en: *The Fa-heng Extracts from the Commentary on the Benevolent Kings’ Sutra for Protecting the State*, Scroll One.
Compiled by the Great Master Yu-rong, who translated the scriptures, verified their meanings, and extensively expounded upon the Sutras, Vinaya, and Shastras.
Now, as the *Prajñāpāramitā* is vast and its scriptural intent profound and subtle, ancient commentaries were composed to explain the sutras; now this extract is being set forth.
The Commentary on the Commentary on this Sūtra is divided into three main sections: first, an explanation of the title of the commentary; second, a presentation of the author of the commentary;

and third, an explanation of the main body of the commentary. The title of the commentary is divided into two parts: first, an explanation of the general name of the entire work, and second, an explanation of the specific title of this particular fascicle.

The general name is divided into two parts: first, an individual explanation (*pṛthag-vyākhyāna*), and second, a combined explanation (*samasta-vyākhyāna*). The individual explanation is divided into two parts: first, an analysis of the object...
After explaining the title of the sūtra, I shall now analyze the words of the commentary that explains it. As for the title of the sūtra:
in the Sanskrit language, it is *Maṇḍalārakṣāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*; in the language of China, it is *The Sūtra of the Benevolent Kings Protecting the State on the Perfection of Wisdom*.
Here, we adopt the phrasing that is elegant and consistent with the common discourse found in all the teachings.

Because this work combines the Chinese and Sanskrit traditions while retaining certain archaic and abbreviated forms, it is titled the *Renwang Huguo Banruo Boluomiduo Jing* (The Benevolent Kings’ Protection of the Nation Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra).
Its commentary is divided into two parts: first, an analytical explanation (*li shi*), and second, a synthetic explanation (*he shi*). The analytical explanation is further divided into two sections:

first, an analysis of the ten characters that constitute the "signified" (*suochuan*), and second, an analysis of the character "sūtra" (*jing*) which constitutes the "signifier" (*nengchuan*). The analysis of the signified is again divided into two: first, an analytical explanation, and second, a synthetic explanation. This concludes the analytical explanation.

This is divided into two parts: first, clarifying the person who requests [the teaching], and second, clarifying the Dharma requested. Regarding the person who requests, this refers to the Benevolent King (*Renwang*).
The *Rites of Zhou* states, "Benevolence possesses six virtues. Master Zheng’s commentary says: "Loving people and things is called benevolence;

mutual affection between superiors and subordinates is called benevolence; honoring the worthy and being close to kin is called benevolence; sacrificing one's own body to complete another is called benevolence. One who possesses these qualities is benevolent."

Patience means to contain and endure both good and evil; this is called benevolence (*ren*). Loving life and detesting killing is called benevolence. The *Mao Shih* says: "The King is one who goes forth; the world goes toward him.
Because he is skilled at nourishing people, the people revere him; because he is skilled at discerning and managing affairs, the people find peace in him;
because he is skilled at pleasing people, the people feel kinship with him; because he is skilled at adorning people, the people rejoice in him. To possess these qualities—
One who possesses the four virtues and whom the world follows is called a "King" (Rāja). Furthermore, a "Benevolent One" (Ren-zhe) is a sage;

because he is compassionate, wise, and endowed with virtuous qualities, the King is the sovereign. His majestic virtue presides over the people, and as he alone is honored and supreme, the *Nyāyapravēśa-śāstra* (Zhengli Lun) states that at the beginning of the kalpa, when the fragrant rice was divided, they collectively established a lord of the fields, King Samantabhadra (translated here as Gongxu Wang, or "King Universally Acknowledged"), whom the multitude authorized.

Because this person possesses virtuous qualities, he receives one-sixth of the fragrant rice harvest as an offering to the king. He is requested to govern what is unjust and acts as the lord of the fields and agriculture;
thus he is called the "Lord of Men" (*manuṣyarāja*) and the "Lord of the People. Because he is uniquely honored and supreme, he is also called the "Son of Heaven" (*devaputra*).
As the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* verse states: "Though born in the human world, because he is most honored and supreme, he is therefore called a 'Deva'."

The various devas who protect and sustain [the Dharma] are also called "sons of heaven" (*devaputra*). Great kings such as Prasenajit and others have long cultivated merit and wisdom and are endowed with benevolence and virtuous qualities;
therefore, they are called "benevolent kings" (*renwang*). When a king possesses benevolent virtue, he is termed a "benevolent king.
This is explained according to the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent determinative) compound. Second, [the term is explained] according to the *bahuvrīhi* (possessive determinative) compound.

Regarding the requester of the Dharma, this is the *Rāṣṭrapālaparipṛcchā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*. This section is divided into two parts: first, an analytical explanation (*vyutpatti*), and second, a synthetic explanation (*samāsa*).

The analytical explanation is further divided into two: first, clarifying the general name "Prajñā" (Wisdom) as reaching the other shore; second, clarifying the specific application of this scripture for Rāṣṭrapāla.

As for the initial passage: "Prajñā" has the meaning of wisdom (*prajñā-jñāna*); it is so called because its discernment (*viveka*) clearly illuminates both principle (*li*) and phenomena (*shi*). Thus, it is "Prajñā."
There are five [aspects]: first, the *prajñā* of true reality (*dharmatā*), which refers to the principle of *tathatā*;
because it is the true nature of *prajñā*, it is called *prajñā*. Thus, the subsequent text states: "The *dharmatā* does not abide in form, nor does it abide in what is non-form;

feeling, perception, mental formations, consciousness, and even the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) and the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) are all called *prajñā*. Second, the *prajñā* of contemplative observation, which refers to that which is pure...
Because wisdom (*prajñā*) observes and illuminates both the nature and characteristics, as well as the ultimate and conventional truths, the subsequent text states:

"By means of profound *prajñā*, one perceives that all phenomena are entirely empty, even unto the equality of their essence and characteristics; this is called the 'knowledge of all modes' (*sarvajñājñāna*), and it is all termed *prajñā*.
Third is the *prajñā* of words (*vyañjana-prajñā*), which refers to the teachings that express [wisdom] because they elucidate *prajñā*; thus, it is also termed *prajñā*.

The following text states: "The Prajñāpāramitā, its words and phrases, has been spoken in common by hundreds of Buddhas, thousands of Buddhas, and all the hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas; the twelve divisions of the teachings are all named Prajñā.
Fourth is the *parivāra-prajñā* (retinue Prajñā), which refers to the wondrous wisdom associated with the six perfections and myriad practices that assists Prajñā; it is also called Prajñā.
Therefore, the subsequent text states: "The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva relies upon the dharma of the five patiences (*pañca-kṣānti*) as the basis for cultivation;
even all the wondrous practices of the three stages of worthiness (*tri-śaikṣa*) and the ten stages (*daśa-bhūmi*) are termed Prajñā.

Fifth is the *viṣaya-prajñā* (wisdom of the objective realm), which refers to the objective realm of the two truths, the three natures (*tri-svabhāva*), and so forth; it is also termed Prajñā because the "Chapter on the Two Truths" and others extensively elucidate its characteristics. This...
Since the meaning of the entire text of this scripture elucidates *prajñā*, it is titled *Prajñā* as its general heading.

In the *Commentary on the Heart Sūtra* by Cien, the five kinds of *prajñā* are explained as follows: "When merit and wisdom are cultivated together and emptiness and existence are illuminated simultaneously, one seeks the expression to reach the intent;

through thorough investigation, understanding arises. The nature of wisdom (*jñāna-svabhāva*), the wisdom that serves as a resource (*upakaraṇa-prajñā*), and all that can remove hindrances and habitual tendencies while realizing the Dharma are termed *prajñā*."
The supreme among all virtues of true emptiness and the guide of myriad practices, it alone is strongly designated as "wisdom" (*prajñā*) because it encompasses all phenomena;
this is precisely what the *Yogācāra* refers to when it says that all phenomena share a single essence and are skillfully integrated, which is termed the "convenience of integration.
By means of wisdom and consciousness, all phenomena are encompassed; thus, the intent is to encompass all phenomena so that they become one single essence. This is because...

Because it is formed by the accumulation of skillful characteristics (*kauśalya-lakṣaṇa*), the very accumulation of skillful characteristics constitutes the meaning of "skillful means" (*upāya*). There are three types of skillful characteristics:

first, skillful characteristics of expression, because the phrasing is skillful and marvelous, with elegant and beautiful wording; second, skillful characteristics of meaning, because various phenomena are revealed through skillful and marvelous meanings;
third, skillful characteristics of substance, such as the skillful and marvelous qualities of painted figures and the like. This is [the explanation].

The characteristics of skillfulness in meaning (*arthakauśalya*) are briefly presented through two gates: namely, wisdom (*jñāna*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*). For the time being, taking wisdom as the gate to encompass all phenomena:
the nature of wisdom, the characteristics of wisdom, the cause of wisdom, the companions of wisdom, and the objects of wisdom—these five types of *prajñā* constitute its essence.

By means of this skillful method of meaning, all phenomena are subsumed into a single essence and designated collectively as "wisdom. This is called the collection of the characteristics of skillfulness.

Regarding the establishment of the means [of inclusion] by taking consciousness as the gateway to encompass all phenomena: (1) the eight consciousnesses, the sovereign minds, are the nature of consciousness;
(2) the fifty-one mental factors are associated with consciousness; (3) the eleven kinds of form are transformations of consciousness;
(4) the twenty-four non-associated formations are states of consciousness; and (5) the six kinds of unconditioned phenomena are the true nature of consciousness. By these five categories...
To subsume all phenomena under the name of "consciousness" is called the skillful means of the integrated collection of characteristics;

the intent of these two gates is that because consciousness is predominant during the causal stage, one establishes the gate of consciousness, whereas because wisdom is predominant during the resultant stage, one establishes the gate of wisdom. Thus, this Prajñā subsumes all phenomena.
*Pāramitā* has the meaning of "the other shore. According to ancient exegesis, there are two [meanings]: namely, Bodhi (enlightenment) and Nirvāṇa; and compassion.

The "En" (恩) explains the five aspects: first, that which is to be known; second, the teaching; third, the principle; fourth, the practice; and fifth, the fruit. Regarding "Prajñāpāramitā," "prajñā" means the sense of "leaving behind" (*li-yi*) and the sense of "reaching" (*dao-yi*).

Taken together, the general meaning is this: by practicing *prajñā*, one leaves behind all obstructive defilements; the objects of perception are exhausted, reaching the limit of both existence and non-existence;

one thoroughly understands the meanings of the six *piṭakas*; one penetrates the ultimate and the conventional; one is fully equipped with the two causes; awakening is perfected and tranquility is fulfilled; thus one ascends to the other shore, wherein essence and function are both complete.

Because it is established based on its destination, this name "Prajñāpāramitā" (Perfection of Wisdom) is used to manifest its meaning according to the shore reached. The term *pāra* means "the other shore," and *mita* means "to reach";
thus, it is interpreted as a *tatpuruṣa* compound (dependent determinative). The essential meaning of *prajñā* applies to both cause and fruit.

At the stage of the cause, the *prajñā* separates from obstructive defilements and reaches the other shore; at the stage of the fruit, the *prajñā* is completely free from obstructive defilements and has ultimately reached [the goal].
Ultimately reaching the other shore, *prajñā* is thus called a *pāramitā*; this is an analysis based on the function of the term (*karmadhāraya*).
According to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, the various practices cultivated must possess seven types of supremacy (*saptavidha-paramatva*) before they can be designated as *pāramitās*.
If even one of these is lacking, they do not constitute "reaching the other shore. In the first eon, they are termed *pāramitās* [only in name].
The first two kalpas are called "near pāramitās," and the third kalpa is called the "great pāramitā. Within the stage of the Buddha-fruit, there is no further distinct designation;
here, because cause and fruit are encompassed together, the general name is employed. The five kinds of *prajñā* encompass the teaching, principle, practice, and fruit:
that is to say, because one relies on the teaching to elucidate the principle, relies on the principle to give rise to practice, and relies on practice to attain the fruit, all are *prajñā*.
The analysis of the intended meaning (*arthaviniścaya*) encompasses both the teachings (*śāsana*) and the principles (*tattva*); the analysis of cause and effect encompasses both cause and effect;
the analysis of merit and wisdom (*puṇyajñāna*) encompasses both merit and wisdom; the analysis of awakening and tranquility encompasses both the truths of cessation and the path;
the analysis of the two benefits encompasses both types of self-benefit and benefit for others; furthermore, because the practitioner cultivates *prajñā*, it encompasses both types of wisdom.

The fundamental and subsequently attained contemplations give rise to the two principles of the emptiness of persons and the emptiness of phenomena; they sever the two obstacles of afflictions and the cognizable;
they bring to rest the two types of death, the intermittent and the transformational; they realize the two fruits of bodhi and nirvāṇa;
and they perfect the two cessations, the cessation without remainder and non-abiding cessation. This is why this Prajñāpāramitā is established as the foremost among the six pāramitās.

The scroll states: The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, employ eighty-four thousand dharma-gates to subdue sentient beings with whom they have a karmic connection, categorizing them into five divisions.

If there are sentient beings who delight in cultivating meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), proper deportment (*īryāpatha*), and the discrimination of essential natures and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), for them he sequentially expounds the Sūtras, the Vinaya, and the Abhidharma.
If they delight in cultivating the true wisdom of the Mahāyāna and are free from the notion of self (*ātman*)...
For those who conceptualize through attachment to phenomena (*dharmābhiniveśa-vikalpa*), the *Prajñāpāramitā* is taught;

for those who are unable to uphold the *Prajñā* of the Tripiṭaka and who have committed various unwholesome acts such as grave offenses, and who desire their extinction and the realization of *nirvāṇa*, the *dhāraṇī* is taught.
The intended meaning of this sūtra is precisely the fourth [aim]: the joyful cultivation of wisdom to become free from attachment to self and phenomena (*ātma-dharmābhiniveśa*).

It explains the *Prajñāpāramitā* so that one may leave behind the notions of self and dharmas and accord with the signless (*animitta*); thus it includes the other four sections as well. Subsequently, it clarifies the specific application of this sutra for protecting the state.
"State" (*rāṣṭra*) carries the meaning of a political domain or territory where beings dwell; it refers to the land and its affairs, upon which both ordinary and holy beings rely.

It denotes the realm governed by kings and ministers through transformation and peace, and the maintenance of the body and the administration of the sovereign—this is termed a "state. "Protecting" (*rakṣā*) means to provide added defense, shelter, and encompassing care.
By the meaning of this, the majestic power of Prajñā adds its protection and encompasses it; thus calamities do not arise and disasters do not occur.
Humans and devas rejoice, while dragons and spirits bestow their grace. As Prajñā flourishes without falling into decline, the sages and worthies provide guardianship and the nation is at peace.
The Dharma relies on people for its propagation, and people rely on the Dharma to establish the state. Is this not the supreme function of Prajñā?

It is thus: this protection of the state consists of both internal protection and external protection. As for internal protection, it is as stated in the following passage where the Buddha told King Prasenajit:

"I shall now first explain for the sake of all bodhisattvas the protection of the fruit of Buddhahood, the protection of the practices of the ten stages, and the protection of the transformation of sentient beings.
As for external protection, it is as the World-Honored One said: "All great kings, listen attentively, listen attentively!"

I shall now explain for you the Dharma for protecting the state. When all kingdoms are about to fall into chaos and various calamities arise—such as when bandits come to destroy them—you kings should receive, uphold, read, and recite this Prajñāpāramitā;
you should adorn the site of practice (maṇḍala), place one hundred images of Buddhas, one hundred images of Bodhisattvas, and one hundred lion thrones, and invite one hundred Dharma masters.

The Master explains this sutra: even if kings, great ministers, and the fourfold assembly listen to, receive, read, recite, and practice it according to the Dharma, calamities and disasters will immediately be extinguished, as detailed extensively in the following text.
That which can protect is called "protection" (*rakṣā*); this protection is the protection of the state, thus it is named "Protection of the State" (*Rakṣā-rāṣṭra*).

That which is protected is called "the protected," and that protection is the state itself; therefore, it is named "Protection of the State. This is the second section, the combined explanation of the title.

Regarding the term "Protector of the Nation" (*Rāṣṭrapāla*), there are two general interpretations. If one follows the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) analysis according to Rāṣṭrapāla, it signifies that this Prajñā is able to protect all nations;

thus, "Protector of the Nation" is the name for Prajñā. This is a *karmadhāraya* (appositional) analysis in which the function is subsumed into the essence, meaning "the Prajñāpāramitā that is the Protector of the Nation.
If one follows the *karmadhāraya* analysis according to Rāṣṭrapāla, it refers to that which can protect the Prajñā.
If one derives its name from the state it protects, it is called the "Prajñā that Protects the State" (*Rāṣṭrapāla-prajñā*);

this is an *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* (genitive determinative) compound. (The conclusion of this section may be understood accordingly. Second, regarding the combined explanation of the ten characters that signify the meaning:
the Dharma requested is named after the person who requests it; thus, the Prajñā that Protects the State by a Benevolent King is called the "Benevolent King’s [Prajñā]."

The *Prajñāpāramitā-rakṣā-deśa* is explained according to the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound analysis (the concluding sections may be understood accordingly). Second, regarding the identification of the words of the scripture that express [the meaning], Vasubandhu’s commentary states:
It is called a "sūtra" because it is able to string together (*sūtrana*) the basis (*āśraya*), the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), the phenomena (*dharma*), and the meanings (*artha*).
That which is spoken of in this context, by means of this, for the sake of this, is designated as the "basis," namely, the ultimate and conventional truths.
The characteristics of the truths are called "characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*); skillful means and so forth are called "dharmas";
and the teachings of various dharmas according to their underlying intent (*saṃdhi*) and so forth are called "meaning" (*artha*). Because it possesses these four meanings, it is called a *sūtra*.

Furthermore, the essence of this *sūtra* generally takes the four factors of phonemes (*śabda*), names (*nāman*), phrases (*pada*), and syllables (*vyañjana*) as its nature, because these four factors are able to express meaning. Moreover, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:

The essence of the sūtra is twofold: first, the text (*vyañjana*), and second, the meaning (*artha*). Regarding the single factor of "text," when taken forward, it subsumes names and phrases (*nāma-pada*); when taken backward, it subsumes sound (*ghoṣa*).

Although it is said that "text" and "meaning" together encompass sound, name, phrase, and sentence, as well as the meanings they express—thus constituting five factors as its essence—the remainder will be explained below (the structural outline may be understood accordingly).
Second, regarding the combined explanation of the title of the sūtra: the aforementioned ten characters are all the expressed text.
The term "letter-prajñā" (*vyañjana-prajñā*) is also that which is elucidated within the sūtra; therefore, the sūtra as the expressive medium is named after that which it expresses.
Thus, the *Renwang Huguo Banruo Boluomiduo Jing* (Benevolent Kings’ Sūtra on the Prajñāpāramitā for Protecting the State) is explained according to the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent determinative) compound.
Furthermore, in terms of the classification of the five prajñās, the "letter" is the expressive medium while the other four are the expressed content. This is based on the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.

The *Prajñāpāramitā-rājā-sūtra* (Renwang huanguo jing), which penetrates both doctrine and principle, is explained here according to the *karmadhāraya* compound (持業釋). (The structural divisions may be understood accordingly.

Second, regarding the explanation of the term "commentary" (*shù* 疏): "Commentary" (*shù*) means "to record. It carries the sense of "compiling and recording," as it compiles the corresponding texts and meanings of various teachings to explain the intent of the sūtra.
Furthermore, "commentary" (*shù*) is pronounced with a level tone (*shū*); it means "to analyze," "to divide," and "to resolve. Thus, it is called a "commentary" (*shù*).

It is called a *śāstra* (commentary) because it penetrates the meaning of the words, distinguishes the underlying intent, and definitively discerns the essential nature and characteristics [of the text].
Thus, the commentary itself takes as its substance five factors: the sounds, names, phrases, and syllables of the commentator, along with the meanings they express.

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that when Bodhisattvas compose treatises to explain the sūtras, they do so through four intentions and five metaphors; the intention behind composing this commentary to explain the sūtra is likewise the same. Now, regarding the four intentions, the first is "adornment."

1. To manifest the adornment of the Buddha’s sūtras by revealing the profound intent of the holy teachings; 2. To subdue the heterodox and manifest the orthodox so that the meaning of the sūtras may be understood and erroneous thoughts do not arise;
3. To cause the Dharma to endure for a long time, so that the teaching may benefit others and the Dharma shall not perish; 4.
To ensure the lineage of the Buddhas is never severed, so that those who understand the meaning may practice and attain Buddhahood. Regarding the five similes: the first is like seeing a flower.

1. Seeing a flower bud and feeling joy is not as good as seeing it in full bloom; likewise, though one may feel joy upon hearing a sutra, it is not as good as obtaining a commentary that reveals its underlying principles.
2. Seeing another’s wealth and feeling joy is not as good as taking possession of it for oneself. 3.
Seeing a letter from home and feeling joy is not as good as opening it to learn of auspicious news. 4. Seeing a gold ingot and feeling joy is not as good as...
The joy arising [from seeing] it is not equal to forging it into a vessel so that one may obtain its utility;

fifth, like encountering a delicious meal when hungry, though seeing it produces joy, it is not equal to eating it—the commentary on the text can be understood according to the passage (the outline of the sections can be understood). Second, regarding the combined explanation of the title of the sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*):
since the original purpose of composing the sub-commentary was to explain the text of the sutra, the sub-commentary that explains is named after the sutra which is being explained.

The title *Zhāngqí mínrénwáng hùguó bōrěbōluómìduō jīng zhī shū* (Commentary on the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra for Humane Kings Protecting the State) is explained by the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent compound) analysis.
Second, regarding the specific title of this fascicle: it is called "Fascicle One. "Fascicle" (*juàn*) signifies the rules of sequential arrangement;

as for the term "fascicle," it refers to the written characters. However, these characters are inscribed using ink and other materials; yet, from the perspective of cause and effect, the intended meaning here refers to sound.
Name, phrase, and syllable constitute its essence. Since phonemes and so forth serve as the cause for the existence of letters, and letters serve as the cause that induces phonemes and so forth;
furthermore, "volume" (varta) carries the meaning of rolling up and unfolding, and palm leaves, paper, and the like constitute its physical basis.
If there were only letters without paper and such materials, the letters would be dispersed and perish; if there were only paper and such materials without letters, it would not [be a volume].
The holy teaching thus relies upon the mutual dependence of the written characters and their supports, such as paper;
the rules for rolling and unrolling these are designated as "volumes" (*juan*). "First" (*di yi*) signifies the beginning of the initial section.

This fascicle is marked as the first because it is the commencement of the entire work, which consists of six volumes. Originally, there were only three volumes, which were later expanded by subsequent generations.
Six fascicles. [Commentary:
Written by the śramaṇa Liangben, a translator and lecturer at Qinglong Monastery. "Fengben" indicates the person who composed the commentary.
This Qinglong Monastery was located in the southeastern corner of Chang'an City. The *Record of Qinglong Monastery* states that formerly, during the Sui...
When Chang’an was first established in the morning [of its founding], this area south of the city had originally been a battlefield where bones were piled up.

The Emperor said, "Since this place is the 'Azure Dragon's Head' (*qīnglóng zhīshǒu*) of the state and contains many tombs, those who have descendants or relatives shall be permitted to relocate their burials there.
As for those without relatives, the government shall provide relocation. It is approximately seven *li* southeast of the city.
After digging a pit more than one *li* away to bury [the remains], there was the sound of ghosts wailing.
When the authorities reported this to the throne, an imperial edict was issued to establish a temple at the site where the bones were buried, naming it Linggan (Manifestation of Response).

Later, during the reign of Emperor Taizong of the Tang dynasty, Princess Chengyang fell ill; she requested the monk Falang of Suzhou to recite the divine mantra of Avalokiteśvara, and she was thereby cured.

When the Empress Dowager recovered from her illness, she petitioned the Emperor for the land of the abolished Linggan Temple so that a new temple might be established there to repay the Imperial Grace.

In the second year of the Longshuo era of the Great Emperor Gaozong, an imperial edict was issued stating that the temple should be re-established according to its former status and renamed Guanyin Temple.
Later, during the reign of Emperor Zhongzong, as the temple stood upon the ridge of Qinglong Hill, an edict was issued in the second year of the Shenlong era.
It was renamed Qinglong Temple. "Temple" (si) signifies succession (si) and administration (si); it is here that those who manage affairs succeed one another in their service.
The *Hanshu* states that the second sovereign of the Later Han, Emperor Xiaoming, dreamed one night of a golden-bodied man sixteen feet tall riding through the air from the west.
He then questioned his court ministers, and Fu Yi submitted a memorial, saying: "According to the *Zhoubi Yiji*, [this refers to] Zhugan..."
After a great sage had appeared and one thousand years had passed, the teachings of his voice and instruction flowed into this land;
that which Your Majesty dreamed of must surely be this. The Emperor dispatched Wang Dao and seventeen others to travel westward to welcome the Buddhist teachings.
Upon reaching the country of Great Yuezhi, they encountered the two monks Kāśyapa Mātanga and Dharmaratna, who were carrying the Sanskrit manuscript of the *Sūtra of Forty-two Sections*.
The physical appearance and characteristics of Śākyamuni were as they had been when he first arrived; he was temporarily housed at the Honglu Temple.

In the seventh year of Yongping, the year of Yichou (or, according to some accounts, Jiawu), he was welcomed from the West. On the thirtieth day of the twelfth month of the tenth year, the year of Wuchen, he returned to Luoyang.
Emperor Ming was filled with joy and specially constructed halls and pavilions to enshrine him. The two monks moved into separate residences, yet they never forgot their origins.

He then designated the name of the monastery; furthermore, because the horse that had carried the scriptures arrived here and died, a stupa was erected within the temple, and it was consequently named Baima Monastery (White Horse Monastery).

The *Sengshi lüe* (Abridged History of the Sangha) states that during the first year of the Shiguang era of Emperor Taizu of the Later Wei dynasty, a *gārala* (monastery) was established and named Zhaoti;
during the Daye era of Emperor Yang of the Sui dynasty, it was renamed Daochang; and this continued into the Tang dynasty.

Furthermore, it is also a temple; in the language of India, it is called *saṃghārāma*, which here [in China] is translated as "Garden of the Assembly" (*zhòngyuán*), because it is the garden where the monastic community resides.

Thus, those who translated the scriptures referred to them simply as "translated scriptures" (*fānjīng*). This is because the Vinaya and Abhidharma are meanings contained within one portion of these scriptures, whereas the *Sūtras* (Kīng) fully encompass the meaning of the entire Tripiṭaka.
"Translation" (*fān*) means "to invert"; it refers to inverting the Indian language to transmit it to this land [of China].
Regarding what is called a "translation śramaṇa," it should properly be rendered as *śramaṇa*. This means "ceasing evil," because it refers to the ceasing and removal of all evils;

it is also called "diligent cessation" (*qín xī*), because it involves diligently cultivating various virtues and ceasing that which is unwholesome. The *Fahua shu* (Commentary on the Lotus Sūtra) states: "The meaning of *śramaṇa* is 'cessation' (*xì*);
because one has attained the Dharma, there is a temporary tranquility, and it is also the cessation of evil. The correct transliteration is *Śramaṇa*.
*Maṇa*, or alternatively *śramaṇa*, means "one who has performed meritorious labor" (*gōngláo*), because one has performed meritorious labor in cultivating the path and its practice.
Here, the original [Sanskrit] is retained in an informal form and further abbreviated; thus it is called *shāmen*. There are four types of *śramaṇas*, as can be known from the usual [explanations].
"Liángbèi" is the name of the author of the commentary (*shū*). Bèi (pronounced *bì yì*)—the author of the commentary was a person from the county of Hézhōng. By secular [status],...
His secular surname was Guo, and his Dharma name was Liangben. His family had held official rank for generations, yet these records were lost and not preserved.

He left home at a young age and, possessing singular virtue, lectured on the *Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā* (Renwang jing), the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, and the *Hetuvidyā*. He was proficient in both Buddhist and secular learning and resided at temples such as Qinglong and Anguo.
His reputation was prominent at the time, and he was held in high esteem by both the monastic and lay communities. He once conferred the Bodhisattva precepts upon Emperor Daizong.
The Master of Commentaries, Sūtra and Śāstra Translator Bukong (Amoghavajra), translated seventy-seven works, of which more than forty were annotated by him with his own hand and refined in style.

On the eleventh day of the second month in the second year of the Yongtai era, he received an imperial edict from Emperor Daizong to compose a commentary on the newly translated *Benevolent Kings Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* at the Southern Peach Garden within the palace. By the tenth month of that same year...

On the eighth day of the first month, the transcription was completed; the text exceeds ten thousand words and consists of three fascicles, together with one fascicle on the ritual for the recitation of the *dhāraṇī*.
Also included is the "Imperial Record of the Lecture on the *Ghanavyūha-sūtra* at the Chengming Hall," one fascicle, all of which were presented together.

The imperial decree praised [the work], but the details have been omitted here. Regarding the phrase "described by imperial decree" (*shuozhe*): "describe" (*shu*) means to narrate or to compose. It refers to that which was personally [recorded].

Having respectfully proclaimed the imperial decree to expound the principles and compile the sacred teachings, this commentary was composed and titled the *Shushi weishi shu* (Commentary on the Exposition of the Principles of Consciousness-Only).
It is called "exposition" (*shu*) because it sets forth the principles; it is called "composition" (*zao*) because previous versions existed, whereas this one is newly produced.

[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "I bow my head," etc., from here below is the explanation of the main text of the sub-commentary (*shu*). As explained according to the sūtra, it is also divided into three parts:
first, the Introduction; second, the Main Body; and third, the Dissemination. Now, regarding the first part, the Introduction, it is further divided into four sections:

first, bowing the head to the Three Honored Ones to express the earnest sincerity of the one who composed the sub-commentary; second, praising the Buddha’s body as the source for the arising of this sūtra.

The three [sections] correctly reveal the profound subtleties of this sūtra’s Prajñā; the fourth interprets the title of the sūtra’s chapters to clarify the essential framework of the general and the specific.

Regarding the sequential order of these four sections of text: first, in wishing to explain the sūtra, one must pay homage to the Triple Gem and express the sincere intention of composing this commentary, seeking the holy power to provide protection; thus, there is the first section. Having already taken refuge...

The Three Jewels should indeed have a commentary composed for them; however, as for the textual style and format, in order to correctly extol those matters, one must first provide a general account of their origins.
This means that while the words concern distant events, the intent concerns what is near, serving as a gradual introduction to the source of the narrative.
This second section consists of such general introductory remarks concerning the fundamental origins and historical development of the teaching, namely:

The Absolute Truth is serene, its nature transcending existence and non-existence; the wondrous wisdom of the Reward Body exhausts the source of both essence and attributes, and only then gives rise to the transformative function of "other-transformation" to benefit beings according to their capacities. Its essence is taught as non-arising, while its function is taught as arising.

Having thus generally described the essence and function, the beginning and the end, [the author] gradually intends to lead the discussion toward the purpose of explaining this sutra; hence there is the second section, which praises the Buddha’s body and his teaching in general.

Having completed the narration, one now distinguishes the auspicious manifestations of this sutra’s assembly on Vulture Peak, wherein the Dharma rain descends from afar to universally moisten both ordinary beings and sages.
The fundamental purpose and great significance of the sutra are set forth: internally, it protects the fruit of Buddhahood through the gates of the five patiences and the two truths;
externally, it manifests the miraculous efficacy of the *Benevolent Kings Prajñāpāramitā*. Flowers fall as auspicious responses, and its virtuous function is inconceivable.

The Master, upholding [the teachings], [observes that] calamities are dispelled and difficulties are stilled through the compassionate mindfulness of the Tathāgata, who bestowed his instructions and entrustment.
Regarding the origins of how the teaching has flowed to this land and been widely expounded, he offers praise and eulogy to express his sincere reverence and veneration.
Desiring that students understand its great significance and thereby develop a sense of solemn respect, there is the third section which correctly reveals the Prajñā of this Sūtra.
Having clarified this meaning through its profound significance, one should now proceed to explain the meaning of the scriptural text in its proper sequence.
However, because there is a title for the scripture preceding the main text, the title of the scripture is explained first, followed by the explanation of the scriptural text itself.

This is because the title of the scripture articulates the general outline of the entire work, while the title of a chapter reveals the essential meaning of that specific chapter; thus, by explaining the title, the purport of the entire work is revealed.

Because it summarizes the general and specific meanings, there is a fourth section explaining the title of the "Chapter on the Preface" (Xingpin). Thus, the sequence of the four sections is as follows.
For this reason, it is said that "Preface" (xu) means "to lead to" (zhì); it leads to the great meaning by conveying the intent of the beginning and the end.

Furthermore, "Preface" (xu) means "thread" (xù); just as a silkworm obtains its thread, so too does one obtain the order (xù) through a commentary, for when the order is exhausted, the single [text] is fully elucidated.

This is the meaning of the section. To speak of "prostrating with the head" (*kāyotsarga*) refers to the physical manifestation of reverence. The "Unsurpassed Awakening" and so forth refer to the Three Jewels who are the objects of veneration.
According to conventional exegesis, "kāya" means "to reach" and "mūrdhan" means "head"; thus, because one brings the head to the ground, it is called "prostration with the head.

This refers to the act of bowing and kneeling until the head touches the ground. However, according to the sūtras and śāstras, "prostration with the head" is distinct from mere ritual salutation (*vandana*).

Regarding the term *namas* (homage): the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states that because one "bows the head to touch the feet," it is called "reverential salutation" (*praṇāma*). Because one deeply reveres those feet, it is called "reverential salutation.
Since such profound veneration surpasses mere speech, it is expressed through the body; for while speech is light, the body can manifest this [veneration].

Since that which arises from the mind is established by implication and need not be stated explicitly, it is only through physical reverence that one generates a sincere and pure mind, exerts superior activity, and extends a heart of true devotion and reliance; therefore, this is called "prostration" (*namaskāra*).
Thus, in various holy teachings, it is sometimes said "bowing the head," which refers to bowing by means of the physical and vocal actions to extend reverence through the three types of activity.

Furthermore, the essence of awakening of the Unsurpassed Buddha is wisdom; because it awakens through discernment, severs hindrances, and illuminates the principles of phenomena, it is called "Awakening" (Bodhi).

Within the stage of Buddhahood, the Dharma-body is the nature of awakening, the Reward-body is the appearance of awakening, and the Transformation-body is the function of awakening; as these are without peer or equal, they are collectively termed "Unsurpassed Awakening.

Next, to specifically indicate this, it is said: "The Dharma-body is omnipresent, the Reward-appearance is perfect and luminous, and it manifests in the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations."
He manifests bodies as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; his wondrous power of great compassion in uprooting suffering is inconceivable, and there is none who can equal the Buddha.
Thus, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "Bodhisattvas have ten kinds of great compassion by which they constantly observe sentient beings:

first, those who have no refuge; second, those who follow false views; third, those who are poor and lack roots of goodness; fourth, those who sleep long in birth and death; fifth, those whose conduct is unwholesome..."

1. Being bound by the fetters of the six desire realms; 2. Remaining within the ocean of birth and death; 3. Suffering from chronic illness for a vast duration; 4. Lacking the wholesome dharmas of desirelessness; 5.
Losing all Buddha-dharmas—by means of these ten kinds of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), the Bodhisattva extracts the suffering of sentient beings.

If this is so even for a Bodhisattva, how much more so for a Tathāgata, whose great compassion is supreme in the work of benefiting others? Therefore, it is specifically said that there is no [compassion] greater than great compassion.
"Equal to [the Buddha].
[Commentary: Regarding the "Dharma of the Deathless (amṛta)" mentioned here, the former refers to the Buddha who can preach it, while this refers to the Dharma that is preached.
The Dharma that is preached is like the deathless nectar (*amṛta*); the nectar of the world has two functions: first, it can eliminate diseases and bring about physical health.

The two kinds of peace can eliminate feverish affliction and attain coolness; the Buddha-dharma is likewise: first, it can eliminate the diseases of birth and death to attain the peace of the noble body;
second, it can eliminate the feverish affliction of obstructive defilements to attain the coolness of *nirvāṇa*.
Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "The World-Honored One bestows the medicine of ambrosia upon all sentient beings; once they have taken it, they do not die."
Nor does it arise [in other cases]—the remaining text is easy to understand.
[Commentary: Those who abide in the path of the fruit or the superior fruit refer to those among the four fruits of the śrāvaka who currently dwell in the first three fruits;

they are called "abiding in the fruit" because they are still in training (*śaikṣa*). As for those who have attained the fourth fruit, they have already realized the state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) and are therefore the most preeminent within their own vehicle.

In the *Shengguodao Linyu Bu xing zunzhe chuxue ji* (Record of the Initial Studies of the Venerable of the Rhinoceros-like Section of the Path of Supreme Fruit), various texts are cited to clarify the appearance of the qilin;
I shall now describe it directly. The qilin is a benevolent beast with the body of a deer, the tail of an ox, a single horn, and the hooves of a horse;

it is yellow in color, its horn-tip is fleshy, and its voice corresponds to the *huangzhong* pitch. When a king possesses ultimate benevolence, one appears, signifying that all within the seas are unified under his virtue.

They share a single sovereign. They are born from fire and roam upon the earth; they embody benevolence and cherish righteousness. Their gait follows the circular compass, and they choose their ground when wandering.

They do not tread upon living insects, nor do they pluck living grass. They do not dwell in groups, nor do they travel in parties. They avoid pitfalls and traps. Their appearance is elegant and refined.
Under the Yellow Emperor, there appeared the Qilin as a sign of his credibility. In the spring of the fourteenth year of Duke Ai of Lu, while on a western hunt—
When the *qilin* was captured and considered an ill omen, Zhongni said, "It is a *qilin*. It appears alone and without a herd;

likewise, the Pratyekabuddha appears alone within the three thousandfold world-system. Because he has but a single horn, he is called a 'unicorn' (*qilin jiao*), serving as a metaphor for the solitary Pratyekabuddha.
Furthermore, there is another class of Pratyekabuddhas who, in their present life, attain realization without receiving the ultimate teachings and without relying upon [a teacher]."
The Buddha who awakens to the Path by himself is called a Pratyekabuddha (Solitary Realizer). Because they practice and travel in groups, there are those known as "group-practicing" Pratyekabuddhas.
Regarding these two types of Pratyekabuddhas, both initially see a Buddha, hear the Dharma, and attain the fruits of holiness through practice.

Among them, the "rhinoceros-horn" type of noble being certainly does not see a Buddha, whereas the group-practicing Pratyekabuddhas may see a Buddha. The former possesses sharp faculties, while the latter possesses dull faculties.

Those of dull faculties who have all abandoned obstructive defilements, realized the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-phala*), and are endowed with untainted virtues (*anāsrava-guṇa*) are therefore called "Venerable.

Regarding the five patiences (*kṣānti*) of the noble ones and ordinary beings: "patience" (*kṣānti*) carries the meaning of acceptance and seal-like verification. Because one verifies the objective realm through sublime wisdom (*prajñā*), it is termed "patience.
Among these five patiences, the initial stage of Subduing Patience (*adhimukti-kṣānti*) occurs prior to the [ten] stages (*bhūmi*) and is thus designated as that of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*).

The four patiences—patience through faith (*śraddhā-kṣānti*), patience through conformity (*anuloma-kṣānti*), patience with the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), and the patience of cessation (*nirodha-kṣānti*)—are termed "noble ones" (*ārya*) from the first stage (*bhūmi*) up to the stage of Buddhahood.
Among these, the patience of cessation pertains to both Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. Here, however, we take the Bodhisattva because [the text] pays homage to the Jewel of the Sangha;
thus, the commentary explains the Sangha Jewel by arranging the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Bodhisattvas in order from the inferior to the superior.
I now offer my full prostration before those whom I revere; I pay homage to the Buddha with words of salutation.
Hereafter, the subsequent phrases clarify the reverence for the Dharma and the Sangha, each mentioned twice. Regarding the Dharma and the noble ones, I offer my full prostration;
these categories of Buddhas and Sangha will be enumerated in detail later in the text, so they are not elaborated upon here.

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "The Three Jewels," etc., this expresses the spirit of taking refuge and paying homage. The Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha are like the gold and jade of the world—worthy of esteem and respect—and are thus termed "Jewels" (*ratna*).
I pray that the Three Jewels, through the power of their compassion and wisdom, will protect me, manifesting their merciful regard so that I am not forsaken.
Now, desiring to praise and explain the true text of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, I pray that the Dharma may long abide for the benefit and salvation of all.

Because it contains all conscious beings, the *Vajraśekhara-yoga-sūtra* states: "Those who take refuge in the Buddha shall receive the protective empowerment of all Buddhas, the Bodhisattvas of the five directions, and their retinues;
those who take refuge in the Dharma shall receive the protective empowerment of Śakra, the Four Heavenly Kings, and their retinues;
and those who take refuge in the Saṅgha shall receive [the protection] of Akaniṣṭha Heaven."
The five Śuddhāvāsa heavens and their retinues have all come to provide protection; by the power of the Triple Gem, all virtuous aspirations are fulfilled and all evils do not arise.
Therefore, I now pay homage and pray for protection: may my mind penetrate the subtle principles as I compose this commentary to explain the sutra, and may my speech be eloquent and my body at ease.

[Commentary: "As for 'the True Principle (zhēnlǐ) being profound and tranquil, transcending the realm of existence and non-existence'—the word 'yuè' (as for) is a particle used to introduce a speech or serve as an introductory phrase in writing.
'Huìng' (transcendence) means solitary or alone; 'biǎo' (realm/surface) means external.
The essence of the True Principle is subtle, clear, and still, unmoving and serene, detached from clamor; it stands out in solitude, far beyond the sphere of existence and non-existence."
[Commentary]: "The mirror of wisdom shines with clarity, penetratingly discerning the source of nature and characteristics. Regarding "mirror," it carries the meaning of reflecting and illuminating.

"The source of nature and characteristics" refers to water, which is called the "source" because it gives rise to streams and tributaries; the Dharma is likewise so. Taking its fundamental basis, nature is the source from which all dharmas arise.
The *Anantaparyāya-dharmaparyāya-sūtra* states: "As for 'infinite meanings,' they arise from a single dharma."
The first principle is so-called *tathatā* (Suchness), for it gives birth to all phenomena (*dharma*).

Alternatively, if one considers the derivative aspects, taking characteristics as the source from which all phenomena arise, this refers to the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), which contains and sustains the seeds of all phenomena across the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).
Through its successive transformations, it manifests the infinite varieties of material and mental phenomena, up to and including the untainted eighth consciousness of the Buddha-fruit.

Because it upholds the seeds of the untainted (*anāsrava*) and manifests through successive transformations an infinite variety of pure phenomena, the nature and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of all dharmas serve as its source.

The four wisdoms (*jñāna*) of the Buddha-fruit are like a bright mirror: clear and pure, they shine everywhere, penetrating and clearly reflecting the source of nature and characteristics, as well as the infinite distinctions between the causes and effects of good and evil. Thus says the Commentary.

[Commentary]: "The ocean of virtue raises its waves, turbidizing the clear currents throughout the dust-like lands" illustrates through both dharma and metaphor how the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) manifests from the ocean of virtue.
The "ocean of virtue" refers to the virtue of truth (*tattva*), which is profound, still, and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*);

the "virtue of wisdom" is like a mirror that clearly reflects conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) phenomena. These two virtues are deep and vast without limit, just like a great ocean. "Raises" means to strike or stir.

The term "yègǔ" (pronounced *gǔ*, meaning "to submerge," or alternatively *yúbǐ* qì, meaning "to draw up"; here the latter pronunciation is adopted) refers to the sense of the vast multitude of worlds within every minute particle of dust.

Just as the great ocean of the world, when struck by the wind, raises surging waves and pure springs flow forth in streams that pervade all rivers and marshes, thereby providing benefit and relief to the common people;
so too is the Tathāgata, whose ocean of virtue is profound and deep, vast and boundless, arising from the power of his original vows.
The union of compassion and wisdom strikes upon the ocean of merit, giving rise to waves of emanation that draw forth wondrous functions;

these pure streams of transformative appearance constitute the *paranirmita-vashavartin* body, which pervades all pure lands. The *nirmāṇakāya* (transformation body) pervades both pure and impure lands, benefiting and bringing joy to ordinary and noble sentient beings according to their needs.
Thus, the tenth chapter of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "The *paranirmita-vashavartin* body relies upon its own land," referring to the level of the *Śuddhāvāsa* (Pure Abodes).

Through the power of equalizing wisdom and great compassion, and by virtue of the maturation of causes and conditions for the pure Buddha-fields cultivated through altruistic, untainted practices in the past, [the Buddha] manifests pure lands—whether small or large, inferior or superior—in accordance with the needs of Bodhisattvas dwelling on the ten stages.
These lands undergo successive transformations, and the Enjoyment Body (*paranirmita-vaśavartin-kāya*) dwells therein; furthermore, there is no fixed measure for the size of this supported body.

Regarding the limit: if the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) relies upon a transformation land, it means that through the power of great compassion and the wisdom of accomplishing activities (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*), based on the ripening of causes and conditions from previously cultivated pure and impure Buddha-lands for the benefit of others, it transforms into a Buddha-land—whether pure or impure, large or small—according to what is appropriate for sentient beings who have not yet entered the stages (*bhūmi*).
Thus, the Buddhas transform [the lands] such that they change and alternate before and after.
The transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) abides by depending upon it, and the dimensions of this supported body are likewise without fixed limit.
[Commentary: Because he is a Great Sage (Mahāmuni), he manifested his traces in a royal palace. In the Sanskrit language, *muni* means "silent" (*jīmò*).
That which is realized—the true nature of reality—is tranquil and free from the clamor of afflictions; therefore, it is called "silent. "Sage" (*shèngzhě*) refers to one who is correct.
Because they correctly accord with the principle through untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*), those of the three vehicles who have seen the truth are all called "sages" (*ārya*).

While those of the two vehicles are sages but not great, and the bodhisattvas of the ten stages are great but not yet perfected, it is now explained that the Buddha-fruit is vast and perfectly complete;
therefore, he is called the "Great Sage" (*mahārya*). Because the Great Sage Śākyamuni has realized the principle of silence, he is called "Muni. As for why he is the Great Sage:
Thus, because the ocean of his prior virtues surged forth as waves, washing the pure currents through the dust-like realms of existence,
the Great Sage Śākyamuni manifested a provisional trace by being born in a royal palace— specifically, the palace of King Śuddhodana in the city of Kapilavastu. Therefore,
the *Sūtra on the Compassionate Lotus of Past Conduct* and other texts state that the Bodhisattva Mahāprabha resided in Tuṣita Heaven.
Passing away from that heaven on the fifteenth day of the seventh month, he mounted the solar disc and, riding a white elephant,

entered the womb of Māyā to manifest the common human state of dwelling in the womb for ten months; on the eighth day of the fourth month he was born, remained as an infant for seven years, was a youth for eight years,
studied the five sciences for four years, indulged in sensual pleasures for ten years, and at the age of twenty-nine he went forth into homelessness.
He practiced austerities for six years on the Snowy Mountains, attained perfect enlightenment at thirty-five years of age, and remained in the world preaching the Dharma for forty-five years;
according to the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, Śākyamuni Buddha’s lifespan was eighty years.
[Commentary: "To arise from the non-arising means that arising has no object of arising. This reveals the manner in which the Tathāgata manifests his body.
"Non-arising" refers to the pure *dharmakāya*, which is immutably and eternally abiding; fundamentally devoid of birth and death, it is called "non-arising.
The perfected *saṃbhogakāya* is uninterrupted and eternally abiding, yet lacks the characteristics of a single period of birth and death; thus, it is also called "non-arising."
From the Dharma-body and Reward-body of the True Buddha, which is non-arising, there arises the provisional body that manifests in response to others through the power of transformation;

this means that while the True Buddha gives rise to that, there is nothing produced in the provisional body of transformation. Alternatively, it may be understood that from the truth of non-arising alone, the body of transformation is produced;
thus, the principle of True Suchness gives rise to that which is produced without being produced. Therefore, the sutra below states: "All..."

All Buddhas are born within Prajñā, transformed within Prajñā, and extinguished within Prajñā; yet in reality, the Buddhas are born where there is no birth, transform where there is no transformation, and are extinguished where there is no extinction.
The commentary on this states: "The *prajñā* of the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa-prajñā) has no birth, transformation, or extinction.
The manifested transformations of the Buddhas respond perfectly throughout the ten directions, manifesting birth, manifestation, and extinction within Prajñā."
"Extinction" refers to his birth in the royal palace, his turning of the wheel of Dharma, his transformation [of beings] at the twin śāla trees, and his subsequent passing into extinction.
[Commentary: "To expound the teaching that is beyond speech is to speak what is unspeakable"—this reveals the characteristic of the Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma.
The essential nature of all phenomena is fundamentally detached from verbal expression; this is called "the unspeakable. The nature of all phenomena is inherently free from words.

Therefore, the Tathāgata employs skillful means to cause people to understand; thus, within the dharma that is devoid of names and marks, he forcibly uses the expedient of names and marks to manifest it, speaking of it by name.
This is because he reveals and explains that which is itself the "dharma of non-explanation.
As the subsequent sutra says: "Before the Buddha appeared in the world, there were no names for the three realms, nor were there the karmic fruits of good and evil."

Regarding the "names of the six destinies": it means that the various Buddhas appear for the sake of sentient beings and speak of the immeasurable names of defilement and purity within the three realms and six destinies.

[Commentary]: "Moving yet quiescent, like the clear moon ascending through the sky. "Moving" refers to the provisional body (*upāyakāya*); "quiescent" refers to the true body (*dharmakāya*). As for "like":...
"Ru" (如) means "to ascend. Just as the clear moon is not a mere reflection in the water, yet its lunar essence ascends in the sky—this is a metaphor for the True Buddha dwelling in the Pure Land;
while the thousandfold variations of the moon's reflections are metaphors for the provisional bodies that appear differently according to the capacities of sentient beings.

Without the moon, the reflections do not exist, yet they are not identical to the moon itself. The True Buddha is the essence (*tǐ*), and the provisional bodies are the function (*yòng*); without the essence, the function does not exist.

The vessel itself is not the water; this is a metaphor for the differences in the faculties and natures of sentient beings. The water is a metaphor for the roots of goodness, such as faith, possessed by sentient beings.
When the vessel is intact and the water is clear, the reflection of the moon appears; when the vessel is broken and the water is turbid, the reflection of the moon sinks.

When the faculties of sentient beings are matured and the water of the mind is clarified, and the vessel of the body is perfectly pure, the Buddha manifests a provisional body to benefit them. If the faculties have not yet matured, the mind...
When water is turbid or a vessel is broken, the Root Buddha does not manifest his body, just as the moon’s reflection sinks when hidden.

The lunar essence is full and ascends into the sky, yet its reflections differ according to the vessels; the True Buddha is tranquil and dwells in stillness, his essence being without distinction, while his provisional bodies move and follow the vessels, their functions appearing in a thousand variations.
To summarize this meaning: due to the preceding ocean of virtue, waves are raised that stir up the clear stream.
Because the Great Sage Muni manifests his traces within royal palaces throughout the dust-motes of all lands, he is born from the unborn;
thus, though born, there is no place of birth. All such phenomena are movement within stillness, like the clear moon ascending through the sky.

[Commentary]: "Speaking while remaining silent" and so forth refers to the *maṇi* jewel illuminating objects. "Speaking" refers to the Buddha manifesting a provisional body (*upāya-kāya*) in the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*) to preach the Dharma;

"silence" refers to the true Buddhas of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) and Reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*), who are beyond words. "Equal" (*sama*) signifies the sense of being identical or similar. "Maṇi" refers to the wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*).
The Buddha resembles that jewel: though silent, he benefits sentient beings; the *maṇi* is brilliant yet devoid of thought, its radiance flowing forth to illuminate objects.
The True Buddha is silent and without speech; yet he manifests a body that possesses speech to proclaim the Dharma for the benefit of sentient beings according to their capacities.

This general meaning is expressed as follows: because the waves of the preceding ocean of virtue surge through the turbid currents across the lands of dust-like atoms, the Great Sage Muni thus manifested his traces within a royal palace.
He expounded the "speech of non-speech," which is to say, he spoke that which is not spoken. All such words as these...
[The Buddha] silently illuminates all things like a mani jewel.

[Commentary: This is a phrase that takes up what preceded to initiate what follows; it is because of the principle that the preceding ocean of virtue raises waves to manifest the body and preach the Dharma.
Thus, in the past, when the Tathāgata dwelt on Vulture Peak, he assembled the multitude and preached the Dharma. Regarding the composition of this commentary...

At that time, when the sutra was being expounded, it was called "In the Past. It is expressed in the correct Sanskrit as *Gṛdhrakūṭa*, which translates as "Vulture Peak" (*Jiùfēng*) and is also known as "Vulture Terrace" (*Jiùtái*).
It is so named because vultures dwell there and it resembles a high terrace. Those who abide in meditative concentration (*samādhi*) dwell securely within that concentration;
they arouse compassion and manifest supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) to assemble the multitude. As the following sutra says: "He entered the Great Quiescence."
"Quiescent and Sublime Samādhi. In Sanskrit, *samādhi* is translated here as "equipoise" (*samāhita*), which is a synonym for meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).

It is called "equipoise" because it is free from dullness and agitation, maintaining the mind with equanimity while focusing one-pointedly on a single object. It is called "sublime" because its functional efficacy is preeminent.
Within this "Great Quiescent and Sublime Equipoise," there are two aspects: first, the arousal of compassion with the desire to benefit [others].
Regarding the two types of sentient beings: "Manifesting and radiating light" (*prabhāsa*) refers to the manner of swift galloping;
the Buddha’s light flashes forth like the gathering of the suns. If a single sun were sufficient for illumination, the brilliance of many gathered suns would reach the ultimate peak of intensity.
The purpose of emitting this light is to assemble those with karmic affinity to come and listen to the Dharma; therefore, the text below states that the Buddha...
From the pores of his body, he emitted great rays of light that universally illuminated Buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions;
furthermore, he emitted immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* rays of light, each of various colors, within which appeared precious lotus flowers,
until Bodhisattvas from all ten directions had come to this place.
[Commentary: Regarding "Prasenajit and others," *Prasenajit* is the Sanskrit name for the King of Śrāvastī; it is translated here as "Victorious Army" (*Shengjun*).

The older transcription "Pusini" is an error. The term "and others" includes other kings, as well as the entire assembly of ordinary and saintly beings who all vied with one another to hasten toward the Dharma assembly.
They gathered like mist, clustering together in such profusion that they resembled dense, billowing smoke.
[Commentary]: "Heavenly flowers fall in disarray, leveling the crags and valleys. "Tàn" (坦) means level; "yí" (夷) means equal.
The heavenly flowers scattered in profusion fall in disarray upon the high crags and deep valleys; because they cover them, all becomes level and even, devoid of any distinction between high and low.
This manifests the Dharma of equality taught by the Buddha; thus, by offering flowers, one symbolizes that having heard the Dharma, one has cultivated the causes [for enlightenment].
The practice of flowers brings forth the fruit of Bodhi; as the text below states:

"When the devas of the desire realm rain down various wondrous flowers, and the devas of the form realm likewise rain down celestial flowers, at that time the devas of the formless realm rain down various fragrant flowers—fragrances like Mount Sumeru and flowers like chariot wheels—which descend like clouds, completely covering the great assembly. It further states: "Bodhisattvas from the ten directions all come to this place."
They held various incenses, scattered various flowers, and performed immeasurable music as offerings to the Tathāgata.
[Commentary: "Thus they attained the Rain of Dharma" reveals the matter of the benefits of preaching this sutra. "Thus they attained" is a phrase that connects the preceding with what follows;

it means that because the assembly had previously gathered, their capacities were matured, and the conditions were harmonized, they desired to hear the wondrous Dharma through the Tathāgata’s compassion.

Out of compassion, the Buddha teaches according to the capacities of sentient beings so that those who hear him may obtain benefit; thus it is said, "they consequently attain," and so forth. Regarding "the Pure Land" and so on:

the Buddha dwells on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, yet beings perceive his appearance differently according to their faculties. If great Bodhisattvas behold the Buddha’s *saṃbhogakāya* (retribution body), they see him residing in a pure land.

If small Bodhisattvas, the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), and other such assemblies behold the Buddha’s *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body), they see him residing in both pure and impure lands. This is because the Buddha’s bodies and lands are one.
This is because, in the various realms, the manifestations of retribution and transformation both appear, and the pure and the defiled are both revealed. The cloud has two meanings:

first, it can provide shade and cover; second, it can produce rain to moisten and benefit the grasses and trees. A compassionate mind is like a cloud that provides shade and cover for those with whom there is a karmic connection, bestowing the rain of the wondrous Dharma to moisten and benefit sentient beings according to their capacities.
Like a cloud that is dense and widespread rather than a sudden, violent storm—this is due to these three factors.
Whether ordinary beings or sages, all who ride upon this vehicle are moistened and nourished, thereby increasing their roots of goodness and attaining the realization of the fruits; thus,

it is said in the subsequent sutra that when the "Chapter on Contemplating the Tathāgata" was taught, the immeasurable great assembly attained the purity of the Dharma-eye, and when the "Chapter on Explaining the Bodhisattva Practice" was taught,
immeasurable multitudes of humans and devas attained the patience of subduing [the passions], the patience of emptiness, the patience of non-arising, and the first, second, and even higher stages.

In the "Ten Stages" [chapter], immeasurable bodhisattvas attain the stage of being "born once more before Buddhahood" (*ekajātipratibaddha*); furthermore, throughout the sections up to the "Chapter on Upholding," there are many instances of realization and attaining the Way.

[Commentary] Regarding the statement that the primary purpose is to protect the state: there is both internal protection and external protection. Internal protection refers to instructing bodhisattvas to protect the Buddha-dharma.
Regarding the protection of the fruits, the protection of the ten stages of practice, and the external protection of transforming sentient beings:

[the latter] involves manifesting to kings and others to protect the state, protecting oneself, and protecting the people by dispelling all calamities so that the country is peaceful and the people are at ease. These forms of internal and external protection are all meanings elucidated in the core doctrine (*zong*) of this sutra;

therefore, it is said that the "core doctrine" (*zong*) here refers to the protection of the state. Within these two types of protection, the principle is found in the "Chapter on Contemplating the Tathāgata."

In this [text], both phenomena (*dharma*) and principle (*dharmatā*) are manifested together; principle and phenomena encompass and integrate the stages from beginning to end. When both object and wisdom are quiescent, what is the mode of activity?
What is clarified in this chapter is that contemplative insight (*prajñā*) is the phenomenon and the wisdom, while true reality (*tathatā*) is the principle and the object.
To dissolve the characteristics and contemplate the nature is called "both object and wisdom being quiescent. As it says below: "The noble wisdom manifests for the first time."
To be fully endowed with eighty-four thousand *pāramitās* in a single thought-moment is called the "Ground of Joy" (*pramuditā-bhūmi*);

this is termed the beginning because it is the initial realization of the principle through untainted noble wisdom (*anāsrava-āryajñāna*). Furthermore, it is said that the equality of essence and appearance is called "the Wisdom of All-Knowledge" (*sarvajñājñāna*);

as this is the fruit of Buddhahood, it is termed the end. Regarding the other five patiences (*kṣānti*) and so forth, I shall briefly outline their general meaning by following the intent of the subsequent text.
The text is clear. [Commentary:
Regarding the phrase "Flowers manifest the power of excellent virtue, appearing as inconceivable," the character *liáng* (令) is read in the departing tone (*qùshēng*) and signifies "good.

In the "Inconceivable Chapter" (*Acintya-parivarta*), the great assembly scatters flowers to manifest the excellent and wondrous virtue of the *prajñā*, while the Tathāgata’s supernatural powers (*ṛddhi-bala*) manifest what is difficult to conceive.

The manifestation of the contemplation of these matters through the divine power of *prajñā* is unfathomable; this refers, for example, to one flower entering into immeasurable flowers, and immeasurable flowers entering into one flower, and so forth.

[Commentary] The "thirteen masters" are Bodhisattvas who uphold the sutras, consisting of those on the three stages of worthiness (*tri-piṭaka*) and the ten stages (*daśa-bhūmi*). They are so named because they possess those dharmas.
To serve as a Dharma Master is itself the "Master"; thus he is called a "Dharma Master. The term *zhāozhāo* (昭昭) and *guìngguìng* (炅炅) describe a state of brilliant and flourishing clarity.
*Fēn* (氛) is identical to *fēn* (芬); it refers to the invasive and baleful vapors of demonic influence.

*Huánqū* (寰區) refers to the universe—the vast expanse of territory under the jurisdiction of emperors throughout all under heaven, which is termed the *huánqū*. Summarizing these meanings, there are thirteen points of doctrine.
The Master upholds the Prajñā; its text is luminous, manifest, and easy to understand, as if one were looking at the back of one's hand.

By virtue of the majestic power of the Prajñā, the seven calamities and the invasion of malevolent vapors are extinguished, and the majestic radiance of the Prajñā shines brilliantly, bringing tranquility to the realm. Therefore, the "Chapter on Upholding" states: "From the initial practice of patience..."
Upon reaching the Vajra-samādhi, practicing the thirteen contemplation gates according to the Dharma serves as the support and foundation for the Dharma Master.
It is further said that if the seven calamities arise, all kings, in order to eliminate these calamities, should uphold and expound the Prajñāpāramitā;
thus the seven calamities will immediately cease, and the land will become peaceful and prosperous.
[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "fearing the final age" (*jì yè*): "final" (*jì*) refers to the end. It is like the image of the end of autumn when grain ripens and forms ears.
Furthermore, "final" (*jì*) refers to siblings (*kùnjì*). When brothers, branches, leaves, sons, and grandsons succeed one another, it is called the "final age" (*jì yè*).

Although the Buddha taught the *Prajñāpāramitā* for the benefit of that time, he feared that within the remaining Dharma of the final age, there would be kings, ministers, the fourfold assembly, and their descendants and branches.
As the leaves gradually wither and fall, the Dharma will perish and calamities will arise within the land; therefore, speaking these words forever as a solemn warning,

he entrusts [the teaching] to kings, so that all monarchs may establish the Buddha-Dharma to protect the state and bring peace to the people, as described in the "Chapter on Entrustment" for those who study it.
[Commentary]: "If it were not... and so forth praises the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma as being able to extinguish suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*).

"Qu" (衢) means a road. The fruit of suffering in birth and death (*saṃsāra*) is that upon which sentient beings depend to travel back and forth; their wandering through the three realms in a state of delusion is called the "dark road" (*huñqu*).

"Zhi" (窒) means extinction. "Yù" (慾)—which is the same as "yù" (欲)—refers to craving and attachment; this is precisely the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), which also subsumes the obstacle of the knowable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

All karma that is produced is comprised within the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*), which is the cause of suffering; because the faults of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) are particularly heavy, they are discussed here with specific emphasis.
As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "The cause of all sufferings is rooted in greed and desire; if greed and desire are extinguished, there will be nothing upon which [suffering] can rely.
Because there are four types of craving, it is said to be "all" (*sarva*). The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 55, asks: "What is meant by 'present craving' (*vidyamāna-tṛṣṇā*)? It refers to..."
What is craving for the existence of one’s own self as it is presently perceived and guarded? It is the craving that accompanies longing and joy for the specific distinctions of one’s future self.
What is craving for delight in this or that? It is the craving that arises as attachment toward the five present sense objects, such as forms and so forth.
What is craving for hope regarding unobtained desirable forms and so forth? This is the general meaning.
If it were not for the Tathāgata’s great brilliance illuminating all and his preaching of the Dharma to dispel delusion,

how could one break through the dark path of the bitter fruits of birth and death? If it were not for the Tathāgata’s great resonance of the Dharma-sound, how could one extinguish the various desires that are the causes of the suffering of birth and death?
[Commentary: "The eighth reign of the August Tang" refers to: 1. Gaozu, 2. Taizong, 3. Gaozong, 4.
Zhongzong, 5. Ruizong, 6. Xuanzong, 7. Suzong, and 8. Daizong. With their golden branches and jade leaves, the descendants succeeded one another;
Daizong was the eighth. "Zào" (造) means transformation; "xuán" (玄) means sagehood; "yín" (垠)—pronounced *jīn*—means boundary. This refers to the former Emperor.

The present Emperor has now brought about a second creation, nurturing all living beings with sagely virtue and sagely transformation that are boundless. His laws and edicts are upright and without crookedness;
his penal codes are pure and clearly defined. "Jie" (截) means to cut; [the punishments] are as uniform as paper being cut with scissors.
[Commentary]: "To spread a fallen net and lift a sagging cord": "to lift" means to raise up; "sagging" means falling downward; and the "cord" is the main rope that governs the net.
One who wishes to spread a fallen net must first lift the main rope, whereupon all parts of the net are spread.

Matters that have not been practiced since antiquity are like a fallen net; Emperor Daizong’s governance and transformation lifted them up and put them into practice, resembling the re-spreading of a fallen net.
"To once again lift the sagging纲 (gāng—meaning 'the guiding cord' or 'order') and spread the net wide once more. What is the intent of this?
