Desiring to make his ministers understand the Bodhisattva’s intelligence and spiritual wonders, he took seven horses and did not give them grass or grain for six days.
On the seventh day, the great assembly of ministers requested the Bodhisattva to preach the Dharma. His discourse flowed like a stream;

his elucidation of the scriptures and his discernment of principles awakened the hearts of the people. Amidst the multitude, the King ordered someone to feed the previously starving horse with grass and grain.
The other horses would not eat, but merely neighed piteously and shed tears as they listened to the Dharma. Thus, throughout the kingdom, everyone came to know that the Bodhisattva was preaching.

The spiritual power of the Dharma is incomparably extraordinary. Regarding Nāgārjuna, the *Preface to the Madhyamaka-śāstra* states: "In the Sanskrit language he is called Nāgāhvaya-cūḍa, which in Chinese means 'Dragon-Winner' (*Longsheng*);
he is also named 'Dragon-Fierce' (*Longmeng*). The old translation 'Dragon-Tree' (*Longshu*) is an error. A verse from the ten-fascicle *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* says:
"After my parinirvāṇa, within the kingdom of South India, there will be a bhikṣu of great virtue whose name is..."

It is said that Nāgārjuna, dwelling in the first stage, the Ground of Extreme Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), skillfully expounded the Mahāyāna Dharma, was able to shatter views of existence and non-existence, and was reborn in the Land of Peace and Bliss;
this is explained in detail as recorded in the original biographies of Nāgārjuna.

[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "up to one thousand years" and so forth: the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, in its fourth fascicle, states that after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the Śrāvaka-piṭaka was divided into many schools beyond the first hundred years;
however, the Bodhisattva-piṭaka remained pure and of a single flavor for a thousand years prior, without any discord or dispute.
Only after a millennium had passed did it come to have divergent doctrines between the two schools of Emptiness (Śūnyavāda) and Existence (Satyavāda). For this reason, the Tathāgata...

The True Dharma shall endure for only a thousand years. Regarding the Master Bhāviveka (translated into Chinese as Qingbian, "Clear Discrimination"), the *Xiyuji* states that not far south of the city of the great country of Andhra in South India, there is a mountain cliff where the master resided.

It was the place where he dwelt in the palace of the Asuras, awaiting the manifestation of Maitreya Bodhisattva’s attainment of Buddhahood. The master possessed a noble and vast magnanimity, and his aspirations were far-reaching.
Cao was profound and reclusive; outwardly he wore the robes of a monk, while inwardly he propagated the teachings of Nāgārjuna.

Hearing that the Dharma-protecting Bodhisattva in the kingdom of Magadha was proclaiming the teachings of the Dharma with several thousand disciples, he felt a desire for discussion and set out on his journey, staff in hand.
Upon reaching the city of Pāṭaliputra, he learned that the Dharma-protecting Bodhisattva was at the Bodhi tree; the master then ordered his gatekeeper to announce his arrival.
The man said, "Go to the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla at the Bodhi tree and speak these words on my behalf:

'The Bodhisattva has proclaimed the bequeathed teachings and guided deluded beings, looking up to your virtue with a humble mind for many days. Yet, because his past vows have not yet been fulfilled, he has been unable to pay his respects.
He has sworn that he will not return from seeing the Bodhi tree empty-handed; upon seeing it, there shall be realization, worthy of the praise of gods and men.'"
The Master, the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla, said to his messenger: "Human existence is like an illusion and life is as fleeting as a bubble.
Though I have been diligent and sincere day after day, I have had no leisure for discussion; though we have traveled back and forth many times, we have ultimately never met.

When the Master returned to his own country, he reflected in silence, saying: "If it were not for Maitreya becoming a Buddha, who would resolve my doubts? He then [prostrated] before an image of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.

While reciting the *Cittamantra* (Heart Mantra) and abstaining from grain while subsisting only on water for three years, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva manifested a body of wondrous color and said to the Master:
"What is your aspiration? He replied: "I wish to retain this body until I may behold Maitreya.
Avalokiteśvara said: "Human life is precarious and fragile; the world is floating and illusory. You should cultivate supreme goodness and aspire to be born in Tuṣita Heaven."
"Regarding this audience, you shall soon succeed in seeing him," the Master said. "Your resolve must not be diverted, and your mind must not be divided.
Avalokiteśvara said, "If that is so, you should go to the country of Dhānakaṭaka. To the south of the city there is a mountain cliff where the Vajrapāṇi deity resides.
If you maintain a sincere resolve and recite the Vajrapāṇi mantra, you shall surely fulfill this vow. Thereupon, the Master...
He went there and recited [the scriptures] for three years, after which the deity spoke to him, saying, "What is it that you require with such diligent effort?

The Master of Treatises replied, "I wish to remain here until I may behold Maitreya. Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva then dispatched the deity to invite him, saying, "Is he not one who shall fulfill my vow?
It rests with you, O deity. The deity then bestowed a secret formula upon the Master of Treatises, saying, "Within this rocky cliff..."
There was a palace of the asuras where, according to the Dharma, they requested that a stone wall be opened; once it was opened, they entered within it to await the sight of the Master.
The Master remarked, "It is dark and desolate, with nothing to be seen; how can I know when the Buddha has appeared? The Vajrapāṇi deity said, "When Maitreya appears in the world, I shall inform you.
Having received this command, the Master applied himself with single-minded diligence to recitation and retention, and another three years passed without any change.

He recited mantras over white mustard seeds and struck the stone wall, which opened up suddenly and completely. At that time, hundreds of thousands of people gazed upon it, so entranced they forgot to leave.
The Master stepped across the threshold and addressed the multitude, saying: "I have long prayed for this, awaiting the manifestation of Maitreya’s sacred spirit and his protective grace;
now that my great vow has been fulfilled, you should enter here together to witness the appearance of the Buddha. Those who heard this were struck with terror and awe.
No one dared to step upon the threshold, fearing it was the lair of a venomous serpent and that they might lose their lives.

After being warned repeatedly, six people followed him inside. When the Master of Śāstras looked back and apologized, the crowd immediately entered; once they had gone in, the stone wall closed back up.
All were filled with lamentation and regret for their previous words. Regarding Dharmapāla, the *Xiyuji* (Records of the Western Regions) states that he was the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla.
This was Dharmananda of the kingdom of Pāṭaliputra. Born into a family of high ministers within the city, he possessed a noble disposition from childhood;
as he grew, he propagated the Way and his learning became as deep as the ocean’s abyss. His understanding was as brilliant as the rising sun; after Vasubandhu, he was the peerless one.
At the age of thirty-two, he passed away at Bodhi Monastery, where a voice resounded from the air, announcing: "Pāṭa..."

These two Bodhisattvas—the former is the master of the ultimate emptiness (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*), and the latter is the master of the perfect reality consistent with reason (*yukti-saṃvṛti*). Each, according to the definitive Mahāyāna teachings, elucidates emptiness and existence respectively.
Specifically, the Bodhisattva Bhāviveka, relying on the *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtras and others, took them as the definitive teaching on the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*)."
All that exists within is empty; this is called the "School of Ultimate Emptiness. Among the three types of teachings, it primarily expounds the teaching of emptiness;

among the teachings of the three periods, it belongs to the second period. The Bodhisattva Dharmapāla, relying on the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* and other texts, established this as a definitive teaching (*nītārtha*).

He clearly elucidated that among all phenomena—both conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), dependent (*paratantra*) and perfected (*pariniṣpanna*)—there exists a self (*ātman*) and what belongs to a self (*ātmīya*) pervading them all.

In the reckoning of the three types of teachings within the "Principled and Perfectly Real" school—which is neither exclusively empty nor exclusively existent—this belongs to the third period of teaching.
Furthermore, regarding the various treatises composed by Aśvaghoṣa and Nāgārjuna mentioned previously, each was established according to their own particular intent as being of the Emptiness school;
however, as for the *Prajñāpāramitā* and other sūtras spoken by the Buddha, their texts merely contain implicit meanings.

Regarding the two schools that maintain that all things are empty from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*), masters such as Nāgārjuna, Āryadeva, and Bhāviveka explain the meaning according to the literal text, asserting that all phenomena are empty;

thus, these belong to the school of the emptiness of ultimate truth. They characterize such sūtras as being of interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*), and they hold that both the words and the meaning are not definitive.
As for the master Maitreya Bodhisattva, who maintains the school of the perfect and true reality (*yathārtha-pariniṣpanna*):
Asaṅga and Vasubandhu each composed treatises to explain the *Prajñāpāramitā* and other sūtras, propagating them extensively;
their many expositions on the teaching of emptiness reveal that while the words of the *Prajñāpāramitā* and other sūtras are cryptic, their meaning is explicit.
Therefore, the *Prajñāpāramitā* and other sūtras are common to both schools and propagate the tenets of both; they are subsumed under the second and third periods of the teachings, respectively.
[Commentary] Regarding the statement "emptiness, existence, and so forth," all phenomena (*dharmas*) are generally categorized into two types: first, emptiness; second, existence.
Because there is no distinction between these phenomena, it is called the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (the nature of being conceptually constructed).

Because this mind of conceptual construction (*parikalpa*) falsely clings to the nature of self and phenomena, it is termed the *parikalpita-svabhāva*. As for the existence of phenomena, there are distinctions.

Briefly, there are two categories: first, impermanent phenomena, which refers to conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*); second, permanent phenomena, which refers to unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
Furthermore, there are two other categories: first, the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*); second, the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).

As for the dependent nature, it refers to phenomena that arise in dependence upon various conditions; these are precisely the conditioned phenomena that possess an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and serve as causes.

That which is produced by conditions is called the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature). This has two categories: The first is the contaminated (*sāsrava*), which refers to the twenty-six afflictions (*kleśa*) including the root and secondary ones, the attainment of non-conception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), the state of non-conception (*asaṃjñika*), the nature of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva*), sleep, and regret—these thirty-one factors in their entirety—as well as a portion of the other sixty-two factors, such as the universal (*sarvatraga*) and object-specific (*viṣayapratiniyata*) mental factors, that are generally categorized as contaminated. The second is the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*). This includes the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), the three gateways to liberation (*vimokṣamukha*), the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*), the nine successive meditative stages (*anupūrvasamāpatti*), the ten totalities (*kṛtsnāyatana*), the eight spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), the three doors of liberation (*vimokṣamukha*), the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), the six supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), the four types of fearlessness (*vaiśāradya*), the four kinds of self-confidence (*pratisaraṇa*), the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*), the great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), the unobstructed knowledge regarding all phenomena (*sarvadharmāsaṅgajñāna*), and so forth. These are all included within the uncontaminated category. Furthermore, the remaining factors not mentioned here are to be understood according to their respective characteristics. Thus, it is established that there are two types of dependent nature: the contaminated and the uncontaminated. Among these, the contaminated is further divided into two: those associated with the mind (*cittasaṃprayukta*) and those dissociated from the mind (*cittaviprayukta*). The former consists of the six root afflictions and the twenty secondary afflictions; the latter consists of the formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayuktasaṃskāra*). The uncontaminated is likewise divided into two: those associated with the mind and those dissociated from the mind. The former consists of the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), the four formless attainments, the three gateways to liberation, the eight liberations, the nine successive meditative stages, the ten totalities, the eight spheres of mastery, the three doors of liberation, the four analytical knowledges, the six supernormal powers, the four types of fearlessness, the four kinds of self-confidence, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, the great compassion, and the unobstructed knowledge regarding all phenomena. The latter consists of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) dharmas, such as space (*ākāśa*), analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*), and non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyānirodha*). Thus, the dependent nature is definitively established as having two categories: the contaminated and the uncontaminated. Regarding the untainted (*anāsrava*), this refers to the entirety of the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) and a portion of the other sixty-two dharmas that are common to the untainted.
These ninety-four dharmas are all of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*). As for the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), there are two types:
first, the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states: "That which is fully accomplished as revealed by the two emptinesses is the reality of all phenomena."

"Nature" (svabhāva) refers to the *pariniṣpanna* (perfected nature). This term reveals that its essence is pervasive and eternal, and that it is not false or erroneous. It distinguishes itself from both the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) and universal (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) characteristics, as well as from space (*ākāśa*) and the self (*ātman*).

This [perfected nature] possesses three meanings: first, its essence is pervasive because it extends to all places; this is the meaning of "perfection" (*pariṇiṣpanna*). Second, its essence is eternal because it is neither produced nor destroyed;
this is the meaning of "accomplishment" (*niṣpanna*). Third, its essence is not false or erroneous because it is the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*); this is the meaning of "reality" (*satya*).
The meaning [of *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*] possesses these three meanings and is thus named *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*.

Second, conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*)—specifically the pure portion (*śuddha-bhāga*) of the previously mentioned uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*)—is also called *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* because it is free from inversion (*viparyāsa*). As the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:

"Uncontaminated conditioned phenomena are free from inversion and possess ultimate, supreme function that is all-pervasive; they also receive this name and likewise possess the three meanings. Because they are free from inversion, they are 'real' (*satya*)."

Because it is ultimate, it constitutes "excellence" (parama); because its function is all-pervasive, it is "perfect" (pariniṣpanna). The treatise establishes "perfection" through these three meanings in sequence;

here, for the sake of convenience regarding the meaning, it is termed "thoroughly established reality" (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva). That which is disputed between the two schools is the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva), categorized by way of its permanence or impermanence.

[Commentary]: Those who are disciples of the *Yogācāra*—such as Vasubandhu, Dharmapāla, and others who followed Maitreya and composed treatises to propagate the teachings of the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* and other scriptures—are all termed *Yogācāra* disciples.
Among them, figures such as Nanda and Sthiramati may have held partial attachments that did not accord with correct principle.
Second, masters such as Bhāviveka and his followers assisted the intent of Nāgārjuna and the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtras*, asserting [the non-dual nature of] the One.
In the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), all phenomena are entirely empty; in the conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*), they may be said to exist.

The third master, Dharmapāla Bodhisattva, refuted these two schools, asserting that both the claim of existence and the claim of emptiness fail to exhaust the principle. Therefore, he established the Middle Way as being neither existent nor empty.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "Now, for the time being," the *Fayuan zhang* states that within the Mahāyāna, those teachings expressed through explicit discourse are called *nītārtha* (definitive) sūtras, while those expressed through implicit discourse are called *anītārtha* (non-definitive) sūtras. The *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* states:

"In the past, during the second period, the World-Honored One turned the wheel of the true Dharma by means of implicit characteristics; it was not yet definitive. During the third period, by means of explicit..."

The turning of the wheel of Dharma that realizes characteristics is the teaching of the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), which explains that the nature of all phenomena is empty and consists of the three absences of intrinsic nature (*trividha-niḥsvabhāvatā*).

Teachings that do not clearly manifest the ultimate reality to be expressed are called "non-definitive" (*neyārtha*). Conversely, those that clearly manifest the ultimate principle to be expressed are called "definitive sutras" (*nītārtha-sūtra*).

Based on this, Dharmapāla elucidates the correct meaning by briefly distinguishing the two truths. *Note: This passage is a commentary on the opening section of Vasubandhu’s *Triṃśikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, specifically the verse concerning the three absences of intrinsic nature.*
Returning to the Middle Way, one brings to rest all contentious debates regarding the attachment to existence and the attachment to emptiness.

[Commentary: This conventional truth is both existent and empty; it is existent because the dependent nature arises through conditions, and it is empty because the imagined nature is a false conceptualization.
[Commentary: "This refers to" means that this is based on the *Prajñāpāramitā*, which directly realizes the true reality (*tattva*) as being beyond words and transcending all marks.

Therefore, it is said that the true nature (*dharmatā*) is empty; it is a void, profound, quiescent, and unobstructed true reality. What is called "emptiness" is not an emptiness that lacks any essence.
[Commentary]: Regarding the *Treatise on the Three Natures* (*Trisvabhāvanirdeśa*) and other texts, they establish three natures: first, the nature of the absence of marks (*lakṣaṇaniḥsvabhāvatā*);

second, the nature of the non-arising of the dependent (*paratantrānutpattiniḥsvabhāvatā*); and third, the nature of the absence of nature in the ultimate reality (*pariniṣpannaniḥsvabhāvatā*). The intention behind establishing these is as follows:

since beginningless time, all sentient beings have engaged in false conceptualization, grasping at persons and grasping at phenomena. To eliminate that affliction, one establishes this "nature of the absence of marks" based upon True Suchness (*tathatā*).

Because the ultimate truth is serene and devoid of such characteristics, there are further sentient beings who falsely cling to the idea that the phenomena of form and mind produced from conditions are substantially real.
To dispel this affliction, it is established—based on *tathatā* (suchness)—that the dependent nature is non-arising and that the true nature is eternally abiding and characterized by non-arising.
Furthermore, there are sentient beings who understand that the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) does not exist, yet they [falsely] claim that the dependent nature is not real.

Because sentient beings give rise to attachment by regarding ultimate truth as a truly existent entity, in order to eliminate that affliction, one establishes "the nature of the lack of nature" based upon *tathatā* (suchness).
Regarding the term "nature": the first "nature" refers to the absence of that truly existent essence which they grasp; the second "nature" refers to being free from such grasping.
It is said that true nature is not non-existent in order to cause sentient beings to dissolve all marks and accord with the signless (*animitta*).
Therefore, based on the one True Suchness (*tathatā*), the three non-natures are established to dispel the [erroneous] three natures.
[Commentary: Regarding the verses of the treatise, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra-kārikā* states: "Precisely by relying on these three abodes, those three non-natures are established;

therefore, the Buddha spoke with intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*) that all phenomena are without nature. First is the non-nature of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-niḥsvabhāvatā*); next is the non-nature of self-existence (*utpatti-niḥsvabhāvatā*); and finally..."

Because one distances oneself from the previously grasped nature of self and phenomena, first clarifying the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) and subsequently the three absences of nature (*triniḥsvabhāvatā*), the text refers back to the former by saying, "it is based on this.
"Intentional meaning" (*saṃdhāya*) carries the sense of being implicit; it is not a teaching of explicit meaning.

The teaching that the nature of all phenomena is entirely empty—the doctrine of the three absences of nature—is called "non-explicit" (*neyārtha*) because it is taught as an antidote for sentient beings who possess the affliction of clinging.

The meaning of these three kinds of lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) was taught with intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*): first, the lack of intrinsic nature in terms of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-niḥsvabhāvatā*), which refers to the fact that the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is entirely empty and devoid of any substantial characteristic;

second, the lack of intrinsic nature in terms of arising (*utpatti-niḥsvabhāvatā*), which refers to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) existing by relying on causes and conditions and lacking any nature of arising spontaneously;
and third, the lack of intrinsic nature in terms of the ultimate (*paramārtha-niḥsvabhāvatā*), which refers to the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).

Regarding the term "ultimate" (*paramārtha*): because it refers to the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), which is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), there is no self-nature (*svabhāva*) of the grasped person or phenomena upon that ultimate;
thus, it is called the "lack of self-nature in the ultimate sense. Furthermore, there is the meaning of the three natures as being clearly manifest, which will be explained below.

[Commentary]: Regarding such passages as these, the *Xinjing Shu* (Commentary on the Heart Sūtra), having already clarified emptiness and existence, offers a general evaluation, stating: "Observing the intent of the Sage, emptiness and existence do not conflict;

the Dharma transcends intellectual designations. What is empty? What is existent? These are provisional teachings of existence and emptiness spoken for the sake of removing attachments according to the capacities of beings.
Subsequently, various disciples have given rise to attachments based on the literal text, claiming that their own understanding accords with the Middle Way while disparaging the views of others."

What has been known thus far may be considered a mistaken exposition; now, in extolling the meaning of the sutras, I shall extend both ends of this marvelous principle so that the wise may discern right from wrong.

(The "two ends" refer to the school of ultimate emptiness and the school of accordant with reason and perfect reality; the commentary below identifies these as the two schools of Nature and Characteristics.)
[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "Fortunately," the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing stated that the Mahāyāna teachings expounded do not exceed two types:
first, Madhyamaka; second, Yogācāra. Madhyamaka holds that while conventional phenomena exist, their ultimate essence is empty and void, like an illusion.

Yogācāra holds that there is nothing external and all internal phenomena are merely consciousness. Since these both follow the holy teachings, which one is right and which one is wrong? They are equally in accord with the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
What is true and what is false? The intent lies in severing hindrances and benefiting sentient beings; how could one wish to extensively cause confusion and further increase the knots of grievance?

If one relies upon practice, both will ascend to the other shore; if one abandons it, both will sink together into the deluded ford. In the Western Land, the two practices proceed together without logical contradiction or dispute.
Since there are no eyes of wisdom, who can discern right from wrong? One need only apply oneself diligently to cultivation; there is no need for self-harm.

Regarding the fundamental and subsequently attained wisdoms of the emptiness of persons and the emptiness of phenomena: the untainted fundamental and subsequently attained wisdoms are precisely the core tenet of this sutra.

Furthermore, the distant preparatory wisdom and the near preparatory wisdom serve as the means for these fundamental and subsequently attained wisdoms; thus, they assist in accomplishing the wisdom of contemplation and are likewise [the core tenet].

The stage of the provisions for the goal (*sambhāra-mārga*) has "patience" (*kṣānti*) as its remote preparation (*dūraprayoga*), while the four stages of the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) constitute its proximate preparation (*āsannaprayoga*), because they are immediately contiguous with the untainted state (*anāsrava*).
[Commentary]:

There is an interpretation that these two together constitute the core tenet (*śāstramata*) of the sutra; that is, the union of the contemplation of the true nature (*dharmatā*) and the contemplation of illumination (*prabhāsvara*) constitutes the core tenet of this sutra.

"Principle" (*zong*) refers to that which is venerated and honored; since this sutra venerates, honors, and takes as its primary focus these two aspects of the Prajñā Dharma, it is titled *Prajñā* to accord with the principle of what the sutra venerates. The three meanings are as explained in the commentary. Now, another interpretation is offered:

according to what is specifically elucidated, Prajñā is the "principle" (*zong*) and protecting the state is the "purport" (*zhi*). The principle is as stated in the commentary, while the purport is...

The intended meaning and purport of this scripture is that the Buddha taught it specifically to manifest the two types of protection (*rakṣā*), which constitute its primary purpose and fundamental intent;
therefore, the title designates it as the *Rāṣṭrapāla Prajñāpāramitā*. As the subsequent text clarifies after explaining *prajñā*, it concludes by stating:
"A bodhisattva mahāsattva protects the fruit of Buddhahood, protects the practice of the ten stages (*bhūmi*), and protects the transformation of sentient beings."
Because it is thus, external protection can be understood. [Commentary:

Regarding the statement that "the essence of the sūtra has two aspects—text and meaning"—here, "text" (*vyañjana*) is so called because, when taken in its forward sense, it serves as the support (*āśraya*) that subsumes the names and phrases (*nāma-pada*);

when taken in its reverse sense, it serves as the supported (*āśrita*) that subsumes the sounds (*ghoṣa*). Therefore, by speaking only of "text," the four dharmas, along with their objects, are fully subsumed.
The five factors that explain the meaning constitute the essence of the sūtra.

[Commentary: Regarding "sound produced by accomplishment," the intended meaning is that the sounds produced and elicited by the establishment of the principles of the teachings by the various noble ones (*ārya*) and their disciples are called "sound produced by accomplishment. Therefore, the sacred teaching takes sound as its essence.

[Commentary]: Regarding the passage from "Only consciousness" to "that which expresses": this refutes the Hīnayāna attachment that names (*nāman*), phrases (*pada*), and syllables (*vyañjana*) exist substantially apart from sound as the actual expressers.
The correct Mahāyāna position is that the triad of name, phrase, and syllable is provisionally established based upon sound and is not separate from it. Thus, he challenges the Hīnayāna:
"It is the winding [modulations] within sound that express and signify all phenomena, giving rise to conceptual understanding in sentient beings; it is the function of sound alone that I [accept]."

Because they are said to be inseparable from the substance of sound, they are capable of signifying meaning; yet according to your own tenet, the three—name, phrase, and phoneme—are asserted to exist substantially apart from sound.

Consequently, like form and other such entities, they would not be capable of signifying meaning. Since form and the rest are all collectively called "form" and so forth, and these are substantially existent forms that are not capable of signifying meaning, it follows that names and the rest, though substantially existent, are likewise not capable of signifying meaning. From this, one must admit that form and the rest [are what truly signify].
There are indeed real entities such as form that are not designators, whereas names and so forth are real entities that are designators.

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "from name up to connection," both the *Mahāvibhāṣā* and the *Abhidharmakośa* contain this expression. A "name-group" (*nāmakāya*) is a sequential arrangement of various names;
it merely designates the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and does not yet manifest the distinctions or establish the meaning. A "phrase-group" (*padakāya*), however, is a sequential establishment...
The body of the text (*vyañjana-kāya*) establishes the distinctions among the meanings of the teachings by linking them sequentially from beginning to end so that their significance is not dispersed;
therefore, it is said that the Buddha’s teaching has names (*nāman*), phrases (*pada*), and phonemes (*vyañjana*) as its essence.

[Commentary]: "All are brought to completion by means of two things" means that "completion" here carries the sense of fulfillment. Because the voice (*śabda*) and the syllables (*vyañjana*) fulfill these two things, they are termed the "Holy Teaching" (*āgama*).
Since the syllable (*vyañjana*) subsumes both the phrase (*pada*) and the sentence (*nāma*), the voice and the syllables collectively encompass these four factors.
Question: What is the mode of establishment regarding their mutual inclusion? Answer: It refers to [the process] upon the voice...

The differentiation of inflections (*vyañjana*) is conventionally designated as "syllables" (*vyañjana*) because they are capable of manifesting meaning. When they turn toward manifesting the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of meaning, they are termed "names" (*nāman*);
when they turn toward manifesting the differentiation (*viśeṣa*) of meaning, they are termed "phrases" (*pada*). In the Sanskrit language, *nāma* is translated here as "name.

This refers to following the meaning, returning to the meaning, and proceeding toward the meaning; that is, it follows sound and returns to or proceeds toward its object, for one calls forth a phenomenon by its name. As it is said: [the verse].
When the term "form" (*rūpa*) expresses the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of form, it is subsumed under what is designated by a single syllable.

If one says "Ānanda" or "Rāhula," these are subsumed under what is designated by two or more syllables; in both cases, they refer to the essence of a phenomenon (*dharmatā*) because they express its intrinsic nature.
In the Sanskrit language, *pada* is translated as "phrase" (*jù*); its precise translation is "trace" (*jì*). Just as there are four traces of an elephant, so too there are four lines in a verse.

By tracing the traces one sees the elephant; by tracing the verses one understands the principles. For example, phrases such as "all conditioned phenomena are impermanent" express the specific meanings of various conditioned phenomena;

therefore, these are sentences that express specific meanings. Furthermore, there are sentences that encompass the dharmas in their entirety, including long sentences, short sentences, and so forth (as explained in other places).
[Commentary]: "Phoneme" (*vyañjana*)—the basis for the two [i.e., name and phrase]—is a Sanskrit term translated here as "phoneme.
A phoneme is that which can manifest meaning; it manifests names and phrases proximately, and it manifests meaning distantly. It universally manifests both self-nature and specific difference.
"Syllable" (*akṣara*) is a Sanskrit term translated here as "syllable," such as the syllables *a* (first tone) and *ha* (third tone). It is precisely by means of these syllables that...
That which possesses expressive power and causes beings to generate understanding is called a *vyañjana* (phoneme/letter); thus, the *vyañjana* is identical to the *akṣara* (syllable).

If there were no expression and it did not produce understanding in beings, it would be merely a *akṣara* and not a *vyañjana*. Because the *vyañjana* is narrow while the *akṣara* is broad, the two types—namely, the *nāma* (name) and the *pada* (phrase)—are established based upon the *vyañjana*, as it is their support;
therefore, it is said that the *vyañjana* is identical to the *akṣara*, serving as the basis for those two. Furthermore, what is this "sound" (*ghoṣa*)? It is the *akṣara*.
Regarding the five factors—phrases (*pada*), names (*nāman*), and syllables (*vyañjana*)—their relative breadth or narrowness when compared to one another is as follows:

If there is sound and syllable, there are phrases and names, though they are not necessarily fixed; this is because if the sound is direct and lacks inflection, there are only sounds and syllables, but no phrases or names.

When syllables are formed, if the phrases and so forth are not fixed, there is no expressive capacity, and thus the syllable is not established. It is only when there is an expressive syllable that it constitutes a phrase.

Only when they form a composition do they constitute a sentence (*pada*). At the time of forming a composition, names (*nāman*) and phrases (*pada*) are not fixed; for instance, the expressions "goes" (*gacchati*) and "comes" (*āgacchati*) are neither names nor phrases.
If one considers names and phrases in relation to one another, there is mutual breadth and narrowness: the terms "form" (*rūpa*) and "sound" (*śabda*) are names but not phrases;
"going," "coming," "sitting," and "standing" are phrases but not names—as in the case of saying "eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, visible form, sound, odor, and taste."

Taste and touch are names; the same principle should be understood to apply to all other phenomena. Here, we clarify that among the four bases of teaching—sound, name, phrase, and syllable—sound is substantial, while name, phrase, and syllable are conventional designations.

These three conventional and substantial factors constitute the essence [of the teaching]. As for the statement that these three are distinct from sound and reach the object through conditions related to sound, this is a passage from the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* (Treatise on Consciousness-Only), intended to refute the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) position that name, phrase, and syllable are substantially real apart from sound.
There is an objection raised against this: "If names, phrases, and syllables are conventionally established based on sound and lack substantial reality, they should not differ from sound.

If they do not differ from sound, then there would be no distinction between the objects of the two types of unimpeded knowledge—those regarding phenomena (*dharma*) and those regarding language (*nirukti*).

If there were no distinction, how could they serve as cognitive objects to constitute the fourfold difference? Therefore, this [text] explains: 'Although these three are separate from sound, they have no distinct essence.'"

Furthermore, the conventional and the real are distinct, yet they are not identical to sound. Since names, phrases, and phonemes differ from the conventional and the real, the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*) takes names and so forth as its object;
the analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*) takes the signified meaning as its object; the analytical knowledge of language (*niruktipratisaṃvid*) takes sound as its object;

and the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhānapratisaṃvid*) is able to speak in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings. Therefore, the objects of these two—the analytical knowledges of phenomena and language—exist [as distinct entities].

To clarify this intention regarding the distinctions: there are differences between the provisional and the real concerning names, phrases, and phonemes; these four dharmas constitute the substance of the teaching.
[Commentary] Regarding "purity" and so forth, the *Anantamukha-sūtra* states: "Because the dispositions and desires of sentient beings are immeasurable, the Dharma is likewise immeasurable."
Because the dharmas of measure are immeasurable, their meanings are also immeasurable. These immeasurable meanings arise from a single dharma;
that single dharma is precisely the signless, wondrous principle of *tathatā*. It continues until it says: "From a single dharma, a hundred thousand meanings arise;
within those hundred thousand meanings, each one further gives rise to hundreds of thousands of millions of others. In this manner, they successively give rise to the infinite and the boundless.
Regarding the meaning of "extremes" (*anta*): all phenomena produced herein are termed "branches," while among the characteristics of things (*vastu-lakṣaṇa*), all dharmas arise from the mind;
thus, the mind is the root. Now, in clarifying the essence of the teaching (*deśanā-tattva*), there is likewise a distinction between root and branch.

If we take the root, it is the mind of the speaker; if we take the branches, it is the mind of the listener. This is as the Buddha said: "All conditioned phenomena are impermanent. By means of... [text continues]
The power of compassionate vows strikes and vibrates the pure consciousness associated with the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*), causing it to manifest the aspects of words and meanings.

The Wondrous Observing Wisdom (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*) takes this as its substrate and transforms it into the reflected images of words and meanings; it then observes the capacities of sentient beings and speaks accordingly.

That which is spoken—using the words and meanings transformed by the Mirror Wisdom as the fundamental substance—is the teaching-body (*deśanā-śarīra*); it consists of the words and meanings transformed by the Wondrous Observing Wisdom.

Regarding the teaching as the body of the doctrine: for ordinary beings and sages who take the words and meanings manifested by the Buddha as their objective basis (*ālambana*), each transforms their own fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) into tainted sound to act as the listener;

this is the objective basis of the teaching-body (*dharmakāya*). For those listeners, each transforms their own auditory consciousness (*śrotravijñāna*) and mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) into the reflected image of sound to act as the listener;
this is the reflected image of the teaching-body. It is the mental consciousness of the listener that takes this as its object.

Regarding the transformation of sound: the phonemes (*akṣara*), phrases (*pada*), and sentences (*vyañjana*), as well as the meanings they express, all constitute the substance of the teaching (*deśanā*).

However, for the speaker, the substance of the teaching consists primarily of the reflection (the mental image) while the actual sound is secondary; this is because the text and meaning manifest from their pure consciousness (*viśuddha-vijñāna*) for the benefit of sentient beings.

For the listener, however, the substance of the teaching consists primarily of the reflection (the auditory perception) while the actual sound is secondary; this is because both the ear-consciousness and the mental consciousness are capable of hearing the Dharma. The preceding explanation concerned only the speaker.

This reveals that while the Buddha taught that all others—both ordinary beings and sages—are capable of speaking and listening, the speaker is taken as the primary factor and the listener as secondary;
this may be understood by analogy with what precedes.
[Commentary: Regarding Vasubandhu and others, the verse states: "Through the successive power of mutual influence, the two consciousnesses become determinate. The treatise says: "As for..."

The commentary explains that "mutual interaction" (*zhuan-zhuan*) signifies reciprocity. Regarding the "two consciousnesses," these refer to the Buddha-consciousness and the sentient-being consciousness.
This means that when sentient beings possess faith and wisdom with certainty, this faith and understanding serve as a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).

Through this dominant power, they strike and stir the original vow and compassion of the Tathāgata. Consequently, the Tathāgata, possessing the certainty of compassionate vows, takes pity upon sentient beings.
Arising within the consciousness of a Buddha, the appearance of words and meanings manifests through the power of compassion and vows acting as the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
Possessing this dominant power, it causes the appearances of words and meanings to arise and continue in succession within the consciousness-minds of all sentient beings.

Regarding the term "body" (*kāya*), there are three senses: the sense of essence (*svabhāva*), the sense of accumulation (*saṃcaya*), and the sense of continuity (*prabandha*). Here, we take the sense of appearance (*lakṣaṇa*).

Regarding the continuity of meaning: because that which has ceased previously gives rise to what is born subsequently, there is constant succession. As for the "others" mentioned above, they refer to the Buddha as the remainder of sentient beings;
as for the "others" mentioned below, they refer to sentient beings as the remainder of the Buddha.

This is because, within the continuous body of the Buddha, a differentiated consciousness manifests, causing a differentiated consciousness to arise within the continuous bodies of other sentient beings. Why is this? Because the Buddha and [the sentient beings]...

Because they arise through mutual interaction as dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*), they are called "discriminative consciousnesses" (*viśeṣa-vijñāna*). This refers to the direct and indirect expression of the characteristics of the meaning of words;
since both the aspect of seeing (*darśana-bhāga*) and the aspect of the seen (*nimitta-bhāga*) are termed "consciousness," they are called discriminative consciousnesses.

[Commentary: "To subsume the characteristics (lakṣaṇa) into the nature (dharmatā)" means that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), with their various phenomenal characteristics and distinctions, are all the functional manifestations (*artha-vyāpāra*) of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
Therefore, by subsuming these characteristics and functions back into the nature of True Suchness, all dharmas take True Suchness as their essence (*svabhāva*).
Now, it is clarified that the teachings (*deśanā-dharma*) are a single portion of the functional manifestations upon True Suchness; thus, Cien says "subsumes."
Because phenomena are governed by the conditioned, it is said that all dharmas are subsumed within consciousness-only (*vijñapti-mātra*);
because phenomena are governed by the unconditioned, it is said that all dharmas are likewise so. Thus, these two gates—consciousness-only and suchness (*tathatā*)—are established.
[Commentary: Regarding the general and specific, and the shallow and deep: these are generally divided into two categories, namely text (*vyañjana*) and meaning (*artha*).

Specifically, they are further opened into five [categories]: three concerning text and two concerning meaning. Within the text and meaning, the text is shallow while the meaning is deep, as their modes of expression differ.

Within the meanings themselves, consciousness (*vijñāna*) is shallow while the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and nature (*dharmatā*) are deep; thus, all are arranged in sequence from the shallow to the deep.
[Commentary: The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and other texts state that the essence of the "Pitaka" (藏) is "teaching" (*śāsana*), in the sense of containing and upholding [the meaning].

When this teaching is presented in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings to contain their underlying principles, two Pitakas are established: the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, so named because it is directed toward Bodhisattvas; and the Śrāvaka-piṭaka, so named because it is directed toward Śrāvakas.

This is because those Pratyekabuddhas—who sever the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and realize the principle of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*)—are identical to the Śrāvakas in their capacity as the "expressers" (*vācaka*).
Because the teaching follows the majority to establish the name "Śrāvaka-piṭaka," treatises such as the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* establish only two piṭakas.

[The Commentary] states that various teachings speak of three because they establish the distinction of the three piṭakas by using the teaching to express practice while containing its underlying principle, thereby manifesting the three trainings (*tri-śikṣā*).
*Sūtra* (素怛纜) is the new name; *sūtra*, *sūtrānta*, and *sūtrālu* are all corruptions. This is translated here as "Agreement" (*kīya*).
Because it accords with the principle (*dharmatā*) and accords with the faculties (*indriya*), it is able to accord; thus, the sūtra that is the object of this accordance is called a *sūtra* (契經).
A *sūtra* is the name for the *piṭaka*, and thus it is called the *Sūtra-piṭaka*. As for *vinaya*, the old term was *vini*; all such forms are corruptions. This is translated as "subduing" (*dameḥ*).
It is so called because it harmonizes, restrains, and controls the actions of body, speech, and mind, thereby subduing and eliminating all afflictions (*kleśa*). Furthermore—
"Discipline" (*vinaya*) refers to both subduing and being subdued; it encompasses both the teaching and the practice. That which the Buddha taught as discipline is called the "Vinaya Piṭaka.
When ordinary beings and sages uphold this treasury of discipline, it is termed the "Vinaya Piṭaka.
As for *Abhidharma*, the old name *Abhidhamma* is a corruption; it means "Dharma in Confrontation" (*pratisaṃvid-dharma*), so called because one confronts and contemplates Nirvāṇa with pure wisdom.

Because it is the counteragent (*pratipakṣa*) to the dharmas of the four truths—both mundane and supramundane—it is called "Abhidharma" (*Abhidharma*). The treasury of Abhidharma is thus named the "Abhidharmapiṭaka. [Commentary: Regarding the question of whether the three piṭakas of Sūtra, Vinaya, and Abhidharma are identical or different, the *Fayuan* (Garden of the Dharma) answers as follows: The three piṭakas of Sūtra, Vinaya, and Abhidharma are established based on the distinctions between the teachings and their respective functions. Specifically: 1. **Sūtra** is established because it primarily explains the meaning of the Dharma; 2. **Vinaya** is established because it primarily governs conduct and discipline; 3. **Abhidharma** is established because it primarily analyzes the characteristics of phenomena. Furthermore, they differ in terms of their essence, purpose, and the individuals for whom they were intended. Their commonality lies in the fact that all three are the word of the Buddha (*buddhavacana*) and serve as the foundation for the path to liberation. Thus, while they are distinct in their specific characteristics and applications, they are not contradictory, as they together constitute the complete body of the Buddha’s teaching.
Regarding the two masters: the first says that the Sūtra, Vinaya, and Abhidharma each constitute distinct categories and are established as three separate Piṭakas;
the second says there are no distinct categories, for the *Mañjuśrī-paripṛcchā-sūtra* and others primarily expound the training in ethical discipline (*śīla*) and are thus called the Vinaya Piṭaka;

the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra* and others primarily expound the training in meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and are thus called the Sūtra Piṭaka; and the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* and others primarily expound the training in wisdom (*prajñā*) and are thus called the Abhidharma Piṭaka.

The Three Pitakas are distinguished according to their predominant subject matter. Furthermore, it is said: if they exclusively explain meditative concentration (*samādhi*), or if they explain all three trainings (*śikṣā*), they are called the Sūtra Piṭaka;

if they exclusively explain ethical discipline (*śīla*), or if they explain both ethical discipline and meditative concentration, they are called the Vinaya Piṭaka, because these pertain to merit (*puṇya*);

if they exclusively explain wisdom (*prajñā*), they are called the Abhidharma Piṭaka; if they explain both meditative concentration and wisdom, they are included in both the Sūtra and Śāstra Piṭakas, because merit and wisdom are distinct. Alternatively, [the classification may be] as follows: the Sūtra...

Because the *sūtra-piṭaka* is broad in its *sūtras*, according to the first master, the title of this scripture indicates "Prajñā" (Wisdom) because it reveals that prajñā is produced from superior meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
This explicitly clarifies the intent of the training in concentration (*samādhi-śikṣā*), instructing one to cultivate concentration so as to induce prajñā;

therefore, according to this [view], this scripture is subsumed within the *sūtra-piṭaka*. According to the latter master, this scripture explicitly reveals the teaching on the training in concentration, demonstrating the practice of eliminating mental signs (*nimitta*).
The contemplation of emptiness causes one to aspire toward it by instructing in its cultivation, while the contemplation of existence causes one to weary of and abandon attachment.

Furthermore, it extinguishes false conceptualization through the gate of emptiness and gives rise to the true mind through the contemplation of existence. By inducing supreme *prajñā* through these two contemplations, the title is designated as "Prajñā.

Moreover, the cultivation of concentration and wisdom necessarily involves the abandonment of killing and other evils, thereby also encompassing the training in ethical discipline (*śīla*). Thus, [it is called] "Prajñāpāramitā."
Although this sutra fully reveals the three trainings, it primarily elucidates the training in concentration while incidentally revealing the trainings in ethical discipline and wisdom;
because it is based on the primary [training] rather than being incidental, it is not a general collection but is specifically subsumed within the Sūtra Piṭaka.
*Commentary on the Benevolent Kings’ Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra for Protecting the State: The Faheng Draft*, Scroll One;
*Phonetic Transcriptions for the Notes on the Benevolent Kings Sūtra*.

*Ki-yang* (Note: These two characters, *ki* and *yang*, are the radical components; they are pronounced with the third tone). *Mǐ-duō* (The first character is pronounced as *bì*). *Yáng* (Pronounced as *yú-liàng*). *Huàn* (Pronounced as *huàn*).
Guān (also pronounced huàn). Guàn (cut by gǔ huàn). Jūn (cut by jū yún; a species of deer). Jìng (pronounced jìng; a pit). Shòu (cut by shū jiù; hunting in winter). Jí (cut by jù yǐ).
Bīnbīn (upper character: pǐ bīn; lower character: fāng wén). Juìng (gǔ huǐng). Zhì (zhé lǜ; meaning "to block"). Tuí (dù huí; vulgar form of 頽). Gòu (gǔ hòu).
Kǎi (cut by kǔ hǎi: to harmonize joyfully). Pú (cut by pǐ jué). Pǒu (cut by pǔ kǒu: to split). Chí (cut by zhí ní: a courtyard or terrace). Wǎng (cut by yú wǎng: to err; also written as kuáng).
Zhǎng (zhī liàng qiè). Sū (pinyin: sū). Zhá (zhāng gé qiè). Kuà (kǔ huà qiè; to leap across). Jùn (sī rùn qiè). Xī (xǔ yí qiè; the light of the sun).
*Commentary on the Benevolent Kings’ Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra for the Protection of the State: The Fa-heng Extracts*, Scroll Two.
Compiled by the Great Master Yu-rong, who translated the scriptures, verified their meanings, and extensively expounded upon the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Śāstras. [Commentary]:

Regarding the "Twelvefold Teachings" (*dvādaśāṅga-dharma-pravacana*), former masters have translated this as the "Twelve Divisions of the Scriptures. This term "divisions" (*aṅga*) contains both the sense of category and that of meaning.
There are two meanings: first, "volumes" (piṭaka); second, "categories" (nikāya). People of the world suspect there are twelve volumes.

Furthermore, the term "sūtra" is also used loosely for the *Kṣayamārga-sūtra* (or *Nidāna-sūtra*), making it difficult to distinguish between the general and the specific. Now, these are translated as the "Twelvefold Teachings" (*dvādaśāṅga-dharma-pravacana*).

"Fold" (*aṅga*) has the meaning of category, branch, and number. "Teaching" (*pravacana*) refers to instruction that admonishes against evil and teaches the cultivation of goodness; therefore, it is called [the Twelvefold Teaching].

The teaching and the body of the teaching are identical; they are divided and thus named "divided teachings" (*vibhāga-śāsana*). There are twelve categories of meaning, and because the branches and classifications differ, they are called the "twelvefold division of the teachings" (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*);
this is an explanation based on enumeration. Question: For what reason is the number exactly this, with neither increase nor decrease? Answer:

The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states that these are what should be heard by those capable of listening to the Dharma. They are taught universally for the three vehicles (*triyāna*) as a turning of the wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra-pravartana*).
The three cycles collectively explain the twelve aspects (*ākāra*) that articulate those teachings, thereby classifying them into twelve;
furthermore, because they serve to counteract the twelve links of existence (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), the Dharma is likewise divided into twelve, as explained in detail in the *Fayuan*.
[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "the sūtras and so forth": these demonstrate the distinctions in the characteristics of the twelve divisions of the teaching (*dvādaśāṅga-dharma-pravacana*).

The text is divided into two parts: first, the definition of their characteristics; second, their correlation with the sūtras. This can be understood according to the text. That which is capable of "conforming" (*kī*) is the sūtra (*sūtra*); the sūtra that is conformed to is called a "sūtra of conformity" (*sūtra-kī* or *sūtra-saṃvāda*).
[Commentary: Regarding "Geya" (Verses to be Chanted): the character *ying* (應) in the second tone means "to accord with" (*qiying*); in the first tone, it means "to harmonize" (*he*).

It signifies harmonizing the meaning of the prose (*changxing*) and harmonizing with the capacities of later audiences. "Geya" means song or praise; because the phrases within these verses are extremely beautiful and subtle, and because they sing and praise the Dharma, they are called "Verses to be Chanted" (*yingsong*).

[Commentary] Regarding "prediction" (*vyākaraṇa*): "prediction" (*vyā*) refers to verifying and cognizing; it is the discernment of various persons and phenomena through such verification and cognition. The essence of the prediction is precisely the act of distinguishing;
the prediction that distinguishes what is to be distinguished is termed "prediction" (*vyākaraṇa*).

[Commentary]: "Verses in measured lines" (geya) is the Sanskrit term *gāthā*, which is translated here as "verse. The *Abhidharmasamuccaya-vyākhyā* states that what is not in prose is called a "repeated verse" (*geya*).
A single line may form a verse, or two, three, four, five, or more lines; all such instances are verses in measured lines.
While one, two, or three lines are often obscure and difficult to understand, most sūtras manifest the characteristics of verses in measured lines through four lines or more.

The words and meanings of the sūtra can be chanted and can be praised; when one both chants and praises, it is called "chanting and praising" (*geya*), which is interpreted according to the *karmadhāraya* compound.
Furthermore, "chanting" (*ge*) refers to the Dharma that is chanted, while "praising" (*ya*) refers to the words that praise;

because one praises what has been chanted, it is called "chanting and praising. Master Ci'en stated: "The *geya* is the teaching itself, for it is solely that which expresses [the meaning]; thus, 'chanting and praising' is..."
This is because it refers to both the teaching and the principle.
[Commentary] "Spoken by oneself" (svayambhūta) refers to the Buddha himself; because these words and teachings were spoken by him personally, they are called "spoken by oneself.
[Commentary] Regarding "dependent origination" (nidāna), the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "In the city of Śrāvastī, there was a man who assisted birds in releasing them from captivity."
Having known this, the World-Honored One spoke these verses: "Do not disregard a small offense, thinking there will be no calamity;
though a drop of water is minute, it gradually fills a large vessel. This was spoken by way of citing this specific matter; the other two cases can be understood accordingly.
Because the teaching is initiated through these three conditions, it is called "dependent origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

[Commentary]: Regarding "Pariyāya" (Exemplification): "Pi" means comparison, analogy, or category; "yu" means to open up, to clarify, or to instruct. Thus, the analogy that clarifies is called "pariyāya.
Since the essence of the analogy is itself the illustration, it is termed "Pariyāya" (Exemplification).
[Commentary]: Regarding "original events" (*pūrvayoga*): according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, this term generally refers to the dharmas of both ordinary persons and sages in the past.
"Original" (*mūla*) refers to the temporal period of the past upon which [the narrative] relies; "events" (*vṛtta*) refers to the activities performed during that time.
Since the essence of the original world is itself the event, it is termed "original events. The two explanations regarding "birth stories" (*jātaka*) should be understood accordingly.

[Commentary: "Vaipulya" (Extensive): "Square" (*fang*) refers to the correctness of principle; "extensive" (*guang*) refers to its comprehensive inclusion. Because it is the extensiveness of the square principle, it is named "Vaipulya.

[Commentary: "Adbhutadharma" (Marvelous Teachings): "Marvelous" (*xi*) refers to extraordinary and unprecedented wondrous events. The teachings that explain these are the marvelous dharmas; thus, they are named "Adbhutadharma."
[Commentary]: Regarding the *Yogācārabhūmi* and other texts, the treatise itself explains:

"In these instances, the Blessed One himself extensively analyzed the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), and his noble disciples, having already perceived the traces of the Truth (*satyapada*), analyzed the essential nature of all phenomena based on their own realization without error;
such are called *mātṛkā*. As for the term 'circulation,' it signifies non-interruption. As for 'investigation' (*vicaya*):"
The meaning of "thorough investigation" (*parīkṣā*) involves a back-and-forth exchange of questions and answers in which the textual meaning remains uninterrupted.

Because it investigates and scrutinizes the nature (*svabhāva*), characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), and the essence of phenomena (*dharmatā*), it is called *vādānuśāsana*. *Abhidharma-mātṛkā* means "Root-Mother"; it is so named because it gives birth to wisdom, just as a mother gives birth to a child.

It is also called *abhidharma*, which means "counter-phenomena" (*prati-dharma*). In terms of its meaning, it is translated as "treatise" (*śāstra*), for it is a treatise that deliberates upon and analyzes the nature and characteristics of phenomena.
Because it deliberates upon profound meanings, it is called a *vāda* (treatise); thus, the essence of a *vāda* is precisely the *vādavāda*.

Among the twelve divisions of the teaching (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*), the *avadāna* (parable), *itivṛttaka* (historical narrative), and *jātaka* (birth stories) are interpreted as *tatpuruṣa* (dependent determinative compounds) when viewed in relation to the categorized teachings;

the remainder are all *karmadhāraya* (appositional determinative compounds). Regarding their inclusion within the two collections (*piṭaka*)—those of the Bodhisattvas and the Śrāvakas—they are present in both.
In the twenty-first section on the Exposition of Yoga (*Yogācārabhūmi-viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī*), its characteristics are fully set forth. Regarding its inclusion within the three preceding Piṭakas:

it is taught in the *Yoga* [treatises] that one portion of dependent origination belongs to the Vinaya Piṭaka, one portion of the treatises (*śāstra*) belongs to the Abhidharma Piṭaka, and the remaining ten portions belong to the Sūtra Piṭaka.
However, because the establishment of precepts based on specific events and the profound reasoning of debate each enter into their respective Piṭakas, they are not [separately categorized].

In the *Sūtras*, there are no other two divisions; the *Itivṛttaka* (Past Deeds), *Jātaka* (Birth Stories), and *Vaineyaka* (Disciplining) are also included, yet these are merely ancillary (*parivāra*) and not the essential nature (*svabhāva*). [Commentary:

Regarding the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and others, they were composed to transform those of indeterminate lineage among the Two Vehicles, causing them to study the One Vehicle. All [these works] function as...
Therefore, the Buddha speaks only of the One Vehicle (ekayāna) and not a second, the Solitary Realizer (pratyekabuddha), nor a third, the Śrāvaka.
Since the initial Great Vehicle is itself the One Vehicle, he speaks only of the One Vehicle to conceal the inferior and manifest the superior.

[Commentary: Regarding the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* and other texts, they speak of the "lineage of the superior vehicle" (*uttarayāna-gotra*) and the "lineage of the inferior vehicle" (*hīnayāna-gotra*), also termed the "nature of the Mahāyāna" and the "nature of the Hīnayāna," because of their distinction in terms of superiority and inferiority;
thus, they employ the general term [lineage] to refer specifically to these two and do not mention the "indeterminate lineage" (*aniyata-gotra*).

[Commentary: Regarding the various sūtras and śāstras, etc., according to the *Fahua shu* (Commentary on the Lotus Sūtra), the three meanings are identical because the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are collectively termed Hīnayāna;
the seven meanings differ because they are distinguished by the sheep, deer, and ox metaphors for the three vehicles. As for the identity of the three meanings:

the obstacles to be abandoned are the same, the principle to be realized is the same, and the provisional *pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha* (cessation through discernment) is the same. As for the difference of the seven meanings: first, the benefit...

1. The difference in dull or sharp faculties; 2. the difference in the two bases from which the Buddha himself emerged; 3. the difference in relying on the teachings to contemplate the principle; 4. the difference in contemplating the truths and dependent origination; 5.

the difference between attaining the fruit of once-returning and the fruit of non-returning; 6. the difference in the duration of time for refining the faculties; and 7. the difference in preaching the Dharma and manifesting supernatural powers.

[Commentary]: Regarding the four vehicles and five vehicles: the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* speaks of the nature of the four vehicles, namely the natures of the three vehicles and the nature of the human and celestial vehicles.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* speaks of the nature of the four vehicles, namely the fixed natures of the three vehicles and the unfixed nature.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* speaks of the nature of the five vehicles, namely the fixed natures of the three vehicles, the unfixed nature, and the human and celestial [natures].

Furthermore, there are four types of indeterminate lineage (*aniyata-gotra*): namely, the śrāvaka lineage, the pratyekabuddha lineage, the śrāvaka-bodhisattva lineage, and the pratyekabuddha-bodhisattva lineage, which possesses the natures of all three vehicles.
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "the sūtra elucidates equality," this refers specifically to Mahāyāna sūtras intended for Bodhisattvas;
however, since Mahāyāna sūtras generally apply to all vehicles (yānas), there are instances in the following text where those who attain the fruit of a Śrāvaka appear.

[Commentary: Regarding those who established "one period" (ekakāla) in antiquity: Bodhiruci established the teaching of one period as being like a single rain that has no differentiation, yet the moisture received differs according to the recipient.
Furthermore, there were ancient masters who established the teaching of two periods: first, the sudden (*tun*), and second, the gradual (*jian*).
The hermit Liu Qiu established the teaching of five periods; all such views have been refuted in the *Fayuan* (Garden of the Dharma).
[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "At first," etc., the meaning of the text concerning the teachings of the initial period consists of five parts: first, the place where the Dharma was preached;
second, the sentient beings who were the recipients [of the teaching]; third, the teaching that was able to reach them; fourth, the fact that this was a rare and marvelous occurrence;

and fifth, the sublation of meanings not yet fully understood. These may be understood according to the text. As for "Vārāṇasī," it is an error for the old name "Póluonà" (Varanasi). "Póluo" (Vāra) means "child."

Regarding "Kṣullakāśrama" (Little Hermitage), it means "the dwelling place of young seers. Because young seers dwelt here and practiced the path, they attained the five mundane supernormal powers (*abhijñā*);

thus, it is named the "Country of the Little Seers' Dwelling. Regarding "Ṛṣipatana" (The Fallen Seers), the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states that in the past, a king led his palace women to a mountain for recreation.
There, he played music and indulged his desires, commanding the women to dance while exposing their bodies. At that time—
There were five hundred ṛṣis who, while traveling upward by means of supernatural powers, lost those powers upon seeing [the Buddha] and fell to this place;
thus, the account of the Mṛgadāva is as described in the seventh fascicle of the *Xiyuji*. Based on its manifest characteristics, it was intended for those of gradualist disposition;

however, in the Mṛgadāva, the Wheel of the Four Truths was turned specifically for those setting out on the Śrāvaka vehicle. In reality, the principle [of this teaching] universally applies to the dispositions of other vehicles as well.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: When the Buddha preached the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths at the Deer Park, immeasurable sentient beings gave rise to the aspiration for the three vehicles, and immeasurable sentient beings attained the fruits of the three vehicles.

Yet, because there were further teachings of the second and third turnings of the wheel that could surpass those [of the first], and because those [subsequent teachings] were superior, it was therefore not yet of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*). Thus, there are twenty schools [of thought].
The polemical treatises of the Hīnayāna are named based on this; it is the foundation upon which all such polemical discourses rest.

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "the second period," etc., during the second period, for the sake of those who have set out to practice the Mahāyāna, he spoke of emptiness through intentional terminology (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*) to cause them to transcend signs.
He nevertheless addressed the Śrāvakas with the intent that they understand the meaning of this emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), so as to achieve [liberation].

In the discourse of those who follow the Dharma of the ignorant, it is taught in general terms that all phenomena (*dharma*) lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). This underlying intention (*abhiprāya*) specifically refers to the three types of non-nature (*tri-niḥsvabhāvatā*):

1. To manifest the non-nature of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-niḥsvabhāvatā*), it is said that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature, because the essential characteristics of both self (*ātman*) and phenomena (*dharma*) lack intrinsic nature. 2. To manifest the non-nature of arising (*utpatti-niḥsvabhāvatā*), it is said that all phenomena are unarisen.
Non-extinction refers to the fact that although phenomena arise through causes and conditions, they lack an inherent nature of spontaneous arising and ceasing.

Third, the revelation of the ultimate lack of self-nature (*paramārtha-niḥsvabhāvatā*) states that all phenomena are primordially quiescent and by nature in *nirvāṇa*. This means that the nature of all phenomena is primordially quiescent, transcending the clamor of birth and death;
it is by nature perfectly still because it lacks the nature of false attachment to birth and death. This is taught through the method of intentional concealment (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*).
Regarding those who turn the wheel of the sublime Dharma: it is said that within this [teaching], there are hidden intentions (*saṃdhāyabhāṣita*) that proclaim the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).

Furthermore, because there is a third-period teaching of the wheel of the Dharma concerning these three natures and emptiness (*śūnyatā*) that surpasses this one, and because that [third teaching] is superior, this [second wheel] remains of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*).
It was from this point that the polemical debates concerning emptiness, held by masters such as Bhāviveka and others, arose.

[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "the third period" and so forth: this refers to the teaching of the Dharma through explicit revelation for the sake of those who have set out to seek the three vehicles.

The subsequent mention of "the nature of lack of intrinsic nature" (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) serves to explain this passage. Based on the characteristic of explicit revelation, the three natures of lack of intrinsic nature are taught:

first, the explicit teaching of the nature of lack of intrinsic nature in terms of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-niḥsvabhāvatā*), stating that all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature. The term "nature" (*svabhāva*) mentioned above indicates the emptiness of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
The first "nature" (svabhāva) mentioned refers to the nature of the parikalpita (imagined), which is characterized by non-existence;

thus, it reveals the lack of intrinsic nature in terms of arising (*utpatti-niḥsvabhāvatā*), stating that all phenomena are neither born nor extinguished. The second "nature" mentioned reveals the absence of an inherent nature of spontaneous arising;

the third "nature" mentioned reveals the presence of a nature arising from conditions. The third [nature] reveals the ultimate lack of intrinsic nature (*paramārtha-niḥsvabhāvatā*), stating that all phenomena are fundamentally...

Regarding the phrase "coming to rest in the nature of quiescent *parinirvāṇa*," the first mention of "nature" (*svabhāva*) reveals that, in terms of the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), there is no such nature as that which is falsely grasped by the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).

The second mention of "nature" reveals the existence of the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), because it clarifies that this differs from the meaning of the three natures taught with intentional ambiguity (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*) during the second period.
Thus, the Sūtra repeats the term "naturelessness" (*niḥsvabhāvatā*); the second instance of the word "nature" is an explicit teaching.
This is precisely the essential nature of the three non-natures.
[Commentary] Regarding those belonging to the various sūtras, as stated in the *Fayuan*: "The Āgamas and so forth constitute the teachings of the first period;

the various sūtras expounding emptiness constitute the teachings of the second period, because they use implicit language to state in general that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature. Thus, the *Avataṃsaka*...

The *Saṃdhinirmocana*, the *Vijñaptimātra* teachings, and others constitute the third period, because they explain the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) through the aspect of explicit manifestation, teaching the path of the Middle Way that is neither empty nor existent.
Regarding the sequence of these three periods: since beginningless time, ordinary beings have been deludedly attached to a self and have failed to realize its non-existence;
thus, submerged in the river of craving and wandering in the ocean of ignorance, the Buddha first taught the Four [Noble Truths].
The Wheel of the Dharma was taught to make known that the self is empty and that there is only the Dharma.

When Kauṇḍinya and others first attained the Path, they heard the teaching that "all selves are empty" and consequently clung to all phenomena as being truly existent. Clinging to the lesser fruit, they did not seek the Great State.
As a skillful means, the Buddha further taught the emptiness of phenomena to destroy their remaining attachment to existence; therefore, he spoke [of this] at a subsequent time.

In such statements as "Prajñāpāramitā," it is taught that the intrinsic nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena is entirely non-existent; yet, Subhūti and others possess a profound inclination toward existence.

Upon hearing these implicit teachings on the emptiness of phenomena, they might then negate the nature and characteristics of all phenomena, asserting that they are utterly non-existent. [They would then ask: "What is there to be cultivated? What is there to be abandoned?

To eliminate this [misconception], the Buddha further taught the doctrines of *vijñaptimātra* (consciousness-only) and the three natures (*trisvabhāva*). Those such as Paramārthasamudgata then gained faith [in this teaching].

In understanding and practicing the cultivation [of the path], one simultaneously discards both the ignorance regarding the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (the imagined nature) and the [clinging to] dharmas and self;
yet, one maintains both the *paratantra-svabhāva* (the dependent nature) and the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (the perfected nature), illuminating both the ultimate and conventional truths.

To speak at length, for those who enter the path gradually according to principle and capacity, the Great arises from the Small, resulting in three stages and a sequence of teachings. If one were to enter the path not gradually, then the Great [would arise directly].
It does not arise from the small [vehicle], for there are no three periods; among the various teachings, the *sudden* (*tun*) and the *gradual* (*jian*) are respectively one and the same.

Yet, within the sudden and gradual methods, there are no distinct teaching-gates (*dharma-mukha*), as they are taught according to what is beneficial within each specific assembly. Thus, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* was preached when śrāvakas were present in the assembly;
in the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra*, there are likewise śrāvakas who resolve upon bodhicitta; and in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, there are eight world-systems [who do so].

Since there are not just one but many such passages in various sutras—such as "sentient beings as numerous as motes of dust resolve their minds on Bodhi"—the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* also reaches those of sudden enlightenment, and the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* also reaches those of gradual enlightenment. Depending on which assembly or which single section one follows, both the sudden and the gradual are universally encompassed.
This classification of the three periods of teaching is based on the attainment of the fruit; however, if one speaks in terms of the human and celestial realms, there are four periods.

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "this sutra now," as explained below in the sutra itself, it first teaches for the sake of bodhisattvas the protection of the Buddha-fruit, the protection of bodhisattva practices, and the protection of sentient beings;

subsequently, it teaches for the sake of various kings the methods for protecting the state, and so forth, extensively explaining throughout the various chapters that there are dharma-gates for realization and awakening belonging to the three vehicles, due to the differences in the capacities of those beings—whether they possess the roots of the Great Vehicle, the Small Vehicle, or the Sudden [Vehicle].
Because they gradually differ, this sutra of the Mahāyāna is primarily taught for those of great capacity;

its exposition of the two types of protection (*saṃvara*) and the meaning of *prajñā* also extends to the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), as it is simultaneously taught for the small vehicle within Mahāyāna sutras. Furthermore, there are two categories of Mahāyāna root-nature:
