[Commentary] First, regarding the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*): knowing the exhaustion of the truth of suffering up to the cultivation of the truth of the path is called the knowledge of exhaustion.
Having attained the knowledge of the fruit, because all afflictions will never again arise, one is further able to realize the principle of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpādajñāna*).
Possessing these two meanings, it is called the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*).

[Commentary: Regarding "those of dull faculties" and so forth, according to the *Abhidharmakośa*, there are three kinds of regression (*parihāṇi*): first, regression from what has already been attained, because one regresses from the various meritorious qualities and dharmas already realized;
second, regression from what has not yet been attained, because one has not yet realized superior meritorious qualities.

Because there is regression, there is "regression from enjoyment" (*parihāṇi-vihāra*); that is, when one wishes to enjoy among the various merits already realized, they do not manifest before one, and thus it is called "regression.
For a Buddha, there is only the latter one—namely, regression from enjoyment—because even though he possesses all virtues, they cannot manifest simultaneously and instantaneously.
An Arhat of sharp faculties possesses both the middle and the latter two types of regression.
Because those with sharp faculties have no falling away from what has already been attained, whereas Arhats with dull faculties possess all three types of falling away.

[Commentary] Regarding the second volume of the *Xianyang lun* (Exposition of the Manifest), it states: "Dharma-knowledge, subsequent knowledge, knowledge of others' minds, conventional knowledge, knowledge of suffering, knowledge of origin, knowledge of cessation, knowledge of the path, knowledge of exhaustion, and knowledge of non-arising."

[Commentary]: "One who has completed what was to be done" (kṛtakṛtya) refers to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, where it is said that having performed what was to be performed and having accomplished what was to be accomplished means one has already departed from suffering and its origin;

this is called "having performed what was to be performed. Having fully perfected the sublime qualities of the Dharma of cessation and the path is called "having accomplished what was to be accomplished."

[Commentary: Regarding wisdom that possesses both the preparatory (*prayoga*) and fundamental (*mūla*) stages: prior to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), when training in this contemplation, it consists solely of contaminated (*sāsrava*) preparatory wisdom.
Once one has entered the noble state (*ārya-avasthā*) and proceeds to cultivate it further, it is also preparatory wisdom, yet it is now both contaminated and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).

This preparatory wisdom universally contemplates the objects of the conventional and ultimate truths, as well as the provisional and real natures; however, fundamental wisdom is exclusively uncontaminated.
Illuminating the realm of ultimate truth, one contemplates that which is real as being neither false nor provisional; the general designation for both the provisional and the real is "dharmas.

This contemplating wisdom derives its name from its object, and thus the contemplation of the provisional and the real among dharmas is called the "contemplation of the provisional and the real of dharmas" (dharmaprajñapti-satyāsatya-vipaśyanā).

[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "the conventional and real contemplations of sensation (*vedanā*)": there are five types of sensation—sensation of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-vedanā*), associated sensation (*samprayukta-vedanā*), objective sensation (*ālambana-vedanā*), karmic sensation (*karman-vedanā*), and resultant sensation (*phala-vedanā*).
These five are all termed "sensation" because they follow one another according to their respective categories.

Because the intrinsic nature of sensation and its associated dharmas experience (*anubhavanti*) objects that are agreeable, disagreeable, or neutral, greed, hatred, and delusion arise; through these, karma is performed and results are received, such that birth and death (*saṃsāra*) do not cease. Therefore, the Tathāgata...
The instruction for the disciple to contemplate the conventional and the real nature of sensation is called "the contemplation of the conventional and real nature of sensation.

The remaining [contemplations] are explained by analogy with what precedes. [Commentary: Regarding the phrase "the self-nature of all phenomena," etc., this explains the reason for the name of the contemplation. All phenomena are by nature beyond verbal expression;
yet sentient beings, lacking wisdom, give rise to deluded and inverted minds, generating arbitrary attachments. Based on expressive names, they falsely calculate and cling to [the objects].

Based on the meanings expressed, one conceives of the designating names; through this conceptual clinging, greed arises toward what is agreeable to the mind, hatred arises toward what is disagreeable, and delusion arises toward what is neither agreeable nor disagreeable.
Driven by these three poisons, one performs karma such as merit-making, which leads to the cycle of birth and death.
Since beginningless time, false conceptualizations have been habituated; by the power of this habituation, they continue in succession, giving rise to rebirth.

Death is endless; therefore, in order to cause sentient beings to sever the root of birth and death, he teaches them to observe that expressive names are merely provisional designations (*prajñapti*).

Since sounds are established based on sound, he further demonstrates that they are illusory and unreal because they depend on others; thus, they are called "provisional. Since the meaning is already provisional, the name itself is also provisional.
Within these names, the true nature (*dharmatā*) is precisely the essence of *tathatā* (suchness); because it is not false or deceptive, it is said to be "real."

Contemplating this is called "the contemplation of the provisional as real. Another interpretation is that it is the "contemplation of the provisional and the real," wherein one observes names as being both provisional and real.

Through such critical observation, one knows that names are merely provisional; thus, one should abandon provisional names and proceed toward the true reality (as explained at length in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*).
[Commentary]: Regarding the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, its commentary on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* lists one thousand two hundred and fifty members of the assembly of śrāvakas;

most of these are bodhisattvas manifesting as śrāvakas. By analogy with that case, these [members] are likewise bodhisattvas. Therefore, they fully cultivate these three contemplations of the provisional and the real.
Now, another interpretation states: the *Prajñāpāramitā* and other sūtras teach the three contemplations of the provisional and the real as Mahāyāna teachings.

The Middle Way encompasses the three vehicles, causing each to practice so as to attain the fruit of their own respective vehicle. Specifically, those of the Mahāyāna rely on the contemplation of the two emptinesses (*dvividha-śūnyatā*), while the Śrāvakas of the Hīnayāna rely on the contemplation of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).
Each observes phenomena and sensations, which are termed "objects" (*viṣaya*); these are distinguished by their depth and shallowness.

Consequently, there is a difference between attaining the fruits of the noble ones (*ārya*) in the Great and Small Vehicles, depending on whether one has completely severed the obstacles. Therefore, this sutra speaks of the three types of Arhats—those who are conventionally real and those who are substantially real.
The contemplations are all fully accomplished.

[Commentary: Regarding the contemplation of the three gates of emptiness: "emptiness" refers to the three natures being devoid of self and what belongs to self, which is termed the "three emptinesses.

"Gate" (mukha) carries the meaning of entering and exiting without obstruction; because these contemplative practices serve as the gate, they constitute the gate for exiting suffering and entering bliss.
This contemplation is called the "Contemplation of the Gates. When practicing this contemplation, one takes the three objects as its focal points;

because it advances through preparatory application (*prayoga*) to remedy obstructing defilements, it is called the "Contemplation of the Three Gates of Emptiness" (*trīṇi śūnyatā-dvārāṇi*). This very contemplative practice has three names in total:

first, it is called the "Contemplation of the Three Gates of Emptiness" because it encompasses both the tainted (*sāsrava*) and untainted (*anāsrava*), as well as both meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and non-concentrated states, by means of the three types of wisdom—those of hearing, reflection, and cultivation (*śruta-mayī*, *cintā-mayī*, and *bhāvanā-mayī* prajñā).

Their substance consists of two [factors] and they are named three; the gates of liberation (*vimokṣamukha*) are exclusively concentration and not distraction, and are exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*), because "liberation" carries the meaning of turning one's back [to defilements].
The three names correspond to the three samādhis; they are exclusively concentration and not distraction, and they are both tainted and untainted.
Next, citing the three treatises, the three names are explained in their respective order.

[Commentary: Regarding the *Abhidharmakośa*, it contemplates the Four Noble Truths through sixteen aspects (*ākāra*). For the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), there are four aspects: impermanence (*anitya*), suffering (*duḥkha*), emptiness (*śūnya*), and non-self (*anātman*). For the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*), there are four aspects:

cause (*hetu*), origination (*samudaya*), production (*prabhava*), and condition (*pratyaya*). For the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*), there are four aspects: cessation (*nirodha*), tranquility (*śānta*), excellence (*praṇīta*), and renunciation (*niḥsaraṇa*).

For the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*), there are four aspects: path (*mārga*), correctness (*nyāya*), practice (*pratipad*), and deliverance (*nairyāṇika*). By means of these Four Noble Truths, all phenomena (*dharma*) are subsumed. Now...
Contemplating the Four Truths through these three contemplations is precisely the comprehensive contemplation of all phenomena.

Cultivating and increasing these modes of practice involves the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and meditation, which encompass the sixteen aspects within these three contemplations, as can be understood from the commentary.

[Commentary: Regarding the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* and other texts, the characteristics of birth, aging, and death are not mentioned because they do not invariably exist; rather, they are observed in relation to the three objects—parikalpita (the imagined), pariniṣpanna (the perfected), and paratantra (the dependent)—respectively.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "the Sarvāstivādins and others," this clarifies that for those in the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), one also includes the preceding stages; based on the state of perfection, there are a total of eighty-nine grades of conditioned merit (*saṃskṛta-guṇa*). These consist of:
the abandonment of the eight categories of intellectually acquired afflictions (*parikalpita-kleśa*) under the four truths during the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*);

and the abandonment of the eighty-one grades of innate afflictions (*sahaja-kleśa*) across the nine stages during the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*). All of these constitute the paths capable of such abandonment.

Regarding conditioned virtues, those realized by the Path consist of the unconditioned analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*); according to the capacity of the realizing path, there are likewise eighty-nine grades of unconditioned merit.
[Sūtra]: As for "bhikṣuṇī," the *Caturvargika-vinaya* states that the Buddha’s maternal aunt, Mahāprajāpatī, together with five...
One hundred Śākya women approached the World-Honored One seeking to go forth [into the religious life], but the Tathāgata did not grant their request.

Later, on another occasion, the maternal aunt and five hundred Śākya women shaved their own heads, each donned a kāṣāya robe, and went to the Jeta Grove Monastery in Śrāvastī, standing outside the gate. When Ānanda saw them, he immediately went to inquire about them. At that time, they—
When they had fully explained their desire to seek ordination and receive the full precepts (*upasampadā*), the World-Honored One did not grant permission.
Ānanda said to them, "Wait at the outer gate; I shall go to the Buddha on your behalf to request it. At that time, Ānanda, having prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Excellent, World-Honored One! I pray that you will allow women to leave the household life within the Buddha-dharma and receive the full precepts."
He said to Ānanda, "Stop, do not speak such words. If you allow women to go forth in the Buddha-dharma and receive the full precepts, it will cause the Buddha-dharma to be unable to endure for long.
For example, if an elder has few sons and many daughters, one knows that his family will gradually decline.
In the same way, Ānanda, if women are allowed to go forth and receive the full precepts, then—"
"The Buddha-dharma will not endure for long; it will be destroyed immediately, like a fine rice field struck by frost and hail.
The ordination of women is likewise. (This was a direct request to the Buddha, though not detailed. Ānanda said to the Buddha: "Mahāprajāpatī has been kind to the Buddha.
After his mother passed away, she nursed the World-Honored One and raised him until he grew up. The Buddha told Ānanda: "So it is, so it is."
She has been kind to me, and I too have been greatly kind to Mahāprajāpatī.
If there is anyone who, through her, attains refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha; upholds the five precepts; understands the Dharma of the Four Truths without doubt;
and attains the fruit of Srotāpanna—thereby severing all evil destinies, entering the right path, and reaching the end of suffering—it is because of her. Thus it is.
The kindness of such a person is difficult to repay; it cannot be repaid through clothing, food, bedding, seating, requisites, or medicine.
Because I have appeared in the world, I have caused Mahāprajāpatī to receive the Three Refuges and even to attain entry into the Right Path;
it is just like this. (This debt of gratitude was not permitted by the Buddha. Ānanda said to the Buddha: "Women [have emerged] within the Buddha-dharma..."
"Can one receive the precepts at home and attain the fruit of *srotāpanna* up to the fruit of *arhat*? The Buddha said, "It is possible.

Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, "If women, within the Buddha-dharma, may go forth and receive the precepts and attain the fruits such as *srotāpanna*, I pray that you will permit them to go forth and receive the precepts.

(This is called a request for the entire assembly to attain the Way. Elsewhere, there is also a passage where Ānanda asks the Buddha about the fourfold assembly of disciples belonging to past Buddhas.)

The Buddha replied, "Yes. Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, "I only pray that the World-Honored One will ordain my maternal aunt so that she may achieve accomplishment within the fourfold assembly.

The Buddha told Ānanda, "Now, for the sake of women, I shall establish eight rules to be observed for as long as life lasts, which must not be transgressed. If one can practice them, this constitutes receiving the precepts.
What are these eight? First, even a bhikṣuṇī who is a hundred years old, upon seeing a newly ordained bhikṣu, should rise to greet him, escort him, and pay him due respect."

Prostrating and arranging seats for them—this rule should be respected, honored, and praised; as long as one lives, it must not be transgressed (the fifteen characters above apply to all subsequent items).

Second, a bhikṣuṇī should not revile a bhikṣu, nor should she scold him, nor should she slander him by saying that he has broken his precepts, broken his views, or broken his deportment. Third, a bhikṣuṇī should not [act] for a bhikṣu...

1. One who has performed an act of formal accusation (*ukkhepana*), one who has performed an act of calling to mind (*sativinaya*), or one who has performed an act of self-exhortation (*pārivāsika*) should not be obstructed;

yet, if they obstruct the search for an offense, obstruct the *poṣadha*, or obstruct the *pravāraṇā*, they should be rebuked by the bhikṣus. 2. A *śikṣamāṇā* (here translated as "one in correct training") who, having completed her training in the precepts, requests the full ordination (*upasampadā*) from the community of bhikṣus.
3. A bhikṣuṇī who has committed a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense should remain before both communities (*ubhayasaṃgha*).
1. Within the Saṃgha, one practices *mānatva* for half a month (*Sudarsana-vinaya-śāstra* explains that this means "to subdue arrogance," and it is also termed "lowering the mind").

2. A bhikṣuṇī must once every half-month request instruction from the Saṃgha. 3. A bhikṣuṇī should not observe the summer retreat (*varṣāvāsa*) in a place where there is no Saṃgha, fearing that in the event of difficulties there would be no one to provide protection or assistance. 4. When a bhikṣuṇī has completed the summer retreat...
One should go before the community of bhikṣus and request the three matters of self-examination regarding offenses seen, heard, or suspected.
Thus, Ānanda, I now declare these eight rules that must not be transgressed; if a woman can practice them, she receives the precepts.
It is like a person who, by establishing a bridge over a great body of water, is able to cross it. Having received these instructions, Ānanda went to his aunt...
The Mother said: "Women may receive ordination and leave the household life within the Buddha-dharma.
The World-Honored One has taught eight rules that women must not transgress; if they can practice these, it is equivalent to receiving the precepts.
He then spoke the eight matters as listed above. Mahāprajāpatī replied: "I and the five hundred Śākya women shall together receive them upon our heads."

It is as if a man or woman, young, pure, and well-adorned, were to have their head washed and anointed, and while standing in a hall, someone were to place various flower garlands upon their head; they would joyfully accept them with reverence.
In this same way, World-Honored One, you have taught these eight rules that must not be transgressed for women, and I, along with five hundred Śākya women, [accept them].
"People should with one mind joyfully receive this. At that time, Ānanda went to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself at his feet, and said to the Buddha:
"The eight rules not to be transgressed have already been spoken for women; having heard them, they joyfully received them with their heads bowed.
The Buddha told Ānanda: "If women had not gone forth from home into the Buddha-dharma, the Buddha-dharma would have lasted for a thousand years."
Having heard that [the Buddha] would remain for five hundred years, Ānanda was displeased; harboring regret and distress in his heart, he wept with streaming tears.
He then prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him, and departed. As for whether the True Dharma will perish or not, there are two interpretations as is customary.
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "based on the four great vows," etc.: it refers to the vow to achieve unsurpassed bodhi and the vow to deliver boundless sentient beings.
Here, it is clarified that because this practitioner possesses that sought-after bodhi and those sentient beings (sattvas) to be delivered, they are called a *bodhisattva*.

This is a possessive compound (*bahuvrīhi*) formed by taking the name of the other [the object] in its entirety; furthermore, it is because this practitioner possesses the functional capacity for seeking bodhi and delivering sentient beings.

"Bodhi" and "sattva" are two functions that share the same basis in the substance of the five aggregates; therefore, they are called "bodhisattva. This is an example of the *dharmadhāraya* (possessive) compound based on a common substratum (*samānādhikaraṇa*).
[Commentary]:
"Sattva" means "valiant. Being courageous, fierce, and sharp, one does not shrink from long periods of time while seeking [enlightenment] in all places.

"Great Bodhi" (Mahābodhi) refers to the "Bodhisattva"; the former term [Bodhi] refers to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), while this [Bodhisattva] refers to the application of diligent practice (*vīrya-pratipatti*). These two are distinguished by their respective bases (*adhiṣṭhāna*).

[Commentary: "Bodhi" is precisely *prajñā* (wisdom), because it is the function of fundamental gnosis (*mūla-jñāna*) for severing [afflictions] and realizing [the truth]. "Sattva" refers to... [the capacity for awakening].

This is because it is the skillful application of subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*); by means of these two dharmas, one brings benefit and happiness to oneself and all sentient beings.

Therefore, the conventional designator is called a "Bodhisattva. Since both functions—enlightenment (*bodhi*) and being (*sattva*)—rely upon the single essence of wisdom, it is termed "Bodhisattva" through a *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound based on a common substratum.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "all *sattvas* who seek bodhi": since *sattvas* of the three vehicles each seek the bodhi of the fruit-stage of their own respective vehicle—being "bodhisattvas" (*bodhi-sattva*) because they seek awakening—they generally belong to all three vehicles.
To distinguish them from those of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*), the term "Mahāsattva" is added.
Nevertheless, various sutras and śāstras often designate those who practice the Mahāyāna specifically as "Bodhisattvas," based on their conduct.
Because they are superior, they receive a collective name; those who cultivate the Lesser Vehicle are specifically termed *pratyekabuddhas* and *śrāvakas*.

[Commentary] Regarding "expedient means" (*upāya*): to rescue and deliver sentient beings is called "direction" (*fang*); to cause others to attain peace is called "benefit" (*bian*); that which is the method for such benefit is termed "expedient means" (*fangbian*).

[Commentary: Regarding "the seventh stage and so forth," among the ten stages, in the first, second, third, and fourth stages, the preparatory (*prayoga*), fundamental (*maula*), and subsequent (*pṛṣṭha*) [wisdoms] arise sequentially.
In the fifth, sixth, and seventh stages, they arise both together and sequentially; even without preparatory effort, they still arise sequentially.
In the eighth, ninth, and tenth stages, they arise spontaneously and simultaneously.

[Commentary]: Those who have attained "compassion of identical essence" (samatā-karuṇā) are also said to have attained the "intentional state of regarding all sentient beings as identical to one's own body.
This means that Tathāgatas, Bodhisattvas of the ten stages, and others perceive all sentient beings as being like themselves;

because they have attained the perception of subsuming others into their own self, they see no sentient beings existing separately outside of their own bodies, and thus constantly deliver them. If, however, they were to see sentient beings as distinct from their own bodies...
Sentient beings, clinging to birth, become weary and thus cannot cross over; even if they do cross over, it is neither extensive nor constant.

[Commentary] Regarding "Manifesting Glory" (*Prakaraṇāryavācā*) and so forth: that text explains the name "Immeasurable" (*apramāṇa*) through four meanings: first, because its mode of understanding is vast; second, because its merit is immeasurable as that of the Great Brahma King;
third, because its fruition and virtue as a Tathāgata are immeasurable; and fourth, because its objects of focus (*ālambana*) are immeasurable.
"Because it is immeasurable.
[Commentary] Furthermore, the *Xianyang lun* and other texts state that sentient beings within the dharma-realm are generally categorized into three types:

first, for those who experience neither suffering nor pleasure, to unerringly bestow happiness is called "loving-kindness" (*maitrī*), which has non-hatred as its essence; second, for those who are suffering, to extract them from their pain is called "compassion" (*karuṇā*).

Non-harming (*avihiṃsā*) is its essence. Third, regarding those who possess happiness, to rejoice in their joy is called sympathetic joy (*muditā*). Its essence is the root of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) that is free from envy.
Furthermore, regarding those who possess suffering, because of their inferior merit, their physical forms are loathsome; thus, foolish people for the most part give rise to hatred toward them.
Regarding those who possess happiness, because of their merit, foolish people for the most part give rise to greed toward them. This [sympathetic joy] is the opposite of that.
Toward those who suffer, one should cultivate the thought of freedom from aversion; toward those who enjoy happiness, one should cultivate the thought of freedom from attachment;
and toward those beings who experience neither suffering nor pleasure, since there is no basis for either attachment or aversion, one should instead cultivate the thought of freedom from delusion.
Toward all sentient beings, one should abandon such uneven states of mind and give rise to impartial conduct, desiring that all beings remain far removed from all evils.

This is the aspect of equanimity (*upekṣā*). Regarding this aspect, a beginner who is by nature benevolent and virtuous, or possesses the power of past habituation, universally cultivates the four practices toward all sentient beings:
bestowing happiness, removing suffering, rejoicing with them, and comforting them, maintaining impartiality.
If one cannot do so, one should practice it gradually; regarding all sentient beings, one should conceive of them in seven categories, dividing kinship into three grades as follows:
The superior, middling, and inferior enemies are likewise divided into three categories—namely, superior, middling, and inferior—as well as those who are neutral, meaning neither friends nor enemies.

Once these seven classes have been established, with the superior friend at the beginning and the superior enemy at the end, and the neutral party in the middle, one should train gradually from the easy to the difficult. Furthermore, pleasant things are also divided into three grades.
That is to say: first, those of superior intimacy are given superior happiness; those of middling intimacy are given middling happiness;
and those of inferior intimacy are given inferior happiness. Next, those of middling intimacy are given superior happiness;

those of inferior intimacy are given middling happiness; and those of neutral status are given inferior happiness. This continues until the seventh round, when even a superior enemy is given superior happiness.
One cultivates loving-kindness by bestowing medium-grade happiness upon superior-grade relatives and inferior-grade happiness upon medium-grade relatives;

thus, one practices loving-kindness toward all sentient beings with equal skillful means in granting them happiness. Compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity are likewise to be understood according to the preceding explanation.

Furthermore, the aspect of equanimity (*upekṣā*) is also divided into three grades—superior, medium, and inferior—taking those sentient beings who were previously categorized as neutral among the seven grades as its object.
First, because it is easiest to arouse equanimity (*upekṣā*), one proceeds from the easy to the difficult:
a minor friend is taken as the second, a minor enemy as the third, a middling friend as the fourth, and so on up to a major enemy as the seventh.

One arouses the three grades of equanimity by proceeding from the easy to the difficult, moving from the beginning toward the end according to the method described above. There are three distinctions regarding the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*).

First, taking sentient beings as the object, one forms the perception of them as sentient beings. Second, taking dharmas as the object, one does not perceive sentient beings but forms the perception of the three categories of phenomena (triskandha-dharma).
Third, being without an object, one is free from discursive thought regarding all phenomena and forms the perception of suchness; this is called "objectless" (anālambana).

Furthermore, as the contemplative practice gradually becomes superior, one contemplates the three objects individually. Regarding the object of dharmas, one takes the teachings as the object, giving rise to the perception that sentient beings do not exist.

Question: Since the latter two types of objects [of these meditative states] do not take sentient beings as their object, and because they cannot bestow happiness or extract suffering [from them], how can they be called "compassion" (*karuṇā*) and so forth?

Answer: Although these latter two arise without taking sentient beings as their focal point, when one takes True Suchness (*tathatā*) as the object through the conditions of non-hatred (*avyāpāda*), non-injury (*avihiṃsā*), and so forth—specifically through non-hatred, non-anger, non-injury, and non-harming—they are designated as such.

Because they are equal, they are termed "loving-kindness" and so forth; that is, taking the teachings or the wish-fulfilling [mind] as their object, they function to extract suffering from and bestow happiness upon all sentient beings.
If one does not awaken to the teachings nor realize the principle of *tathatā* (suchness), one's benefit for beings will be narrow and inferior rather than vast and great.

[Commentary: Regarding the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* and other texts, its essence consists of the mental states (*cittakalāpa*) associated with the four aggregates that serve as the companions for the elicitation of superior concentration and wisdom;
its retinue consists of the five aggregates, because concentration, the path, and ethical discipline constitute the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "Loving-kindness alone," etc., the question is asked: What is the distinction between this [loving-kindness] and Great Loving-kindness, Great Compassion, Great Sympathetic Joy, and Great Equanimity?

The answer is: According to the *Fahua shu* (Commentary on the Lotus Sutra), there are four points of difference. 1. That [Great Compassion, etc. is exclusively a contemplation of reality (*bhūta-darśana*) and arises only from a Buddha;

this [loving-kindness] encompasses both the conventional and the real, and arises in both ordinary beings and sages. 2. That [Great Compassion, etc. takes as its object sentient beings within the three realms; this [loving-kindness] takes as its object an indeterminate realm. 3. That [Great Compassion, etc. is accompanied by non-delusion (*amoha*); this [loving-kindness] may or may not be accompanied by non-delusion.
For this reason, those four are exclusively uncommon virtues, whereas these are common virtues because they pertain to all three vehicles.

*Commentary on the Benevolent Kings’ Sūtra for the Protection of the State (Renwang Huguo Banruo Jing Shu):

Faheng’s Extracts, Scroll Three.* Compiled by the Great Master Yurong, who translated the scriptures, verified their meanings, and extensively expounded upon the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Abhidharma. [Commentary]:

Regarding "the realization and clear verification through the wisdom of recollecting past lives" (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñānasākṣātkriyāvidhi*): "wisdom-realization" (*jñānasākṣātkriyā*) refers to the name given to the sovereign mastery of noble wisdom that realizes and clearly mirrors [reality].
"Clear knowledge" (vidyā) is the proof; "knowledge of proof" (vidyā-sākṣātkriyā-jñāna) is the recollection that follows. Regarding "recollection" (anusmṛti):

it is the clear mindfulness and non-forgetfulness of past events as they are recalled; the recollection that is followed is called "recollection," or the recollection that can follow is called "recollection.

Alternatively, that which is followed is the recollection, and that which follows is the knowledge; because one knows the past by following the recollection, that which is followed is the recollection.

Furthermore, because this knowledge of realization (jñānasākṣātkriyā) is proximate to mindfulness (smṛti), it is called "knowledge of realization through recollection" (*anusmṛtijñānasākṣātkriyā*); this is an etymological explanation based on its proximity [to mindfulness].
This knowledge is named after its object; thus, it is the "knowledge of realization through recollection of past lives" (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñānasākṣātkriyā*).

As for "death and rebirth" (*cyutyupapāda*), because one is able to know all sentient beings as they die here and are born there, experiencing various retributions—whether good or foul—it is called the "knowledge of death and rebirth" (*cyutyupapādajñāna*).
"Knowledge" (*vidyā*) refers to the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*). "Outflows" are defined as the faults of the afflictions (*kleśa*);

because the noble path (*āryamārga*) exhausts those outflowing phenomena, the nature of cessation (*nirodhasvabhāva*) manifested thereby is called the "exhaustion of outflows. Because this knowledge realizes the principle of that exhaustion of outflows, it is the "knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows" (*āsravakṣayajñāna*).
Alternatively, this knowledge clearly discerns whether the defiled phenomena of outflows in oneself and others have been exhausted or not yet exhausted.

It is also the realization through the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya-jñāna-sākṣātkriyā*). The three knowledges (*tisro vidyāḥ*) are established as such because they respectively cognize the objects of the three periods of time—past, future, and present—and thereby counteract the darkness of ignorance regarding these three temporal limits. Among the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍ-abhijñā*), why are three specifically designated as the "three knowledges"?

[Question: Since the divine eye power (*divya-cakṣur-abhijñā*) is a wisdom associated with visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna-samprayukta-prajñā*) that takes present objects as its domain, how can it [be considered a knowledge]?

This knowledge of death and rebirth (*cyutyupapādajñāna*) is the realization that clearly knows future events. It is answered: by means of the supernormal power of the divine eye (*divyacakṣurabhijñā*), one observes how sentient beings die here and are born there;
from this, the knowledge of death and rebirth is induced, whereby one clearly knows how sentient beings of the five destinies in future lives die here and are born there.
Since it now returns to what induces it, they are considered identical in nature.

[Commentary]: Regarding the essence of the three types of clear knowledge (*vidyā*): among the ten knowledges (*jñāna*) in the *Abhidharmakośa*, the first, conventional knowledge (*saṃvṛti-jñāna*), is exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*).

The eighth, the knowledge of others' minds (*paracitta-jñāna*), is both contaminated and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*). The remaining eight knowledges are all uncontaminated. Of these, the first two types of clear knowledge take conventional phenomena as their objects;

thus, they are conventional knowledge and are exclusively contaminated. As for the clear knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-vidyā*), it consists of the knowledges of the four noble truths...

The knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) have six knowledges as their essence. Because they realize the principles of the various truths and possess the nature of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*), they are exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*) knowledges.
However, within the context of objective observation, when they take the principles of the four truths as their objects, they may be either tainted or untainted.

Alternatively, when one knows that the outflows of one's own afflictions are exhausted, and that within this body of exhausted outflows there exist these ten knowledges as the clear evidence of the realized realm, this is termed the "clear vision of the exhaustion of outflows" (*āsravakṣayajñānadarśana*). Taken collectively, [this constitutes the tenth power].

The ten knowledges (*jñāna*) constitute its essence, encompassing both the outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*) and the outflow-free (*anāsrava*). [Commentary]: Regarding the supernormal power of the realization of the knowledge of the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhiviṣayajñānasākṣātkriyābhijñā*): "psychic power" (*ṛddhi*) refers to the quality of miraculous and wondrous transformation, which has meditative concentration (*samādhi*) as its essence.

"Bases" (*viṣaya*) refers to the objects—the things transformed. The objects transformed by psychic power are called the "bases of psychic power" (*ṛddhiviṣaya*), or alternatively, it may refer to the objects themselves that are transformed.
That which can be measured is called "divine" (*divya*); this "divine" is the objective sphere, hence it is named the "divine sphere" (*ṛddhiviṣaya*).

The noble wisdom that functions with mastery, realizing and penetrating without obstruction, is called the "supernormal power of realization through wisdom" (*jñānasākṣātkriyābhijñā*). This wisdom—the supernormal power of realization—is the wisdom of the divine sphere; thus, it is called the "supernormal power of realization through wisdom regarding the divine sphere" (*ṛddhivisayajñānasākṣātkriyābhijñā*).

Regarding the "divine eye" (*divyacakṣus*): "divine" refers to the sentient beings of the celestial realms within the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), whose pure physical sense faculties give rise to consciousness.
That which illuminates objects is called the "eye"; that which relies upon the divine eye is called the "divine eye" (*divyacakṣus*), referring to that obtained as a karmic retribution (*vipākaja*).
As for that obtained through cultivation (*bhāvanāja*), regarding the supernormal power of the body (*kāyavibhūti*) within the desire and form realms:

when a noble being (*ārya*) belonging to a certain class resides in the desire realm, by the power of cultivation, they cause the seeds of the eye-faculty (*cakṣurindriya*) belonging to a higher stage to arise as a manifest activity (*samudācāra*) within their own body, which belongs to a lower stage.

Although there are differences in the superior or inferior qualities of perceiving obstructed, subtle, distant, and other such forms—whether acquired as a result of karmic retribution (*vipākaja*) or through cultivation (*bhāvanāja*)—their essential nature is not distinct, for they both have the pure sense-faculties (*rūpīndriya*) as their substance.

It is by means of this that the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) gives rise to knowledge and realizes the supernormal power (*abhijñā*). The same applies to the supernormal power of the divine ear (*divyaśrotra*).

[Commentary]: If one proceeds from the perspective of the fundamental [knowledge] (*mūla*)—wherein it is known that the mind is not an object of knowledge and what is not mind is not mind—the subsequent mention of "preparatory application" (*prayoga*) serves as a contrast to clarify this term "fundamental.

This refers to the stage where cultivation has reached completion. Within this stage of perfected cultivation, one knows that the other's mind-king (*citta-rāja*), whether wholesome, defiled, or indeterminate, is not an object known by [one's own] mind;
likewise, the other's mental factors (*caitasika*), whether wholesome, defiled, or indeterminate, are not [objects known by one's own mind].

When this mental sovereign (*cittarāja*) practices preparatory application (*prayoga*), it contemplates the aggregate of mental states of other sentient beings—whether virtuous, afflicted, or neutral—and is thus designated as the supernormal power of knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna-abhijñā*);
its designation as the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-abhijñā*) is as explained in the commentary on the "Three Knowledges" (*traividya*).

[Commentary] Regarding the clarification of the five bodies: since the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) is specifically for the severing of hindrances and does not give rise to the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), it is the wisdom of the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) that constitutes the essence of the five supernormal powers.
The method for extracting their essential nature from the ten types of knowledge (*daśa-jñāna*) previously cited, as well as what is to be included or excluded, is as set forth in the commentary.

[Commentary: Only the four fundamental stages are relied upon because, in these four dhyāna fundamental grounds, concentration and wisdom are balanced and further enhanced, thereby enabling the manifestation of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
As for the four preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*), concentration and wisdom are not superior and thus it is difficult to manifest supernormal powers;
therefore, one does not rely upon them.

[Commentary]: Regarding the *Prakaraṇāryavācā* and other texts, the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*) have wisdom (*prajñā*) as their essential nature when considered in terms of their intrinsic character (*svabhāva*). When considered in terms of their induced nature (*ākṣepa-svabhāva*), they have both meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom as their nature.

When considered in terms of their associated nature (*saṃprayukta-svabhāva*), they have the four aggregates (*catuḥ-skandha*) within the mental complex that arises simultaneously with that wisdom as their nature; including their attendants (*parivāra*), they have the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) as their nature.

[Commentary] The thirty-seven [factors of enlightenment] are divided into seven stages. First, the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*): one contemplates the body, feelings, mind, and phenomena internally and externally.

Because they contemplate both self and others, they are termed "internal and external. This means contemplating the body as being like empty space; contemplating feelings as being neither internal nor external; contemplating the mind as being merely a name;
and contemplating phenomena as being ungraspable in terms of good or evil—this is called the Bodhisattva’s four [foundations of mindfulness].

Because mindfulness dwells through the observation [of objects], it is called "foundation of mindfulness" (*smṛtyupasthāna*). The foundation of mindfulness is itself the observation; thus, it is called the "observation-foundation of mindfulness.

Regarding these two—the foundations of mindfulness and the observations—they both have right exertion (*samyakprahāṇa*) as their essence. Their nature is that of capability, for they are able to abandon. Their substance is wisdom (*prajñā*), because right exertion universally stimulates and assists wisdom in abandoning.
Therefore, the name "right exertion" is established. That is to say: for unarisen unwholesome dharmas, one practices the abandonment of abandonment (*prahāṇaprahāṇa*); for unarisen unwholesome...

Dharmas that ought to be abandoned are said to be "abandoned" because they are prevented from arising through the power of diligence; this is called the abandonment of abandonment (*prahāṇa-prahāṇa*).
Regarding the abandonment of arisen unwholesome dharmas, one cultivates restraint (*saṃvara*); this method for extinguishing evil, consisting of rules and regulations, is called restraint.
Since restraint is itself abandonment, it is termed the abandonment of restraint (*saṃvara-prahāṇa*). Regarding unarisen wholesome dharmas, one cultivates their cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
Abandonment through the power of diligence consists of cultivating and increasing unarisen wholesome dharmas so that unwholesome ones do not arise;
this cultivation is called abandonment. Cultivating abandonment means guarding against the arising of unwholesome states once they have already arisen.

Through the power of diligence, one protects already arisen wholesome dharmas so that they further increase and unwholesome states do not arise; this protection is called abandonment. Guarding abandonment is...

The abandonment [of defilements] is called "abandonment through protection" (ārakṣa-prahāṇa). Regarding the three [types of abandonment], the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) have meditative concentration (*samādhi*) as their essence.
"Power" (*ṛddhi*) refers to the quality of miraculous and wondrous transformation; "base" (*pāda*) is that upon which the power relies. Thus, they are called "bases of power" (*ṛddhipāda*).

Because one attains the bases of power by taking the four factors—desire (*chanda*), effort (*vīrya*), mind (*citta*), and investigation (*mīmāṃsā*)—as causes, these four bases of power are termed the "four bases of psychic power. Therefore, in contrast [to the other types of abandonment], [this is designated as such].
The "Cloud of Dharma" refers to the performance of various miraculous feats through the power of perfected *samādhi*. It involves the cultivation of four practices:
desire, exertion, mind, and investigation. Regarding "desire for *samādhi*": it refers to attaining *samādhi* through the skillful means of earnest, intense longing and reverence.
Regarding "exertion for *samādhi*": it refers to touching [upon *samādhi*] through uninterrupted skillful means.

Regarding "one-pointedness of mind" (*cittaikāgratā*) and constant diligence without even a moment's interval, "mental samādhi" (*citta-samādhi*) refers to first cultivating meditative concentration (*samādhi*) to touch one-pointedness of mind.
Due to the power of having repeatedly cultivated the force of concentration in previous lives, the potential of those seeds increases.
By the power of these seeds, the mind spontaneously undergoes a transformation that accords with samādhi; it is for this reason [that it is so called].
One swiftly realizes one-pointedness of mind (inferior concentration is termed "mind," while superior concentration is termed *samādhi*). Regarding the *vipaśyanā-samādhi*:

through hearing the teachings, one internally discriminates within oneself and touches upon one-pointedness of mind (the wisdoms of hearing and reflection are termed *vipaśyanā*). Fourth, the five faculties (*indriya*); fifth, the five powers (*bala*):

these are called "faculties" because they give rise to various virtues, and they are called "powers" because they are superior and difficult to be overcome. Sixth, the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*).
The "factors of enlightenment" (*bodhipakṣa*) refer to the factors of the Noble Path; the meaning of being a "factor" is that they serve as the causes for enlightenment.

That which is called "tranquility" (*praśrabdhi*), the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states, has the nature of removing heaviness (*dausthulya*), harmonizing and refreshing body and mind, and providing functional capacity (*karmanyatā*).

Its function is to counteract lethargy (*styāna*) and to effect the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*). It is called "tranquility" because, by subduing the obstacles to meditative concentration, it causes the body that serves as the support...

Equanimity (*upekṣā*) is so called because it brings about a state of well-being. Its essence is precisely "equanimity of application" (*praśaṭha-upekṣā*). The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: What is equanimity of application?

It has the nature of causing the mind to abide in a state of evenness, rectitude, and effortlessness through the three roots of goodness and diligence; its function is to counteract restlessness (*auddhatya*) and to bring about tranquil abiding (*sthiti*).
That is to say, by means of diligence and the three roots of goodness, one counteracts restlessness and abides in a state of rectitude and tranquility; therefore, it is so named.

In order to distinguish it from equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*), it is called "equanimity of application" (*praśrabdhi-upekṣā*); the names of the others can be understood accordingly. Seventh, regarding the Eightfold Noble Path:

Right View (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*) and Right Thought (*samyak-saṃkalpa*) both have wisdom (*prajñā*) as their essential nature. One might ask: why is thought (*cetanā*) not taken as the essence of Right Thought?

The answer is that it is because Right Thought is capable of initiating speech to instruct and inform others; if it were not wisdom, nothing else would possess this capacity. Therefore, [it is defined as wisdom].
"Right reflection on the Dharma-cloud" has the meaning of instruction, because it establishes expedient means through the utterance of speech according to what has been realized.
"Right view" has the meaning of discernment, because it makes distinctions based on what was previously realized. As for "right speech" and so forth:
that which is produced by the absence of hatred and delusion is called right speech and right action; that which is produced by the absence of greed is [right livelihood]. In total:

Right livelihood is named as such because these three [precepts] prevent and ward off unwholesome physical actions; they are provisionally designated by the name "unmanifest form" (*avijñapti-rūpa*), taking form and volition as their essence.
The names of the others can be understood accordingly.
[Commentary: Therefore, although there are thirty-seven [factors], their essence consists of only ten. According to the Mahāyāna, these ten consist of nine dharmas as their essence.

Because it eliminates discursive thought (*vitarka*), the Abhidharma states that wisdom (*prajñā*) is able to produce speech and instruct others; therefore, it is called "right reflection" (*samyak-saṃkalpa*).

The rest is the same as in the *Abhidharmakośa*. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* says: "The factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*) are numerous, but the most excellent are thirty-seven. It further states:
"Based on the bodhisattva’s unimpeded analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), there is wondrous wisdom encompassed by skillful means regarding the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment."
The Dharma is understood as it truly is; nevertheless, there are five points of difference between the practice of the Mahāyāna and the Hīnayāna: first, the difference in seeking the fruit;

second, the difference in severing hindrances; third, the difference in the two types of death—the Hīnayāna practice exhausts *paricchinna-jarāmaraṇa* (death and rebirth within the realms of分段), while the Mahāyāna practice exhausts *pariṇāmi-jarāmaraṇa* (death and rebirth through transformation);
fourth, the difference in compassion and wisdom—the Mahāyāna practices out of compassion, whereas the Hīnayāna [practices] out of...
Because of wisdom, one cultivates the five beneficial practices (*pañca-kuśala-caryā*), which differ from the Great Vehicle’s two benefits in that the Lesser Vehicle emphasizes self-benefit.

[Commentary: Regarding the cultivation of the contemplations on the truths (*satya-vipaśyanā*): Bodhisattvas of the ten stages (*daśa-bhūmi*) cultivate the practices of the ten perfections (*daśa-pāramitā*) and traverse the contemplation of the two emptinesses (*dvaya-śūnyatā*).

However, for the purpose of subduing those of the Two Vehicles, they subsequently cultivate the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) and the truths in sequence during the fourth, fifth, and sixth stages.
Contemplation of Dependent Origination.
[Commentary] Regarding "discerning contemplation based on conditions," this refers to discerning the three contemplations based on the twelve links of dependent origination.

In the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, after first clarifying dependent origination, it subsequently states: "The bodhisattvas of this stage, by contemplating the aforementioned dependent origination, attain entry into emptiness and signlessness."
The Gate of Wishlessness (as cited in the Commentary). [Commentary]:

Regarding "vipāka" and so forth, the body consisting of the five aggregates of grasping (*pañcopādānaskandha*) is called the *vipākaphala* (ripened fruit). Self-harming and self-inflicted injury are termed the "māra of the aggregates.
The karma that can summon this is the *puruṣakārahetu* (human-effort cause). At the precise moment of relinquishing life, the five aggregates that exist at that time are designated as such.
Death and this fruit of death are named "fruits of human effort" (*puruṣakāra-phala*) based on their causes.

The existence at the moment of death (*maraṇabhava*) that inflicts harm upon itself is called the "demon of death" (*mṛtyu-māra*) or the "demon of the aggregates" (*skandha-māra*). The demon of death who delights in abiding and the demon of death who delights in the cessation of the aggregates are the two demons that mutually inflict harm upon one another.

[Commentary: As for "the essence is wisdom," the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) primarily take post-attainment wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) as their essence, because they take phenomena as objects.

Since the analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*) also penetrates correct wisdom (*samyagjñāna*) by realizing ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), it is attained partially in the first stage (*bhūmi*).
In the ninth stage, one spontaneously transcends obstacles and perfectly fulfills the fruit of Buddhahood.
[Commentary: Regarding the ten powers (*daśabala*) of the Buddha-fruit, they are called "powers" (*bala*) because they have the sense of being able to crush enemies and the sense of being invincible.

It is said that there are ten powers of wisdom (*jñānabala*); since the essence of wisdom itself is power, it is termed "power of wisdom. There are ten such powers of wisdom, hence they are called the "ten powers of wisdom.

First is the power of knowing what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñānabala*): when cause and effect correspond to one another, it is termed "possible" (*sthāna*); if they do not correspond...
That which is called "the power of non-locus" (asthāna-jñāna-bala) is so named because it establishes the meaning of what is not a locus, the meaning of dependence, and the arising of meaning;
it is able to establish results as dependent and to give rise to various respective results. Regarding this, one correctly knows it; this is the second [power].

As for the power of knowledge regarding one's own karma (karma-svaka-jñāna-bala), it is the correct knowledge that all sentient beings each create their own karma and undergo the ripening of its results (vipāka-phala). Regarding this, one correctly knows it.

Regarding these three powers of knowledge: first, the power of knowledge regarding dhyānas, liberations, concentrations (*samādhi*), and attainments (*samāpatti*). This refers to the four dhyānas and eight liberations;
"concentrations" refers to all meditative states with mental activity, while "attainments" refers to both meditative states with and without mental activity.

To have correct knowledge of these is called this power of knowledge. Fourth, the power of knowledge regarding the superior and inferior faculties. This refers to the capacities of the Great and Small Vehicles, which may be weak, middling, or [superior].
The former is called the "superiority or inferiority of faculties" (*indriya-parāpara-jñāna-bala*); here, it is correctly known as the "power of knowledge regarding faculties.

Fifth is the power of knowledge regarding various inclinations (*nānādhimukti-jñāna-bala*). Whether one practices preceded by faith in others or preceded by the contemplation of all phenomena, the resulting soft, medium, or superior degrees of affectionate inclination are called "various inclinations. Here, it is correctly known as this [power].
The sixth is the power of knowledge regarding various elements (*nānā-dhātu-jñāna-bala*). "Element" (*dhātu*) has the meaning of "nature.

To establish them extensively, there are various natures, ranging from the single vehicle (*ekayāna*) and the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*) up to the eighty-four thousand types of temperaments and behaviors; because one knows these, it is called the power of knowledge regarding various elements.

The seventh is the power of knowledge regarding the paths leading everywhere (*sarvatraga-gāminī-pratipad-jñāna-bala*). Among the various doors of rebirth, one follows correct practice accordingly; for example, in the case of one whose temperament is characterized by greed (*rāga-carita*).

The cultivation of the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) and so forth is called the "path leading everywhere" (*sarvatraga-gāminī-pratipad*), or it is called the "path leading everywhere" because it is the gateway to all five destinies (*pañca-gati*);
it is the eighth [power] because one knows this. Regarding the power of the knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna-bala*):

among those various assemblies of sentient beings, within the four directions, names are conventionally established and categories are differentiated according to where they previously dwelt in the past.

Because he is able to know all the immeasurable varieties of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of phenomena, this power of knowledge is called "the power of knowledge consisting in recollection" (*anusmṛti-jñāna-bala*), as it closely follows recollection;
this is an etymological explanation based on proximity. Because he correctly understands the objects of past abodes (*pūrvanivāsa*), [this is the ninth power].

Ninth is the power of knowledge regarding death and rebirth (*cyutyupapāda-jñāna-bala*): when sentient beings pass away from their lives, it is called "death," and when they abide in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), it is called "rebirth."

Because one is able to know [the death and rebirth] in both the good and evil realms at the time of death and the time of birth, the tenth is the power of the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣayajñānabala*).

It is called the "power of the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows" because it manifests the reality characterized by the permanent and complete severance of all outflows and other latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) without remainder;
alternatively, it is called the "power of the knowledge of the destruction of the outflows" because it knows the exhaustion of the defilements of sentient beings. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:

These ten powers of knowledge (*jñānabala*) have wisdom (*prajñā*) as their essence. If their nature is that of an induced state (*samudānīta-svabhāva*), they consist of both meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom.

If their nature is that of an associated complex (*saṃprayukta-svabhāva*), they consist of the four aggregates (*skandha*) of the mental category. Thus, the *Abhidharma* states: "Whether it be meditative concentration or wisdom, along with their respective associated minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*), these constitute the essence of the power of knowledge.
If one considers their substantial essence (*dravya-svabhāva*), the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states that they have the five faculties, such as faith (*śraddhā*), as their nature.

The nature of the retinue consists of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). Since the morality of the fixed path constitutes the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), the remaining four aggregates can be understood accordingly.
[Commentary: Regarding the ten entities as they correspond: the first, the power of firmness, and the sixth, seventh, eighth, ninth, and tenth—these six have wisdom (*prajñā*) as their essence.

The second, the power of loving-kindness (*maitrī-bala*), has non-hatred (*adveṣa*) as its essence. The third, the power of compassion (*karuṇā-bala*), has non-harming (*avihiṃsā*) as its essence. The fourth... [text continues].
The fourth is diligence and the fifth is meditative concentration; each corresponds to its respective name.

[Commentary: Thus, regarding "the first and so forth," the Vajra-samādhi belongs to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), which is the position of the Bodhisattva of the tenth stage (*daśama-bhūmi*) who is close to the fruit of Buddhahood that is "equal to the unequaled" (*asamasama*).
It is the position of the Vajra-samādhi that is proximate to the stage of Equal Enlightenment.

[Commentary: Regarding the "Seven Worthies" and so forth, both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna teachings explain that there are distinct characteristics for the practices of the five stages of the three vehicles;

thus, each should be explained separately. For now, following the intent of this commentary, I shall set forth the Hīnayāna teaching to supplement what was omitted or brief. First, regarding the Śrāvaka vehicle:

from the initial arousal of the mind and the commencement of practice, starting from the stage of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and proceeding toward the fruit, it is generally divided into two parts: first, the stage of external ordinary beings (*bāhyapṛthagjana*); second, [the stage of internal ordinary beings].

Regarding those who have already transcended the stage of the outer ordinary person (*bāhyapṛthagjana*) and belong to the inner ordinary persons (*adhyātmapṛthagjana*), the *Abhidharmakośa*, chapter twenty-two, states:
"What is the method for diligently cultivating the path leading to the realization of the truths? One should first abide securely in pure ethical discipline (*śīla*), as it is the foundation.

Next, one should diligently cultivate the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and meditation (*śrutamayī-, cintāmayī-, bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*). That is to say, by first abiding in ethical discipline, one purifies the 'vessel' of the body, thereby becoming fit to perform the various preparatory virtues (*prayoga-kuśala*)."

The basis for the qualities of the Dharma should possess a profound intention toward liberation and a joyful contemplation of the virtues of *nirvāṇa*, while turning away from the faults of *saṃsāra*.
One should draw near to virtuous friends, listen to the true Dharma, and—possessing wisdom derived from hearing and so forth—cause the wisdom of cultivation to be swiftly perfected.
Next, one must possess three causes: first, physical and mental seclusion. Physical seclusion means being free from signs and free from dwelling [in attachment], remaining at a distance.

Those who distance themselves from the mind of evil factions abandon evil discursive thoughts; second, they have few desires and are content; third, they should next abide in the four noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*):
first, the noble lineage of contentment with clothing; second, the noble lineage of contentment with food and drink;

third, the noble lineage of contentment with bedding and seats; and fourth, the noble lineage of delighting in abandonment and delighting in cultivation. These four are capable of bringing about realization.

They are called the "noble lineages" (*āryavaṃśa*) because they are the seeds of the noble ones. Among these four, the first three are all contentment, while the fourth is the delight in abandoning afflictions and the delight in cultivating the noble path.
The first three are the requisites for generating the aids to the path, while the fourth is the activity of the aids to the path.
Because the disciples who have gone forth from the world under the Buddha have abandoned worldly requisites and worldly activities, the World-Honored One, out of compassion, established [these four].
These aids to the path provide the requisites for the practice of the path and cause the practitioner to attain liberation before long;

as the *Kṣudrakavastu* states: "Because sentient beings give rise to craving for 'I' and 'mine,' the Tathāgata established the first three noble lineages (*āryavaṃśa*) to cause such craving to cease temporarily, and established the fourth noble lineage to eliminate it forever. These four noble lineages are without...

Greed is the primary affliction within the body. Having already departed from that state, there are five stages; when these five are combined with the two stages of the preparatory aids (*upakāra*), they are called the seven stages of skillful means (*saptaprayoga*), namely the five contemplations for settling the mind (*pañcanivaraṇa-viśuddhi*) and so forth. "Skillful means" (*prayoga*) signifies the sense of employing methods and expedients as causes.

Because one enters the stage of the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) by means of these causes, the virtuous qualities possessed through these skillful means are also called the Seven Virtuous Practices (*saptakalyāṇapudgala*).

The first three of the middle [section] belong to the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*), and the latter four belong to the stage of application (*prayoga-avasthā*) (as may be understood from the Commentary).

[Commentary]: Regarding the five contemplations for settling the mind (*pañca-viṣaya-sthiti-citta-bhāvanā*): because sentient beings have, since beginningless time, wandered through birth and death and given rise to various faults that follow after objects, they find no means to attain meditative concentration or realize the fruits of the noble ones; therefore, the Buddha enjoined them to practice these five kinds [of contemplation].
In the practice of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), the mind is brought to rest; generally speaking, its faults number eighty-four thousand, yet when categorized by type, they do not exceed five kinds:
first, excessive greed; second, excessive hatred; third, excessive delusion; fourth, attachment to a self; and fifth, discursive thought (*vitarka-vicāra*).

To counteract these five types of afflictions, the Tathāgata taught the cultivation of the five *sthāpanā-citta* (stabilizing the mind) contemplations, whereby one attains meditative concentration (*samādhi*). If...

Whether through self-awareness or by instructing others, if one has excessive greed, one should practice the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*); if one has excessive hatred, one should practice the contemplation of loving-kindness and compassion (*maitrī-karuṇā-bhāvanā*);

if one has excessive delusion, one should practice the contemplation of the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda-bhāvanā*); if one is attached to a self, one should practice the contemplation of the analysis of the elements (*dhātu-vibhaṅga-bhāvanā*);

and if one has excessive discursive thought and investigation (*vitarka-vicāra*), one should practice the mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpāna-smṛti-bhāvanā*). The *Abhidharmakośa* further states that although there are five such contemplations, they are essential.
There are two [meditations]: first, the meditation on impurity (aśubha-bhāvanā), and second, the meditation on mindfulness of breathing (ānāpāna-smṛti).

Because these two types of faults are prevalent among sentient beings—namely, because their craving is so intense that it frequently manifests before them—such sentient beings are called "those who act out of desire" (rāga-carita).
By contemplating impurity, they are able to correctly enter into cultivation; for sentient beings generally give rise to craving and attachment toward exquisite forms.
There are four kinds of greed: first, greed for color; second, greed for shape; third, greed for exquisite touch; and fourth, greed for service and honor.
This means that because one encounters beautiful colors, physical forms, excellent bodies, softness, graceful movements, and acts of service and honor, these four types of greed arise.
To counteract these four types of greed, one contemplates four objects through the power of imaginative resolve (*adhimokṣa*) and performs four meditative practices.

One cultivates the meditation on impurity by taking the bluish discoloration (*vinīlaka*) and so forth as the object to counteract greed for color; by taking the being devoured by worms and so forth as the object to counteract greed for shape;

by taking the presence of maggots and so forth as the object to counteract greed for exquisite touch; and by taking the unmoving corpse and so forth as the object to counteract greed for honor and service.

By practicing these repeatedly, greed is prevented from arising. Furthermore, that verse states: "To universally counteract the four types of greed, one shall first explain the contemplation of the skeleton."

Contemplating [the skeleton] extensively until it reaches the ocean, then contracting it again, is called the stage of "initial practice" (*ādikarmika*). From the feet up to the midpoint of the head, it is called the stage of "mature cultivation" (*kṛtaparicaya*).
Fixing the mind between the eyebrows is called the stage of "transcending mental attention" (*atikrāntamanasikāra*).

The intent of this verse is to explain that the contemplation of the "skeleton chain" (*asthisaṃkalā*) serves as a universal remedy for the four types of craving, because within the skeleton chain there are no objects of those four cravings; thus, there are three distinct stages in the cultivation of this meditative practice.
There are three stages: first, the stage of initial practice; second, the stage of mature cultivation; and third, the stage of transcending mental attention (*manasikāra*). Regarding the first stage:

one should practice the meditation on the chain of bones (*asthi-śaṅkalā*) by first fixing the mind upon a part of one's own body—whether it be the toes, the forehead, or any other place as desired—and having established the mind there, one should, through the power of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), engage in conceptual reflection upon the skin.
The flesh decays and falls away, gradually revealing the bones, until one contemplates the entire body as a skeleton.
Having contemplated one such body, one likewise contemplates others decaying and falling away in the same manner.

After contemplating the second body, one proceeds sequentially through a single room, a single monastery, a single village, and finally the entire earth bounded by the ocean, filled with skeletons, in order to cause the growth of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*).

Gradually contracting the visualization until one contemplates only a single set of white bones—up to this point, the gradual contraction of the contemplation of impurity is perfected, and one enters the stage of "initial practice.

Second, in order to facilitate this contracted visualization through the power of resolute conviction (*adhimukti*), one first removes the bones of the feet from within that single set and contemplates the remaining bones;
proceeding gradually until the half-bone of the head is removed, one contemplates that remaining half-bone.
This transition from the abbreviated meditation on impurity to the stage of "mastery through cultivation" consists of three parts:

first, in order to attain mastery over the resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) of the abbreviated observation, one removes the skull and half-bones and fixes the mind between the eyebrows, concentrating on a single object until it dwells in profound stillness;

at this point, the abbreviated meditation on impurity is perfected and one enters the stage of "transcending mental attention" (*atikrāntamanasikāra*). One practices in this manner until meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is attained.
The contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) has non-attachment as its essence because it remedies greed. Regarding the mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpāna-smṛti*):
*āna* is translated here as "sending forth" (or "bringing in"), meaning the holding of the breath as it enters, which signifies drawing the wind into the body;
*apāna* is translated as "sending away" (or "expelling"), meaning the holding of the breath as it exits, which signifies leading the internal wind out of the body.

In terms of meaning, "ānāpānasmṛti" (mindfulness of breathing) is translated as "holding the breath through mindfulness. Its essential nature is wisdom (*prajñā*). "Breath" (*āna-apāna*) refers to the wind;

because mindfulness can hold that breath, it is called "mindfulness of holding the breath" (*ānāpānasmṛti*), which is analyzed according to the *tatpuruṣa* (possessive) compound. Now, when we refer to it specifically as "wisdom," it is due to the power of mindfulness that wisdom becomes distinct regarding its object;

thus, it is called "mindfulness of holding the breath" (*ānāpānasmṛti*), which is analyzed according to the *sāmīpya* (proximate) compound. There are differences in the cultivation of these meditative practices.
There are six further points: first, counting; second, following; third, stopping; fourth, contemplating; fifth, transforming; and sixth, purifying. Regarding counting:
this refers to counting from one to ten, with the inhalation as the beginning and the exhalation as the end. Only when four conditions are met does the breath proceed.

The basis for a single breath consists of the desire realm and the first three dhyānas, which are called the "stages where breath exists. Second, the pathways of wind refer to the mouth and [the nostrils].
The three nostril pores open at birth from the mother’s womb; the stage of inhalation and exhalation refers to when coarse consciousness manifests.

Entering the mindless meditative attainments lacks coarse consciousness; while remaining in the mother’s womb, the four conditions are incomplete; and in the formless realm, all four conditions are absent.
In these various states, because the conditions are not complete, the breaths do not circulate. Where the four conditions are complete, [the breaths circulate].
Mindfully maintaining the count of inhalations and exhalations while remaining free from the three faults is called "correct counting.
First, the fault of undercounting: taking two to be one. Second, the fault of overcounting: taking one to be two. Third, the fault of confusion:
taking an inhalation to be an exhalation, or an exhalation to be an inhalation. If the mind becomes distracted in the midst of counting to ten, one should begin again from one.

Counting them in sequence, one completes the count and begins again until stability is attained. Furthermore, counting "one" consists of taking the inhalation as the first entry and the exhalation as the subsequent exit;

the same applies to "two," "three," and so forth. Regarding "following," this means fixing the mind on the object of the inhalation and exhalation without applying deliberate effort (*prayoga*), following the breath as it moves.
When the breath enters, does it travel far, reaching the end of the body, or does it travel only a portion of the body? One should observe this.
Following that breath as it enters, one’s mindfulness constantly follows it through the heart, navel, hips, thighs, calves, and even down to the toes.
"Stilling" means binding the mind exclusively to the tip of the nose, or between the eyebrows, or even down to the toes—whichever place one prefers—and settling the mind there.
One contemplates the breath abiding in the body like a thread within a pearl, observing whether it is cold or warm, and whether it is harmful or beneficial.

"Observing" refers to having observed the substance of the breath-wind (*āśvāsa-praśvāsa*), while simultaneously observing the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) co-arising with the breath, as well as the mind (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitasika*) that abide based upon that matter;
thus, one takes the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) as the object of observation.

"Shifting" refers to shifting the awareness of the breath-wind and placing it within progressively superior roots of goodness (*kuśala-mūla*), up to the stage of the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgra-dharma*). "Purifying" refers to what is called "superior."
Upon entering the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and so forth, one attains untainted (*anāsrava*) and pure (*śuddha*) applied and sustained thought (*vitarka-vicāra*);

because these are causes of distraction, by repeatedly focusing on the inhalation and exhalation, one is able to abandon distraction and prevent the arising of applied and sustained thought, which is non-distraction.
[Commentary: Regarding "the mind is detached," etc., this refers to being free from afflicted attention (*kliṣṭa-manasikāra*) and free from neutral attention (*avyākṛta-manasikāra*).
It is the opposite of those two types; it refers to the cultivation of the practice of attending to the meditative states (*samāhita-bhūmi*) that lead to meaningful benefit.

[Commentary: Regarding "the contemplation of dependent origination" and so forth: one contemplates the twelve links of dependent origination as arising from conditions, wherein each link undergoes transformation;
they are impermanent, suffering, empty, and without self, being merely a provisional combination. Because of this, saṃsāra does not cease.
Thus, by observing that ignorance is the root of saṃsāra, one counteracts delusion.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "the contemplation of the differentiation of the elements (*dhātu*) can eliminate pride," this refers to eliminating pride according to the specific affliction of the practitioner.

While the preceding contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) was sufficient to verify the absence of self (*anātman*), the subsequent contemplations of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) and the differentiation of the six elements (*ṣaḍ-dhātu*) fully demonstrate impermanence (*anitya*), suffering (*duḥkha*), emptiness (*śūnyatā*), and non-self; therefore, they differ from what is countered in the *Abhidharmakośa*.

[Commentary] To summarize, the *Yogācārabhūmi* further states: "If one is a practitioner whose afflictions are slight, they may simply abide in mindfulness directed toward the object (*pratyakṣa-smṛti*) without necessarily practicing the five contemplations for stabilizing the mind (*pañca-vipaśyanā-sthiti-citta-vidarśanā*)."

[Commentary]: Regarding the "application of mindfulness to specific characteristics" (*viśeṣalakṣaṇasmṛtyupasthāna*) and so forth, the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*, chapter twenty-three, states that after one has already cultivated the contemplation of impurity (*aśubhabhāvanā*) and so on to achieve superior *śamatha* (here translated as "the category of cessation"), one subsequently cultivates the four applications of mindfulness—body, sensation, mind, and phenomena—in order to achieve the category of *vipaśyanā*.

These are called "specific" because regarding these four objects, one contemplates them either by way of their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) or by way of their general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
