Because one contemplates these, they are called the applications of mindfulness of specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa-smṛtyupasthāna*). With the exception of body, sensation, and mind, all others are called phenomena (*dharma*). That is to say:
contemplating the body as impure, contemplating sensation as suffering, contemplating the mind as impermanent, and contemplating phenomena as non-self.

These four objects of contemplation, each having its own distinct intrinsic nature, are called "specific characteristics" (*svalakṣaṇa*). As for "common characteristics" (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), it refers to those characteristics that are shared by all phenomena. This is what is meant by [the term].
They say to one another: "All conditioned phenomena have the characteristic of impermanence; all contaminated phenomena have the characteristic of suffering;

all dharmas have the characteristics of emptiness and non-self. When contemplating the body, there is only the nature of impurity—meaning it is composed of thirty-six constituent substances—and this is called its specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). If one contemplates this body as being identical to all conditioned phenomena...

The characteristic of impermanence is common to all contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena; the characteristic of suffering is common to all phenomena; and the characteristics of emptiness and non-self are common to all phenomena.
Regarding "emptiness," it means emptying that which belongs to a self (*ātmiya*); regarding "non-self," it means there is no real self.

The original intent was merely to contemplate the body, not to contemplate all phenomena in their entirety; therefore, this is called the "contemplation of common characteristics. Since the contemplation of the body is thus, so it is with the others.

The same applies to the [remaining] three. Although they differ in two categories—specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*)—they are collectively termed the "applications of mindfulness to specific characteristics" (*viśeṣalakṣaṇasmṛtyupasthāna*).
This is because all sentient beings, from time immemorial, have transmigrated through birth and death due to the four inversions;

they give rise to the four inversions of purity, pleasure, permanence, and self regarding various objects and phenomena. Therefore, for the sake of practitioners who seek to transcend birth and death, these serve as the antidotes (*pratipakṣa*).

This refers to the perfection of the nature of the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*). It is the practice of observing the body—without diminishing or augmenting it—even down to a single infinitesimal particle (*paramāṇu*) and a single moment (*kṣaṇa*), seeing that it is of the nature of suffering (*duḥkha*), impermanence (*anitya*), emptiness (*śūnya*), and non-self (*anātman*).
Regarding the etymological explanation according to the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, there are two senses: first, it is said that wisdom (*prajñā*) is sustained by the power of mindfulness (*smṛti*).

The dwelling upon the object is called "foundation of mindfulness" (*smṛtyupasthāna*). Its essence is wisdom (*prajñā*). Second, it is said that by the power of wisdom, mindfulness is made to dwell upon the object;
regarding the object under investigation, mindfulness attains clarity and stability. Because mindfulness thus dwells, it is called a "foundation of mindfulness.
Now, as for why wisdom is here termed "mindfulness": because it is closely associated with that [actual] mindfulness, it is called a "foundation of mindfulness" through proximity (*sāmantaka*).
This is the explanation.
[Commentary]: Regarding "the application of mindfulness to phenomena with mixed objects" (*miśrālambana-dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) and so forth, the citation from the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* is abbreviated.

That treatise states that among the four objects observed by the application of mindfulness to specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-smṛtyupasthāna*), the first three observe only unmixed objects, whereas the fourth, the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*), applies to both mixed and unmixed phenomena.
Because it is named "broad" (*viśāla*) as it encompasses other objects, and because one contemplates individual phenomena (*dharma*), it is called "non-confused object" (*asaṃbhinnālambana*).

If one contemplates by combining two of the four objects together, or three together, or by contemplating all four objects collectively, and furthermore combines them collectively by way of both specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), this is the object of the application of mindfulness to phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) with confused objects.
When the cultivation of this is perfected, it constitutes the application of mindfulness to specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇasmṛtyupasthāna*).

Following the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), and prior to the foundations of mindfulness in their general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa-smṛtyupasthāna*), one cultivates the practice of the non-self (*anātman*). Next, one contemplates arising and ceasing; next, one contemplates dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*);

and next, one contemplates the three meanings, namely the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*). Subsequently, based on the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*), one trains in the sixteen aspects (*ṣoḍaśākāra*);

then, based on the wisdom derived from reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*), one trains in the sixteen aspects. All of these constitute the preparatory stages (*prayoga*) for the foundations of mindfulness in their general characteristics. This, then—

Tracing back from this point, one arises from the *smṛtyupasthāna* of mindfulness of dharmas with miscellaneous objects (*nānālambana-dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) to practice a general contemplation of the four objects that encompasses all phenomena.

One cultivates the four aspects (*ākāra*), namely: impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self; this is called the *smṛtyupasthāna* of general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa-smṛtyupasthāna*). It also has wisdom as its essence.

Among the seven stages of the virtuous practices (*saptakalyāṇakāraka*), these three preceding positions are termed the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*). "Equipment" refers to that which is intended for the distant pursuit of enlightenment (*bodhi*).
Because it is a fruit, the stage in which the two types of provisions—merit and wisdom—are accumulated is called the *sambhāra-avasthā* (the stage of provisions);

it is also called the *mokṣabhāgīya* (conducive to liberation). "Liberation" (*mokṣa*) refers to the fruit, which is *nirvāṇa*; "part" (*bhāga*) has the sense of a cause, because the cause can lead toward the fruit of liberation.
Thus, "conducive" (*anuloma*) is itself the part; the "part conducive to liberation" is termed *mokṣabhāgīya*.

[Commentary]: Regarding "the roots of goodness such as Heat" (*ūṣmagata-kuśalamūla*), these latter four among the seven stages of the virtuous practitioner (*saptakalyāṇapudgala*) are called the stage of application (*prayogāvasthā*).
Because one has practiced this stage of application for a long time and is close to the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), it can serve as the preparatory application for the Path of Seeing;

therefore, it is named the stage of application. It is also called the "Aids to Penetration" (*nirvedhabhāgīya*). "Penetration" (*nirveda*) refers to the untainted noble wisdom (*anāsravāryaprajñā*); the "aids" (*bhāgīya*) are as explained previously.
Because these preparatory causes (*prayoga-hetu*) accord with and lead toward that [decisive penetration], they are called "factors conducive to decisive penetration" (*nirvedha-bhāgīya*).

Furthermore, the *Nyāyānusāra* states that "factor" (*bhāga*) means a "portion. Since the wisdom of the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) is comprised within a portion of decisive penetration, decisive penetration itself is the factor.

Because the roots of goodness such as "heat" (*uṣmagata*) accord with and lead toward that [path of seeing], they are called "factors conducive to decisive penetration" by virtue of being factors that accord with the portion of decisive penetration.

[Commentary: This refers to those subsumed under the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), specifically taking up the wholesome dharmas associated with meditative concentration and wisdom (*samādhi-prajñā*) that are cultivated through cultivation (*bhāvanā-mayī-prajñā*).

According to the Hīnayāna school, among the four roots of goodness (*catvāri kuśalamūlāni*), the first two are movable while the latter two are immovable; each of these has lower and higher, inferior and superior [distinctions].

Because they differ, the four roots of goodness (*catur-kuśala-mūla*) are established: namely, during the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*), one may still commit immediate transgressions (*ānantarya-karma*) and so forth;

however, by virtue of this merit, one will swiftly escape the miserable destinies and inevitably reach *nirvāṇa*. During the stage of "Summit" (*mūrdhan*), one does not commit immediate transgressions, though one may still commit other evil deeds.
At the stages of "Patience" (*kṣānti*) and "Supreme Worldly Dharmas" (*laukikāgradharma*), one performs no evil deeds and is thus called "immovable. As the *Abhidharmakośa* verse states: "Heat..."

One will certainly reach the summit of *nirvāṇa*, never severing the patience of the wholesome, nor falling into the evil destinies; this is the "Supreme Worldly Dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*) which transcends the state of ordinary birth.

[Commentary] Regarding these [categories], the sub-commentary (*śū*) merely states that there are eight types based on their objects (*ālambana*). That is to say, it speaks of the objects as the fundamental truths (*satya*), but does not speak of their modes of activity (*ākāra*).
This means that each individual truth has three modes of activity, and across the eight truths—four upper and four lower—there are [twelve modes].
The fourteen aspects (*ākāra*), whether considered as objects (*ālambana*) or modes of activity, amount to thirty-two when combined.

One diligently cultivates these—from the broad to the concise—within the three grades of patience (*kṣānti*) and the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*), proceeding in accordance with the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*).

Specifically, the inferior grade of patience involves contemplating the sixteen aspects of the Four Noble Truths; that is, one contemplates the suffering of the desire realm by cultivating four aspects: impermanence (*anitya*), suffering (*duḥkha*), emptiness (*śūnya*), and selflessness (*anātman*).
Contemplating the suffering of the higher realms as "not-self" through its four aspects, and so on, up to contemplating the path of the higher realms by cultivating its four aspects—
namely, viewing it as the path, as right practice, as emergence, and as departure— this is called the stage of inferior patience (*mṛdu-kṣānti*). Once this inferior patience has been accomplished,

one again contemplates the object of the Noble Truth of Suffering in the desire realm through its four aspects, and so on, until contemplating the Truth of the Path in the higher realms, which is cultivated only [in its four aspects].
The three aspects of practice refer to the path; when one aspect is reduced from these, it constitutes medium-grade patience (*madhya-kṣānti*), which is the first cycle.

Furthermore, one contemplates the truths of the desire realm up to the upper realms, cultivating two aspects of practice: namely, the path and suchness (*tathatā*); this reduction of two aspects constitutes the second cycle.
Again, one contemplates the suffering of the desire realm up to the path of the upper realms, cultivating only one aspect of practice; this is the [third cycle].

In the third cycle, one reduces three modes of practice; furthermore, one contemplates the suffering of the desire realm up to the path-factors of the desire realm, cultivating four modes of practice while not contemplating the path-truth of the higher realms.
This is the reduction of one object; when reducing one object, one also reduces one mode of practice because the reduction of objects subsumes the reduction of practices.
Thus, only three cycles of reducing practice and one cycle of reducing objects are mentioned. In this manner, one gradually performs a concise contemplation.

When one reaches the stage of observing only the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) by cultivating four aspects (*ākāra*) without observing the Truths of Suffering and so forth of the higher realms, this constitutes twenty-one cycles of reducing the objects (*ālambana*) and seven cycles of reducing the aspects. Then, observing the suffering of the desire realm again while cultivating the first three aspects is the twenty-second cycle;
continuing in this manner until one observes only the suffering of the desire realm while cultivating only two aspects takes two moments (*kṣaṇa*).
When that mind reaches the completion of the stage of medium patience (*madhyakṣānti*), one again contemplates this suffering by practicing the first of the four aspects;
a single momentary mind constitutes the stage of supreme patience (*adhimātrakṣānti*). Taken collectively, this is called the perfection of the stage of patience.

According to the *Abhidharmakośa-vyākhyā*, regarding the four aspects of the Truth of Suffering in the sixth chapter, there is no logical prohibition against retaining any particular aspect. This is because there are two types of persons who practice these contemplative aspects: the first is...
Regarding those of sharp faculties, there are two types: if one is attached to a self, they are established in the practice of non-self;
if one is attached to "mine," they are established in the practice of emptiness. Regarding those of dull faculties, there are also two types:

if one is characterized by the conceit of "I am," they are established in the practice of impermanence—because such a person is deluded regarding the principle of impermanence due to their physical existence, and because they give rise to pride through attachment, their indolence increases, they are thus established in the practice of suffering. Indolence...
Because of indolence, one is unable to exert oneself with vigor; therefore, by contemplating the truths as suffering and as unstable, one advances toward renunciation.
Whichever practice one maintains, one enters the Path of Seeing through that very practice.

[Commentary: Regarding "the worldly supreme roots of goodness" (*laukikāgradharma*), immediately following the stage of "supreme patience" (*adhimātrākṣānti*), there arises a root of goodness consisting of a single moment of mind that takes as its object one aspect of the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*).
This is called the "worldly supreme dharma. What is the distinction between this and the "supreme patience"?
The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* (Treatise on the Correct Principles), fascicle 61, states: "Wholesome karma of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) is of nine grades; namely, the inferior..."

The three grades [of goodness] subsumed under the stage of *uṣmagata* (Heat); the middle three grades subsumed under the stage of *mūrdhan* (Summits); and the lower-upper, upper-middle, and upper-lower grades are named the stage of *kṣānti* (Patience).
Regarding these two grades of goodness subsumed under the three types of *kṣānti*: the lower-upper and lower-middle grades of goodness are subsumed under the two lower *kṣāntis*;

the upper-middle grade of goodness is subsumed under the upper *kṣānti*; and the upper-upper grade of goodness is subsumed under the *laukikāgradharma* (Supreme Mundane Dharma). This is due to their relative superiority and inferiority.

Because they are distinct, they constitute a differentiation; this [root of merit] lasts for only a single moment and necessarily does not continue as an equal-and-immediate condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), yet it is able to induce the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*). These four roots of goodness have wisdom as their essence, with the four aggregates (*skandha*) as their associated factors and the five aggregates as their retinue.

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "the power of the human effort" (*puruṣakāra-bala*) and so forth: contaminated mental states (*sāsrava-citta*) induce other contaminated mental states, and uncontaminated mental states (*anāsrava-citta*) induce other uncontaminated mental states.
These two categories—where the preceding cause induces its subsequent effect within its own kind—are called "homogeneous causes" (*sabhāga-hetu*) and "homogeneous effects" (*niṣyanda-phala*).
However, the first stage (*ādikṣānti*) of this present life induces the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*); it does not precede [its result] by way of a homogeneous cause.
A single *kṣaṇa* is the cause with outflows (*sāsrava*) that induces the subsequent moment of the untainted noble path (*anāsrava-āryamārga*).

Because the preceding cause and the succeeding fruit differ—being tainted and untainted respectively—and because the fruit arises from that [cause] through the power of human effort (*puruṣakāra*) without any interval, it is called the "uninterrupted fruit of human effort" (*anantara-puruṣakāra-phala*).
"Only practicing to that extent" means practicing by taking only the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) of the Desire Realm as the object and cultivating a single aspect (*ākāra*).

Because it serves as the condition for entering the noble state (*ārya*), not practicing much is equivalent to this single practice of a single moment of mind resembling the "patience regarding the dharma-knowledge of suffering" (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*) on the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).

[Commentary] Regarding the "eight bases of mastery" (*abhibhvāyatana*) and so forth: within the first two bases of mastery, one has not yet subdued or eliminated the craving for the perception of form (*rūpa-saṃjñā*) in those who see.

The six subsequent spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) are called "having internal perception of form" because, through long-term cultivation, one has already suppressed and eliminated the perception of form and craving for form within oneself.
Regarding "having internal perception of no-form": "limited form" refers to the forms of sentient beings and the forms of their requisites;

"vast form" refers to the forms of the great earth, mountains, rivers, and so forth. When contemplating those limited and vast forms, one further cultivates seven types [of meditative observation] for each.
The modes of activity (*ākāra*) are as follows: first, pleasant forms, meaning those that are exclusively pure and exquisite;

second, unpleasant forms, which are the opposite of the former; third, inferior forms, meaning those that are disagreeable; fourth, superior forms, which are the opposite of the former; fifth, superior knowledge, meaning the path of *śamatha*;
sixth, superior vision, meaning the path of *vipaśyanā* (here translated as "contemplation"); seventh, attaining the suchness of reality (*yathābhūta-lakṣaṇa*). Regarding these...
Within the two categories of the "conquered" and the "unconquered," one is free from overweening pride (*adhimāna*) and gives rise to the perception of mastery.
Following this, among the four remaining spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), there are four modes of appearance (*ākāra*) for each of the colors blue, yellow, red, and white.

Regarding these four, the first is the general term and the other three are specific terms. "Blue-appearing" (*nīlanidarśana*) refers to innate blue, such as the color of a blue flower; "blue-manifesting" (*nīlanirbhāsa*) refers to...
This refers to the combination of blue, such as the blue of a garment and so forth, and the blue light; this latter is the fresh and pure light inherent within the aforementioned three types of blue.

Just as it is with blue, so it is with yellow and the others. When one performs such superior contemplations, the mind abides in a superior object, which is called a "sphere of mastery" (*abhibhvāyatana*).
This is unlike other births where the mind is inferior while the object is superior, leading to confusion as one is dragged away by the object.

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "the first two are superior," etc., according to the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra*, the first three liberations (*vimokṣa*) sequentially induce the first two, the next two, and the final four spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*).
As for the primary derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*), it is subsumed under the secondary derived matter (*bhautika-rūpa*); thus, the earth and other elements are not mentioned.
The first four spheres of mastery rely on the first and second dhyānas; they observe the signs of impurity in small and large quantities of form, and function as the antidote to the desire realm.
Because there is attachment to visible forms within the first dhyāna, the latter four bases of mastery rely on the fourth dhyāna;
they observe the pure aspects of the forms of the desire realm, causing the mind to rejoice and thereby bringing them to thorough fulfillment.
[Commentary]: Regarding the "ten spheres of totality" (*daśa kṛtsnāyatana*) and so forth, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states that they are induced by means of the third liberation.
The latter two spheres of totality are precisely the spheres of totality of space and consciousness. These also involve the absence of internal perception of form while observing external forms;
that is, one observes the derivative forms—blue, yellow, red, and white—as pervading all places, and further observes the primary elements, such as earth.

Because water, fire, and wind pervade all that is derived [from the primary elements], they collectively constitute eight [perceptual spheres]. This is for the purpose of fulfilling the meaning of the aforementioned eight pervasive bases.
Since the pervasion of the object does not exceed space and the pervasion of the subject does not exceed consciousness, one practices the latter two universal bases;
because they pervade the entire objective field, they are called "universal bases" (kṛtsnāyatana).

[Commentary]: Regarding the latter two, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states that the latter two *kṛtsnāyatana*s (totalities) have, respectively, the meditative wholesome states (*dhyāna-kuśala*) of the Sphere of Infinite Space and the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness as their intrinsic nature;
they are neither neutral (*avyākṛta*) nor defiled (*kliṣṭa*), nor are they the nature of mundane wholesome states (*vairāgya-kuśala*), because the latter are weak and inferior.

However, they extend to both the preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) and the fundamental stages (*maula*) of these concentrations. As for those wholesome states that take the space or consciousness of their own respective levels as objects, this is explained in the *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 80.
Regarding the four clouds: it is said that a beginner first dwells in contemplation of the signs of space;
having grasped these signs, they cultivate the preparatory application by means of imaginative resolve (*adhimokṣa*) to observe and clearly comprehend the sign of infinite space.

Because this sequentially induces the first formless attainment (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), this attainment is called the Sphere of Infinite Space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*). Now, to clarify the All-pervading Sphere of Space (*ākāśakṛtsnāyatana*): it is...
This samādhi takes emptiness as its object; by analogy, it can be understood that consciousness likewise takes it as its object.
[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "and those associated with the Path" (*mārga-samprayukta*), etc., this refers to the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) such as arising (*jāti*).

According to the Hīnayāna, these have a distinct substantial nature (*svabhāva*) and possess auxiliary powers that assist in severing all afflictions (*kleśa*). Because they share the same activity (*karma*) as the clear realization (*abhisamaya*), they are mentioned collectively.

This is called the "clear realization of names and things" (*nāma-vastu-abhisamaya*). [Commentary: "Desire" refers to the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*), so called because within this realm there exist those three objects of desire: sexual intercourse, food, and sleep. It comprises the five destinies (*gati*).
Now, to clarify the destiny of humans: O Benevolent Lord, there are six names, namely the Six Desire Heavens (*ṣaḍ-kāmāvacara-deva*).

"King. [Commentary: As for the Heaven of the Four Great Kings (*Cāturmahārājakāyika*), it is so called because these celestial kings govern the four great continents; thus they are called the "Four Great Kings.
Furthermore, because there is one king for each continent and they are not a single entity, they are also called a "host" (*kāya*). On each of the four sides of Mount Sumeru, there is one [king].
The King [Indra] said: "The one in the east is named Dhṛtarāṣṭra; the one in the south is named Virūḍhaka; the one in the west is named Virūpākṣa, also known as Ugra;
and the one in the north is named Vaiśravaṇa. These four Heavenly Kings preside over various spirits and ghosts, each protecting the classes of sentient beings in their respective directions.
As for Mount Sumeru, in the Sanskrit language it is called Meru; this mountain is thus named 'Wondrously High. Now, we shall follow the local dialect."
It is named Mount *Sumeru* (the "Wondrous High Mountain"; its former name, *Xumi*, is a corruption).

This means that the northern side is made of gold, the eastern of silver, the southern of lapis lazuli, and the western of *sphatika* (translated here as "crystal"); because the body of the mountain is composed of these four jewels, it is called "Wondrous.
It is called "High" because its extent both above and below the water is eighty thousand *yojanas*. *Yojana* is a term for measurement. [End of section. West.
The *Dharmottarābhidharma-śāstra* (Chuyou ji) states that one march (*yōjana*) of the ancient military expeditions was eighty *li* according to worldly convention, or forty *li*;
however, that which is taught in the Noble Teachings is sixteen *li*. As the verse in the *Abhidharmakośa* says: "The four tiers of Mount Sumeru are each ten thousand [yojanas] apart;
Extending outward, they measure sixteen, eight, four, and two thousand [yojanas]; They are the abodes of the Karoṭapāṇis, the Mālādharas, The Sadāmattas, and the Mahārājikas."
The assembly of kings resides sequentially upon the four tiers; they also dwell on the other seven mountains.
That is to say, the form of Mount Sumeru is like a *dardura* drum—broad at both the top and bottom, with a narrow waist in the middle.

From its lower half, extending from the surface of the water up to its summit, there are four tiers, each measuring forty thousand *yojanas*. These four tiers are separated from one another by ten thousand *yojanas* each.

Extending outward, it encircles Mount Sumeru; from the surface of the water, the first terrace extends for sixteen thousand *yojanas*, the second for eight thousand, the third for four thousand, and the fourth for two thousand.
Yakṣa deities named Dṛḍhapāṇi guard the first terrace, those named Mālādhāra reside on the second, and those named... [reside] on the third.

Nitya-pramada (Ever-Arrogant) dwells on the third tier; the fourth tier is the abode of the Four Great Kings, who also reside upon the other seven golden mountains—these being their separate settlements.
In Sanskrit, *Trāyastriṃśa-deva* means "the Heaven of the Thirty-three.
Atop the summit of Mount Sumeru, there are eight palaces in each of the four directions, with one celestial being as the Indra for each palace.
Your servant, Śakra, dwells in the center of the Sudharmā Hall as their sovereign; thus, sovereign and subjects together speak of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
As for the Yāma Heaven, it is translated here as the "Time-Portion" (Śīdāna) Heaven, because those devas experience their joys and pleasures according to specific time-portions.
Furthermore, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states that above the midpoint of Mount Sumeru, there are no sun or moon, and the devas [reside there].

Because they rely on the light of their own bodies or the light of jewels and so forth to provide illumination and guidance, they establish day and night based on the opening and closing of flowers or the clamor and silence of birds, or based on the waking and sleeping of the celestial hosts.

Furthermore, they establish day when blue lotuses close and yellow lotuses open, and the reverse for night. Based on such signs, the divisions of time are established; this is called "time-period" (*velā*).

The *Tuṣita* Heaven is here translated as the "Heaven of Contentment," because the devas of that realm do not excessively crave the objects of the five sensory dusts (*pañca-viṣaya*), knowing their desire for pleasure to be sufficient. The *Nirmāṇarati* Heaven is so called because they delight in utilizing and enjoying the requisites they themselves transform;
this is unlike the requisites used by the two lower heavens, which grow from trees. [The next heaven is] *Paranirmita-vaśavartin*.
The Lord of Sovereignty (Īśvara) refers to an inferior deva who transforms his requisites to be enjoyed by a superior deva;
if both are inferior, they transform them for mutual enjoyment, because the dispositions and desires of those sentient beings are such.
[Commentary]: Regarding "the kingdom of Magadha" and so forth, the child [of the Buddha] was established as an official of this region.

Because his nature was benevolent and he did not commit acts of poisonous harm, he was named by virtue of his character "King Without Poisonous Harm" (Amṛtāśoka). Consequently, the name of the kingdom became the Kingdom Without Poisonous Harm.
In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, it is recorded according to worldly convention that the place was named "The Abode of Ambrosia" (Amṛtasthāna).
[Commentary: Regarding the passage "In the past, Śakra [Indra]," the old manuscript states: In a previous life, Śakra was a slave in the household of the Kausika family.

The people held him in great respect and faith, so the King granted him his freedom. He joined thirty-two other men in governing the streets and sweeping the roads, encouraging people to perform virtuous deeds; thus his reputation spread upward.
When the King wished to appoint him to an official post, a sycophantic minister slandered him, and he was handed over to an elephant to be killed. Once the elephant had already—

Having been granted the rank of official in his native commandery for abstaining from killing, he subsequently took four wives: the first was named Shanfa (Dharmā), the second Yuansheng (Udyānajā), the third Huankui (Nandā), and the fourth Qingjie (Śuddhā).
At that time, the Commandant of the Commandery, together with the multitude, constructed a Dharma Hall;
Lady Shanfa fashioned a dew-receptacle (*amalakapātra*), Lady Huankui surrounded the hall by laying out a garden, and Lady Yuansheng planted within it.
After the Lady Śuddhāśayā failed to cultivate meritorious deeds and her life came to an end, she was all reborn in the second heaven of the desire realm;

because one receives fruits according to their causes, there exist such places as the Hall of Good Dharma (Sudharmā). However, because the Lady Śuddhāśayā had previously failed to cultivate merit, she was born among the water-ruddy geese.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, perceived this with his divine eye and manifested a transformation body identical to theirs to instruct them in maintaining [the precepts].
Regarding the precept against killing: due to her original jealousy, she abandoned the water-geese and was reborn in the palace of the asuras, named Śacī.
Indra took her as his wife and returned to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; "Śacī" is also called Śachi, which translates here as "Bondage.
Because her beauty was extraordinary and bound men [to her], the asuras produced ugly sons when they fathered children by her, but beautiful daughters.
Because Śakra married her, and since there was the flavor of *suda* (translated here as "ambrosia") within Śakra’s palace,
this led to the gods and asuras contending with one another over its color and flavor, frequently giving rise to strife and conflict.

[Commentary]: "The four dhyānas of the form realm" refers to the four dhyānas of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*). The commentary explains that *dhyāna* is designated as such because it is both meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and discernment (*prajñā*).
Furthermore, it is explained that the Sanskrit term *dhyāna* is translated here as "calm discernment" (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*). "Calm" (*śama*) is a synonym for tranquility or meditative concentration;

"discernment" (*vipaśyanā*) is a specific designation for investigative wisdom (*prajñā*). In the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*), there is discernment but no calm; in the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), calm is abundant while discernment is scarce.

Only that which consists of the concentration and wisdom of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), being balanced and characterized by tranquility and reflection, is called *dhyāna* (meditative absorption); this refers to the realm of the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*). Regarding its four distinct types, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:

the first is the *dhyāna* with applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), joy (*prīti*), and tranquility; the second is the *dhyāna* free from applied and sustained thought, possessing joy and bliss (*sukha*);
the third is the *dhyāna* free from joy, possessing bliss; and the fourth is the *dhyāna* free from both joy and bliss, possessing equanimity (*upekṣā*).
The meditative concentration of pure mindfulness.
[Commentary: Regarding the Brahmakāyika devas and others, "Brahmā" (梵) is translated as "Pure" (清淨); it is also called "Utterly Pure.

Because they are free from the defiled dharmas of the desire realm, they receive the name "Utterly Pure" within the form realm. Nevertheless, all four dhyānas are called "Brahma-heavens," beginning with the first.

Because dhyāna is the foremost, it is specifically called "Brahma" (the intermediate dhyāna). Regarding the intermediate dhyāna: among the deities of the two lower heavens, there is both vitarka (applied thought) and vicāra (sustained thought);
from the second dhyāna upward, there is neither vitarka nor vicāra. This Great Brahmā Heaven possesses vicāra but lacks vitarka; thus it is named the intermediate dhyāna.

[Commentary]: Regarding those who practice the "intermingled cultivation" (*vyavakīrṇa-bhāvanā*) of the dhyānas, the *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā* states: "First, one intermingles the fourth [dhyāna]; its accomplishment is by means of a single moment of intermingling.
This is for the sake of rebirth, for present happiness, and to prevent falling away through afflictions. By intermingling five grades, there arise the five Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*).

As for "intermingled cultivation," it refers to the alternating cultivation of the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) states; therefore, one must first intermingle the fourth dhyāna.
Because the fourth dhyāna is the most capable, when an Arhat or a Non-returner intends to practice the mixed cultivation (vyavakiraṇa),
they must first enter the fourth dhyāna so that a continuous succession of many moments of untainted (anāsrava) states manifests before them;
from this, they induce many moments of tainted (sāsrava) states, followed again by many moments of untainted states— this is the initial application of the mixed cultivation concentration.

Having practiced such a cycle of alternating and returning, the subsequent moments gradually decrease until finally, two moments of untainted (anāsrava) consciousness are followed immediately by two moments of tainted (sāsrava) consciousness appearing before one;
this is called the completion of the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) for the mixed cultivation of meditative concentration (*vyavakīrṇa-bhāvanā-samādhi*).
Thereafter, from a single moment of untainted consciousness, one induces a single moment of tainted consciousness to appear before one, which is immediately followed by...

When one gives rise to a single moment of outflow-free (anāsrava) thought, such that the intermediate moments of outflow (sāsrava) are interspersed with preceding and succeeding moments of the outflow-free, it is therefore called "mixed cultivation" (*miśra-bhāvanā*).

The fundamental stage of this mixed cultivation is perfected through these [moments]: the first two moments resemble the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*), while the third moment resembles the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).

By means of this, one is able to sever the obstacles to mixed cultivation. However, regarding the superior or inferior nature of mixed cultivation— *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the available content.*

Collectively, there are five grades, namely: first, the inferior grade; second, the middling grade; third, the superior grade; fourth, the superior-superior grade; and fifth, the supreme-superior grade.

The obstructions to be abandoned likewise consist of five grades: first, the inferior grade; second, the middling grade; third, the inferior-superior grade; fourth, the superior-middling grade; and fifth, the superior-superior grade.
By practicing these five grades of meditative concentration, one abandons these five grades of obstructions in both forward and reverse order.

In contrast, because the abandonment of afflictions through the mixed cultivation of meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) and the abandonment of their respective obstacles each consist of five stages, the five Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*) arise in that order.

Since ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) are not born in the five Pure Abodes—being inhabited only by Non-returners (*anāgāmin*) and Arhats—they are called the "Pure Abode Devas" (*śuddhāvāsakāyika*).
Furthermore, since ordinary worldlings have never been born there from time immemorial, if one should attain [them]...

Once they have realized the state of an Arhat through that concentration, they no longer create new karma, nor do they possess any remaining old karma. How, then, can those Non-returners (anāgāmin) be born there?

Therefore, they rely on one of the lower three heavens, or initially rely solely on the Heaven of Vast Results (Bṛhatphala). By means of the meditative cultivation of the mixed dhyāna (vyavakīrṇa-dhyāna), they repeatedly cultivate it before and after;
in the interim, they cultivate the contaminated (sāsrava) states to assist that previous birth, which was produced during their stage as ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) in the lower realms.

Thus, through karma, one’s state is transformed into something superior, resulting in rebirth in the Śuddhāvāsa heavens. Consequently, there are three general conditions for the noble cultivation of the mixed meditative absorption (*miśrabhāvanā*):

first, for the sake of being born in the Śuddhāvāsa; second, for the sake of enjoying the blissful dwelling in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*); and third, for the sake of preventing the regression caused by afflictions.
Regarding the stage upon which this concentration relies, it initially exists only in the fourth dhyāna; once its cultivation is perfected, one relies upon this.

By the power of this [attainment], one is also able to practice the mixed cultivation (*vyavakīrṇa-bhāvanā*) of the lower three dhyānas. Regarding the physical basis (*āśraya-deha*), it was previously in the human realm of the three continents within the desire realm;

having later fallen away from that, one is subsequently born in the form realm. Relying on the power of the former [attainment] and supported by a body in the form realm, one likewise gives rise to the mixed cultivation of dhyāna.
In the commentary, the first and last heavens are omitted for brevity and are not mentioned as practicing mixed cultivation.
[Commentary: "Saha" (娑婆) is properly called *Sahā*, which translates as "Endurance.

This is because when various Bodhisattvas and others practice for the benefit and happiness of beings, they encounter many enemies, jealousy, and the oppression of manifold sufferings; they endure these wearinesses and accept them, and thus it is named accordingly.
The *Karunāpuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "Because all classes of sentient beings endure their afflictions without giving rise to weariness or aversion, it is therefore named [Saha]."
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* concerning the Sahā World states: "What is meant by 'world' (*loka*)? 'World' refers to the world of time (*loka*) and the realm of space (*dhātu*).
The ten directions constitute the realm; the three periods of time constitute the world. Therefore, it is called the 'world'."

[Commentary]: Regarding the transformation of the land by the nirmāṇakāya: those Brahmā kings may arise as transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) through the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi-bala*) and come to the Buddha’s assembly;

or, through the power of meditative concentration, they transport themselves here. However, the ground of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is coarse and porous, and cannot support the subtle body of a Brahmā king.
Due to the power of the Brahmā king’s merit and virtue, his palace transforms spontaneously as a receptacle-world (*bhājana-loka*) following his own body.
The realms abide by depending upon it.

[Sūtra]: Regarding those who transform among the various destinies—"transformation" (vikāra) refers to changing, such as transforming the small into the large, the large into the small, or the beautiful into the ugly;
"emanation" (nirmāṇa) refers to that which suddenly appears where there was nothing. Whether it be transformation or emanation, all the infinite forms and types [are included therein].
"Come to the assembly.

[Commentary: As for the statement that "humans possess only four [types of attainment] because they lack those acquired through non-arising," the principle of the three vehicles cultivating the supernormal powers is as commonly discussed.

The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states that there is a *dhāraṇī* called "holding the cause" (*hetu-dhāraṇī*) and "holding the benefit" (*anuśaṃsa-dhāraṇī*); this is what enables one to travel to the worlds of the ten directions and is termed a "mantra."

Attaining supernormal powers through medicinal substances is like the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna, who possessed a supreme, wondrous medicine that enabled him to become invisible, soar through the air, and enter water without drowning;

this is called attaining powers through medicine. Attaining powers through karmic force is like King Pāṇḍu, who, by the power of his karma, traveled back and forth via supernormal powers; this is called attaining powers through karma.

It should be understood that such powers exist within the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*). Within the animal realm (*tiryagyoni*), beings such as nāgas and garuḍas possess both innate and acquired supernormal powers, as explained in the *Abhidharmakośa*.

The treatises state that when one first takes birth within the hell realm, one attains the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*) and is thus able to know the evil karma one committed in the past;

however, at the time of actually undergoing suffering, because one is oppressed by that pain, one is unable to remember it. Regarding those who possess the power of karma, the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra*—as cited in the sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*)—explains this in successive order.

[Commentary]: As for "those beings," by means of the Buddha’s earth-shaking great compassion and miraculous transformations, those in the three miserable realms and the eight states of no leisure are all caused to leave behind their suffering and hardships and proceed together to the Buddha's presence.
Furthermore, a certain class of beings, having passed away from those realms, are reborn among humans or devas;
they remember their past lives and, rejoicing in the Buddha’s profound kindness, proceed together to the Buddha's presence.
[Commentary]: *Rāhu* (羅睺) here means "Grasper of the Sun" (*sūryagraha*). When the Asuras wage war against the Devas, the Four Heavenly Kings first engage them in battle.
The Sun and Moon Devas assist the Four Heavenly Kings by emitting intense radiance and shooting it at the Asuras.

Since these serve as the vanguard for the Asuras, they seize the sun with their hands to obstruct its light; therefore, he is called the "Grasper of the Sun. Regarding "Valiant and Strong" (*vīrabala*), this is the old [translation].
Pāñcika (newly transliterated as *Bázhìkā*); this means "one with a round and full body," so called because his physical strength is abundant and possesses superior utility;
in meaning, it is translated as "valiant. Next is the Holder of the Sun (*Āditya-bandhin*); when he fought with the gods, he possessed valiant strength.

As for Mālādhāra, the Sanskrit is *Kharaskandha* (*khara* is pronounced with the departing tone, *skandha* with the level tone); this means "Broad Shoulders," so called because his physical appearance is most massive.
Regarding the names: "Huaman" (Mālā) is translated as "wife," and "Gong" (Pitṛ) refers to the father.
[Commentary: As for the "devas," since the scriptural text has already listed the celestial hosts of the three realms, it mentions the *asuras* and so forth.
According to the *Śāriputra-paripṛcchā-sūtra*, there is a distinct class of spirits within the deva realm who possess supernatural powers and transformations; these are called "devas."
The divine body possesses radiance and dwells within a palace in the realm of empty space.
[Commentary] As for the "dragon spirits" (nāgas), they are those capable of transformation, entering the water, soaring through the air, raising clouds, and measuring the rain.
The *Āgama* Sūtras state that there are four kinds of dragons: first, the celestial dragons (*deva-nāga*), who uphold the celestial palaces so that they do not fall; second, the... [text continues].

Because humans raise clouds and rain; because the dragons of the third stage support the great earth; and because the dragons of the Four Kings guard the royal treasuries—as cited in the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra*, Chapter on Reverent Upholding.

[Commentary: *Yakṣa* was formerly called *yecha*. Paramārtha translated it as "light and agile deity" (*qīngjiàn shén*), while Cien translated it as "valiant and robust" (*yǒngjiàn*) or "violent and malevolent.
It refers to those who fly through the air and devour living beings; this is the male form.
The female, who travels upon the earth, is called *rākṣasī*, which means "terrifying ghost."
[Commentary]: *Gandharva* means "one who moves seeking fragrance" (*gandha-hārī*), because they seek out music by searching for the scent of food.
The *Jing yinyi* (Meanings of Words in the Sutras) states that they exist within the ocean and belong to the Asuras; they dwell among the ten precious mountains as musicians.
When the sons of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven desire music, these deities possess extraordinary physical characteristics through which they perceive the intentions of the gods.
They go there to amuse themselves; those with horns are called *kiṃnara*, and those without horns are called *gandharva*.

[Commentary]: Regarding the "wondrous-winged birds" (*garuḍa*), in the *Āgama* sūtras the Buddha told the bhikṣus that there are four types of birth for wondrous-winged birds—namely, egg-born, womb-born, moisture-born, and transformation-born—and likewise four types of birth for dragons—egg-born, womb-born, moisture-born, and transformation-born. The egg-born wondrous-winged bird eats eggs.
If a garuḍa born from an egg intends to eat a nāga born from a womb, the bird’s life is immediately lost.

Thus, a garuḍa born from a womb who eats nāgas born from eggs or wombs, a garuḍa born from moisture who eats nāgas born from the three [other] modes, and a garuḍa born through transformation who eats nāgas born from all four modes—there are four such types of garuḍas.
Among them, the Greatly Majestic Garuḍa King possesses such great majesty that all nāgas are terrified of him.
Thus, first, its two great bodies and two wings span three million three hundred and sixty thousand *li*;
second, its belly is fully distended with dragons, which it constantly devours until satiated; third, beneath its chin is a wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*);

and fourth, as the *Loutan jing* (Kāraṇḍavyūha-sūtra) states, the King of the Golden-Winged Birds dwells on the southern side of Mount Sumeru, facing the northern side of the great ocean, each possessing a palace of vast extent.

It is twenty-four thousand li in length; its sevenfold city walls are all made of the seven treasures, and it has sevenfold railings, trees, groves, and gardens where small birds warble in harmony as if of a single kind.
[Commentary] *Kinnara* is translated by Cien as "Singing Deity" (*gāna-deva*), because they sing in accordance with what the Buddha has taught, just as worldly musicians sing of a ruler's virtues.

In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, both the *Gandharva-caryā* and this singing deity are referred to as "Heavenly Sons" (*devaputra*), which clarifies that they belong to the celestial realm (*devagati*).
There are four types of singing deities, as described in the *Lotus Sūtra*.
[Commentary]: "Large-bellied" (*mahodara*) refers to having a large belly. "Great python" (*mahābhujaṅga*) means a great serpent, a king of snakes.
"Field-cricket" (*kṣetrakarkaṭaka*): *karkaṭaka* is pronounced *fu* (as in *fǔ*). The *Qieyun* states it is a specific name for the *qián* and *kǎng* insects.
Because these are numerous in the fields, they are called "field-crickets. Those without legs are pythons, while those with legs are crickets; both are termed "large-bellied."
[Commentary]: Regarding the two types of karma—general retribution for evil karma and specific retribution for good karma—one receives their fruits within a single realm of existence.
[Commentary]: From "humans and non-humans" up to "the True Dharma," among the eight classes of beings (*aṣṭa-nikāya*), there are those with human forms and those with non-human forms.

The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states that there are four types of spiritual capacities (*indriya*): first, those whose vehicle is urgent but whose precepts are lax; because their precepts are lax, they fall [into lower realms].

Among those in the animal realm, there are four types: first, those whose vehicle is swift but whose vision is slow; because they are swift in their vehicle, they see the Buddha and hear the Dharma. Second, those whose vehicle is slow but whose discipline is swift;

because they are swift in their discipline and strictly maintain the precepts, they are born among humans or devas, yet because their vehicle is slow, they do not hear the true Dharma. Third, those for whom both vehicle and discipline are swift;

these include wise ordinary beings as well as all noble sages, who are constantly born among humans or devas, seeing the Buddha and hearing the Dharma. Fourth, those for whom both vehicle and discipline are... [slow].

Those who are lax regarding the precepts constantly dwell in the three miserable realms and do not hear the True Dharma; it is said that those who are lax regarding the precepts are not truly considered lax because they still manage to hear the Dharma.
However, those who are lax regarding the Vehicle (yāna) are truly considered lax, for they do not hear the True Dharma and sink into the evil paths.
Thus, most of these eight classes of beings are those who are lax regarding the precepts but urgent regarding the Vehicle.
[Commentary]: Regarding the "land that is transformed," the *Fahua shu* (Commentary on the Lotus Sutra) states:

"The purity of the buddha-lands is manifested because they are born from supramundane roots of goodness that are incomparably superior; thus they are vast and pure. Those born from mundane roots of goodness are neither pure nor vast.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, among its eighteen transformations, includes four types of this [transformation]. First:

First, it is the manifestation of the appearance of the pure lands of the ten directions; second, it is transformation, which refers to the transformation of the pure land within this very sutra text;
third, it is mastery over what is produced, meaning the manifestation of lion thrones and various kinds of flowers and so forth;
fourth, it is the ability to bestow peace and happiness, meaning that upon the lion thrones, Buddhas appear to preach the Dharma, thereby bestowing the joy of the Dharma.

[Commentary: Regarding the "lion throne," just as the Buddha is able to subdue Māra as a lion can subdue all beasts, the Buddha’s majestic virtue and sovereign power within the assembly are like those of a lion among animals;

because a seat upon which a person sits is called a "lion throne," he manifests a pure land here to indicate that the pure land is the cause for teaching the *Prajñāpāramitā*, and thus he manifests ten billion [lands].
The seated ones represent that ten billion Tathāgatas throughout the great trichiliocosm are simultaneously preaching the *Prajñāpāramitā* and have attained fearlessness.
[Sūtra]: Regarding the phrase "among them," one might ask: it is sufficient to manifest the gathering of the transformed assembly; why is it necessary to manifest the Buddhas preaching the Dharma?
The intended meaning of the answer is to show that when Śākyamuni wishes to preach the *Prajñāpāramitā*, all Buddhas do likewise, thereby signifying their simultaneous teaching.
[Commentary: Regarding the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and other texts, sentient beings of the second dhyāna perceive the kalpa-ending conflagration of the lower realms;

yet my Buddha’s pure land remains as it was, peaceful and secure, filled with bodhisattvas, devas, and humans. This is because within a single location of a Buddha-land, both the distinct and the dual aspects of purity and impurity are manifested.
[Commentary]: Regarding the "White Day of the Lotus Sūtra," the scripture states: "Today the Tathāgata shall preach the Mahāyāna sūtra named *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the *Anantārthasthiti*.
Whether in terms of teaching (*śāsana*) or principle (*nyāya*), these are all the "locus" (*sthiti*) from which the True Suchness (*tathatā*) flows.

"Locus" (*sthiti*) carries the meaning of that from which things are produced; it signifies the immeasurable teachings and principles produced from that [True Suchness], thereby manifesting its nature.
The name "Infinite Meanings" refers to the Samādhi of the Place of Infinite Meanings; it is named after its object, thus it is the Samādhi of the Place of Infinite Meanings.

[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "Now, at this time," etc.: when the Buddha first preached this sutra on the eighth day of the month, he entered meditative concentration and emitted light to signify his intention to preach.
Because the essence of the Eightfold Path of Prajñā is the foremost among all dharmas, the Sūtra speaks of the "eighth day" to signify that it is not night;
it further states, "Today the Tathāgata emits a great radiance," signifying that the sun of Prajñā-wisdom is brilliantly clear, shattering the darkness of delusion.
It is like the white sun illuminating all things; thus, Vimalakīrti says, "The Tathāgata moves..."

The use of giving is capable of subduing those sentient beings to be converted; all matters concerning the turning of the Wheel of Dharma are not established in vain, for each has its manifest purpose. [Commentary:

"The Imperial Tang governs the calendar, taking the month of Yin as the beginning of the year. Here, "Imperial" (Huang) means "Great" (Dai). The "Calendar Office" (Liluan Guan) refers to those who manage the imperial edicts regarding calendrical calculations.

It was named after the creation of the calendar; the establishment of the beginning of the year falls in the month of Yin (the first lunar month). In ancient times, the Xia, Yin, and Zhou dynasties each established their beginnings differently.
The Xia dynasty established the beginning of the year in Yin; "Yin" implies drawing forth, as it is the month when all things draw forth and begin to grow.
The Yin dynasty established the beginning of the year in Chou; "Chou" denotes a state of obscurity, as it is the month when all things have begun to grow but have not yet sprouted.

During the Zhou dynasty, the first month was established as the beginning of the year; "zi" (rat) signifies the appearance of initial birth, and since each [month] marks the commencement of the first yang-energy, it serves as the head of the year.
Regarding the three seasons of the Western Heaven (India), there are briefly two explanations:

one, according to the *Lokadhātu-sūtra*, the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra*, and various Vinaya texts, the period from the sixteenth day of the twelfth month to the fifteenth day of the fourth month constitutes the spring season. From... [text continues]
From the sixteenth day of the fourth month to the fifteenth day of the eighth month is the summer season;

from the sixteenth day of the eighth month to the fifteenth day of the twelfth month is the winter season. Each season lasts four months. Each month has a "dark" (kṛṣṇa) and a "bright" (śukla) fortnight;

in the Western Heaven (India), the dark fortnight comes first followed by the bright, which together constitute one month. According to this reckoning, the month of *Chou* (丑) is the first month, which corresponds to the current twelfth month.

The twenty-third day of the month is the first day of the spring season; the eighth day is the second [day]. According to the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* and the *Xiyu ji*, there are three seasons in a year:
from the sixteenth day of the first month to the fifteenth day of the fifth month is the hot season (*uṣṇa-kāla*);
from the sixteenth day of the fifth month to the fifteenth day of the ninth month is the rainy season (*varṣā-kāla*). From... [the winter season].
From the sixteenth day of the ninth month to the fifteenth day of the first month constitutes the period of cold (*śīta-ṛtu*).

According to this reckoning, if the first month is the second lunar month (*yǐn*), then the twenty-third day of the current first month is the beginning of the period of heat (*uṣṇa-ṛtu*); since it is the eighth day of the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*) of that month, it is said to be the "eighth day of the eighth month of the year.

However, the translators [of the Chinese canon] discarded the system of the first month being the eleventh lunar month (*zǐyuè*) established during the Zhou dynasty at the time of the Buddha's appearance.
However, according to the current usage in this region, the first month of the year is established as the month of Yīn (the Tiger).

[Commentary] "Great Tranquility" (*mahā-śānti*) refers to the object realized through meditative concentration (*samādhi*). That is to say, because Prajñā is profound, vast, and infinite, it is called "Great";
because it is free from afflictions, karma, and suffering, it is called "Tranquil. Because its essential nature is tranquility, it is termed "Great Tranquility. 3.
"Mati" (samādhi) is translated here as "equal holding" (*samāhita*). Because the mind is held equally and turns toward a single object with one-pointedness, it is called "equal holding.

This equal holding is attained by both ordinary beings and noble ones; however, because that which is attained by the Tathāgata is superior to that of other ordinary beings and noble ones, it is further termed "wondrous.
Thus, this wondrous equal holding is named "Wondrous Samādhi. This samādhi is designated by way of its object as the "Great Tranquility."
This is the wondrous samādhi associated with the wondrous wisdom of observation (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*).

Having observed the Dharma to be taught through this supreme concentration, one subsequently emerges from meditative absorption and teaches the Dharma according to what was realized. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-śāstra* states that the accomplishment of *samādhi* has two aspects:

first, the accomplishment of sovereign power, because the body and mind are unmoving; second, the departure from all hindrances in accordance with that sovereign power. This refers to the initial power.
The meaning is this: if one does not enter meditative concentration (*samādhi*), there is conceptual discrimination and mental agitation, whereby one cannot realize or teach mastery over phenomena.
Now, having entered *samādhi*, body and mind are unmoving; being free from conceptual discrimination and mental agitation regarding phenomena, one is able to realize and teach mastery.
Regarding the subsequent power: it means that by entering *samādhi* and being free from all obstacles to concentration, one accords with the Dharma and realizes mastery in teaching.

Because if there were meditative obstacles (*samādhi-āvaraṇa*), one would lack mastery over realization and teaching (as explained at length in that commentary). Regarding the stage upon which concentration relies:

it is the fourth dhyāna, because its qualities of balanced concentration and wisdom are superior; the Buddha mostly relies on this stage, whereas other stages are not superior and he mostly does not rely on them.

[Commentary] Regarding the answer concerning the Buddha and others: the Buddha has no distracted mind and is always in a state of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Briefly stated, he manifests the signs of entering concentration for five reasons:

first, to serve as a model for later students so that they may practice concentration; second, to demonstrate that wisdom must be induced by relying upon concentration, thereby manifesting the signs of entering concentration to give rise to supreme wisdom;
third, to ensure that the dual cultivation of concentration and wisdom remains unshakable; [and fourth and fifth... to enter [concentration].

First, [the Buddha] is unshakable in the fulfillment of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) despite agitation and distraction; second, he is unshakable in the fulfillment of the wisdom of teaching the Dharma (*dharmadeśanā*) despite difficult questions;

third, because he enters meditative concentration to emit light and manifest supernormal transformations (*ṛddhiprātihārya*), for if he did not enter concentration, one might fear it were not an auspicious omen of a Buddha;

and fourth, to manifest the guidance of the three karmas (*trikarma*) of teaching the Dharma for the benefit of sentient beings—being able to "show" and "guide" is called "guidance," wherein bodily karma (*kāyakarman*) is able to initiate supernormal transformations.

The *Abhidharmakośa* states that these are called the three *prātihāryas* (modes of guidance): because they benefit sentient beings through the miraculous power of supernatural manifestation (*ṛddhi-prātihārya*), verbal action can give rise to the guidance of mind-reading (*ādeśanā-prātihārya*), which involves discerning and explaining the mental states of others;

and because it instructs in the cultivation of virtue and admonishes the abandonment of evil, mental action can give rise to the guidance of instruction (*anuśāsanī-prātihārya*). Furthermore, in the Mahāyāna teachings, these are termed the three wheels (*trimaṇḍala*).

This entry into meditative concentration (*samādhi*) manifests the fulfillment of the Tathāgata’s three secrets: emitting light is the secret of body (*kāyaguhyaka*), preaching the Dharma is the secret of speech (*vāgguhyaka*), and entering concentration is the secret of mind (*manoguhyaka*).
Because these three activities are profoundly secret and peerless, they cannot be fathomed by those in lower stages; thus, the fifth meaning is as explained in the commentary.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "attainment" (*samāpatti*) applies to both states with and without mind—such that within the nine successive attainments (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*), the mindless attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) is called an "attainment"—there are two interpretations.
First, "equal" (*sama*) refers to being in the state of meditative equipoise where body and mind are tranquil and balanced;
thus it is termed "attainment. In the attainment of cessation, even though the seventh and eighth consciousnesses are present, they are also termed the "equality of body and mind."

"Peaceful arrival" (*samāpatti*) means that the essential nature of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is able to arrive; thus it is called "arrival. This arrival of such [concentration] is termed "attainment" (*samāpatti*). Second, regarding the term "equal" (*sama*):

because one is far removed from the faults of dullness (*laya*), agitation (*auddhatya*), and the fluctuations of high and low during the preparatory application (*prayoga*) preceding concentration, it is called "equal.

Because one practices this equal application until reaching the state of concentration itself, what is reached is called "arrival. Thus, it is the arrival of such [equality] that is termed "attainment."

Regarding the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), the first eight have concentration as their essence, while the ninth, the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*)—the nature of which will be explained below—does not.

"Equanimity" (*samāhita*) refers to the aforementioned eight types of conscious meditative concentrations; their names are explained according to the two meanings previously applied to the attainments.
[Commentary]: Regarding this term "Abundant Virtue" (Śrāvastī), the *Shangsheng shu* states: "Śrāvastī; formerly called Shewei [Śrāvastī], it is a corruption and abbreviation.
This means 'Abundant Virtue. It is the name of the capital city of the kingdom of Kośala within the region of India.
To distinguish it from Southern Kośala, the capital city is used as the designation for the kingdom. That [city] is located within the kingdom."
The city of Śrāvastī is the ancient land of Abhaya-rāṣṭra.
[Commentary: Regarding Prasenajit, the *Shangsheng shu* (Commentary on the Superior Birth) states: *Prasenajit* is the former name for King Bimbasāra;
it means "King of Victorious Army," as he was victorious with the fourfold army of elephants, cavalry, chariots, and infantry. Aṅgulimāla—this...
"Cloud-Finger-Garland" (Aṅgulimāla) refers to his vow to kill a thousand people and take their fingers as a garland, from which he derived his name.
[Commentary] Śāriputra: To speak fully, his name is Śāriputtra. "Śāri" means "spring warbler," also known as the "stork" or the "cuckoo" (the hundred-tongued bird).
If it drinks spring water, it can speak with exquisite skill; if it drinks autumn... [text ends]
Because water cannot speak, it receives two names. The Venerable One’s mother was skilled in eloquent discourse due to having conceived him;
however, after giving birth, she lacked such rhetorical skill. Furthermore, his eyes were sharp and clear like those of a śāli bird;
because the son was born from her, he is called *Bhadrika* (Son of Bhadrikā). Since he is the son of Śāri, he is briefly called Śāriputra (Son of Śāri).

[Commentary: Subhūti is properly called *Subhūti*, which means "Good Appearance" (*Śubhavyūha*). At the time of his birth, the house and other surroundings were all empty, and auspicious signs appeared;
thus he was named accordingly. He is also called "Good Fortune" (*Śubhamati*) and "Empty-Born" (*Śūnyatā-ja*).
Both Śāriputra and Subhūti were of the Brahmin caste; the causes and conditions for their entry into the Dharma are explained elsewhere.
[Commentary: "Maitreya" is the correct transliteration of *Meṭṛiyaya*, which is translated as "Compassion" (*maitrī*). He receives this name based on three meanings:

first, because his mother, while pregnant with him, practiced loving-kindness (*maitrī*), the son is named after the mother; second, he establishes the name for himself, as it represents his own essential nature (*svabhāva-maitrī*);
and third, the name is established by his past vows, having made great aspirational prayers under a former Buddha Maitreya.

The vow to become Maitreya is also based on his clan name; because he established his surname through the practice of compassion, he is called the "Compassionate Clan" (Maitreya), using his clan name as his designation.
As for the "Lion’s Roar," it refers to the roar of the Dharma from one who has internally realized fearlessness, thereby subduing the māras.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "these and others," the term "others" refers to three categories of people; because it says "etcetera," it indicates that the inquiry is universal. The intent of the question is as follows:
What is the underlying purpose of the Tathāgata’s manifestation of signs? What kind of Buddha-work does he perform? What sublime Dharma does he preach?
For there are these various extraordinary auspicious signs. Regarding this question, there are briefly two interpretations. The first states that it was King Prasenajit [who asked].
Because those at the stage of the causal ground did not understand the Buddha’s intention, they questioned the assembly.

Second, although King Prasenajit did not fully know the entire realm of the Buddha’s fruition, he nevertheless possessed partial knowledge; he knew that the Buddha intended to preach the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, as stated in the subsequent text.
During the time of Dragon-Light King Buddha (*Nāgaprabhāsa-rāja-buddha*), the king was a Bodhisattva of the fourth ground, while the Buddha was a Bodhisattva of the eighth ground.
That he has reached this point today is sufficient proof that his rank is high and the conditions he has encountered have not been few; the karma he has planted must be abundant.

How could it be otherwise? He beheld the emission of light yet did not recognize it, and observed the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) yet did not understand it. This was merely a demonstration of the appearance of ignorance, intended to provoke questions and awaken the minds of the multitude.
[Commentary: "The Dharma is extremely profound" refers to the meaning of the teaching that the Buddha intends to expound.
Because those in lower stages do not know the intentions of those in higher stages, there is no one capable of answering.

[Sūtra] Regarding the extensive performance of music: it is offered as a musical tribute to express that the Buddha’s voice, emerging from meditative absorption to preach the Dharma, delights the minds of the assembly.
[Sūtra] Regarding the "trichiliocosm": this refers to one thousand sets of four continents, suns, moons, and so forth, up to the first dhyāna heaven.
Encompassed all around by the Cakravāḍa Mountains, its extent equal to that of the Second Dhyāna, it is called a Small Thousandfold World System (*sāhasracūdika-lokadhātu*).

Furthermore, ten such small thousandfold world systems constitute one ten-thousandfold; a hundred such small thousandfold world systems constitute one hundred-thousandfold; and a thousand such small thousandfold world systems constitute one millionfold.

Encompassed all around by the Cakravāḍa Mountains, its extent equal to that of the Third Dhyāna, it is called a Medium Thousandfold World System (*dvisāhasramadhyama-lokadhātu*). Furthermore, ten such medium [thousandfold world systems]...
A thousand [small chiliocosms] constitutes a *koṭi* (ten million); these ten million together form one *arbuda* (one hundred million).

A hundred such intermediate *dvisāhasra-lokadhātus* constitute one *niyuta* (one billion), and a thousand such intermediate *dvisāhasra-lokadhātus* constitute one *vibhūta* (ten billion). These thousand intermediate *dvisāhasra-lokadhātus* are the great *trisāhasra-mahāsāhasra-lokadhātu*.
It is entirely encircled by the Cakravāḍa Mountains; its magnitude is equal to the fourth *dhyāna* heaven. By combining the small, the intermediate, and the great, they form this great trichiliocosm.
It is called the trichiliocosm.

[Sūtra] Regarding the phrase "in each and every ray of light," it means that immeasurable and innumerable rays of light are emitted to signify that in immeasurable and innumerable worlds, all Buddhas are preaching the Prajñāpāramitā;
and that within each and every ray of light, immeasurable and innumerable flowers appear to signify that the multitude hears [the teaching].
Dharmakāra, by means of practicing the flower, brings forth the fruit of Bodhi;
its thousand petals are all golden in color, signifying that this teaching is the foremost treasure for all sentient beings throughout the great trichiliocosm.
Since the Tathāgata’s three karmas—whether lifting or setting down his feet—all turn the wheel of Dharma, they all possess symbolic significance.

[Sūtra] Regarding "Ganges sands": because there is a goddess named Ganga who dwells in the river, it is called the Ganges; it is correctly transliterated as *Gaṅgā*, though it is vulgarly abbreviated as "Gang.

The *Record of the Western Regions* states that to the northwest of the kingdom of Magadha are the Nine Black Mountains (*Kṛṣṇagiri*). To the north of the Black Mountains is the Great Snow Mountain (*Himavat*).
To the north of the Great Snow Mountain is Mount Gandhamādana; its fragrance is so pervasive that those who smell it become intoxicated. [The text continues with: "Snow Mountain..."
To the south of Mount Gandhamādana in the north lies the Lake Anavatapta. This lake measures fifty *yojana*s in length and breadth;
only those who have attained spiritual penetration can reach it. Its four shores are composed of the four jewels—gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal—and its bottom is strewn with golden sand.
The water is fragrant and delicious, possessing the eight meritorious qualities, and great Bodhisattvas [dwell there].
By the power of his vows, he dwells secretly within it and brings forth clear, cool water to provide relief for all sentient beings of Jambudvīpa.

From each of the four sides of the lake, a river issues forth: the one to the east is named Gaṅgā, the one to the south is named Sindhu, the one to the west is named Vakṣu, and the one to the north is named Sītā.
As each flows out, it circles the lake once and then flows into the great ocean according to its own original direction. Alternatively, [it may flow directly].
It is said that the underground currents flow beneath the earth, traversing the borders of China; this is the Dead River (*Mṛta-nadī*), which serves as the upper source of the Mengjin River.
As for the Gaṅgā River, it possesses five significant meanings and is therefore frequently used as a metaphor in the sūtras: first, because its sands are so abundant;

second, because worldly people collectively regard it as a water of merit, such that by bathing in it, sins are extinguished, and by casting oneself into it, one is reborn in heaven; third, because even though it passes through the period of cosmic destruction (*kalpa-saṃvarta*), its name remains.
It is always fixed that the four Buddhas frequently preach the sublime Dharma near this place because it is well known to the five classes of beings; therefore, it is often used as a metaphor.
Specifically, it takes as its metaphor the sand at the mouth of the pond when first emerging, which is forty *li* long and twenty *li* wide.
[Sūtra] Regarding "the eastern direction, etc.," the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (Chapter 401) states:

In the eastern direction, beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there is a final world named Ratnāvatī. Therein dwells a Buddha named Ratnagotra, who is currently expounding the Prajñāpāramitā to bodhisattvas.
A bodhisattva named Samantaprabha, seeing this radiance, the rain of flowers, and the shaking of the earth, questioned him.
The Buddha explained this in detail to that Buddha, and that Buddha granted his permission. At that time, Samantaprabha and his retinue arrived at this assembly;
having made offerings, praised the Buddha, and prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, they withdrew to sit to one side.
The manner in which the bodhisattvas from other directions came was likewise the same.
[Commentary: Regarding "hearing, reflection, and so forth," the essence of wisdom (*prajñā*) is one; however, based on its functions and its objects, there are many different names. These include:

the wisdom consisting of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*), the wisdom consisting of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*), and the wisdom consisting of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*); the wisdom of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā-jñāna*), the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā-jñāna*), and the wisdom of the emptiness of both;

the preparatory wisdom (*prayoga-jñāna*), the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), and the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*). All of these constitute the essence of contemplation. The *Fayuan zhang* states that the wisdom of hearing takes only...

The nature of this [wisdom] is the wisdom associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), and its accompanying factors also include the nature of the wisdom associated with the five sensory consciousnesses.

The seven consciousnesses do not externally perceive objects; they arise at the stage of Buddhahood from the eighth consciousness. All of these consist solely of the wisdom associated with the mental consciousness;

the first five consciousnesses lack the capacity for investigative mental activity (*ākāra*). Furthermore, the wisdom associated with the seventh consciousness does not function in the untainted state (*anāsrava*).
Because it is profound, supreme, and beyond conceptual deliberation, the Buddha possesses no wisdom consisting of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*); nor does it coexist with the eighth consciousness.

Regarding the essence of wisdom consisting of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*), when discussed in terms of both cause and effect, it is said to coexist with all eight consciousnesses. As for "wisdom consisting of hearing" (*śrutamayī-prajñā*):

"hearing" (*śruta*) refers to that which is able to listen, which is the ear-consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*), capable of hearing sounds; "consisting of" (*maya*) has the meaning of growth, development, and fulfillment; and "wisdom" (*prajñā*) has the meaning of discernment. [This arises] from hearing.

Because it arises from the Dharma, this wisdom is called "wisdom derived from hearing" (*śrutamayī-prajñā*). "Reflection" (*cintā*) refers to the mental factor of volition (*cetanā*); through the deliberation of volition, superior wisdom is subsequently produced.
Since this wisdom is accomplished by means of volition that is associated with its cause, and because this resulting wisdom is proximate to volition, it is called "wisdom derived from reflection.

This is an explanation based on the sense of proximity (*upapada-samāsa*). Alternatively, it may be explained as a *tatpuruṣa* compound: "reflection" has the sense of "realization," meaning that it clearly realizes the object.
