As for "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*), it has the sense of "attestation," meaning that it clearly attests the object.

The essence [of this wisdom] is precisely the number of concentrations; because this wisdom is accomplished through association with concentration, it is a *tatpuruṣa* compound based on proximity, as explained in the case of "wisdom consisting of reflection" (*cintāmayī-prajñā*).

The term "accomplished" (*bhāvanā*) is used in all cases to indicate that these three types of wisdom are accomplished by means of those three causes: hearing, reflection, and cultivation (*śruta-cintā-bhāvanā*).

However, using the terms "wisdom of hearing" (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) and so forth would lead to confusion with *karmadhāraya* compounds; thus, the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (vol. 42) states that "wisdom accomplished through hearing" pertains to all [three].

At that time, relying on names, one contemplates the definitive teachings of the Tripiṭaka and the instructions of teachers and friends; according to what is thus contemplated, one is able to understand them clearly.

In the stage of full maturation, one truly relies only on the meaning. Based on this initial stage, it is said that one relies only on names. This is called wisdom accomplished through reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*), which takes both name and meaning as its objects.
Sometimes the meaning is drawn out by the text, and sometimes the text is drawn out by the meaning; at this point, one has not yet completely abandoned reliance on names.
Because one observes the meaning by relying on the words, the wisdom produced through cultivation (*bhāvanā-mayī-prajñā*) takes only the meaning as its object;
having already been able to abandon the words to observe the meaning, it is like a person swimming in deep, swift water: one who has not yet learned does not let go of their support;
one whose learning is incomplete may either let go or cling; but one who is well-trained does not depend on a support, crossing over by their own power. The three types of wisdom are likewise.
Thus, these three types of wisdom are accessible to all practitioners of the three vehicles—whether ordinary beings or noble ones—and can all be aroused.

Once the mind of the three vehicles has been generated, prior to the Path of Seeing, during the Stage of Accumulation (*sambhāra-mārga*), there is much distraction and little concentration; one dwells mostly in the wisdom of hearing (*śruta*) and reflection (*cintā*), while the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanā*) is rarely aroused.

During the Stage of Application (*prayoga-mārga*), concentration is much greater than distraction; one dwells mostly in the wisdom of cultivation, while the wisdom of hearing and reflection is rarely aroused. As for the Path of Seeing of the three vehicles, it is exclusively [the wisdom of cultivation].

The wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanā-prajñā*) arises through internal contemplation of the principles of the truths, for it does not occur within a distracted mind. Thus, the three types of wisdom may arise during the paths of cultivation and no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-mārga*) of the two vehicles.
During the bodhisattva’s path of cultivation prior to the seventh stage, the states of concentration and distraction alternate, and the three types of wisdom may arise.

From the eighth stage upward, the untainted state (*anāsrava*) is continuous and there is no distracted mind at all; thus, there is exclusively the wisdom of cultivation. This is based on the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*. 8.

Regarding the phrase "above the stage [of the path]": the *Commentary on the Maitreya-śāstra* (Cien shi) explains that within a single moment of the essence of cultivated wisdom (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*), the ability to grasp external teachings and investigate their principles is called "wisdom derived from hearing" (*śrutamayī-prajñā*);
the ability to deeply deliberate upon the sequence of principle followed by text is called "wisdom derived from reflection" (*cintāmayī-prajñā*);
and the ability to realize and manifest clarity within these two is called "cultivated wisdom. Because noble wisdom is so rapid, it...

In a single moment of thought, the meaning is divided into three types of wisdom (*prajñā*), yet in reality they have no distinct essence, as they are solely the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*). Within the three realms:

in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there is no wisdom of cultivation, but there are the wisdoms of hearing (*śrutamayī*) and reflection (*cintāmayī*); in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), there is no wisdom of reflection—since whenever one gives rise to thought, one immediately enters meditative absorption—but there are the wisdoms of hearing and cultivation;
in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), there is no wisdom of hearing or reflection, but only the wisdom of cultivation. As for those [wisdoms of] hearing and reflection...

Regarding the fundamental [wisdom], it consists exclusively of cultivated wisdom (*bhāvanā-mayī-prajñā*), which encompasses both the preparatory (*prayoga*) and the subsequent (*pṛṣṭhalabdha*) wisdoms.
However, the intent of this sutra is that since practitioners of all three vehicles—whether ordinary beings or noble ones—all contemplate the Tathāgata, it includes all three types of wisdom.

Among them, for Bodhisattvas from the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) onward, they perceive the Buddha’s *dharmakāya* through the fundamental wisdom of the two emptinesses (*dvividha-śūnyatā*), while they perceive the *saṃbhogakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya* through preparatory and subsequent wisdoms during their stage as ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).

By means of preparatory wisdom (*prayoga-jñāna*), one contemplates the three bodies of the Buddha; by means of the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) following preparation, one contemplates the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) of the Buddha.
Although those [of the two vehicles] have realized the principle, it is not called the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), because it is not the locus upon which the qualities of merit depend.

The general purport of the sutra text is to instruct the practitioners of the three vehicles—both ordinary beings and sages—in observing the physical form of the Tathāgata, which is itself the signless dharma (*animitta-dharma*).
The Body. [Commentary]:
According to the intent of the *Treatise on the Awakening of Faith*, the fundamental essence of the mind-source is serene and eternally abiding; it is neither born nor extinguished.

Its nature is free from delusion and confusion, and it alone illuminates with clarity; this is termed "Original Enlightenment. Based upon this Original Enlightenment, a single thought-moment of the mind arises.
This is called non-awakening; because of this non-awakening, one is deluded regarding original awakening (prakṛti-pratibhāsa), and thus falsely undergoes the cycle of birth and death in other lands.
From those other lands, by following the sublime practices of others, one returns toward original awakening. Because it is as if coming from outside, it is called "Tathāgata" (Thus-Come One).

When returning to original awakening, all that is false and illusory is extinguished; the phenomena of the dream-like cycle of birth and death are simultaneously stilled, and there remains only the Dharma-body (dharmakāya) as suchness (tathatā).
It is like the great ocean when its waves have subsided and it is profoundly still and tranquil. [Commentary]:

Regarding "corresponding to the characteristics" (*dangxiang*—both characters pronounced with the departing tone): because the title of this chapter corresponds to the characteristics of the practice (*xingxiang*) expounded in the main text, it is named "corresponding to the characteristics."

[Commentary]: Regarding "sitting in the full lotus posture" (*paryaṅka-bandha*), the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "To place the two feet' insteps upon the two thighs is called sitting in the full lotus posture. [Commentary]:
Regarding "like an overturned vessel," the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* says: "One should listen attentively with a focused mind, so that it is not like an overturned vessel, thereby ensuring clarity."
Listen with reverence so that you do not act like a leaking vessel; reflect well so that you do not act like a defiled vessel;
and maintain mindfulness in sequence so that the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation arise, just as one would with an upright vessel, a complete vessel, and a clean vessel.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "How does one abide until the arousal of mental reflection?"—this is the treatise clarifying that the Bodhisattvas, out of their intense compassion, earnestly seek to exhort sentient beings to practice so as to emerge from the suffering of birth and death. "Arousal" (zuò) means to initiate;
at all times, they initiate mental reflection, vowing to transform those born through the four modes of birth without weariness.

[Commentary: Regarding those who are male and so forth, at the final stage of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), a male being conceives birth in the mother; he gives rise to desire for the mother and anger toward the father, competing with him over the female form.
Because of this hatred, he dwells within the mother’s womb leaning against her abdomen and facing her spine, as he is oriented toward the mother at the time of conception.
A female being, conversely, conceives birth by giving rise to desire for the father and anger toward the mother, competing with her over the male form; thus she dwells within the mother’s womb.

The fetus rests with its spine toward the mother's abdomen because at the time of birth it faces the father; thus, for a male, the activity is oriented forward, dwelling on the right side of the mother’s womb, while for a female, the activity is directed backward, winding in a contrary direction, and therefore dwelling on the left side.

[Commentary]: Regarding "the birth [state] and so forth," the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that for one newly receiving birth, the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) originally lasts for a maximum of seven days;
even if it does not perish then, it remains for no more than seven times seven days.

Those who have committed evil deeds possess an intermediate state like the light of a black sheep or a dark, overcast night (reflecting the superiority or inferiority of their karma, there are two types of intermediate states). Those who have performed virtuous deeds possess an intermediate state like the light of white clothing or a clear sky.

In the intermediate state (antarābhava) of the following night—of which there are two types, as explained according to their evil karma—one proceeds without obstruction toward the place of rebirth corresponding to the signs of that birth.
One sees one's own kindred and the place of rebirth. Those who have committed evil deeds see it as impure; they walk with their faces cast down. Those bound for the heavenly realms proceed upward;
those bound for the human realm proceed horizontally. If one has committed an act of non-restraint (asaṃvara) and is to be born in hell, one sees former companions and feels joy.
Rushing forward, they are then obstructed; this applies equally to the realms of hungry ghosts and animals, which are characterized by pure suffering.
As for other miscellaneous karmas, one is born in various places according to the goodness or evil of those specific actions.

Within the first seven days after entering the mother’s womb, it is called *kalala*, which means "mixture" (*miśra*) because it is a combination of the impurities of the father and mother, and "loathsome" (*kaluṣa*) because it is deeply disgusting. Once it has coagulated...
Because it remains solid yet is still thin within, during the second week it is called *arbuda*, which means "blister";
its shape is like that of a blister on a pea, with an interior and exterior like curd, as flesh has not yet formed. During the third week it is called *peśī*, which means "congealed mass";
because it is like warm blood that has slightly congealed, although it has already become flesh, it remains extremely soft.
Within the fourth seven-day period, it is called *ghanam*, which means "thickening"; because it gradually thickens, it becomes firm and solid enough to be slightly touched.
Within the fifth seven-day period, it is called *praśākhā*, which means "the stage of limbs";
like five lumps of clay joined together, the internal winds strike outward to produce the distinct forms of the body's four limbs and trunk.
Therefore, the preceding mass of flesh increases its limbs and features; within six or seven days, it is called the stage of hair, body hair, and nails because hair and body hair begin to grow.
Within seven weeks, it is called the stage of possessing the sense organs because the five faculties become fully developed, clear, and prominent.

Only after passing through these initial and final stages does it undergo the various accomplishments of the three months. If there is neither increase nor decrease, it thus conforms to the duration of the pregnancy.
When thirty-eight weeks have passed in the womb, it becomes fully developed; after four more days, the head turns downward and the two feet turn upward.
The fetal membrane then tears, and as one is forced toward the birth canal, various kinds of suffering arise.

At that time, though one is being pressed, depending on previous karma, the child’s hair and body hair may be sparse if the mother has consumed ash or salt during pregnancy, or [sparse] if the mother has consumed [certain substances] due to previous karma.

The embryo is born with a dark or reddish complexion that is warm and hot; or, due to the mother’s prior karma or her consumption of cold food or proximity to a cold chamber, the child is often dull-witted.
If the mother indulges in sexual desire, the child is often born with scabies, ringworm, and other such ailments.
If the mother is prone to jumping and leaping and lacks dignified deportment, the child will have deficient limbs, be crooked, and be restless. Thus is this foul body first grasped.
It dwells in dependence upon the impurity of the parents, and is subsequently nourished and grown by the mother’s impurity.
Since the present conditions are thus, it is brought about by karma as a body composed of one hundred evils and thirty-six impure substances.
Such an evil body cannot experience pleasure; its transmigration is inexhaustible, and it grows from conception through successive lifetimes (as described at length in the *Ratnakūṭa*).

[Commentary] Regarding the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and other texts, the four modes of birth (*yoni*) are discussed collectively as having four causes and conditions: first, karma-intention; second, the egg-shell; third, the womb;

and fourth, moisture (corresponding to the four births as explained in the commentary). Among these, transformation-birth (*upapāduka*) is the most excellent because it possesses the fewest conditions. Nevertheless, when a Buddha appears in the world, he mostly takes birth in the human realm through transformation, following the example of those born from a womb.
As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "The Tathāgata does not undergo transformation-birth"—this refers to [the Buddha's] manifestation of transformation.
Because there was no remaining physical body after birth and death, and because the Buddha wished to leave behind his physical form as *śarīra* relics, he accepted birth from a womb.

[Commentary] Regarding "equal to humans," the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states that when the Queen of the Pañcāla king gave birth to five hundred egg-born beings, she felt ashamed and placed them in a casket to cast away into the Gaṅgā River, where they drifted with the current. A neighboring kingdom collected them, and after some time had passed...
Each month thereafter, they each gave birth to a son; as they grew up, they were all valiant and fierce, such that everyone they encountered was subdued.

They then engaged in battle with King Pañcāla by force. When the queen learned of this, she recounted the previous events in detail, saying: "If my sons see me, they will certainly not cause you harm.
The queen ascended the city wall and addressed the five hundred men, explaining the prior circumstances: "If you do not believe me, you should all open your mouths."
The queen pressed her two breasts, and from five hundred channels of milk, each flowed into his mouth; at that moment, he was converted with faith, and both kingdoms became peaceful and secure.

King Pupuśata developed a boil on the crown of his head, from which a son was born with a countenance so dignified and handsome that when the king took him into the palace, everyone said, "I wish to nourish him.
This King Mūrdhaja (Crown-Born) was thus born from moisture; at the beginning of the kalpa, there were beings born by transformation, and later those born from the womb.

Regarding those who always possess all four modes of birth among animals: as for the four types of birth, the *Miāochì* (Garuda) eats dragons of all four types; ghosts are mostly born by transformation (*aupapāduka*) and only rarely by birth from a womb (*jarāyuja*).
For example, a ghost mother told Maudgalyāyana: "I give birth to five hundred sons by day, and likewise five hundred by night;

as soon as they are born, I eat them, yet in the end I can never satisfy my hunger. This refers specifically to ghosts born from a womb. As the *Abhidharmakośa* states: [the hungry ghosts are of four kinds...]

Humans and animals possess all four modes of birth; ghosts possess both womb-birth and transformation-birth; those in the hells, the various heavens, and the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) are born only by transformation.
[Commentary on] the dimensions of their bodies: The *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā* states: "The stature of humans in Jambudvīpa is three and a half cubits or four cubits;
for humans of the eastern, western, and northern continents, it doubles successively. For the gods of the desire realm, it increases by one-quarter of a *krośa* for each successive level."
In the *rūpa*-heaven *yojanas* increase by half a *yojana* for each of the first four levels; above these, they double successively, except that in the *Anabhraka* heaven they are reduced by three.
After one thousand years following the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, Vasubandhu composed a treatise stating that the body size of humans in Jambudvīpa corresponds to their own cubit (*hasta*):
they are three and a half cubits or four cubits tall according to the size of their respective bodies. As for the people of Pūrvavideha...
For the people of this continent (Jambudvīpa), a square measuring seven *hasta* [of their own] is equal to three and a half *hasta* of their own measure;
for the people of the western continent (Aparagodānīya), a square measuring fourteen *hasta* [of their own] is equal to three and a half *hasta* of their own measure;

and for the people of the northern continent (Uttarakuru), a square measuring twenty-eight *hasta* [of their own] is equal to three and a half *hasta* of their own measure, or four *hasta*. These proportions may be understood by applying the same logic accordingly.
*Rucaka* (盧舍) means "the bellowing great ox"; its size corresponds to two *li*, hence it is so named.
These two *li* are divided into four parts, with each part being half a *li*. The gods of the Four Great Kings (*Cāturmahārājika*) are half a *li* in height;
those of the Thirty-three (*Trāyastriṃśa*) are one *li*; those of Yāma are one and a half *li*; those of Tuṣita are two *li*; and those of Nirmāṇarati...

The Heaven of the Gods Who Control Others' Emanations (Paranirmita-vaśavartin) is two and a half *yojanas*; the Heaven of the Gods Who Enjoy Emanations (Nirmāṇarati) is three *yojanas*. A *yojana* signifies a measure of sixteen *li*.
The height of the gods in the Heaven of the Brahma Assembly (Brahmakāyika) is half a *yojana*; the gods in the Heaven of the Ministers of Brahmā (Brahmapurohita) are one *yojana*;
the Great Brahmā King (Mahābrahmā) is one and a half *yojanas*; the Heaven of Limited Light (Parīttābha) is two *yojanas*; and the Heaven of Immeasurable Light (Apramāṇābha) is four *yojanas*.
The Ābhāsvara Heaven is eight *yojana*s; the Parīttaśubha Heaven is sixteen *yojana*s; the Apramāṇaśubha Heaven is thirty-two *yojana*s;
and the Śubhakṛtsna Heaven is sixty-four *yojana*s. As for the Anabhraka Heaven, if one follows the rule of doubling, it would be one hundred and twenty-eight *yojana*s;
however, the treatises state that three are subtracted, resulting in a height of one hundred *yojana*s.

Twenty-five *yojanas* less three; why? Because they transcend the variable sensations (*vipariṇāma-vedanā*) of the third dhyāna and cultivate exclusively the sensation of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*), their bodily dimensions decrease.

Furthermore, because the retribution experienced is such due to differences in the karmic power of sentient beings, it cannot be questioned by way of ordinary phenomena, nor can it be increased or decreased. In the Puṇyaprasava Heaven, [the height] is two hundred and five [yojanas].

The gods of the Vast Fruit (*Bṛhatphala*) heaven are ten *yojana* in height; the Unconscious Beings (*asaṃjñisattva*) are the same as those of the Vast Fruit. The gods of the Unafflicted (*Avṛha*) heaven are five hundred *yojana*;

the Heatless (*Atapa*) heaven are one thousand; the Excellent Appearance (*Sudṛśa*) heaven are two thousand; the Good Vision (*Sudarśana*) heaven are four thousand; and the Ultimate Form (*Akaniṣṭha*) heaven are eight thousand.

Thus are the differences in the physical dimensions of the gods of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*). As for the sentient beings of the hells, the hungry ghost realm (*preta*), and the animal realm (*tiryagyoni*): [their measurements follow accordingly].
The dimensions of beings who fly through the air, those of water, and those of land vary infinitely in size; their physical proportions are not fixed.
Nevertheless, sentient beings born by transformation arise and perish instantaneously, whereas those born from eggs, wombs, or moisture all grow gradually and likewise decay and perish gradually.

[Commentary]: This "equality" clarifies that when Bodhisattvas benefit sentient beings within the three realms, they do so based on the categories of the four types of birth within the realm of sentient beings;
it does not refer to the container world (the physical environment) as the primary object of their aspiration. The following passage describes those who are not [such aspirants].

[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "Although the Bodhisattva... and so forth: this asks how those among the four modes of birth (*catur-yoni*) who are to be converted—specifically those within the three miserable realms (*durgati*) and the eight difficult conditions (*aṣṭākṣaṇa*)—are to be transformed.
Furthermore, it asks how those within the human or celestial realms whose faculties (*indriya*) have not yet matured are to be strengthened.

To explain this, it says: although the Bodhisattva’s vow is to transform beings through the four modes of birth and so forth, in reality, the sentient beings to be converted are transformed according to their respective circumstances.

The faculties [of those in] the eight difficult states and those not in such states wait for the time when their potential ripens, providing aid at the appropriate moment rather than through forced exertion.

[Commentary: Regarding those proceeding to the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), there is no intermediate state for the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*); thus, one does not depart from the two realms of desire and form.
Because one is established in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) and because there is no destination to which one proceeds, there is no intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
[Commentary: If one is associated with the non-conceptual ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), then the mind of contemplation that possesses signs is called "conceptualization.

Once one has attained non-conceptual contemplation and is in profound accord with the subtle contemplation of the ultimate truth, even the cultivation of a single hair’s breadth of goodness constitutes the departure from the world.

Those who proceed toward the noble state will certainly attain the fruit of Buddhahood; how much more so those with abundant merit! Therefore, one should not contemplate the characteristics of form (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*), nor contemplate the suchness of form (*rūpa-tathatā*).
[Commentary: This non-discrimination applies generally to what follows below. This refers to the term "not contemplating" found in the Sūtra;

it should be stated as "not contemplating the characteristics of sensation (*vedanā-lakṣaṇa*)" and "not contemplating the suchness of sensation (*vedanā-tathatā*)," and the same applies to perception (*saṃjñā*) and the others. [This also includes] the inversions of self, person, knower, seer, permanence, bliss, and purity.
Furthermore, one does not contemplate the marks nor the suchness of all conditioned phenomena, including even the powers and fearlessnesses; one does not contemplate their marks nor their suchness.

[Commentary] "Regarding 'etcetera'" means that regarding the four aggregates, having already abandoned conceptualization because they are devoid of the characteristics of an aggregate, one subsumes the characteristics back into [the nature].

The nature is like waves returning to water; apart from water there are no waves, for the waves are themselves water. Apart from the nature there are no characteristics, for the characteristics are themselves the nature.
Therefore, nature and characteristics are equal, and both object and cognition are suchness (*tathatā*). Observing in this way, one dissolves all characteristics;
this is intended as an antidote to the affliction of grasping at existence. Thus, even the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) upon which the discriminating mind relies is likewise eliminated.
[Commentary]: Based on the aggregates (*skandha*), sentient beings have since beginningless time been blindly devoid of the eye of wisdom.

Failing to understand that the five aggregates are empty and illusory, arising from conditions, they falsely conceptualize these aggregates as having a real self (*ātman*) and real phenomena (*dharma*).
If one grasps this body of the five aggregates as having a real, sovereign, supreme, and autonomous master, it is called "real."

Regarding the characteristic of a self (*ātman-lakṣaṇa*), there is a distinct attachment to each of these aggregates as having the superior function of maintaining its own essence through its own mode of being;

this is called the characteristic of a real entity (*dravya-sat-lakṣaṇa*). When the various differences in the emotional views of ordinary people and non-Buddhists are summarized, there are four categories for both the attachment to a self and the attachment to phenomena;
thus, there are four inversions for each (the numerical assignments are as in the commentary).

[Commentary]: "Self" (*ātman*) refers to that which exercises sovereign control. It is like a sovereign ruler because it possesses actual autonomy; it is like a minister because it is capable of decisive action.

Furthermore, the "sovereign" (*prabhu*) is the essence of the self, while the "minister" (*amātya*) is its function. Alternatively, the sovereign is the essence of the self, and the minister is what belongs to the self.

Within the twenty views, the notion of "self" based on the aggregates (*skandha*) corresponds to the meaning of being a sovereign, while the notion of "self" based on something apart from the aggregates corresponds to the meaning of being a minister. These two are combined [to form the view of self].

The ten views regarding the aggregates (*skandha*) that are clung to as objects of conception are all termed "the controller" (*īśvara*); the deluded sentiment that performs the conceiving is termed the "master" (*svāmin*).
This "self" (*ātman*) is the general designation, while "person" (*pudgala*) and "cognition and vision" (*jñāna-darśana*) are its specific characteristics.

[Commentary]: To conceive of a self apart from the aggregates (*skandha*) is like imagining a person exists apart from the chariot; to conceive of a self apart from the aggregates is called "conceiving of a self apart from the aggregates.
[Commentary]: Regarding "discriminating the self": to discriminate and cling to "self" and "what belongs to the self" (*ātman* and *ātmīya*) is entirely a perversion of mind (*viparyāsa*).

[Commentary: The *Asaṅga-śāstra* states that the "characteristic of self" (*ātma-lakṣaṇa*) refers to the continuity of the essence of grasping (*upādāna*). "Continuity" has the meaning of non-interruption;
it is the total grasping of the essence of the five aggregates as being permanent and uninterrupted that is called the characteristic of self.
Because one grasps the "self" of a previous life as the "mine" (*mama*) of this present life, [the treatise] now clarifies that which is grasped: the "self" of the previous life.

[Commentary]: Regarding "person" (*pudgala*), the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states that it refers to the successive transition to other realms of existence (*gati*) while taking on the characteristics of a human.
This means that the "I" of the present human realm who can transition to other realms such as the heavenly realms in future lives is what is called the "characteristic of a person.
To grasp at a future birth in a different realm—that is, the "I" of a future life—is precisely what is meant here.

[Commentary]: Regarding the term "knower," all treatises state that the Sāṃkhya non-Buddhists maintain the existence of a real self (*ātman*), and that this self is precisely volition (*cetanā*) which experiences all phenomena; this knower is the present self.

[Commentary]: "View" (*dṛṣṭi*) refers to the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*). To universally grasp the three periods of time and, through investigation and calculation, posit a self is called "view";
this is precisely the view of a self-body (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*). To grasp the body as the essence of the self and to regard it as a substantially existent body is called the view of a self-body.

[Commentary: "By these" means that taking self-grasping (*ātma-grāha*) as the head gives rise to all afflictive obstructions (*kleśa-āvaraṇa*), while taking grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*) as the head gives rise to all cognitive obstructions (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*).
Because of these two obstructions, one either gives rise to or creates karma, resulting in the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) and eternal sinking into the ocean of suffering.
Since these obstructions are so grave, they cause Bodhisattvas to cultivate the practice of non-abiding to remedy self and phenomena.

To be attached to these four kinds [of views] while failing to contemplate their inverted nature, yet failing to contemplate True Suchness (tathatā) so as to attain mastery over a clear mind— vast, empty, limpid, and tranquil—
and thus practicing without practice and crossing over without crossing, is called the Bodhisattva’s cultivation of the non-abiding dwelling.

[Commentary]: Only that which is non-conceptual is free from the marks of conceptualization. The meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) that are signless (*animitta*) are able to remedy the two kinds of inversion regarding self (*ātman*) and phenomena (*dharma*).

If there is contemplation with signs (*sanimitta*), such as conceptually observing the characteristics of the aggregates (*skandha*), or perceiving the aggregates as a self, a person, a knower, a viewer, or as permanent, blissful, and pure—then inverted attachments to these marks will not be eliminated, and this is itself a sickness. Such states will certainly be unable to eliminate the two inversions of self and phenomena.

Because the Bodhisattva employs the contemplation of the signless (*animitta*) as an antidote to the two inversions, the Buddha shows this by saying: "One does not contemplate the characteristics of form (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*), nor does one contemplate the suchness of form (*rūpa-tathatā*)," and so forth.

[Commentary]: This means that contemplating the signless within signs is itself the signless. Because essence (*svabhāva*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are mutually integrated, there is no duality between this and that. Therefore—

To contemplate form as formless is itself formlessness as form. The intent behind teaching this contemplative practice is to cause those who follow the current to return to the source, those lost on the path to awaken to the Way, those attached to existence to dissolve their marks, and those dwelling in causes to realize the fruit;
it is to cease delusion, return to the truth, and ultimately abide in eternal stillness.

[Commentary: "To cause [them] to be equal" means that for the sake of causing the bodhisattvas’ superior contemplation of signlessness (*animitta*) to manifest before them, all the superior practices they cultivate are entirely signless.

Thus, their ability to abide [in this state] is precisely because the great bodhisattvas who are the objects of observation reflect upon themselves and do not perceive signs, nor do they perceive suchness (*tathatā*).
Alternatively, there may be a certain class of practitioners whose superior practices are so lofty that they have already transcended signs.
Therefore, observing that which is capable of abiding is itself the object of observation; now, by demonstrating this again, one prevents the arising of a discriminating mind.

Thus, by observing that neither signs nor suchness are perceived—thereby subsuming these two categories—one correctly abandons the discriminating mind of self and other and abides in the practice of signlessness (*animitta*).

[Commentary] Furthermore, regarding the phrase "and so forth," this is based on the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* to provide a further explanation of the meaning of the three preceding sections of the text through the three practices of abiding, cultivation, and subduing.
"One should abide thus" means to abide in a signless mind (*animitta-citta*) in order to advance toward great enlightenment.

"To transform and teach the four modes of birth" means to cultivate altruistic practice in order to transform sentient beings. This includes not observing the characteristics of the aggregates (*skandha-lakṣaṇa*), not observing the suchness of the aggregates (*skandha-tathatā*), and so forth.
Regarding the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas as well, one does not observe their marks nor such [characteristics];
this is to demonstrate the subduing of the mind that clings to marks and discriminates, thereby causing it to relinquish marks and accord with the principle of marklessness to realize parinirvāṇa.
Thus, these three serve as the causes for attaining the three virtues and the fruit of Buddhahood as the three bodies (the three virtues are as follows).

[Sūtra] Why is this so? It is because it was previously stated that one does not contemplate the characteristics of the aggregates (*skandha*), nor does one contemplate the suchness (*tathatā*) of the aggregates;
even contemplating the Buddha or Bodhisattvas is likewise non-contemplation. Why is this "non-contemplation" so called?
[Sūtra] By means of the various "equalities," this section reiterates and expands upon the meaning of the three preceding passages concerning the non-contemplation of form and so forth.

Although the preceding text explained the principle of the practice of dispelling marks (*lakṣaṇa*), its full significance was not yet exhausted; therefore, this inquiry is raised to provide a detailed exposition.

By subsuming marks back into their nature, the five aggregates and all phenomena are the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Consequently, one does not contemplate the marks of the aggregates, nor does one contemplate the suchness (*tathatā*) of the aggregates.
This is the reason why [the text says] "and so forth.

[The Commentary] explains the four inversions regarding phenomena (*dharma*) and so on: sentient beings, from time immemorial, rely upon the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and falsely cling to permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
Taking the eighth consciousness as the grasping mind, they perfumate it; because of this perfuming, the perfuming of self-clinging (*ātma-grāha) is formed.

Habits reside within the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*); from this, the waves of consciousness flow without ceasing, with the four characteristics cycling in succession—coming and going, arising and ceasing.

If one realizes that the essence of what is falsely grasped through inverted conceptualization is itself emptiness, then it is merely the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), which neither comes nor goes, neither arises nor ceases. Therefore, it is said to be permanent, blissful, and pure.
"Inversion does not contemplate characteristics, nor does it contemplate suchness. [Commentary:

"To be identical with the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*)" means to be free from delusion, which is termed "True" (*zhen*). The "Dharma-base" (*dharmatā*) is termed the "limit" (*koṭi*); the myriad practices are its function, while the limit of reality is its essence (*tattva*).
Because the function extensively pervades and resembles the essence, it is said to be "identical with the limit of reality. Among all practices, one performs them all.

Their practice is empty, harmonious, and unimpeded, equal to the *dharmatā*. For this reason, regarding all practices such as the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), they do not contemplate their marks (*lakṣaṇa*) nor contemplate their suchness (*tathatā*).
[Commentary]: Although all [phenomena]... [Question]: The *dharmatā* of all phenomena is fundamentally eternally abiding, nameless, ineffable, and by nature detached.

For what reason are names established through verbal expression to extensively differentiate between various inverted and non-inverted phenomena, up to and including the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*), the six perfections (*pāramitā*), and conventional and ultimate truths—causing those who hear them to engage in conceptual speculation based on words and give rise to all manner of delusions?
Why, therefore, would the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas speak of these? This [text] explains it as follows: "It is indeed as you have questioned."

Although the nature of all phenomena is primordially abiding, nameless and ineffable, its nature transcending verbal expression, sentient beings are born without wisdom or understanding and fail to recognize right from wrong.
If one does not manifest right and wrong through words, deluded and confused sentient beings would have no means to awaken, cultivate, realize, and attain liberation;
therefore, within that nameless dharma, one employs skillful means by means of speech.
He manifests this by using speech to teach the wordless Dharma, so that beings may understand it,
abandon their inversions, cultivate non-inverted practice, undertake the six perfections, and realize the fruit of true permanence; thus,

Buddhas and Bodhisattvas appear in the world to extensively reveal various Dharma gates and instruct sentient beings to study these means of abandonment, for it is not otherwise for those who would learn.

Although one practices according to the teachings, if one has not yet transcended signs—meaning that one still perceives distinctions between speaker and spoken, ordinary and holy, self and other—one is obstructed by these signs from attaining the superior merit of signlessness on higher stages.

Therefore, the Buddha instructs one to contemplate Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and so forth as being non-dual, undifferentiated, and without distinction, just like space; this is the meaning of the second interpretation.

This extensively elaborates upon the meaning of the preceding five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). As for the true nature (*tathatā*) that serves as the substratum for all phenomena of the five aggregates, its essence is real;
therefore, it is said that the nature of all phenomena is itself reality. When this nature is perfumed by delusion, it is like a pearl being smoked:
the pearl itself does not receive the perfume, yet because of the smoke, soot and dust arise as an obscuration upon the bright pearl.
When people do not see the pearl, they see only the appearance of smoke and dust upon it; the true nature is likewise so, yet it is defiled by the deluded consciousness of sentient beings.
The true nature does not receive this defilement, but because of the influence of delusion, illusory dust arises upon that nature.
This dust obscures the true nature, such that people do not see the nature but see only illusory appearances—the phenomena of the five aggregates coming and going, arising and ceasing.

Now, I shall explain for you that the nature of the five aggregates and all phenomena is fundamentally empty and quiescent; it is the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), without coming or going, and without arising or ceasing.
The meaning of the next two lines is that because the nature exists within the characteristics, the characteristics are called by the same name as the nature, and thus they are said to be "equal.
The meaning of the final two lines is to instruct the Bodhisattva to settle the mind in śamatha and vipaśyanā, so that nature is obliterated and characteristics are extinguished.
The object of observation is perfectly interfused, beyond all dependence, non-dual, and undifferentiated, like space, which is neither distinct nor dual.

This is the meaning of the third interpretation. As previously stated, the World-Honored One instructed the Bodhisattvas not to observe the characteristics of the aggregates (*skandha*) nor the suchness (*tathatā*) of the aggregates;
these are all differentiated marks that should not be observed. Instead, one should observe the eternally abiding true reality of the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*).

That which is called the dharmatā is eternally abiding because it transcends the three periods of time; thus, there is no coming and no going. It is eternally abiding and unchanging because it transcends arising and ceasing;
thus, there is no birth and no extinction. The rest of the text may be understood accordingly.

[Sūtra] Regarding the characteristics of the aggregates (skandha), bases (āyatana), and elements (dhātu): while the teachings of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna differ slightly and agree largely on the meaning of these three categories, I shall now explain the Mahāyāna sūtras by briefly summarizing the Mahāyāna exposition as taught in the second fascicle of the Abhidharmasamuccaya. There are three meanings of "aggregate" (skandha):
first, the sense of accumulation (*caya*). This refers to form (*rūpa*), which is of eleven kinds: first, the past; second, the future; third, the present...

The essential nature of the aggregates (*skandha*) is explained as the concise summary of ten types of form: (1) the four internal forms of the five sense faculties; (2) the five external forms of the five sense objects;
(3) coarse resistant form; (4) subtle non-resistant form; (5) inferior disagreeable form; (6) superior agreeable form; (7) proximate form of one’s own realm; and (8–10) distant form of other realms.
Because they cannot be gathered together, yet possess the meaning of being a "gathering," they are called aggregates (*skandha*). This applies to feeling (*vedanā*) as well.

The meaning of the aggregates of perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) is to be understood by analogy with these two [preceding] ones. Third is the sense of "vastness," because the characteristic of suffering is vast;

and fourth is the sense of "bearing the burden," because one bears the burden of affliction (*saṃkleśa*). The first [aggregate, form] applies universally to both ordinary beings and sages, whereas the latter two do not.

This sequence is as follows: one abides in accordance with consciousness; first, the aggregate of form is established because one experiences [objects] according to their formal characteristics, and one grasps them as they are experienced.

Because one knows as it is known, because one intends and acts as it is intended, and because one discerns as it is intended and acted upon, form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness follow this sequence.
However, according to worldly convention, there are five bases for the notion of a self:

the basis of the self’s body and possessions, the basis of the self’s enjoyment, the basis of the self’s speech, the basis of the self’s activity, and the basis of the self’s own essence; these are now being revealed.

These aggregates (*skandha*) are merely the functional capacity of phenomena (*dharma*), lacking any real intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and being neither the self (*ātman*) nor what belongs to the self (*ātmīya*);

therefore, they are taught as five, neither less nor more. That treatise further states that the meaning of the bases (*āyatana*) is threefold: first, the sense of growth and production, because they produce the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*);
second, the sense of seed, because they are the causes of all phenomena; and third, the sense of encompassing the distinctions of all phenomena, because they include them all.

It is so because of various meanings; for it is by means of seeing worldly signs, inquiring after one's health, receiving ointments and incense, accepting food, and providing service that distinctions are made.
Therefore, the Buddha taught the sequence of the bases (*āyatana*) in this manner. As for the elements (*dhātu*), there are three meanings:

first, the meaning of maintaining their own nature, because the faculties, objects, and consciousnesses each maintain their own nature; second, the meaning of maintaining the nature of cause and effect, because of the faculties and the objects...

Because they can sustain the six consciousnesses, the third [meaning] is the sense of "lineage" (*gotra*), for these six categories—the faculties, objects, and consciousnesses—each constitute a lineage.
Because the consciousness element arises in accordance with the sequence of the preceding bases, the sequence of the eighteen elements is thus established.

That which can grasp an object consists of the six internal faculty-elements, such as the eye; that which is grasped consists of the six external objective spheres; and the object depends upon the faculty as its condition.
The characteristic of the six consciousness-elements (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna-dhātu*) is the discernment of objects that appear as objects.

Because non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) and others cling to the existence of a real self (*ātman*) that can sustain all phenomena, the Buddha established the "elements" (*dhātu*) in order to refute them; for an element is that which sustains phenomena, not a self that sustains them.

Furthermore, when the *Prajñāpāramitā* teaches that the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth are all empty, it is because non-Buddhists and others cling to a real self possessing various superior functions.

Those who rely on birth and learning sink forever into saṃsāra; therefore, in order to shatter their false attachment to a self, the Buddha employs skillful means to establish and teach that which is inexpressible—beyond the aggregates and so forth—as being the aggregates and so forth, instructing sentient beings to abandon what they have learned and lead them toward the truth so that they may forever emerge from saṃsāra.
However, those of the two vehicles and others do not understand this as a conventional expression of skillful means, and thus...

Regarding those who grasp at the existence of the dharmas of the aggregates (skandhas), bases (āyatanas), and elements (dhātus), the Tathāgata reveals that those grasped-at aggregates and so forth are entirely devoid of intrinsic nature.

Within causes and conditions, there is no reality of such dharmas as the aggregates; their nature is emptiness. Because there is no dependence upon aggregates and so forth, he teaches the emptiness of the aggregates through the doctrine of the three natures.
Thus, the Sūtra says: "The five aggregates are all empty," and it further states: "The eye-base is merely a name," and so on.

The sphere of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) exists merely as a name; from the emptiness of the eye-sphere up to the emptiness of the dharma-sphere, all eighteen elements (*dhātus*) are sequentially empty.

Nevertheless, the Buddha taught the Dharma—whether wholesome, defiled, or neutral; form or mind; cause or effect; conditioned or unconditioned—revealing infinite distinctions according to the capacities of sentient beings.
The Bodhisattva Vasubandhu established one hundred dharmas to encompass all phenomena, further [categorizing them] by means of three...

The one hundred dharmas are categorized under the [five] aggregates (*skandha*) so that they may be easily understood. Thus, the mental factors (*caitta*) are explained in detail while matter (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*) are explained briefly, clarifying how the one hundred dharmas are subsumed within the five aggregates.

The verse says: Matter comprises the eleven [categories] in their entirety; Sensation (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) each comprise one; The aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) comprises seventy-three;

And the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) comprises [the remaining] eight. Unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) are not included in the category of aggregates because they are not accumulations (*cita*). [This concludes] the brief explanation of matter. [Now follows] the detailed explanation of matter.
A brief explanation of the Dharma: the mind and mental factors clarify how the one hundred dharmas are subsumed within the twelve bases (*āyatana*). The verse says:

The five internal and five external bases, Ten material [bases] according to their own names, Eight are included in the base of mind (*manāyatana*), And eighty-two are all the base of phenomena (*dharmāyatana*).

An extensive explanation of matter and a brief explanation of mind clarify how the one hundred dharmas are subsumed within the eighteen elements (*dhātu*). The verse says: The five elements of the faculties and five of the objects, each...
The ten material [dharmas] follow their own names; the eight sovereigns (ādhipatya) are subsumed under seven minds; and all eighty-two are mental objects (dharma). [Commentary:

Regarding the meaning of "lineage" (gotra) and "realm" (dhātu): the eye faculty, its object of form, and the eye-consciousness constitute one lineage, and so on, up to the mind faculty, its object of phenomena (dharma), and the mind-consciousness, which constitute one lineage.
This very lineage serves as the homogeneous cause (sabhāga-hetu) to project and produce its own kind.
Because it is a result of uniform outflow (*niṣyanda-phala*), the realm (*dhātu*) itself has the meaning of being the cause.
[Commentary: Those who cling to a self as one and permanent give rise to false conceptualizations and attachments based on various views regarding sentient beings;

they either cling to the essence of this self as being unitary and its nature as eternally abiding, or they cling to this self as having the superior function of experiencing and receiving [objects], or they cling to this self as that which cognizes and grasps images, or they cling...

Regarding this notion that "I" am the agent of actions, the Buddha taught the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) in order to refute it. Within these five aggregates: it is by feeling (*vedanā*) that one experiences, not the self that experiences;
it is by perception (*saṃjñā*) that one grasps images, not the self that grasps images; it is by formations (*saṃskāra*) that one performs actions, not the self that performs actions.
The various non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*) hold diverse views and attachments regarding a self; they propagate false doctrines based on their deluded perceptions to deceive and mislead others.

The Tathāgata, out of compassion for sentient beings, teaches the aggregates (skandha), bases (āyatana), and elements (dhātu) in accordance with their various attachments, using this or that teaching to dismantle them;
thus, they are collectively established as the five aggregates, the twelve bases, and the eighteen elements.
[Sūtra]: "If for a bodhisattva the nature of sentient beings is non-dual," as previously stated, "a bodhisattva should abide thus to transform and teach the four modes of birth;

they do not contemplate the characteristics of the aggregates, nor do they contemplate the suchness of the aggregates," and so forth, up to "the bodhisattva and the Tathāgata likewise do not contemplate characteristics, nor do they contemplate suchness.
The sūtra itself explains this by saying: "Non-dual and without distinction, just like empty space. This intends to reveal that all phenomena are [thus].
Dharmas, sentient beings, bodhisattvas, and Tathāgatas are all non-dual; therefore, the word "therefore" (hi) serves to recapitulate the preceding question.

These three kinds of prajñā explained here further elaborate upon the meaning of the previous text regarding the practice of the signless contemplation (*animitta-vipaśyanā*) while abiding in the transformation of sentient beings.
[Commentary: Regarding the subsequent listing of the four inversions—permanence, bliss, self, and purity—this is a reiteration of the preceding text.

Because sentient beings, from time immemorial, have conceptualized and clung to the five aggregates, asserting that they possess permanence, bliss, self, and purity, [the text] first designates these aggregates and the four inversions, and subsequently reveals their emptiness.

[Sūtra] Regarding the meaning of the phrase "the nature of phenomena" (*dharmatā*) in the sūtra text: the nature of phenomena, which is suchness (*tathatā*), refers to the *prajñā* of the ultimate reality (*bhūtārtha*).
It does not abide within the five aggregates (*skandha*) or the four inversions (*viparyāsa*). Why is this? Because the nature of all phenomena is entirely empty.
When one returns to the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), all phenomena are nothing but absolute emptiness (*śūnyatā*); it can no longer be said that they abide in this or that place. Therefore...
The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) does not abide within the five aggregates.
[Commentary: Regarding "permanence, bliss, self, and purity," one should state in full that it does not abide in permanence, nor does it abide in non-permanence, and so on, up to:

it does not abide in purity, nor does it abide in non-purity. "Purity" refers to the inversion of purity; the others are termed "non-purity. This applies equally to permanence and the other [attributes]. The nature of phenomena...
Because one does not abide within the four inversions.

[Commentary] The phrase "fundamental" (*mūla*) and so forth intends to reveal that both object and wisdom are empty. By practicing the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*), one perceives that all phenomena are entirely true emptiness;
this gradually induces noble wisdom to perceive the realm of true emptiness—the object realized and the wisdom that realizes it.
All are entirely empty; therefore, it cannot be further said that the bodhisattvas who manifest emanations and the sentient beings who are manifested abide in this or that place.

This is because, according to the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), all things are empty and lack the characteristic of manifestation. If there were the characteristic of manifestation, it would constitute conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*), which belongs to the subsequent section of the text.

[Sūtra]: Regarding the phrase "because the nature of all dharmas is entirely empty," a general discussion of the meaning of emptiness comprises four categories in brief: First, the emptiness of non-existence (*abhāva-śūnyatā*):

Nāgārjuna and others teach that in the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), nothing is established; it is vast, still, and silent, and is therefore called "empty. Second, the emptiness of the imagined (*parikalpita-śūnyatā*):
This refers to the real self and real dharmas grasped by the deluded mind; while they appear to exist emotionally, they lack existence in reality.

Therefore, it is called "emptiness. Maitreya and others explain that the meaning of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) is all distinguished based on this. Regarding the first, the emptiness of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*):

Nāgārjuna’s *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states that all minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) are originally without intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), being provisionally established in dependence upon four kinds of conditions.
First, the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) refers to the various seeds (*bīja*). Second, the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) refers to the objective referent.
The three types of objects and the immediately preceding condition refer to how the former induces the latter; the four predominant conditions refer to the assistance provided by external conditions.
It is through these four conditions that mind and mental factors are collectively established; for if these four conditions were absent, no mind or mental factors would exist.

Thus, all minds and mental factors are empty, and all material phenomena (rūpa-dharma) originally lack intrinsic nature, being only provisionally established in dependence upon two kinds of conditions.

There are two conditions: the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*). From the synthesis of these two conditions, material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) arise;

since material phenomena do not exist apart from these two conditions, all matter is empty. Thus, the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of both matter and mind is fundamentally empty, yet the foolish do not know this and stubbornly claim they truly exist.
Therefore, the Buddha said: "The five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are all empty. This is spoken in accordance with conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

The emptiness of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya-śūnyatā*) is also called "illusory" in order to refute the view of nihilism; it has four aspects. First, the emptiness of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*), also called the emptiness of true nature (*tathatā-śūnyatā*).

Briefly stated, this refers to "true emptiness," meaning that the principle of *tathatā* is void, harmonious, and unimpeded, and because its very nature is emptiness, it is designated as "empty" by virtue of being revealed through emptiness.
This meaning of true emptiness is discussed in common across all teachings, as seen in the commentaries of the higher and lower vehicles.
The meaning of emptiness primarily relies on the fourth [emptiness], while also manifesting the remaining types of emptiness as can be seen according to the text.

[Commentary: To know, abandon, realize, and cultivate—by speaking of the True (paramārtha), one instructs others to know it; by speaking of the conventional (saṃvṛti), one encourages them to resolve their false attachments, realize it, and cultivate the study of the True Emptiness and Conventional Existence; the sequence is thus clearly elucidated.

[Sūtra] Regarding "meritorious action" (*puṇya*) and so forth: "merit" has the sense of excellence. Because the nature and fruit of various wholesome karmas are excellent and desirable, they are called merit.
Because the nature and fruit of unwholesome karmas are base and undesirable, they are called non-merit (*apuṇya*).

Karma that brings about rebirth in the celestial realms of the two upper realms is called "immovable action" (*āniñjya-karman*). It is not [the case that it is immovable in the sense of being entirely inactive].
Because one undergoes transformation by changing to another plane of existence, these can induce the fruits of the higher meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) and the formless realms (*ārūpya*).

Within these three types of action, there are further distinctions corresponding to the three time periods; therefore, it is said that "equal causes and effects both possess fetters" (*saṃyojana*), as indicated by the concluding text.

[Commentary]: Although [the sūtra] mentions "the eight afflictions" (*aṣṭau doṣāḥ*)—namely vitarka, vicāra, sorrow, suffering, joy, pleasure, inhalation, and exhalation—the first dhyāna eliminates sorrow, the second eliminates suffering and vitarka-vicāra, the third eliminates joy, and the fourth eliminates pleasure;
furthermore, the calamities of fire, water, and wind destroy the first, second, and third dhyānas respectively, while only the fourth dhyāna is free from these three calamities.

Regarding the purity of equanimity and mindfulness free from the eight afflictions: although the lower three dhyānas possess calamities and fluctuations, here we refer to the stages of the higher absorptions as "unshakable" (*aniñjya*).
Karma that brings about the fruit of this unshakable stage is called "unshakable karma. A second interpretation states:
furthermore, karma of the first dhyāna that draws forth the fruit of the first dhyāna cannot be altered; because its fruition is certain, it is termed "unshakable."

[Commentary]: Regarding the establishment of the name "immovable" (*āniñjya*) based on the fixed nature of karma and its fruit, this serves as a double conclusion for the two interpretations. Thus, Cien said:

"If 'immovable' refers to the fixed stage [of dhyāna], it applies to all [such stages]. If, however, it is named 'immovable' because one is not reborn in a different location, this is spoken from the perspective of the majority of cases.

For instance, when those who have practiced the mixed meditations (*miśra-dhyāna*) are reborn in the five Pure Abodes (*śuddhāvāsa*) due to their lower-tier karma, there is still movement and transition."

[Commentary]: Regarding "not being equal" and so forth: for example, within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), pure tenfold wholesome karma (*daśakuśalakarmapatha*) induces the fruit of the celestial realms (*devagati*), while interrupted tenfold wholesome karma induces the fruit of the human realm (*manuṣyagati*).
That is to say, if a person first cultivates pure tenfold wholesome karma, they will necessarily induce the fruit of the celestial realms;

however, if at a later time they commit evil that interrupts that wholesome karma, it instead induces the fruit of the human realm—this is called "shifting karma" (*calakarma*). The other realms should be understood by analogy.
[Commentary: Regarding the remaining three fruits: by exhausting the afflictions of discrimination within the three realms, one realizes the fruit of *srotāpanna*;
if one abandons the first six grades of innate afflictions of the desire realm, one realizes the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin*; by abandoning the final three grades, one realizes the fruit of *anāgāmin*;
and by exhausting the innate afflictions of the two upper realms, one realizes the fruit of *arhat*.

[Commentary] Regarding "the stage of the Pratyekabuddha," etc.: based on the Mahāyāna teachings, there are four types of lineages for the cultivation and attainment of the fruit by those of the Pratyekabuddha nature—those who are definite or indefinite in their nature.
There is one type with a single nature, namely, those of the definite Pratyekabuddha nature.

There are two types with dual natures, namely, those of the Śrāvaka-Pratyekabuddha nature and those of the Pratyekabuddha-Mahāyāna nature. There is one type with triple natures, namely, those who possess all three.

Regarding those who possess the dispositions for the three vehicles: if they are of a fixed disposition, they cultivate the provisions (*sambhāra*) and so forth just like the *śrāvakas*, for their practice is no different from that of the *śrāvakas*.

Among those of an unfixed disposition, if one lacks the Mahāyāna disposition, they are able to turn away from the stages of the *śrāvaka*—namely, the provisions, the application (*prayoga*), and the noble state of training (*śaikṣa*)—and instead proceed toward the enlightenment of a *pratyekabuddha*. However, this applies provided they do not possess the Mahāyāna disposition of the unfixed type.

Those belonging to the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle—whether they are in the stage of equipment (*saṃbhāra*), application (*prayoga*), training (*śaikṣa*), or beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)—are all capable of turning toward unsurpassed enlightenment (*anuttara-bodhi*).
However, there is no case where one who has already attained the noble fruit (*ārya-phala*) as a Pratyekabuddha turns toward the Śrāvaka Vehicle, because the Śrāvaka is inferior.

At the time of attaining the noble fruit, one who realizes it for oneself without a teacher is called a Pratyekabuddha; since such a self-realized one possesses that awakening (*bodha*), he is named "Pratyekabuddha" (Solitary Realizer).
"Bodhi" (Awakening) or "Buddha" refers specifically to the Pratyekabuddha. In Sanskrit, *pratyekabuddha* is translated as "Solitary Awakened One" (*dujue*).
Because they realize awakening by contemplating dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), they are also called "Dependently Awakened Ones.

From the initial generation of the mind until the fruit of No-More-Learning (*aśaikṣa-phala*), this stage is divided into two: first, the stage of external ordinary beings (*bāhyapṛthagjana*); second, the stage of internal ordinary beings (*adhyātmapṛthagjana*) and above. First, regarding the external...
Regarding those in the stage of ordinary beings, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, at the end of the thirty-fourth fascicle, states:
"What is the lineage of the Pratyekabuddha? It should be correctly understood through three characteristics: first, the lineage of attenuated afflictions;

that is, because the afflictions of that lineage are subtle and thin, for this reason, one does not take pleasure in places of clamor and commotion, but takes deep delight in places of tranquility. Second, attenuated compassion..."
Due to these causes and conditions, those of the lineage whose mental disposition is characterized by pride find no joy in teaching the True Dharma or in benefiting sentient beings;
rather, they take deep delight in internal reflection and dwelling in tranquility. Regarding these three types of lineages with middling faculties, the summary states:
"By virtue of these causes and conditions, they deeply aspire to realize *bodhi* for themselves, without a teacher and without a rival."
Regarding this treatise: if one of the *pratyekabuddha* lineage encounters a Buddha in the world, they are transformed and led to practice;

if they do not encounter a Buddha, they nonetheless cultivate the practices of a *śrāvaka* by relying on the Dharma themselves. Whether in the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*), the stage of application (*prayoga-avasthā*), or having already attained the noble fruit of a *śrāvaka*, at whichever stage they may be, even until they turn toward the enlightenment of a *pratyekabuddha*, they give rise to the aspiration for wholesome qualities (*kuśala-dharma-chanda*).

All those who have already departed are subsumed under the stage of the ordinary outsider of the Pratyekabuddhas. Regarding those from the second stage, the inner noble one (ārya), there are two types:
the rhinoceros-like (*khadgaviṣāṇakalpa*) and the group-practitioner (*vargacārin*). Both possess the five stages of practice and realization, beginning with the stage of equipment (*sambhāra*).

Now, concerning the stage of equipment for the rhinoceros-like Pratyekabuddha: prior to this, they have not yet produced the aids to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) of the Śrāvaka; thus, from the stage of equipment...

Turning [the roots of merit] toward the state of a Pratyekabuddha, they may either encounter a Buddha or not encounter one; nevertheless, their mental continuum is matured as they single-mindedly seek to realize the enlightenment of a Pratyekabuddha.

At the initial stage of the *sambhāra-mārga* (path of accumulation), they do not need to further cultivate the five *sthāpanā-cittas* (stabilizing meditations) and so forth, because these were already cultivated to maturity during their previous stage as Śrāvakas.

According to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, within the *sambhāra-mārga*, they cultivate the six types of expertise (*kauśalya*), namely: the aggregates (*skandha*), the sense bases (*āyatana*), and so on.
One practices skillfulness regarding the elements (*dhātu*), dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), the possible and impossible (*sthānāsthāna*), and the truths (*satya*);
however, one practices skillfulness regarding dependent origination most extensively, because this is the distinct object of focus for the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle.

For instance, after practicing for more than a hundred eons, one emerges in a world without a Buddha and, being without a teacher, is able to personally contemplate dependent origination; thus, one is able to practice the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣyadharma*).

That is to say: the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, and the four bases of psychic power; following these, for the sake of initiating application, one cultivates the five faculties;

furthermore, one cultivates the aforementioned five types of skillfulness—namely, the aggregates, the sense bases, the elements, dependent origination, and the contemplation of what is possible and impossible (*sthānāsthāna*), since the meaning of possibility and impossibility is precisely a specific aspect of dependent origination. One cultivates these seven...

Next, one further cultivates forty-four types of knowledge, which consist of contemplating dependent origination through the gateway of the Four Noble Truths; this constitutes skillfulness regarding the [Four] Truths.

Up to this point, it is collectively termed the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*). Following this, one enters what is subsumed under the stage of application (*prayoga-avasthā*), wherein one contemplates the Four Truths and cultivates the sixteen aspects (*ṣoḍaśākāra*), giving rise to the stages of Heat (*uṣmagata*), Summits (*mūrdhan*), Patience (*kṣānti*), and the Supreme Worldly Dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*), identical to those of the Śrāvakas.
It is taught that up to this point, these are collectively termed the stage of application (*prayoga-mārga*). Regarding the stage of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), it is likewise as follows:

for a śrāvaka, after giving rise to the single-moment true path of seeing, one subsequently gives rise to two moments and sixteen moments, which are termed the path of seeing with aspects (*lakṣaṇa-darśana-mārga*);

all moments up to the sixteenth are subsumed within the stage of seeing. As for the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), one has already practiced during the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-mārga*) for a hundred kalpas.

Sublime practice necessarily suppresses the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation of the lower eight stages by means of the mundane path; although their seeds have not yet been severed, they have already been impaired by the power of the mundane path.
Thus, when entering the Path of Seeing, at the stage of the True Path of Seeing, the seeds of the afflictions of conceptual discrimination are simultaneously severed.
Only those belonging to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) are not suppressed by the mundane path, yet this noble one gives rise to the nine paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*).

The ninth path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) that abandons obstacles and realizes the principle is called the "Vajra Path" (*vajra-mārga*), which constitutes the ninth stage of the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*).

Up to this point, it is collectively designated as being subsumed within the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*). This ninth path of liberation is precisely the attainment of the enlightenment of a Pratyekabuddha, termed the "knowledge of exhaustion" (*kṣaya-jñāna*).

Immediately following the knowledge of exhaustion, the "knowledge of non-arising" (*anutpāda-jñāna*) arises; thus, one fully accomplishes the merits of the fruit-stage. This refers to those of fixed nature (*niyata-gotra*).

Regarding those of indeterminate nature from the stage of awakening up to nirvāṇa who have not yet entered the Mahāyāna, they are collectively designated as belonging to the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).

Those termed "rhinoceros-like" (*khadgaviṣāṇakalpa*) are those who exclusively delight in dwelling in solitary forests and even take pleasure in abiding in the three gates of liberation—emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*).
This means that when observing the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*), they cultivate the practices of emptiness and non-self; this is the gate of emptiness.

Regarding the doors of liberation: if one contemplates the Truth of Suffering by cultivating the practices of suffering and impermanence, as well as the four aspects of the Truth of Origination, this is the Door of Liberation of Wishlessness (*apraṇihita-vimokṣa-mukha*), because one does not take delight in these two truths.
If one contemplates the Truth of Cessation by cultivating its four aspects, this is the Door of Liberation of Signlessness (*animitta-vimokṣa-mukha*).
[The Truth of] the Path is itself the practice of purity; therefore, it is not included among the three contemplations.
The "solitary" (khaḍgaviṣāṇakalpa) pratyekabuddhas are those who are like the horn of a rhinoceros. Regarding the second type, the "group-practicing" (vargacārin) pratyekabuddhas:

these are those who, in a previous life, having practiced according to the Śrāvaka vehicle and reached the stages of *uṣmagata* and *mūrdhan* within the levels conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*), subsequently turned toward the state of a pratyekabuddha.

Because their remaining time was short, they did not proceed through the stage of the "supreme mundane dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*) toward the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), but instead focused exclusively on the [four] truths.

Those who do not turn their minds [toward the Great Vehicle], or those who, having already practiced, have attained the fruit of a Śrāvaka but then turn toward the fruit of a Pratyekabuddha—once they have departed from the desire for the Dharma [of the Śrāvakas] and so forth, they are all categorized within the stage of the outer ordinary person (bāhyapṛthagjana) of the Pratyekabuddhas. From this point onward, they belong to the stage of the Requisites (sambhārāvasthā).

Within the stage of the Requisites, they extensively practice the five contemplations for settling the mind (pañca-viṣaya-sthāpana-bhāvanā) and predominantly contemplate dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda).

The six types of skillfulness are extremely swift, while the four types of birth are extremely slow; the sequence of their cultivation over a hundred kalpas is explained by analogy with what precedes.

Alternatively, one may pass through many lifetimes during the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*), or even during the stages of heat, summits, and patience within the stage of application (*prayoga-avasthā*).
During the stage of equipment, there may be occasions when one encounters a Buddha or does not encounter one; when the cultivation reaches completion, one emerges due to those causes and conditions.
In an age without a Buddha, one is able to cultivate the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma) spontaneously;

proceeding from the four foundations of mindfulness through the stage of the five faculties, one further cultivates the six stages of skillfulness, performs the contemplations of the seventy-seven knowledges and the forty-four knowledges, and subsequently gives rise to the stages of application (prayoga-avasthā) until the full realization of pratyekabuddha-bodhi. Such a person is called a "solitary practitioner" (vargacārin-pratyekabuddha).
The realization of the great meaning is the same as in the preceding section. Having attained the noble fruit as a pratyekabuddha through solitary practice, one may be permitted to see a Buddha;

however, a pratyekabuddha who is like a rhinoceros horn will certainly not see a Buddha. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states that when a bodhisattva is about to descend from Tuṣita Heaven, he emits a great light from the palm of his right hand called "Adorned and Purified World. If there is a pratyekabuddha within the three thousandfold world system...

Upon encountering this light, those who have awakened will swiftly enter *nirvāṇa*; if they do not, by the power of the Buddha’s light, they shall be transported to another realm where they cannot see the Buddha.

[Commentary: Among these three, those whose faculty-nature is that of the "dull-witted" (māna-carita) class have somewhat thicker defilements than the previous two classes, and their compassionate heart...

Those who are slightly superior are called those of middling faculties; because their defilements are somewhat thickened by these [afflictions], they are termed the "type characterized by pride" (*mānacarita*). [Commentary] Regarding the second point, "the paths," etc.:

it is explained that three types of persons cultivate merit and wisdom based on the six kinds of skillfulness (*ṣaḍpāramitākauśalya*), and this is designated as the "paths. Of these, the first two types of persons cultivate the six kinds of skillfulness while relying on an ordinary person’s body (*pṛthagjana-kāya*);

the third type of person relies on [the attainment of... (Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment from a Buddhist scholastic commentary, likely concerning the classification of practitioners according to their faculties and the stages of their cultivation.)
The noble ones cultivate the six *kauśalyas* (skillful means), each seeking awakening.

[Commentary: Regarding the "one hundred eons," the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states that a Pratyekabuddha practices for one hundred periods of increase and decrease (*utsarpiṇī-avasarpiṇī-kalpa*) before attaining the fruit of sainthood; this refers to such individuals.

As for "the possible and the impossible" (*sthānāsthāna*), "possible" (*sthāna*) has the meaning of dependence upon causes and the sense of establishment; it refers to relying on the causes of good and evil.
Because effects are established, the correspondence between cause and effect is called the "proper" (*sthāna*).

The false calculations of non-Buddhists—who seek birth in the Brahma-world through the merit of killing and sacrificing to the gods—are contrary to the above and are thus called the "improper" (*asthāna*). By taking these as objects and practicing with diligent application, one thereby enters the state of a noble one (*ārya*);
hence, this is termed "skillfulness regarding the proper and the improper" (*sthānāsthāna-kauśalya*).
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "There is one class... and so forth, the *Fahua shu* (Commentary on the Lotus Sutra) states:
