"If one has not yet entered the Śrāvaka stage of the *ānulomika-vimokṣa-bhāga* (the stage conducive to liberation) but becomes a Pratyekabuddha, one becomes a *khaḍgaviṣāṇakalpa* (rhinoceros-like). Those who become [Pratyekabuddhas] after having entered the *nirvedhabhāga* (the stage of penetration) all become *vargacārin* (group-dwelling).
One who becomes a Pratyekabuddha while still in the indeterminate period of the *vimokṣa-bhāga* may become a *khaḍgaviṣāṇakalpa*, because the number of births [required] is many."
Those already destined for birth also constitute the *vargacārin* (group-dwelling) type because their number of births is small;

therefore, it is said that those who practice through refinement have many births relative to this, as the period of their refinement is long and their faculties are sharp, being named "rhinoceros-like" (*khadgaviṣāṇakalpa*) because their number of births is few, as the period of their refinement is short and their faculties are dull, being named "group-dwelling.
Regarding the first category mentioned above, the *niyata-rāśi-pratyekabuddha* (solitary realizers of fixed destiny) and those who practice...

Regarding those śrāvakas who possess the factors conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya*) but have not yet fixed their birth, they may proceed toward the state of a pratyekabuddha and become rhinoceros-like (*khadgaviṣāṇakalpa*);

this second category consists of those whose lineage is already fixed. Thus, they form a group (*vargacārin*). Based on this ordinary body, it is said that in a future life they will gradually realize the path of seeing and the path of cultivation, attain that pratyekabuddha enlightenment, and achieve the ultimate fruit of a śramaṇa, which is the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "a certain class of those in the three realms" and so forth: this third category refers to those who, relying on the Śrāvaka vehicle, practice and attain the realization of the noble [state], observing the objects of the Four Truths through the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*). Thus, they are called "those who have realized the direct observation of phenomena.

Accordingly, they obtain the first, second, or third fruit; however, due to the power of their spiritual lineage (*gotra*), they lack the capacity to reach the ultimate, final stage of a Śrāvaka Arhat.

Therefore, turning toward the path of the Pratyekabuddha, one further cultivates the six kinds of skillfulness regarding the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth. It is possible for such a noble person to undergo further births;

by relying on the supramundane path, they shall attain the ultimate fruit in a future life. "Ultimately free from defilement" means that the accumulation of afflictions (*kleśa*) is exhausted and the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*) has ceased.
The Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*) is named *brahma* because it signifies purity; the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*) is named "practice" (*caryā*) because it is the practice of cultivation.

Because they have understood the meaning [of the Dharma], their cessation and path are perfected; thus, they are called "Pratyekabuddhas who have reached the limit" (*prāntakoṭika*) and "Arhats who have attained no-more-learning" (*aśaikṣa*).

[Commentary: Regarding the third section on "cultivation" (*abhyāsa*), etc., this explains the mode of cultivation for the three preceding categories. As that treatise states: "What is the cultivation of a Pratyekabuddha?

It is said there are three types" (as cited in the commentary). The intent of the first type is as follows: having cultivated the six types of skillfulness (*kauśalya*) for more than a hundred [eons]...

When a kalpa has passed and there is no Buddha in the world, by the power of their spiritual lineage (*gotra*), they are able to cultivate the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) on their own without a teacher.
They realize the dharma of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) through the superior insight of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and attain the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-phala*).

Because they have severed all afflictions using an ordinary body and have perfected the ultimate fruit, they become rhinoceros-like [solitary realizers]. The latter two categories are the two types of group-dwelling [solitary realizers] mentioned in the preceding text.
Those who train as śrāvakas, by the power of the causes and conditions of that spiritual lineage (*gotra*), emerge into a world where no Buddha exists and turn toward the state of a pratyekabuddha;
though they lack teachers and companions, they are able to cultivate the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) on their own.

These individuals correspond respectively to those who, from among the previously mentioned second and third stages—both mundane and supramundane—turn their minds toward the state of a pratyekabuddha. Furthermore, throughout these stages of practice, they all cultivate the six kinds of skillfulness (*kauśalya*).
Because it was already explained previously, the fourth dwelling is omitted here;
as for the fifth practice, it refers to the transformative activities of the three preceding classes of persons, which can be understood according to the text.

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "only by manifesting [signs]," it is because while for those who preach the Dharma one must produce understanding in others through speech, for Pratyekabuddhas they manifest signs of supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) to cause people to resolve their doubts and give rise to faith. Thus, in accordance with their seeking the fulfillment of vows, they do not utter words when preaching the Dharma.
This is because the nature of all Pratyekabuddhas is fond of tranquility; if they were to engage in verbal discourse, they would inevitably gather a crowd, and there is a fear of such commotion.
Therefore, [the Commentary] states: "Although that which is grasped by non-Buddhists and others does not exist, the mind that grasps it is of the nature of dependence (*paratantra-svabhāva*);
thus, even the sixty-two views are said to 'exist'."
[Commentary: Regarding the "Worthy Eon" (*bhadrakalpa*) and so forth, many types of non-Buddhists give rise to such views as:
"Form is the self," because form is the ornaments and finery that adorn the self; or "Form is my servant," because it belongs to me and is driven by my commands;
or "Form is my dwelling," because I reside within it. The same applies to the other four aggregates.
[Sūtra]: "If one who distinguishes phenomena by clinging to names and marks... The commentary explains: "Distinguishing" means attachment.

This teaches practitioners not to cling to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), but rather to understand that causes and conditions are like illusions and to realize that these causes and conditions are empty.

If one clings to names, clings to marks, or clings to things—being deluded by the characteristics of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa*)—one will be unable to see the reality of all phenomena."

[The section on] Nature. [Commentary]: The *Xianyang lun* (Exposition of the Manifest) and the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* rely upon the gate of the permanent and the impermanent; all dharmas are fully subsumed within five categories.

The first four, being impermanent, subsume all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) and are termed the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature). The fifth, the permanent dharma, subsumes all unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
It is called the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) because it is devoid of the essence of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) and is not subsumed within the five dharmas.

Regarding the aforementioned four [categories], the first three are with-outflows (*sāsrava*) and the fourth is without-outflows (*anāsrava*). Regarding the aforementioned three, the first two are the objects (*ālambana*) and the third is the subject (*ālambaka*).

Regarding the aforementioned two, the "characteristic" (*nimitta*) is that which is signified, and the "name" (*nāman*) is that which signifies. Because one does not understand the characteristic, one expresses it by means of a name; thus, by means of the five...
The Dharma encompasses all dharmas.

[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "the characteristic of awakening" (*bodha-lakṣaṇa*): it means to awaken to and fully comprehend. Because it is able to discern the objective characteristics of its own sphere—including all delusive, illusory mental conceptions—it is called the "characteristic of awakening.
Regarding the two characteristics of self-nature: this explains the aforementioned three dharmas—parikalpita-svabhāva (imagined nature) and paratantra-svabhāva (dependent nature).
The two modes of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) as suchness (*tathatā*) are precisely *tathatā*; it is designated by these two characters.

In terms of the gates of the tainted (*sāsrava*) and the untainted (*anāsrava*), all conditioned phenomena and the untainted are subsumed within correct gnosis (*samyag-jñāna*), for they are free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).

Therefore, it is called the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) that is free from inversion. Because the essence of all unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) is immovable, it is called the eternally abiding perfected nature.
Therefore, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* combines correct cognition (*samyag-jñāna*) and suchness (*tathatā*) as the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). [Commentary:

Regarding the phrase "the later world," etc., I have now examined the text on the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) of the later period; it applies to the preceding four dharmas and possesses the meaning of the three natures (*tri-svabhāva*).

The characteristics of birth-and-death as cause and effect within the triple world consist of discrimination and false imagination (*vikalpa-mithyā-parikalpa*); these three rely upon the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*). The causes and effects of the Three Vehicles likewise pertain to this.

Regarding the outflows (*āsrava*) and the outflow-free (*anāsrava*): if they are with outflows, they are called "conceptualization" and are subsumed under the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*);

if they are outflow-free, they are called "correct wisdom" and are subsumed under the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). The sixty-two views are as explained in the commentary on the *Vivaraṇa*.

[Commentary: The *Xiányáng* and *Yúqié* [śāstras] belong to this sūtra. The statement that "the true nature of all phenomena (dharmatā) does not abide in form, nor does it abide in non-form," and so forth, clarifies that they are subsumed under ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*) as suchness (*tathatā*).

Furthermore, the causal and resultant conditioned virtues (*saṃskṛtaguṇa*) of the three vehicles—comprising both the tainted (*sāsrava*) and untainted (*anāsrava*)—are subsumed by the aforementioned four categories.

Specifically, those that are tainted consist of characteristics (*nimitta*), names (*nāman*), and conceptualization (*vikalpa*); those that are untainted are subsumed under correct knowledge (*samyagjñāna*).
However, the unconditioned merits realized by those of the three vehicles belong to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) and are not what is elucidated here;

for they are subsumed within the three realms, the five destinies, the four modes of birth, and the sixty-two views, as their characteristics, names, and conceptualizations are all with outflows (*sāsrava*).

[Commentary: Regarding the "Two Truths" and so forth: previously, the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) was explained to reveal the emptiness of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*). Here, the causes and effects of the three realms and the three vehicles are explained to reveal that conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) possesses its own meaning.
Because this point was not yet fully understood, it is now expanded upon. The sequence of the "Chapter on the Two Truths"—first the ultimate and then the conventional—is as follows:

first, the ultimate truth is clarified to cause the elimination of conceptual signs (*nimitta*) and to bring about accord with the principle of signlessness; subsequently, the conventional truth is taught to provide exhortation.
To cause practitioners to cultivate and learn so as to understand the illusory nature of phenomena, the "Chapter on the Two Truths" extensively elucidates the ultimate and conventional truths,
instructing bodhisattvas to rely on the gateway of the two truths to cultivate the causes and proceed toward the fruit, thereby perfecting great awakening.

[Commentary]: Regarding the "six elements of the gentleman" (*puruṣa*), all sentient beings are termed "gentlemen" (*puruṣa*) because they possess what appears to be powerful functional activity.

Earth, water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness are called the six elements (*ṣaḍ-dhātu*). "Element" (*dhātu*) has the meaning of "nature. By means of these six factors of the person (*pudgala*), one's own nature is maintained;
it is not as the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) maintain, that a self (*ātman*) maintains [the aggregates].

[Commentary] "This is the correct [view]" means that Consciousness-Only (Vijñaptimātra) is the correct [position]. Of the three phases—arising, abiding, and change—all reside in the present, because they exist in the present.

Cessation resides in the past, because it has already lost its substance. The name "past" belongs to the preceding stage, while the name "future" refers to what is subsequent, as it is directed toward the future.
[Commentary] Regarding the two interpretations in the treatise, it says: "The Sūtra speaks of three characteristics; why does it not speak of four? There are three explanations. The first says:

Just as arising is called *udaya* and cessation is called *nirodha*, one should know that the characteristic of change (*anyathātva*) is called *sthiti* (abiding), and abiding while undergoing transformation is called the characteristic of abiding-and-change (*sthity-anyathātva*).

The second says: Unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) possess their own intrinsic abiding (*sva-lakṣaṇa-sthiti*); [if a separate characteristic of abiding were taught], it would be confused with that.

The Sūtra does not speak of "abiding" as three [separate entities]. As for the Sūtra’s statement that "abiding and change" are combined into a single name, the intention behind explaining them in combination is as follows:

it is like the case of the woman Darkness (Tamasī) and the goddess Śrī, where honor and disgrace follow one another; they are explained together so as to engender revulsion [toward conditioned phenomena].

The first interpretation clarifies the names of abiding and change, while the latter two interpretations clarify the meaning of the three characteristics; therefore, this present commentary [proceeds accordingly].
The Master refers to the latter two interpretations.
[Commentary]: Regarding "the absence of the two marks of permanence": true nature is eternally present, while the horns of a rabbit are eternally absent.
Because these conditioned phenomena lack those two marks of permanence, they are called "impermanent."
[Commentary]: A *kṣaṇa* (moment) is the smallest unit of time. The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* explains the meaning of the three "smallest units":

first, the smallest unit among material forms (*rūpa*) is one *paramāṇu* (atom); second, the smallest unit among names (*nāman*) is a single syllable; third, the smallest unit among time is one *kṣaṇa*.
Within the category of material phenomena, that which reaches the ultimate degree of subtlety is called an *paramāṇu*; it refers to [the interval between] arising and ceasing.

Regarding the two [categories], the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that "arising" (*jāti*) and "change-while-abiding" (*sthity-anyathātva*) together constitute the category of arising (*utpāda-pakṣa*), while "cessation" (*nirodha*) constitutes the category of cessation (*nirodha-pakṣa*).

It instructs disciples to contemplate all phenomena as arising and ceasing moment by moment, and to settle their minds upon this arising and cessation which is endowed with the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).
Furthermore, there are two types: first, the four characteristics of a single moment (*kṣaṇika-lakṣaṇa*), also known as the subtle four characteristics, which are universally present.

Regarding the Dharma being thus, this sutra explains the meaning of emptiness through arising and ceasing. Second, the four characteristics of a single period [of existence] are also called the "coarse four characteristics.
These are distinguished based on the specific temporal limits of the abiding world of sentient beings and their environment.

For example, in the human realm, the initial entry into the womb, the dwelling in the womb, and the emergence from the womb are all termed the characteristic of arising; once arisen, the dwelling in the world for the duration of one's lifespan is [the characteristic of abiding].
Life is collectively termed the characteristic of duration (*sthiti-lakṣaṇa*); the successive transformations from youth to old age are all termed the characteristic of change (*anyathātva-lakṣaṇa*);
and the actual relinquishing of life at a single moment, as well as the state of the intermediate existence (*antarābhava*), are all termed the characteristic of cessation (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*).

Master Ci'en cites the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, which states that the body of the intermediate existence is called the suffering of death; therefore, the body of the intermediate existence is subsumed under the characteristic of cessation. [The characteristics of] birth, duration, and change...

Cessation is also termed birth, old age, sickness, and death; these four intersect and invade one another, and thus one should feel weary of them and seek liberation from them, as will be explained below.
[Commentary] Regarding "the harmony of conditions" and so forth, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, chapter twelve, states:

"When a collection of various conditions brings about a dharma that acquires its own essence instantaneously, or when a moving dharma traverses the distance of a single atom (*paramāṇu*), this is called one *kṣaṇa*. It is, for example, like the snap of a strong man's fingers."
There are sixty-five *kṣaṇas* in the time it takes to snap one's fingers; this is called the measure of a single *kṣaṇa*. The first explanation is easily understood;
the intent of the latter explanation is that the time taken for a particle (*paramāṇu*) to traverse [one unit of space] is the measure of a single *kṣaṇa*.
The *Vibhāṣā*, fascicle 136, cites a sūtra in which the Buddha told the bhikṣus: "For example, four men, all skilled archers, each holding a bow..."
The arrows were all braced together, pointing toward the four directions, as a swift man approached and said to them, "You may now release your arrows all at once;
I can catch them all so that none fall to the ground. What do you think? Is this man not swift?
The bhikṣus replied, "He is indeed very swift. The Blessed One said, "That man’s swiftness does not equal that of a medicinal herb that travels upon the earth."
The speed of the *khaḍgaviṣāṇa-cara* yakṣas does not equal that of the *antarīkṣa-cara* yakṣas;
the speed of the *antarīkṣa-cara* yakṣas does not equal that of the Cāturmahārājika devas; the speed of those devas does not equal that of the two wheels of the sun and moon;
the speed of those two wheels does not equal that of the Devaputra Dṛḍhavrata, who guides the wheels of the sun and moon—the speed of these various devas increases progressively in this manner.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "The arising and ceasing of the life-process (āyus-saṃskāra) is more rapid than that; it flows through moments without even a moment's pause.

[Commentary] Regarding the response beginning with "However," etc., if one calculates according to the subsequent scriptural text, there are eight [moments] in total within a single thought-instant (ekakṣaṇa).

If eleven thousand instances of arising and ceasing are thus [simultaneous], how can one distinguish between their prior and posterior moments? The answer is: it is because the duration of time is extremely brief.

For example, when a sharp blade suddenly cuts through nine hundred layers of paper in a single kṣaṇa, although there is a sequence of prior and posterior moments in the cutting of that paper, the arising and ceasing are likewise [simultaneous].
Ordinary people have dull consciousness and are unaware of this existence; only the Great Sages perceive it directly.
The *Pramāṇa* (Logic) school teaches this to show sentient beings that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) are empty because they arise and perish.
[Commentary: Regarding the *Avataṃsaka* and other sutras, it is said that when a long wind blows upon the water, it generates a momentum of movement which is called "waves.
As each preceding wave perishes and each succeeding wave arises, these two—the arising and perishing of the waves—do not know one another; the arising and perishing of phenomena is likewise so.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement "herein, the eye is empty of the eye" and so forth: according to the meaning of Nāgārjuna, the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) are composed of four conditions, while the sense faculties, objects, and other material forms are composed of two conditions. Since there is no form or mind apart from these causal conditions, all things are empty.
According to the meaning of Maitreya, "internal emptiness" refers to the fact that within the six internal bases (*āyatana*), there is no grasped real self or phenomena.

Therefore, it is said that "emptiness" does not mean the absence of a fundamental substance; as it is said that a house is empty because there are no people within it, rather than the substance of the house itself being empty.
According to the general meaning, the characteristics [of phenomena] are subsumed into their nature: all dharmas are themselves true emptiness.
Just as waves depend upon water—being neither identical to nor separate from it—the sutra below states: "All dharmas are like suchness. All...
The Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha are likewise suchness. The preceding and following sections should be interpreted according to these three meanings. [Commentary]:

Regarding the "six internal bases" and so forth herein: because the six external bases, which are the objects of apprehension, are empty, the six internal bases, which are the subjects of apprehension, are empty;
because the six external bases, which are the objects of apprehension, are empty due to the emptiness of the six internal bases, which are the subjects of apprehension, the external bases are empty.
Because they exist in dependence upon one another through their spatial characteristics, both the internal and external are empty; this is the meaning of these three types of emptiness.

First, one contemplates the internal separately, then one contemplates the external separately, and both are entirely empty. Furthermore, if one contemplates the internal and external together as a whole, they are likewise all empty.

[Commentary]: What is meant by "emptiness of emptiness"? The first mention of "emptiness" refers to the great void that pervades all phenomena. The second mention of "emptiness" reveals that even that [void] is non-existent.
The intended meaning is that the characteristic of the void of the ten directions is itself non-existent; therefore, it is called the "emptiness of emptiness.
Consequently, it is further explained that the vessel-world and its material phenomena throughout the ten directions are all non-existent, which is termed [the emptiness of emptiness].
The *Mahāśūnyatā-prakāśana-śāstra* states: "Great emptiness (*mahāśūnyatā*) refers to the emptiness of the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*).

[Commentary]: That which is empty by virtue of being unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is called "unconditioned. If a dharma possesses such activities as arising and so forth, it is termed a conditioned dharma (*saṃskṛta-dharma*);
if a dharma lacks those activities of arising and so forth, it is termed an unconditioned dharma. This demonstrates that even the unconditioned is ultimately non-existent.
Because it is attained, it is called "emptiness of the unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta-śūnyatā*).

[Commentary]: Regarding "ultimate emptiness" (*atyanta-śūnyatā*): whereas the preceding "emptiness of the beginningless" (*anavarāgra-śūnyatā*) clarifies the emptiness of the three periods of time, this ultimate emptiness clarifies the emptiness of what is not of the world.
This is because the true nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena does not belong to the three periods of time.

[Commentary]: Regarding "emptiness of dispersion" (*vibhava-śūnyatā*), the various phenomena of form and mind are called "dispersed," while the true nature (*dharmatā*) of these phenomena is called "non-dispersed.

Because dispersion and non-dispersion are mutually dependent, the Sūtra speaks only of dispersion, which necessarily implies its counterpart, non-dispersion; it is merely through the shadow of this contrast that [the latter] is revealed.
In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, emptiness of dispersion and emptiness of non-alteration (*avikāra-śūnyatā*) are explained by way of their mutual opposition. That which is "non-altered" is...
The meaning of non-dispersal.

[Commentary: Regarding such [categories] as these, each of the bases (*āyatana*) and elements (*dhātu*) possesses its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). Furthermore, the three categories (*triskandha*) are subsumed into two:

namely, the specific characteristic of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-svalakṣaṇa*) and the specific characteristic of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-svalakṣaṇa*). That sutra further mentions "emptiness of common characteristics" (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*), which refers, for example, to how suffering is characterized by being contaminated (*sāsrava*).
The common characteristic of conditioned phenomena is impermanence; the common characteristic of all phenomena is emptiness and selflessness.
There are countless such common characteristics, and these common characteristics are empty of common characteristics.

[Commentary] Regarding the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and other texts, among the eighteen kinds of emptiness (*aṣṭādaśa-śūnyatā*), there is the separate contemplation of internal faculties, the separate contemplation of external objects, and the collective contemplation of both internal faculties and external objects;

these twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*) encompass all phenomena, and all are empty. Within this, the distinctions of various categories are further elaborated, explaining the subsequent eleven kinds of emptiness:
namely, the emptiness of the ten directions, of space, and of the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*). All of these are...

Because they are empty, one speaks of the emptiness of emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*) and the great emptiness (*mahā-śūnyatā*). In contrast to these conventional [truths], one further speaks of the ultimate (*paramārtha*), clarifying that the ultimate is empty;

thus, the emptiness of those two truths returns to the gates of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), which are themselves also empty. Therefore, one speaks of the emptiness of the conditioned and the emptiness of the unconditioned.

Because the conditioned falls within the world while the unconditioned is not of the world, one speaks of the emptiness of the beginningless (*anavarāgra-śūnyatā*) and the ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*). Worldly phenomena are...
Because that which is dispersed is not non-dispersed, it is called "dispersed emptiness" (*vibhava-śūnyatā*).

Because both that world and this world are found to possess neither intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) nor self-characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), it is called "emptiness of intrinsic nature" (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*) and "emptiness of self-characteristics" (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*).

Because they collectively encompass all phenomena—whether mundane or supramundane, material or immaterial, characterized by defilement or purity—it is called "emptiness of all phenomena" (*sarvadharma-śūnyatā*). These first fourteen types [of emptiness] constitute the general [classification].

It clarifies that the nature and characteristics of both the objects and the wisdom regarding the defiled and pure states of all phenomena are empty. Next, three sections specifically clarify the emergence of cause and effect:

first, the general clarification of cause and effect; second, the cause; and third, the result. By means of wisdom, one illuminates that all these are empty, using the seventeen types of emptiness to counteract and dismantle all forms of existence (*bhava*).
However, fearing that sentient beings might become attached to this "emptiness that refutes" and thereby develop the "sickness of emptiness," the eighteenth emptiness is taught.

"Because it is empty, it is empty. The second mention of "emptiness" refers to the emptiness that is the object to be eliminated (*prahātavya*), while the initial and final mentions of "emptiness" refer to the emptiness that is the means of elimination (*prahāṇaka*).
By means of this single emptiness, one eliminates all those various forms of emptiness; thus, even the emptiness that performs the elimination is itself empty. It is like a wedge removing a wedge:
for example, if there is an obstruction within a hole in wood, one uses a wedge to remove it. Once the obstruction is removed, the wedge remains; yet the wedge, too, is an obstruction. Furthermore—
By using one wedge to drive out another wedge, both wedges are removed; when the obstruction of the object is eliminated, the wooden hole becomes empty and unobstructed.

By means of this one emptiness, that [other] emptiness is driven out, and once both emptinesses are discarded, the mind that clings to their removal is also cleared away. However, one must not establish a third emptiness as a principle, for it would be useless and lead to error.
First, eliminate the sickness of existence; next, eliminate the sickness of emptiness; finally, through the illumination of wisdom, realize the true nature.
"That it is neither existent nor non-existent, that marks are extinguished and dependencies severed—this is the great purport of this sutra.
[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "fearing that... and so forth: [Question] Sentient beings cling to phenomena as being existent; thus, emptiness is used to refute existence.

When sentient beings become attached to emptiness, existence should be used to refute emptiness. [Answer] This objection is not so. It is like a person who, having a disease, uses medicine to treat the disease.

One fears that medicine might become an illness and thus uses medicine to dispel the toxicity of the medicine; sentient beings are attached to the illness of existence and thus use emptiness to shatter existence.

One fears that emptiness might become an illness and thus uses emptiness to expel emptiness. It is only by using medicine that one can treat illness, but it is not by using illness that one can treat medicine.
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "it exists because it is gathered by names": this means that when names invoke and express various phenomena (*dharma*), they infuse seeds;
thus, because these seeds are gathered by means of names, they are said to exist. If there were no infusion, the very substance of the newly infused seeds would not exist.

[Sūtra] Regarding "due to the accumulation" (*hetu-samudaya*) and so forth: that which accumulates and that which is accumulated are both termed "accumulation. Afflictions (*kleśa*) and karma are termed the "accumulation as cause" (*hetu-samudaya*) because they act as the inducers;
sentient beings and the receptacle world are termed the "accumulation as fruit" (*phala-samudaya*) because they are what is induced.

Since there are distinctions among the six destinies of sentient beings within the realm of fruition, it is not non-existent. Thus, among the three phrases [of the verse], the first is the cause, and the latter...
The second [section] concerns the fruit and the fruits thereof; within this, the first is general while the latter is specific.

[Sūtra]: "The ten stages and the fruit of Buddhahood. This clarifies that the supramundane, superior meritorious qualities (guṇa-dharma) pertain exclusively to the untainted (anāsrava) merit and wisdom of the ten stages and the fruit of Buddhahood.
It does not refer here to the tainted merit and wisdom of the three stages of worthiness prior to the ten stages. Alternatively, it may be interpreted as follows:
The Three Worthies (*trayaḥ pāṇḍitāḥ*) are omitted here for brevity.

[Commentary: Furthermore, regarding the headings and conclusions, they are the same as previously explained. In the "Three Collections," it is generally shown that both mundane and supramundane dharmas possess causes and effects;
the "Six Realms" specifically show that the mundane has ten stages (*daśabhūmi*); and the "Buddha-fruit" specifically shows the supramundane.
Some parts can be understood by following the sutra itself.

[Commentary: One who mistakes a stump for a person does so because they are deluded regarding the wooden stump and falsely claim it to be a person; if one were not deluded regarding the stump, one would not grasp it as being a person.

This failure to comprehend the stump is analogous to the attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*), which fails to realize the emptiness of phenomena and instead clings to them as having real existence.
To falsely grasp at others as being persons is like the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*); it is a failure to understand non-self and a false grasping at the existence of a self.

Just as one is deluded by mistaking a tree stump for a person—where both the person and the stump are objects of delusion—it is logically certain that the grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*) and the grasping at a self are both delusions regarding both phenomena and the self. Therefore, the Buddha said:
"If a bodhisattva dwells in the signs of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), he is not a bodhisattva. To "dwell" means to be attached; because of attachment to phenomena, [he is not a bodhisattva].
"You must certainly give rise to the grasping of a self; you should not dwell in attachment to the marks of dharmas. [Commentary:

*Upāya* means "expedient means" (*upāya-kauśalya*), and *mau-hsi* (未始) means "never yet" (*an-ādi*). This reveals that the Bodhisattva, possessing the gate of *prajñā*, contemplates the emptiness of dharmas;
possessing the gate of *upāya*, he engages in the realm of existence. He thus surpasses other ordinary persons and those of the Two Vehicles.
Question: Regarding the practice of Prajñā and the skillful means (*upāya*) of observing emptiness (*śūnyatā*) while engaging with existence (*saṃsāra*), what is the superiority of these two? Answer:
Because one who employs skillful means while engaging with existence has never been deluded regarding emptiness, they remain within existence without being defiled by it.

This is unlike ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), who are deluded regarding emptiness and thus become defiled while remaining in existence. Because one possesses signless (*animitta*) Prajñā and does not weary of existence while contemplating emptiness, although one contemplates...
Though empty, one does not realize [the ultimate] quiescence as the two vehicles do, who, weary of birth-and-death, seek to enter extinction.
[Commentary: Just as the space within three different vessels is not distinct from the space-element itself, though the vessels that contain it differ, the space contained within them is one;
this illustrates the Dharma-nature according to the text.

[Commentary]: Regarding the "counteractive practices according to reality," some masters interpret this by fixing the number either according to the literal text or according to the underlying meaning, asserting that such explanations do not point to the correct meaning.

Thus, it says "according to reality": according to the correct meaning of reality, there are eighty-four thousand afflictive obstacles (*kleśa-āvaraṇa*) to be countered, and the number of counteractive practices (*pratipakṣa*) is likewise the same.
This is just as the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) serves as a counteractive practice [for specific afflictions].
Since the number of the dharmas that the Tathāgata taught to elucidate [the antidotes to] greed and so forth is likewise the same, that verse states:
"The Muni’s aggregates of Dharma number eighty thousand. "Eighty thousand" means eighty-thousand; this refers to the total number when complete, which should be stated as eighty-four thousand.

[Commentary: Regarding the ten types of afflictions: first, greed; second, anger; third, delusion; fourth, pride; fifth, doubt; sixth, the view of a self-entity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*); seventh, the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*);
eighth, false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*); ninth, the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*); and tenth, the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).

Each of these takes the other nine as its "expedient means" (*upāya*), thereby completing the total of one hundred. As for the term "expedient means," it signifies the sense of employing methods, skillful means, or causes. For example, in the case of greed...
The "head" and the remaining nine "assistants" are established as follows: because of hatred (*dveṣa*), greed (*rāga*) arises; because of delusion (*moha*), greed arises;

and so on, up to because of the clinging to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), greed arises. These ten types of afflictions act as heads for one another, with each set of ten forming a hundred.

In the Śrāvaka vehicle, that which is yet to come is called "future" (*anāgata*) and that which has already passed is called "past" (*atīta*). Since the durations of the past and future are long, they possess the sense of mutual support; [this is not the case for] the present time.

To urge the meaning of mutual support through non-characteristics (*animitta*): future dharmas have some that are acquired prior to their arising; past dharmas have some that are acquired subsequent to their cessation;
and present dharmas have some that are acquired simultaneously with them. Because the power of the "attaining" (*prāpti*) is efficacious, the dharmas thus attained persist and do not perish;
this is why afflictions (*kleśa*) are all categorized as either already arisen or yet to arise.

[Commentary]: Although it is said that "the true [path] and so forth," this refers to the numerical categories of those dharmas used to explain this sūtra’s section on the single-mind True Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*).
While the True Path of Seeing itself does not possess these many distinct varieties, the types of afflictive obstructions to be eliminated do exist in such numbers;

consequently, the number of noble paths (*āryamārga*) that serve as their antidotes is likewise the same. Therefore, it is said that the first moment when noble wisdom manifests is endowed with eight [qualities].
[There are] fourteen thousand *pāramitās*. [Commentary:

Regarding "the Worthy Eon (*bhadrakalpa*) and so forth," this means that by taking each of the ten afflictions, such as greed (*rāga*), as a primary head, they induce the remaining ninety [afflictions], totaling one hundred.
These are capable of arising across the three periods of time; specifically, one hundred [instances] in the past constitute one thousand, and likewise for the future.
It is likewise for the present [afflictions]; because the time is brief, they lack the capacity to mutually support one another, thus totaling two thousand one hundred.
Based on the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*), each gives rise to two thousand one hundred; these combined total twenty-one thousand.

Since those with excessive greed, excessive hatred, excessive delusion, and those of equal proportions—these four types of persons—each give rise to twenty-one thousand, when all are totaled together...
The Tathāgata has proclaimed eighty-four thousand medicines of pure Dharma to treat the diseases of the eighty-four thousand roots of affliction (*kleśa*).

As stated in the *Bhadra-kalpika Sūtra*, this begins with the descent from Tuṣita to Jambudvīpa, known as the "Light-Radiance" (*Prabhāsa*) stage, and extends through to the distribution of relics at the Twin Trees; these stages comprise three [sections] in total.

One hundred and fifty times each of these expounds the six *pāramitās*, totaling two thousand one hundred gates of *pāramitā* (the remainder is as explained in the commentary). [Commentary] Furthermore,
regarding the phrase "another interpretation," etc., the previous interpretation held that the World-Honored One appeared in the world at all times to preach this and that dharma.
The general meaning of the eighty-four thousand practices that serve as remedies for the various diseases of affliction is as commonly explained;

they do not belong to the categories of the Dharma of the Path of Seeing found in this sutra. Furthermore, regarding the explanation of these categories of the Path of Seeing according to that [other] commentary:
because those two obstacles (āvaraṇa) obscure the nature, characteristics, and qualities of pure wisdom, the qualities [of that wisdom] are obstructed accordingly.

There are many categories of obstacles that can hinder [realization]. Now, upon reaching the moment of the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), when wisdom arises, eighty-four thousand defiled obstacles are suddenly severed, and eighty-four thousand pure merits are suddenly manifested. This is like polishing a mirror:

as one portion of dust is removed, one portion of clarity appears; as more portions of dust are removed, more portions of clarity appear. Regarding the "coarseness" (*dauṣṭhulya*) of the two obstacles:
The general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) reveals that the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*) are designated as "heavy burdens" (*dauṣṭhulya*), not merely as habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
[Commentary: Regarding the term "Omniscient One" (*sarvajña*), Ci'en provides three interpretations. First: "The Omniscient One" refers to the Buddha;

furthermore, "the Wise One" (*jñānin*) refers to the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) and the subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*). These two are the functions of the two wisdoms, while their true nature (*tattva*) is True Suchness (*tathatā*). If...
When its function is conjoined with its nature, it is called "wisdom" (*jñāna*); the wisdom of an All-Knowing One (*sarvajña*) is called "the wisdom of an all-knower" (*sarvajñajñāna*).

The second [commentary] states in the *Tongshu* (Concordant Commentary), section three: "All-knower" refers to the function of wisdom, which is enlightenment (*bodhi*); the repeated term "wisdom" refers to the nature of wisdom, which is nirvana.
Now, to reveal that both of these are unsurpassed, this excellence is praised to inspire aspiration.
[Commentary: Regarding "Vimalakīrti and others," it means that whatever is seen, heard, sensed, or known all constitutes the work of a Buddha.
The *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra* states that in the world-system of Fragrant Accumulation (Gandhavyuha) in the zenith, there is no verbal teaching;

when the assembly of bodhisattvas sits beneath the fragrant trees and smells this wondrous fragrance, they immediately attain the Samādhi of the Treasury of All Virtues. There may also be buddha-fields where there is no speech at all.
The mental intention constitutes the Buddha-work; seeing forms and hearing sounds is as explained in the *Śāstra*.
[Commentary: "Ā" (the upper character is pronounced with the second tone, the lower with the third tone, as previously explained).
[Commentary] To translate "yi" (meaning) as "ju" (phrase/sentence): it is called a "zhāngjù" (chapter-phrase) because it expresses the ultimate sense of the meaning of differentiation.
[Sūtra] Regarding the seven treasures: the *Amitāyus Sūtra* states they are gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, coral, agate, and musaragalva;
the *Gaṅgā Sūtra* states they are gold, silver, coral, pearl, musaragalva, moonstone, and maṇi-jewel. The Buddha...
The *Dilun* states: first, gold; second, silver; third, vaidūrya; fourth, sphaṭika;
fifth, musāragalva (which corresponds to *carcā*; sixth, aśmagarbha (which corresponds to *mǎnǎo*); seventh, red pearl.
As for the differences in the textual versions, these are distinct enumerations of names based on variations in the preferences of different regions.
[Commentary]: Regarding these four [types of practitioners], those who have heard the three [teachings] once and contemplate them once receive and uphold these;

that which understands even a single phrase through the wisdom derived from hearing is the wisdom of contemplation (*cintāmayī-prajñā*). Briefly citing these four as examples, one should practice all the remaining six modes of conduct accordingly.
[Sūtra] That the nature of syllables is detached means that they are empty of causes and conditions; because syllables arise dependently, their intrinsic nature is empty.

Because their intrinsic nature is empty, they lack the characteristics of syllables. Returning to the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), the nature of syllables is detached; the characteristics of syllables are extinguished, and there is only true nature.

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "without increase," the intent of that sutra is to explain the nature (*dhātu*) according to its manifestations. That is to say, the pure *dharmakāya* exists within the bodies of sentient beings;
as it follows sentient beings through their coming and going in birth and death, this aspect of coming and going is termed "sentient being.
If those sentient beings go against the flow of birth and death, returning to the root and source, they revert to their original nature and abide therein as before.
This is called "attaining Buddhahood," which is like an actor who transforms his appearance and then returns to his original form.

[Commentary] Regarding the "Desire Realm" (*kāmadhātu*): "desire" refers to the three desires, namely, sexual desire, the desire for food, and the desire for sleep. "Realm" (*dhātu*) has the meanings of striking and dividing.

It extends from the wind-circle below up to the Heaven of Controlling Others' Emanations (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*) above. It comprises the sentient beings of the five destinies as well as the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*).

Because it is divided into three realms of desire (*kāmadhātu*) by this intermediate boundary, it is called the "Desire Realm. Furthermore, this Desire Realm is known as the "Ground of Mixed Dwelling of the Five Destinies" (*pañcagatimiśravāsa-bhūmi*).

Together with the four meditative concentrations of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*) and the four spheres of the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), they constitute the nine stages (*navabhūmi*). (This may be understood according to the text).
[Commentary]: Regarding the "four emptinesses" and so forth, this refers to the four formless abodes (*ārūpya*) of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), which are called the "four formless emptinesses.
The *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* (Vibhāṣā), fascicle 141, asks: "Why are these four called 'formless'? It answers:

"Because they transcend all material phenomena (*rūpadharma*), and because there is no possibility for material phenomena to arise therein. Fascicle 84 states: "This refers to those who are first practicing the karma [of meditation]."

The practitioner first dwells in contemplation upon the characteristics of space; having grasped these characteristics, they cultivate the preparatory application by means of conceptualization, resolute conviction, observation, and clear illumination of the boundless characteristic of space, thereby successively inducing the first formless absorption.
Therefore, this absorption is called the Sphere of Infinite Space. Regarding the second [absorption], "space" refers to the six kinds [of objects] which the practitioner should first contemplate.

The characteristics of consciousness are to be understood according to what was previously explained. As for the third emptiness, it is called "nothingness" (*ākiṃcanya*) because of the absence of "mine" and "self.
If this is so, then all stages are likewise [devoid of self]; why then is "absence of mine" (*nir-mama*) attributed to this stage alone? Answer:

Because the power of "I" and "mine" has become weak and diminished, and there is no other stage like this one. As for the fourth emptiness, it refers to the absence of ignorance (*avidyā*) within this stage.
Because one has realized that characteristics are not non-characteristics, it is called the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception.
These four "spheres" (āyatana) are all places where various states of existence (bhava) grow and develop; they are places where various karmas and afflictions (kleśa) arise.

Because [beings] mistakenly reckon these as nirvāṇa, the Buddha taught them to be "places where existence grows. Their essential nature is meditative concentration (samādhi); the names are derived from their objects—namely, emptiness (śūnya) and nothingness (ākiṃcanya).
The term "limit" (*anta*) is explained according to the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent) compound; the remaining three [terms] are to be understood accordingly.

If one asks what the characteristics of entering the two types of meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) are, and how they differ: the characteristics of the dhyāna attainments are like being inside a room, because they depend upon form (*rūpa*).
The characteristics of entering the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) are like being in open space, because they do not depend upon form.
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "based on these preparatory stages (*sāmantaka*) and so forth," the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* states:

"The mundane paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) and liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) take, respectively, the lower and upper stages as their objects, [perceiving them] as coarse (*audārika*), suffering (*duḥkha*), and obstructive (*ādīnava*), and as calm (*śānta*), sublime (*praṇīta*), and renounced (*niḥsaraṇa*).

This means that the path of uninterrupted transition takes the various contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) of the immediately lower stage as its object, and among the three aspects (*ākāra*)—coarse, suffering, and obstructive—it adopts whichever single aspect is appropriate.

In the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*), one contemplates the various contaminated phenomena (*sāsravadharma*) of the immediately higher stage through the three aspects of "calm" (*śānta*), "excellent" (*praṇīta*), and "separation" (*niḥsaraṇa*).

Among these, because [the lower stage] is not calm in any respect, it is called "gross" (*audārika*); because it can only be transcended with great exertion and is not exquisite, it is called "painful" (*duḥkha*);
and because it is characterized by much heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*) that causes obstruction and harm, and lacks true renunciation, it is so designated.

These are called "obstructions" because they can hinder one from transcending their own level (*bhūmi*). The three—*śānta*, *praṇīta*, and *niḥsaraṇa*—should be understood as the opposites of these. The meaning is as follows: whether it be through aversion for the coarse and aspiration for the calm, or aversion for suffering and aspiration for the sublime, or aversion for obstructions and aspiration for liberation—whichever of these occurs, one becomes established in the subduing of the innate afflictions (*kleśa*) of the lower level and is born in the higher level.
