Regarding the first dhyāna and the joy of the second dhyāna up to the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), this now clarifies that among the three types of mental application (*manasikāra*) within the four formless spheres of emptiness (*ārūpya-āyatana*), by cultivating any one of these as the cause for attaining meditative absorption, one is born there as the result. As for "homogeneity" (*nikāya-sabhāga*), the Ci'en commentary explains:
"Homogeneous group" (*nikāya*) means "category"; "same" (*sama*) means "one"; and "division" (*bhāga*) means "similarity. This refers to many dharmas being unified into one.

Based on similarity, the "homogeneity" (*nikāya-sabhāga*) is established; since the gods of the formless realm lack material bodies, their homogeneity is established solely based on the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*).
Because each of the four classes is similar to itself, a single homogeneity is established for each.

[Commentary: Regarding the sixth [category] and so forth: because the ever-present ignorance (*nitya-carita-avidyā*) associated with the seventh consciousness does not initiate karma, it is not the primary focus here.
The ignorance associated with the sixth consciousness that deludes regarding principles (*tattva*) is precisely what can initiate karma;

while that which arises from deluding regarding phenomena (*vastu*) can assist in initiating karma, this ignorance—which is both the primary initiator and the assistant of the three types of karma such as merit (*puṇya*)—is called the "root" (*mūla*), being the foremost of all dependently originated phenomena.
This ignorance is, in fact, the root of the fruits of suffering within the three realms. [Commentary:
Regarding the phrase "from the *Qixin lun* to the branches and tips," this refers to the fundamental non-enlightenment and the derivative non-enlightenment within that treatise.
That work explains the arising of delusion from the Truth through five successive layers of root and branch: first, the single mind, which is called the source; second, the reliance upon...
The One Mind opens two gates: first, the gate of the True Suchness of the mind, which means that the nature of the mind is neither born nor extinguished;
second, the gate of the arising and ceasing of the mind, which means that the Tathāgatagarbha conjoined with arising and ceasing is called the Ālayavijñāna.

Third, based on this consciousness, two meanings are clarified: first, the meaning of awakening, which means that the essence of the mind is free from thought, equal to the realm of empty space; second, [the meaning of] non-...

The meaning of "awakening" (*jue*) refers to not awakening because one does not know the *tathatā* (suchness) of phenomena as they truly are; thus, the mind arises. Fourth, based on the meaning of non-awakening, the three subtle states (*sanxi*) arise:

first, because of non-awakening, the mind moves, which is called the "mark of karma" (*yesiang*); second, because of movement, there is the capacity to perceive, which is called the "mark of transformation" (*zhuanxiang*);
third, because of perception, objects falsely appear, which is called the "mark of manifestation" (*xianxiang*). Fifth, based on the mark of manifestation...

There arise six coarse states: first, the mark of cognition (the innate clinging to dharmas based on objects); second, the mark of continuity (the uninterrupted arising of thoughts, which is the discriminative clinging to dharmas);

third, the mark of grasping (the arising of attachment in the mind, which is the innate clinging to a self); fourth, the mark of calculating names (discriminative views of a self; these four are all afflictions); fifth, the mark of initiating karma (caused by karma);
and sixth, the mark of suffering bound by karma (the fruit of suffering). One should know that ignorance can give rise to all these, which are called the three realms.
The Root. [Commentary:

Regarding the "branches, ends, subtle characteristics, and so forth," these are based on the Mind’s Gate of Arising and Ceasing (*citta-utpāda-nirodha-mukha*), which is opened into two meanings: namely, the meaning of awakening (*bodhi*) and the meaning of non-awakening (*abodhi*).
This meaning of non-awakening has two aspects: first, fundamental non-awakening (*mūla-abodhi*), which, in contrast to True Suchness (*tathatā*), is beginningless.
This fundamental awakening is called "beginningless non-awakening"; the very first moment of delusion that turns its back on fundamental awakening is called "fundamental non-awakening.
Second is "branching non-awakening," which arises with fundamental awakening as the cause and non-awakening as the condition, producing the three subtle marks:

first, the mark of karma; second, the mark of transformation; and third, the mark of manifestation. These three are precisely the eighth consciousness, which is capable of manifesting through transformation.

Therefore, it is called the manifesting consciousness (*khyāti-vijñāna*). Based on this manifesting consciousness, the preceding seven object-consciousnesses arise, manifesting the six coarse characteristics.
These six coarsenesses are collectively termed the "branch-end non-awakening."
[Commentary]: Regarding "Laṅkā," a verse states: "Just as when the ocean encounters the condition of wind, various waves arise and manifest their functions in continuous, uninterrupted succession;

so too is it with the ocean of the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna). Struck by the winds of objects and the like, the waves of the various consciousnesses constantly arise and manifest their functions in succession.
When the waters of the sea give rise to waves, their successive manifestations of function are without interruption."
When the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) is severed, it is like the ocean; the waves of the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) arise when struck by conditions such as objects.

The preceding seven evolving consciousnesses manifest according to conditions, inducing the subsequent ones and following upon the preceding ones, their functions unfolding one after another so that the continuity of birth and death proceeds without interruption.

[Commentary: "Just as, for example," and so forth, means: suppose there is a person who, upon first arriving at a mountain range or entering a village, becomes mentally confused and takes the east for the west.
Once one direction is mistaken, all other directions shift accordingly. While in this state of confusion, the directions themselves do not actually change;
yet, when one suddenly awakens, one realizes that the previous confusion left no trace whatsoever, leaving only the four [cardinal directions].
Whether one is lost or awakened, both rely upon the compass; sentient beings are likewise. At the very first moment of delusion, they turn their backs on original enlightenment (*prakṛti-vijñāna*).
Once deluded, original enlightenment follows that delusion in its turning. Yet, at the very moment of being deluded, original enlightenment does not itself turn.

When awakening occurs suddenly, it is also simply this original enlightenment. Whether deluded or awakened, both rely upon original enlightenment. Enlightenment is itself awakening; non-enlightenment is not.

Delusion and awakening are contrasted to distinguish their respective characteristics; here, we take the initial moment of the mind’s non-awakening and name it "fundamental non-awakening," which is precisely what this sutra refers to as the fundamental ignorance of the triple world.

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "the stages of the sages" (*ārya-bhūmi*), the old version of the *Ratnaketuparipṛcchā-sūtra* (Renwang jing) speaks only of the eighth, ninth, and tenth stages as receiving the body of transformation (*nirmāṇakāya*).

This is explained in terms of those who have attained universal equality; that is, from the eighth stage upward, both those of sudden and gradual enlightenment who have attained universal equality all receive the body of transformation.

Therefore, following the broad and comprehensive textual intent of this present sutra regarding the various stages of the sage-positions, it is revealed that the Śrāvakas of the two vehicles—both those still in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)—turn [toward Mahāyāna].

Those whose minds are directed toward the great transformation of the *parināmika-śarīra* (the body of transformation) are all Bodhisattvas of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*); they are all considered persons. Generally speaking, regarding the two types of transformation, those of the Two Vehicles do not attain it;
only Bodhisattvas attain it. There are two categories of Bodhisattvas: first, those of sudden enlightenment (*tongwu*), and second, those of gradual enlightenment (*jianwu*).

After entering the first stage (*prathamā-bhūmi*), they are further divided into three classes: those in whom compassion (*karuṇā*) predominates, those in whom wisdom (*jñāna*) predominates, and those in whom compassion and wisdom are equal. Among these, [we shall discuss] those in whom compassion predominates.
For those who enter the eighth stage (*bhūmi*), the category of contemplation on the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) continues for a long duration, such that afflictions do not arise;
because they do not retain delusions to moisten rebirth, they do not undergo *paricchinna-vedanīya* (segmented) birth, but must instead enter *pariṇāmi-vedanīya* (transformative) birth.

For those whose wisdom predominates, after entering the first stage (*bhūmi*), they eternally suppress the afflictions and receive a transformative body. For those whose compassion and wisdom are equal, it depends upon the different modes of practice preferred by those bodhisattvas.

From the first stage through the second up to the completion of the seventh stage, those who wish to fear the afflictions enter the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) first and enter the transformation [of the basis] later;

those who do not fear the afflictions enter the transformation [of the basis] first and enter the transformation body later. These two types of gradual awakening all undergo the transformation body upon turning their minds toward the five fruits.

However, there is a distinction: when those of the Two Vehicles who have attained the state of no-more-learning turn their minds toward the Great Vehicle, they receive [the transformation body] immediately.

Because those who have undergone transformation (*parivṛtti*) have no further existence, they do not turn their minds toward future birth; whereas those in training (*śaikṣa*), because they still have future existence, may—whether in the present body or after passing through a birth—attain a transformed body according to the will of the Noble One and as appropriate.

[Commentary: Regarding "Mahāmati and others," this refers to those of the two vehicles who have turned their minds [toward the Mahāyāna] prior to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) but have not yet realized the principle of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*).

Nevertheless, by means of the power of the untainted concentration and vows regarding the emptiness of persons (*pudgalanairātmya*), they support their past karma and receive an inconceivable *nirmāṇacitta* (transformation) body.
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "The *Puruṣa-sūtra* and others," the sūtras state that the two vehicles (*dvayāyāna*) are those who have already turned their minds [toward Mahāyāna];

they are called by their former names because they are bodhisattvas of gradual enlightenment (*anupūrva-abhisambodhi*). When it says that all three vehicles (*triyāna*) receive the name "transformation body" (*nirmāṇakāya*) and attain mastery over marks (*lakṣaṇa*) and lands (*kṣetra*), the seventh fascicle of Vasubandhu’s *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* states that this refers to the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) realized in the eighth stage (*bhūmi*).
These two are the bases for mastery: when the desired characteristics are about to manifest, they can manifest immediately according to one's resolute conviction;

this is called mastery over characteristics (*lakṣaṇavaśitā*). When the lands of gold, jewels, and so forth that one aspires for manifest according to one's resolute conviction, this is called mastery over lands (*kṣetravaśitā*).

[Commentary: Regarding the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, chapter three, and so forth, it states: "First, the *manomaya-kāya* (mind-made body) of the bliss of *samāpatti*. *Samāpatti* here is translated as 'equilibrium' (*ting-zhi*);

it refers to meditative absorption that encompasses both states with mind and without mind. At this stage, the Bodhisattva, by the power of samādhi, receives a *parināmika-kāya* (body of transformation) that arises according to his will;
it is also called the *manomaya-kāya*. What is now termed the 'body formed by mind' (*yi-cheng-shen*) is this same [concept]."

Because it is accomplished according to one's wishes and does not arise anew, it is not termed "birth. The Sūtras state that one attains this body through mastery over the meditative concentrations (dhyāna) of the third, fourth, and fifth stages;
subsequently, having attained it, one also attains it in the preceding first and second stages.

Second, the mind-made body that realizes the self-nature of phenomena (*dharmasvabhāva-avabodha-manomaya-kāya*): by observing and realizing that all phenomena, such as illusions and the like, are entirely non-existent.
The third is the "body born of mind" (*manomaya-kāya*) of the same class and innate, characterized by effortless activity (*anabhisamskāra*).

Bodhisattvas of the eighth stage attain this through the realization of signlessness (*animitta-darśana*), whereby they immediately perceive that all phenomena are like illusions and lack intrinsic substance. However, [this body] does not exist for the six [stages], nor does it persist for a long time in the seventh;
although that sūtra speaks specifically of its attainment in the eighth stage, in reality, it is attained throughout the sixth, seventh, and eighth stages.
Regarding those born simultaneously (*sahaja*): according to the various species of sentient beings, Bodhisattvas are able to manifest bodies identical to them;

yet, while they can manifest hundreds, thousands, and tens of millions of such identical bodies simultaneously, this occurs without deliberate effort (*anābhoga*) and arises spontaneously, hence it is called the "body made of mind through effortless action" (*anabhisamskāra-manomaya-kāya*).
It is like many images appearing instantaneously in a mirror, for the mirror requires no effort; [this is the case] in the ninth stage.
The manifestation of the body on the ten stages is likewise so.
[Commentary] Regarding the three texts that are identical: these are the four-fascicle *Old Benevolent Kings Sūtra* and the *Laṅkāvatāra-bhagavatī-sūtra*.

Both the fourth fascicle of the *Laṅkāvatāra* and the *Bhagavatī-sūtra* state that even before those of the two vehicles who have attained the stage of no-more-learning turn their minds toward the great stages (*mahābhūmi*), they already obtain [the bodhisattva path].

If even those who undergo the body of transformation (pariṇāma-kāya) [attain this], how much more so those who have ascended the stages (*bhūmi*)? The three types of mind-made bodies (*manomaya-kāya*) are attained throughout the ten stages;
as this sutra states, these correspond to the various stages of the noble ones (*ārya*).

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "there are two kinds of hindrances," there is the afflictive hindrance (*kleśāvaraṇa*), which acts as the condition for moistening [the seeds] to bring about the segmented body (*prātibhāsika-kāya*); it is from this that the body of transformation is attained.

Because the *yì* (transformation) is free from afflictions (*kleśa*), only the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) serve as the conditions for deluded attachment and as the conditions to be severed;

it brings about the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*). [Commentary] Regarding these three names: first, it is called the "inconceivable transformation body" because the coarse body is transformed into a subtle essence.
It transforms a short lifespan into a long one; because its body is subtle and wondrous, and its lower state is unfathomable, it is called "inconceivable" (*acintya*).

As the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "By the power of compassion and vows, one transforms the body and life so that they have no fixed limit; therefore it is called 'transformation' (*pariṇāmanika*).
Its wondrous function is difficult to fathom, hence it is called 'inconceivable. (The other two names are as cited in the commentary)."

[Commentary: Regarding those who rely on bodies of the desire or form realms according to their respective spheres and stages: those in the first and second fruits who turn their minds toward the Great Vehicle do so from the desire realm;

those in the third fruit who turn their minds do so from both the desire and form realms; and those of the two vehicles in the stage of no-more-learning who turn their minds do so from the desire realm, or those in the fourth fruit who turn their minds toward the Great Vehicle do so from within the form realm. These various noble ones, as appropriate, abide in those [realms]—the desire realm or the four dhyānas.
Relying immediately upon that very body, they undergo transformation through the conditions of the teaching and transformation by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Those who have attained sudden awakening, relying on a superior basis, are born among the Bṛhatphala gods of the Fourth Dhyāna;

there, they utilize the karma that induced their present existence from a lower stage to receive a transformation body, whereby the five aggregates are transmuted into something subtle and wondrous. Thus, it is not a body of the Formless Realm, because [that body] is subtle.
Because they are wondrous, only those of the same class see one another;

those in higher, superior stages—Buddhas and Bodhisattvas—see the bodies of those in lower stages, yet inferior sages of lower stages do not see the superior transformation-bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) of higher stages.

The phrase "Bodhisattvas and others" is equivalent to "Buddhas," while "not the objects of inferior or equal [beings]" is equivalent to "ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*). All of this clarifies that those in lower stages do not see the superior [bodies] of higher stages.

Because it is a transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), it is called "subtle and wondrous. Furthermore, Ci'en explains that because they belong to the same class, those in lower stations can also see the transformation bodies of those in higher stations.

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "because one has personally realized *bodhi* for the sake of benefiting and gladdening others," this is because one desires to accomplish these two matters. Thus, the reason is...
Because it is secretly supported by the power of the vow of untainted meditative concentration (*anāsrava-samādhi*), karma induces a body of transformation (*nirmāṇakāya*).

Just as the method for extending life supports the causal karma of the present body, making it superior and causing that karma to continue uninterruptedly with the fruit of transformation for a long duration;
when its momentum is perceived to be exhausted, one again supports it. In this way, through repeated support and induction, one relies upon the body of transformation.
From the time one personally realizes bodhi and delivers sentient beings until the moment of attaining Buddhahood— specifically during the path of liberation following the vajra-path—
this body of transformation is discarded simultaneously with the vajra-path, leaving no trace behind, just as a lamp is extinguished.
As for the method of prolonging life, it is like an arhat of definitive nature who will not undergo rebirth again.

One who has no desire for future existence but wishes to cause this body to remain long in the world first discards clothing and ornaments, performs various meritorious deeds, and makes a formal vow and commitment.
Then, entering the *prāntakoṭika-samādhi* (the meditative concentration of the ultimate limit) in a secluded place, they use the power of that concentration and vow to secretly support that [body].

Because of the causes from former times, the karmic actions of the past are supported; their functional efficacy becomes exceedingly powerful, thereby sustaining the *paricchinna-kāya* (the segmented, physical body).

Although Yan-ian remains in the world, the essence of his meditative vows is tainted (sāsrava); as he now draws upon the latent support of his past karma, and because the characteristics of that past karma are similar [to the present], he is cited as an analogy.
[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "since they have not yet," etc.: because of the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), they grasp at phenomena as being existent;

they see that there is *bodhi* which can be sought and realized, and they see that there are sentient beings who can be delivered. For this reason, this obscuration is called the "condition" (*pratyaya*).

Due to this condition, they intend to remain for a long time, cultivating the practices of *bodhi* and delivering the classes of sentient beings. However, because the power of their causal karma is weak...

Because the aspiration of untainted meditative concentration (*anāsrava-samādhi*) supports the karma capable of inducing the present body, it causes that karma to become preeminent, thereby inducing a transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) that abides long in the world.
This is for the purpose of seeking great enlightenment and delivering sentient beings; the reverse explanation follows the commentary.

[Commentary: Furthermore, regarding the phrase "that which is equalized" (*so-teng*): because the cognitive obstacles (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) obstruct great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*), in order to sever those obstacles, one maintains the body for a long duration and gradually eliminates them.

How does one maintain the body for a long duration and sever the obstacles? One should do so by utilizing the power of untainted meditative concentration and vows (*anāsrava-samādhi-praṇidhāna-bala*) to sustain the karmic seeds that produce the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*). Relying upon this transformation body, one gradually severs those obstacles and perfectly realizes enlightenment.
[Commentary]:
Regarding "the *Laṅkāvatāra* and other [sūtras]," this refers to recollecting how, in the past, one made great vows to seek supreme enlightenment above and to deliver sentient beings below.
Through these causes and conditions, one provides the necessary support for transformation, and by means of a transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), fulfills the mind of one's original vow.

[Commentary]: Regarding "the holy teachings" and so forth, there are scriptural statements that those who undergo untainted transformation (*anāsrava-nairmāṇika*) and transcend the three realms do so by taking untainted meditative concentration and vows as the auxiliary cause (*sahakāri-hetu*) and tainted karma as the primary cause (*upādāna-hetu*).

Because these two causes induce the fruit of transformation, it is said—according to its fundamental auxiliary cause—that the fruit of transformation transcends the three realms; it is not that the fruit itself does not [belong to the realms].
Question: Since the outflow-free (anāsrava) dharmas destroy the three realms of existence (trai-bhava), how can that which is outflow-free induce an outflowing body?

Answer: It is not so. Rather, through the power of concentration and vows (samādhi-praṇidhāna) associated with the outflow-free state, and supported by the longing [for enlightenment], one induces the karma for manifesting a present body.
This causes the karma to become preeminent, ensuring that the fruit does not cease. In reality, it is an outflowing karma that induces this, just like a tree in the world.
Just as wood depends upon water and so forth, because the roots receive superior support, the branches and leaves flourish luxuriantly.

[Commentary: Regarding the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* and other texts, if the five and eight consciousnesses of Bodhisattvas transform into lands, these are contaminated lands belonging to the bonds of the three realms.
However, the pure lands transformed by the sixth and seventh consciousnesses during their uncontaminated state are themselves uncontaminated in essence; they do not belong to the three realms.
Just as a portion of the consciousness that undergoes transformation is untainted (*anāsrava*) and transcends the three realms when it pertains to the pure lands (*śuddhakṣetra*),
so too, regarding this transformation, its portion that serves as the auxiliary cause is untainted and thus transcends the three realms.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "How is it that... and so forth, [the question is] how it is that even at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (samyaksambodhi), there still remains the cause for the segmented [birth] (*bhavāgra-cheda*).

There are three interpretations in the *Śāstra*: 1. One interpretation states: The seeds of innate afflictions (*sahaja-kleśa-bīja*) are the cause for moistening and producing that segmented birth. If one observes [the continuity of the mind] as uninterrupted, it does not admit of moistening for the production of birth;

however, if one observes [the continuity] as interrupted, it will necessarily be able to moisten [the seeds] so that one receives a body of segmented birth. Thus, at the stage of Equal Enlightenment, there still remains [the cause for] segmentation.

Regarding the two aspects of the power of cause and effect in the *duàn* (segmented) [rebirth]: first, it is said that the cause and effect of the *biànyì* (transformational) body are fundamentally the *duànfēn* (segmented) [rebirth], which is transformed from the segmented state into the transformational body by means of the untainted (*anāsrava*) [virtue] sustaining past karma;

this is discussed in terms of the point of exhaustion, where both deaths are eternally exhausted before one attains Great Enlightenment, and thus even at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*), there still remain the two deaths as cause and effect. Third, it is said that Original Enlightenment (*benjue*) serves as the root-cause.
Taking fundamental ignorance as a condition, the three subtle states arise; from the three subtle states, the six coarse states arise.
These three and six together are termed "branch-final ignorance," which is itself the two kinds of birth and death. This is what is meant by proceeding from the root toward the branches.

If one can resolve to cultivate practice and advance toward the holy, proceeding from the branches back to the root, one transforms the body of segmented existence into a body of transformational change and returns to the source.
Awakening is called the state of the Tathāgata; at this stage of equal awakening, there is only the death of transformation (*pariṇāmiki-maraṇa*), whether as cause or as fruit.

As for the body of segmented existence (*aupapāduka-kāya*), there is the cause but no fruit. Thus, speaking in terms of general characteristics, there are two types of death: those consisting of cause and those consisting of fruit.
[Commentary: Regarding the three bodies and three virtues: the two types of cessation and the dharma-realm constitute the Dharma-body; the two wisdoms constitute the Reward-body;

and the equality of nature and characteristics, which pervades both the Dharma and Reward bodies, along with their functional application, constitutes the Transformation-body. Thus, the Dharma, Reward, and Transformation bodies correspond respectively to the three virtues of eradication, wisdom, and grace.
[Commentary]: The two lines clarify the person; now, examining the three lines that clarify the person, it refers to the one who studies and practices Prajñāpāramitā.
When observing the speaker and the listener, they are like illusory beings who appear to move and act, yet lack the characteristics of speaking and listening, because their intrinsic nature is empty.
[Commentary: Regarding "flowing through the three periods of time," all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) arise and perish moment by moment, yet their substance flows on;
that is to say, they flow from the future into the present, and then from the present into the past.

What has already passed is called the past, what has not yet come is called the future, and that which stands between these two is called the present phenomenon. As for "phenomena moving through the three periods," it refers to the movement of the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).

The flux is like the traveler who relies [upon it], while form and mind are like the road; arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing proceed in dependence upon these factors, which is called "dharma-practice" (the three time periods are as explained in the commentary).

[Commentary: The *Vibhāṣā-śāstra* states that there are four types of fields: first, the field of destiny (*gati-kṣetra*), referring to animals, hungry ghosts, and so forth; second, the field of suffering (*duḥkha-kṣetra*), referring to travelers, the sick, and so forth;
third, the field of gratitude (*upakārin-kṣetra*), referring to parents, Dharma masters, and so forth; and fourth, the field of virtue (*guṇa-kṣetra*), referring to the Buddha-jewel and so forth.
Within these four objects, that which causes benefit and merit to grow is called a "field of merit" (*puṇya-kṣetra*).

[Sūtra]: That which is not "seeing" and so forth refers to seeing with the eye and hearing with the ear, because these are free from grasping at forms and sounds; therefore they are called "seeing" and "hearing.

The three faculties of nose, tongue, and body cognize through their conjunction [with objects], and thus are collectively termed "awareness" (*buddhi*). The mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) apprehends its objects and discerns all phenomena; because it functions through both conjunction and non-conjunction, it is called "cognition" (*jñāna*).
[Commentary]: "Only practicing the cultivation of existence while not [practicing] emptiness"—the phrase "not emptiness" explains the aforementioned "cultivation of existence.
Because one clings to existence and the deluded mind increases further, the Bodhisattva is instructed to extinguish this clinging to existence and the mind of false conceptualization;

thus, they are led to practice the cultivation of emptiness. "Only practicing the cultivation of emptiness while not [practicing] existence"—the phrase "not existence" explains the aforementioned "emptiness."
Because one practices the cultivation of emptiness, one becomes attached to emptiness; therefore, it is taught that the truly untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*) does not arise without a cause.

To instruct Bodhisattvas to give rise to the true mind and cultivate the contemplation of existence (*bhāvālambana*), within this contemplation of existence, the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation (*śruta-mati*, *cintā-mati*, *bhāvanā-mati*) perfume the original seeds, thereby giving rise to the truly untainted mind of the noble stages (*ārya-bhūmi*). Through this instruction, one practices the simultaneous cultivation of both emptiness and existence.

[Commentary: Regarding the three kinds of sublime contemplation: the sublime contemplation of the mind that feels weary of and seeks detachment from conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) serves as the cause for the quality of cessation (*prahāṇa-guṇa*), realizing the fruit of the *dharmakāya*.

The sublime contemplation of the mind seeking *bodhi* serves as the cause for the quality of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*), attaining the fruit of the *saṃbhogakāya*. The sublime contemplation of the mind of compassion for sentient beings serves as the cause for the quality of grace (*anugraha-guṇa*), accomplishing the fruit of the *nirmāṇakāya*.
[Commentary]: Regarding "the patience of subduing" (*vītarṣa-kṣānti*) and so forth among the five [patiences], the patience of subduing is impure wisdom (*sāsrava-prajñā*).

"Patience" (*kṣānti*) here carries the sense of accepting and upholding through conviction. The remaining four patiences are both pure and impure; "patience" here carries the sense of investigating, verifying, and realizing. Furthermore, as for the patience of subduing:

because this patience is able to suppress the two obstacles of conceptualization (*vikalpa-āvaraṇa*) so that they do not arise, it is called "subduing. That which is subdued by this patience is the very act of subduing itself.

"Endurance" (*kṣānti*) is called "subduing endurance" (*vinīlaka-kṣānti*). "Faith-endurance" (*adhimukti-kṣānti*) is so named because those who possess faith and endurance are close to [the stage of] faith;

this is an etymological explanation based on proximity. "Compliance-endurance" (*anuloma-kṣānti*) refers to the endurance that accords with what is to be accorded; since one can comply, that endurance is called compliance-endurance. "Non-arising endurance" (*anutpāda-kṣānti*) is the natural non-arising itself as endurance;
the three types of endurance regarding non-arising are termed non-arising endurance. "Cessation-endurance" (*nirodha-kṣānti*) is first explained as follows: [text continues].

Regarding the "dependent designation" (yǐzhǔ) [compound] and so forth, the meaning of the latter interpretation is as follows: this patience (*kṣānti*) can pacify birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and can extinguish obstructive defilements; thus it is called "patience of pacification" (*jīmèi rěn*).
This is explained according to the *adhikaraṇasamāsa* (locative determinative compound).

[Commentary: The *tathāgatagarbha* (the womb/embryo of the Tathāgata) is precisely the innate, untainted seeds (*anāsravabīja*). It is termed the "power of the Dharma" (*dharmabala*) and also the "power of the causal basis" (*niśraya-hetu-bala*).
"Garbha" has the meaning of being a causal nature; its name is established by way of the future manifestation of the fruit of Buddhahood.
Because it is the womb of the Tathāgata, it is called the *tathāgatagarbha*.
[Commentary: The "Three Jewels of One Substance" (yiti sānbǎo) are also called the "Three Jewels of Identical Substance" (tóngti sānbǎo).

Because the Jewels of Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha share the same True Suchness (*tathatā*) as their essential nature, and because True Suchness and Awakening constitute the true nature, they are termed the "Buddha Jewel. Because it has the meaning of providing a track and support, it is termed the "Dharma Jewel.
Because it has the meaning of non-opposition, it is termed the "Sangha Jewel. The "Three Jewels of Distinct Characteristics" (biexiang sānbǎo) are also called "distinct [jewels]."
Because the essential nature and characteristics of the three bodies of the Tathāgata are distinct from one another, they are called the Buddha Jewel;
because the untainted teachings, principles, practices, and fruits of the Three Vehicles are distinct, they are called the Dharma Jewel;

and because the noble assemblies of the Three Vehicles possess the harmony of principle and phenomena, they are called the Saṃgha Jewel—only by possessing the untainted precepts, views, and so forth are they designated as the Saṃgha Jewel. As for those who maintain the Three Jewels:
The relics of the physical form and other Buddha images are called the Jewel of the Buddha. After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the Dharma has three periods:

the True (Śāsana), the Semblance (Pratirūpaka), and the Final (Anta). Within these, all contaminated teachings and practices, as well as the written words on palm leaves, are called the Jewel of the Dharma;

those that are uncontaminated are the true Jewel of the Dharma. Thus, among the two types of śramaṇas—those who demonstrate the Path and those who live by the Path—the ordinary beings possess both ethical discipline and right view.
Those who are able to maintain the True Dharma, the Semblance Dharma, and the Final Dharma are called the Sangha Jewel (the meaning of the Three Jewels is as explained in the *Fayuan*).

[Sūtra] Regarding those who give rise to the Ten Faiths: they give rise to these ten mental states; faith is the primary leader, while the other nine assist in its accomplishment. Collectively, these are termed the "Ten Faiths."

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "certainly not regressing" and so forth: one certainly does not regress from faith when one gives rise to superior-grade wrong views and completely severs the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*).

Both the roots of goodness and the wrong views are each divided into nine grades. By severing the roots of goodness in reverse order, up until the point where the superior-superior grade of wrong view severs the inferior-inferior grade of the roots of goodness, this is called "severing the roots of goodness.
Because the roots of goodness have been exhausted, the roots of goodness that are severed are exclusively those that are *sāsrava* (with outflows).

The wholesome dharmas acquired at birth (*upapatti-lābhika-kuśala*) within the tainted conditioned realm exist only as active manifestations; they do not refer to the cutting off of the seeds of goodness in those who are *icchantikas*.
Regarding this term "without nature" (*abhavya*), there are two types: first, the absence of the untainted seed-nature of the three vehicles;
second, the current absence of the causal seed-nature for practicing wholesome deeds. It should be understood that the "cutting off of goodness" refers to the latter type of lack of nature.

[Commentary: Regarding "entering the stage of right determination" (*samyaktva-niyāma*), the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* states: "Within the stage of the ten wholesome actions, one grows weary of the suffering of birth and death and seeks supreme enlightenment.

Encountering Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, one serves and makes offerings to them, performing these various practices for ten thousand kalpas until faith is perfected and one is able to resolve the mind [for enlightenment].
Once the mind has been resolved, one enters the stage of right determination and dwells in the state of a Buddha, never again falling back."
Regarding the statement that "generating the mind" (bodhicitta) corresponds to the superior cause of the lineage (*gotra*): it refers to the generation of the mind through the perfection of faith.

Because this marks the initial entry into the stage of the inner ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), it is called "entering the assembly of those fixed in the rightness" (*samyaktva-niyāma*). This is established as the three assemblies (*tri-nikāya*) which collectively encompass both ordinary persons and noble ones (*ārya*).

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that those of the icchantika class are called the "assembly of those fixed in the wrongness" (*mithyātva-niyāma*), those from the first bhūmi upward are called the "assembly of those fixed in the rightness," and those prior to the bhūmis, as well as others, are [the assembly of those not yet fixed].

The indeterminate group (*aniyata-rāśi*) is also called those lacking the nature for *nirvāṇa*, who constitute the wrongly fixed group (*mithyātva-niyata-rāśi*). Among the ten stages (*bhūmi*), those prior to the seventh stage, the Stage of Non-retrogression (*avaivartika-bhūmi*), are termed the indeterminate group;

from that point onward, they are the rightly fixed group (*samyaktva-niyata-rāśi*). According to this sutra and the *Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna* (*Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra*), those at the stage of non-retrogression through faith are named the rightly fixed group, while those who have severed their roots of goodness (*kuśala-mūla*) are named the wrongly fixed group; all others are the indeterminate group.
Sentient beings are called the "indefinite group" (*aniyata-rāśi*). There are four types of non-retrogression: first, non-retrogression through faith;

the sixth of the ten faiths is named the "non-retrogressive mind," because from this point onward one no longer retrogresses into the arising of false views. Second, non-retrogression through position;

the seventh of the ten abodes is named the "non-retrogressive abode," because from this point onward one no longer retrogresses into entering the two vehicles (*dviyāna*). Third, non-retrogression through realization; from the first stage (*bhūmi*) upward, one has already realized [the truth].

Because wisdom and discernment are not lost, one does not regress from the four practices; from the eighth stage upward, it is called the "stage of non-retrogression" because both the conditioned and the unconditioned are cultivated and realized, and because one proceeds spontaneously within the swift current of the Dharma.
[Commentary] Regarding the *Yingluo jing* and other texts: each of the ten minds has its own minor, major, and complete portions;

whether practiced for a short time, a long time, or throughout one's life, by performing them oneself, teaching others, and encouraging and consoling them, these ten in each category form a hundred practices.

Alternatively, when one practice among these ten faiths arises, the remaining nine assist it; thus, through mutual support among the ten, they constitute a hundred practices. These are the hundred practices.
The Dharma is the basis for the wisdom of those in training; because it serves as the gateway for entering higher and higher stages, it is called the "Gate of Illumination.

When practicing the hundred activities, one constantly generates immeasurable aspirational vows with signs (*sanimitta*) to benefit sentient beings, and aspirational vows without signs (*animitta*) to realize the true and eternal.
By practicing in this manner, one attains entry into the stage of the Nature of Cultivation (*śikṣamāṇa-gotra*).

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that there are no separate ten stages of faith (śraddhā) apart from the ten abodes (bhūmi), the ten stages of faith are subsumed within the Abode of Initial Resolve (prathamacittotpādabhūmi).

From the ten abodes onward is termed the stage of the Inner Ordinary Person (antarapṛthagjana), the nature of the Cultivated Seed (śrutavāsanāgotra), entry into the assembly of those fixed in rightness (samyaktvaniyāma), and the stage of the lower-grade Patience of Subduing (mṛdu-kṣānti).
[Commentary: Regarding "diligently studying the ten dharmas" and so forth, the first four dharmas each consist of one phrase, while the latter six each consist of two phrases;
their meanings may be understood according to the text. [Commentary:
Regarding the attainment of Buddhahood through the eight phases: first, the phase of entering the womb; second, the infant; third, the youth; fourth, asceticism; fifth...
The manifestation of the eight aspects of attaining Buddhahood— namely, (1) attaining enlightenment, (2) subduing Māra, (3) turning the wheel of Dharma, and (4) entering nirvāṇa—
is thus called "attaining Buddhahood through the eight aspects" for the sake of delivering all sentient beings (as explained at length in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*).

[Commentary: The Stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā-bhūmi*) is so called because within the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*), the water of meditative concentration is scant; thus, the two types of wisdom—through hearing and reflection—are termed "dry wisdom.
The Stage of Seed-Nature (*gotra-bhūmi*) is so called because within the stage of application (*prayoga-avasthā*), one's lineage and family gradually become more noble.

The Stage of the Eight Persons (*aṣṭamaka-bhūmi*) is so called because when counting the four candidates and four fruits from the superior to the inferior, it corresponds to the eighth; it is precisely the beginning of the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*).
Regarding the stages of fruition and the paths of progress: the stage of one who possesses vision refers to the first fruit, because one has fully realized the truths (*satya*).
The stage of attenuation refers to the second fruit, because six categories of afflictions have been abandoned and the remaining three categories are extremely subtle and thin.

The stage of detachment from desire refers to the third fruit, because one has realized the state of being free from desire. The stage of having completed what was to be done refers to the fourth fruit, because the fruits have been fully perfected.

(The remainder of the text may be understood). [the stage of the stream-enterer]; 8. [the stage of the once-returner]; 9. [the stage of the non-returner]; 10. [the stage of the arhat]. (The rest is as previously explained). The stage of Stream-enterer (8), the stage of Once-returner (9), the stage of Non-returner (10), and the stage of Arhat; the ten stages of the Pratyekabuddha:

1) the stage of perfection in ascetic practices, 2) the stage of self-awakening to causes and conditions, 3) the stage of awakening to the Four Noble Truths, 4) the stage of profound and sharp wisdom, 5) the stage of the Eightfold Noble Path, and 6) the stage of awakening to the Dharma-realm, the realm of empty space, and sentient beings.

1. The Stage of Birth; 2. The Stage of the Grounds; 3. The Stage of the Seven Realizations; 4. The Stage of Quiescence; 5. The Stage of the Six Supernatural Powers (referring to the six types of skillfulness);

6. The Stage of Subtle Secrets; 7. The Stage of the Gradual Thinning of Habit-Energies. These are the ten stages of the Bodhisattva as usually described. Regarding the ten stages of the Buddha-fruit: 1.
The Stage of Profound and Difficult-to-know Nature, because it can eliminate habit-energies; 2. The Stage of Majestic and Radiant Virtue, for the purpose of teaching all Bodhisattvas.

1. Because it is the profound Dharma, it is called the Ground of the True Reality of the Three Natures; 2. because it teaches the Triple Vehicle, it is called the Ground of the Virtue of the Wisdom of Supernatural Powers; 3.

because it subdues the four Māras through eighty-four thousand Dharma-gates, it is called the Ground of the Radiance of the Fire-Wheel; 4. because it subdues non-Buddhists, it is called the Ground of Stainless Nirvāṇa; 5.
because it manifests the eight aspects of attaining enlightenment, it is called the Ground of the Vast and Supreme Dharmadhātu; 6. regarding the Ground of... [text continues].
37. The Stage of the Non-existence and Non-attachment of the Thirty-seven Factors of Enlightenment, because there is nothing that exists and nothing to which one is attached; 38.

The Stage of Universal Awakening Wisdom and Penetration, because of the bestowing of the prophecy upon Bodhisattvas; 39. The Stage of Illumination through Dedication, because of manifesting skillful means for all Bodhisattvas; 40.
The Stage of Vairocana’s Wisdom and Virtue, because of teaching all phenomena as being originally quiescent for all Bodhisattvas.
Because it is the quiescent Great Nirvāṇa.

[Commentary] Regarding the "Pure Dharma-realm" (*dharmadhātu*): "realm" (*dhātu*) has the meaning of "nature" (*svabhāva*) and the meaning of "cause" (*hetu*). Taking the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) as the cause, the twelvefold teaching flows forth equally;
because the teachings thus flowing forth resemble the Dharma-realm, they are called "outflowing teachings" (*niṣyanda-dharma*). Hearing these teachings perfumes the mind.
The untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*) increase, differing from their original state, and are nurtured until they become superior, just as a fetus in the womb is nourished.

At the stage of the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*), the noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*) manifests, like the birth of a fetus; the *dharmatā* realized therein possesses the sense of being a support, and by way of this metaphor, it is called the "noble family.

Because the noble wisdom arises based on that realization, it is termed "born into the Buddha-family. Now, it is clarified that the period prior to the Path of Seeing is designated as the "noble embryo" (*āryagarbha*). As for the noble...
Because it is conceived in the womb, it is called the "Noble Womb" (*āryagarbha*).
[Commentary: Regarding the "nature-lineage" (*gotra*), the various types of untainted wisdom (*anāsravajñāna*) are themselves the nature.

The "nature" mentioned above refers to the fact that through hearing the true Dharma, the original untainted seeds—perfumed by hearing and so forth—increase and become distinct from their original state; this is what is designated as "nature. This nature is...
Because it is the nature that increases and brings about accomplishment, its very nature (*prakṛti*) is called "nature-lineage" (*prakṛti-gotra*).
[Commentary] Regarding the "naturally abiding lineage," the term "lineage" used below refers to the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of the originally existing untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*).

In the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra-ṭīkā*, this is categorized under the character "surname" (*xing*). Both "essential nature" (*svabhāva*) and "surname" (*gotra*) may be used; they both signify that which is primordial.
There are distinctions among the essential nature (*svabhāva*), lineage (*gotra*), and category (*jāti*) of these seeds, which do not exist [as such] at present;

thus, this "seed-lineage" (*bīja-gotra*) has two meanings: first, to distinguish it from newly perfumed seeds, it is called the "original nature" (*prakṛti-gotra*), because its essential nature is originally present;

second, to distinguish it from already perfumed seeds, it is called "abiding," because it remains guarding its original state without increasing. As for the seed-lineage accomplished through cultivation (*abhyāsa-saṃskṛta-gotra*), it refers to that which arises upon generating the Great... [text fragment ends].

Following the mind, one listens to and receives the true Dharma; through the perfuming of hearing and so forth, the seeds that are the nature of things (*dharmatā-bīja*) increase and transform from their original state, and are thus termed "the lineage accomplished through practice" (*abhyāsa-niṣpanna-gotra*). This lineage also has two meanings: first, the meaning of "practice," because the three types of wisdom (*prajñā*) perfume [the mind] and cause it to increase;
second, the meaning of "accomplishment," because the excellence of the perfuming brings about the perfection of this lineage.

[Commentary: Regarding the "treatise" (*śāstra*), it refers to the fundamental seeds (*bīja*). Those that have existed from the beginning and have never been cultivated through practice are called the "nature-abiding lineage" (*prakṛti-stha-gotra*).
If they have already been cultivated and increased beyond their original state, they are called the "cultivated lineage" (*samudānīta-gotra*). Therefore, nature comes first and cultivation follows.

The scriptural text, however, establishes these two names solely with reference to the lineage of cultivation from the point of generating the mind of awakening (*cittotpāda*) onwards; thus, [it speaks of] the first...

Cultivation is called the "nature of cultivated seeds" (*śikṣāgotra*). When cultivation has been practiced for a long time and the nature has become established through that practice, it is called the "nature of innate seeds" (*prakṛtisthagotra*).
Therefore, cultivation comes first and the innate nature follows. [Commentary:

Regarding the practitioner of the ten perfections, one adds skillful means (*upāya*), aspiration (*praṇidhāna*), power (*bala*), and wisdom (*jñāna*) to the six perfections; thus, they together constitute the ten perfections. This is the intended meaning.

[This section] explains how Bodhisattvas at the stage of the ten practices cultivate according to their respective inclinations, interpreting the thirty types of mind as being like the "Chapter on Receiving and Upholding.
[Commentary]: Regarding the patience that contemplates the causes arising from past karma—for instance, although the substance of the wholesome karma performed in the past...

Having already ceased, yet having once served as a cause that summoned the maturation (*vipāka*) of a happy rebirth (*sugati*) in this present life—one carefully examines and confirms that causal karma;

this is called "acceptance of the former cause. That the present maturation is the fruit summoned by the former causal karma of a previous life—one carefully examines and doubly confirms and accepts this.
Furthermore, that one creates causal karma within this very body to summon future fruits—one carefully examines and doubly confirms and accepts both.

The acceptance of the cause and the present result is called "acceptance of the cause"; the thorough investigation and firm conviction that a present virtuous cause will necessarily induce the maturation of a future happy rebirth is called "acceptance of the future result."

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "Although only," etc., the question is raised: while it can be said that present causes and effects exist, how can one further speak of past causes and future effects arising—the former having already ceased and the latter not yet existing—in order to give rise to the patient acceptance of cause and effect (*hetu-phala-kṣānti*)? This [passage] provides the explanation for this.

[Commentary: Regarding "dependent origination" and so forth, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that the twelve links of dependent origination are collectively categorized into four types: namely, ignorance (*avidyā*) and volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) are the "projectors";
consciousness (*vijñāna*) and the other five [links] are the "projected"; craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and existence (*bhava*) are the "producers";

and birth (*jāti*) and old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) are the "produced. To investigate and examine these causes and effects with precision and to then accept them through conviction is termed "acceptance of past causes" (*pūrvahetu-kṣānti*) and so forth.
[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "and so forth," these five names are all alternative designations for the "self" as conceived by non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).

Because they conceive that the self will have further existence in future lives, it is called the "life-possessor" (*jīvaka*). Because they conceive that the self is currently capable of performing actions, it is called [the agent].
Because the self as the agent possesses a permanent and indestructible life-force, it is called the "vitalizer" (*jīvaka*).

To conceive of the self as having superior function is, for example, like calling a strong man a "hero" (*puruṣa*); to conceive of the self as having exquisite and peerless function is to call it a "youth" (*maṇavaka*), where "youthful" (*maṇava*) means beautiful and "child" (*ka*) means young; thus, the divine self is both exquisite and youthful and vigorous.
[Commentary] "Perverse perception" (*saṃjñā-viparyāsa*) refers to the perception that occurs when the four perversions arise simultaneously. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"Because one gives rise to false conceptualizations and discriminations such as 'permanence' regarding what is impermanent and so forth, it is called perverse perception (*saṃjñā-viparyāsa*).

Because one endures, desires, establishes, and clings to those objects discriminated by such false conceptualization, it is called perverse view (*dṛṣṭi-viparyāsa*). Within that which is clung to, one gives rise to craving and the like."
The delusions are called "inversions of the mind"; there are four inversions of perception, and these three types together constitute seven inversions of delusion.
The meaning of the sutra is that the inverted false imaginings of non-Buddhists deny [reality] and do not destroy the correct practice of Bodhisattvas.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "by means of contemplation" and so forth, various sūtras and śāstras explain the virtues of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) as follows: first, the aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīla-skandha*), which is the prātimokṣa vows;

second, the aggregate of meditative concentration (*samādhi-skandha*), which consists of the nine successive attainments (*navānupūrva-samāpatti*); third, the aggregate of wisdom (*prajñā-skandha*), which is the wisdom directed toward conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*); fourth, the aggregate of liberation (*vimukti-skandha*), which refers to the faculty of resolve (*adhimukti*);

and fifth, the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimukti-jñāna-darśana-skandha*), which is the wisdom directed toward unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*). Bodhisattvas attain these partially, while Tathāgatas realize them perfectly.

The virtues of those five aggregates are the dharmas certified by these five patiences; because the Bodhisattva in this stage cultivates the practice of patience and is certified as progressing toward the noble stages through the superior merits of the five aggregates, the patience regarding the five aggregates is termed the "five patiences."

[Commentary]: Regarding the patience of the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimukti-jñāna-darśana-kṣānti*): "knowledge" (*jñāna*) refers to realization through direct perception, while "vision" (*darśana*) refers to contemplative observation.

Its essence is wisdom (*prajñā*). Because it both knows and sees, it is called "knowledge-vision. Because this knowledge and vision takes the unconditioned liberation as its object, it is termed "the knowledge and vision of liberation.

Bodhisattvas prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) cultivate patience in order to incline toward and realize the virtues of that noble stage of knowledge and vision; therefore, it is called the "knowledge and vision of liberation."
The patience [regarding] this is called the patience of the knowledge and vision of liberation; the remaining four are to be understood by analogy. [Commentary:
Regarding these two, it is because these two patiences induce the two paths of vision (*darśanamārga*) of the true nature and the conventional characteristics. What are their aspects?

One contemplates the conventional truth as a provisional designation and realizes that phenomena are impermanent, thereby attaining the patience of impermanence; yet this object of contemplation relies upon the established [conventional] basis.

Based on these truths, one induces the sixteen moments of mind that constitute the相见道 (the path of vision as characterized by images). Through the contemplation of the established truths (*vyavasthāpita-satya*), one contemplates the reality of the ultimate truth;
by realizing the emptiness of all phenomena, one attains the patient acceptance of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

However, this object of observation is the non-established truth (*avyavasthāpita-satya*), which involves contemplating either the single principle of True Suchness (*tathatā*) or the two types of emptiness. From this, one induces the single-moment path of true vision (*eka-citta-tattva-darśana-mārga*).
And the three minds of the path of vision (*darśanamārga*) consist of the contemplation of the non-established truths (*apratiṣṭhita-satya*).

[Commentary: Regarding the four verified convictions (*pratyakṣa-śraddhā*): because untainted faith (*anāsrava-śraddhā*) together with the fundamental and subsequent wisdoms (*mūla-anvaya-jñāna*) verify the four objects—the True Treasures (*ratna*) and the purity of ethical discipline (*śīla*)—they are called "verified convictions. Because these can verify the four objects, they are termed the "four verified convictions."
It is also called the "Fourfold Verified Pure Faith" (*caturvidhā avetyaprasāda*), because its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is pure mind and it takes the verified objects of faith as its domain.

[Commentary: Regarding the "Joyful Stage" (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), all commentaries on the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* follow the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*. This Joyful Stage receives its name based on three meanings:

first, because one initially attains the nature of a noble one (*ārya*) and abandons the nature of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*); second, because one possesses the realization of the two kinds of emptiness (*dvividha-śūnyatā*), which is not like that of the Hīnayāna.

Because one realizes the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), the three [joyful roots] benefit both oneself and others by cultivating the two types of welfare. As the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra* states:
"Seeing the truth and benefiting sentient beings are both called the roots of joy"; thus, both the fundamental and subsequent attainments are joyful. Regarding the "ground" (*bhūmi*):

its essence is the union of wisdom and phenomena (*jñāna-dharma*). It is so called because it serves as the basis for the various practices of the noble ones and because it sustains their meritorious qualities, preventing them from being lost.
Because it gives rise to wondrous conduct and increases excellence, and because it possesses these three meanings, it is called a "ground" (*bhūmi*). As the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
"Because it serves as a superior support for the practices being cultivated, allowing them to grow and flourish, it is called a 'ground.
The ground of joy is named the 'Joyous Ground' (*pramuditā-bhūmi*). The remaining grounds are to be explained accordingly."
[Commentary]: *Śīla* means "coolness," which is the fruit of ethical discipline (*śīla*). For a Bodhisattva on the second stage, the nature-precept (*prakṛti-śīla*) is perfected;
it is not like the guarding of precepts through deliberation on the first stage, and thus it is named the "Stainless Stage" (*Vimalā-bhūmi*).

[Commentary]: Regarding those within the afflictive obstacles (*kleśāvaraṇa*): the ten afflictions consist of doubt (*vicikitsā*), wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), view-grasping (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), and precept-and-vow-grasping (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).

These four arise solely through conceptual construction (*vikalpaja*). Greed, hatred, delusion, pride, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*)—these six—pervade both innate (*sahaja*) and conceptually constructed [arising].

In total, there are ten [conceptual] types. Because these [first four] are conceptually constructed and arise from delusion regarding the principles (*tattva*), they are abandoned instantaneously by the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*). As for the six [remaining] innate types, they arise from delusion regarding phenomena (*vastu*).

In the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), these are severed bit by bit. Regarding the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* treats them as analogous to the afflictions;
both the categories of delusion regarding principles (*tattva*) and delusion regarding phenomena (*vastu*) are identical in number (as explained in detail below according to this interpretation).
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "this sutra and so forth," in these three stages, one respectively abandons one obstacle (*āvaraṇa*).

Since these three obstacles predominantly manifest as bodily and vocal forms, and because they arise largely by taking form-objects (*rūpaviṣaya*) as their conditions, they are termed "afflictions of form" (*rūpakleśa*).

They are called "bonds" (*bandhana*) because they bind the Bodhisattva, making it difficult to ascend to the increasingly superior and sublime stages. Furthermore, there are three categories of phenomena among those abandoned: first, afflictions (*kleśa*); [the other two are]...

The two types of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) that act as obstacles are: first, the seeds of the cognitive obstacles (*jñeyāvaraṇa*); second, the habitual tendencies of the cognitive obstacles. According to the *Sūtra*, based on their general characteristics, these are collectively termed "form" (*rūpa*).

Regarding the bondage of afflictions: because giving (*dāna*) directly opposes greed (*lobha*), it is practiced in the first stage (*bhūmi*). Because the cultivation of the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*) directly opposes hatred (*dveṣa*) and so forth, it is practiced in the second stage.
In the third stage, one accomplishes superior meditative concentrations (*samādhi*), great dhāraṇīs, and is able to give rise to boundless sublime wisdom (*prajñā*).
Because light opposes the darkness of delusion (the remaining cases may be understood by analogy).

[Commentary: Regarding the ten *paryavasthānas* (envelopments), the *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā* states: "The eight envelopments are lack of shame (*āhrīkya*), lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*), envy (*īrṣyā*), avarice (*mātsarya*), along with regret (*kaukṛtya*), sleep (*middha*), restlessness (*auddhatya*), and torpor (*styāna*);
or ten, adding anger (*krodha*) and concealment (*mrakṣa*). Regarding the five *nīvaraṇas* (hindrances): first, greed; second, hatred; third, delusion; fourth, restlessness; [fifth, doubt].
The five [factors]—remorse, lethargy, and sleep—obscure the principle by these five kinds; because they shroud wisdom and prevent its arising, they are established as "hindrances" (*nīvaraṇa*).
Furthermore, the afflictions (*kleśa*) and cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) of both the paths of seeing and cultivation bind sentient beings and shroud their wisdom and insight;
such obstacles as these he vows to sever.

[Sūtra] Regarding "benefit and happiness," the *Abhidharmasamuccayabhāṣya* explains that there are eight distinct meanings: 1) benefiting future lives is called "benefit," while benefiting the present life is called "happiness";
2) benefiting the present life and bringing happiness to future lives; 3) gathering what is wholesome and abandoning what is unwholesome;
4) abandoning evil and cultivating goodness; 5) uprooting suffering and bestowing happiness; 6) bestowing supramundane goodness and bestowing mundane goodness.
The seventh [stage] bestows wisdom and merit; the eighth bestows the fruits of the Hīnayāna and the fruits of the Mahāyāna. These eight meanings correspond respectively to benefit and happiness.

[Commentary]: Regarding the Stage of Blazing Wisdom (Arciṣmatī-bhūmi), the first, second, third, fourth, fifth, sixth, and seventh stages are similar to ordinary beings in their cultivation of generosity, ethical discipline, and patience. The fourth, fifth, and sixth [stages]...

This fourth ground is similar to that of the two vehicles; it is similar to the śrāvakas in their cultivation of the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), yet it is superior to the practices previously cultivated.

Among the thirty-seven [factors], there are those whose essence is not wisdom, which nevertheless assist wisdom in severing hindrances and burning the fuel of afflictions, for dharmas such as the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) within the sixth consciousness are what are to be burned.

[Commentary]: Regarding the "Difficult to Conquer" (Sudurjaya) stage, according to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, the non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) realizes the realm of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), while the conceptual wisdom (*savikalpa-jñāna*) takes the realm of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) as its object. In the first, second, third, and fourth stages, these two arise sequentially;

in the fifth, sixth, seventh, and eighth stages, they arise together with the preparatory application (*prayoga*); and in the ninth, tenth, and eleventh stages, they arise spontaneously (*anābhoga*). This [refers to] the preparatory application of this fifth stage.

Because the mental application (*manasikāra*) that realizes the ultimate and the one that penetrates the conventional arise simultaneously, they enable the two types of wisdom to be mutually non-contradictory;
because they can unite what is difficult to unite, it is named the "Extremely Difficult to Conquer" stage (*sudurjayā bhūmiḥ*).

[Commentary] Regarding the "Manifesting" stage (*abhimukhī bhūmi*): this sixth stage involves contemplating the twelve links of dependent origination, which is termed the "wisdom dwelling in dependent origination. Furthermore...
It is called the "Manifesting Ground" (*Abhimukhī-bhūmi*) because it is able to induce the most excellent *prajñā* and cause it to become manifest.

[Commentary: Regarding the three obstacles being associated with the three types of pride respectively: first, the pride of self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-māna*), which refers to conceit arising from clinging to a self and clinging to phenomena;
this encompasses both obstacles. Second, the pride of conceptualizing the purity of the body (*kāya-śuddhi-vikalpa-māna*); "conceptualizing" refers to attachment.
The meaning is this: because he practices the contemplation of the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), he counteracts the defilements of the hindrances.

Consequently, regarding his own body as pure, he gives rise to pride. Third, there is the pride of discriminating between the defiled and the pure: "defiled" refers to suffering and its origin (*duḥkha* and *samudaya*), while "pure" refers to cessation and the path (*nirodha* and *mārga*).

At this stage, the Bodhisattva observes the Four Noble Truths and, becoming attached to their marks (*nimitta*), gives rise to pride. Most of these [forms of pride] belong to the category of the cognitive hindrance (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) arising from the notion of self.

Pride is called an affliction (*kleśa*) because it shares these three characteristics. As for the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), it is designated by the name "affliction" and is called a mental affliction.

[Commentary]: Regarding "skin, flesh, and heart," etc.: because they take the six sense objects as their conditions, they are shallow and easy to know, and are thus like skin; if they take the internal...
Those who cling to the person and the phenomena of self give rise to the notion of "I" and so forth; because they are difficult to discern, they are like flesh.

If one is deluded regarding ultimate truth and clings to the difference between the ultimate and the conventional, this subtle clinging to phenomena is profound and difficult to perceive, like the mind.
[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "the coarseness and heaviness in the skin," the seeds, manifestations, and habitual tendencies are collectively termed "coarseness and heaviness" (*dauṣṭhulya*).

Among these, the medium grade is somewhat difficult to sever, while the inferior grade is subtle and extremely difficult to sever. This is like first damaging the skin, then subsequently damaging the [flesh], bone, and so forth;
this refers to the actual reality.

[Commentary] Regarding the "Sūtras and Śāstras" and so forth: the *Śīla-samvara-yoga* (The Yoga of Ethical Discipline) and the stages of abandoning hindrances (*prahāṇa-bhūmi*)—the dharmic entities metaphorically represented by the skin, flesh, and so on—pertain to both types of hindrances (*āvaraṇa*). Based upon those [metaphors], these afflictions of form and mind are revealed.
[Commentary]: All explain that the three natures are called "unborn" (*anutpāda*). First, "intrinsic non-arising" refers to the nature of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*);
because what is grasped as existing has no essence whatsoever, its fundamental nature does not arise, and is thus termed "intrinsic non-arising.
Second, "spontaneous non-arising" refers to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*); although phenomena such as form and mind arise from causes and conditions, they do not arise spontaneously.
The nature of arising is called the "nature of non-arising" regarding the three delusions and suffering; this refers to the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).

Because its self-nature is pure and delusions and suffering do not arise, it is called the "non-arising of delusions and suffering. By means of the seal of the three types of non-arising, one realizes and witnesses them;
therefore, it is named "patience toward non-arising" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
[Commentary]: Regarding "the patience that is itself patience": among the three types of patience, the essence of non-arising is naturally wisdom;
therefore, the essence of non-arising is called patience, specifically the "patience of non-arising. This refers to the three types of patience regarding non-arising.
[Commentary]: The "Ground of Far-Going" (*dūraṃgamā-bhūmi*) receives its name through three meanings: first, it reaches the limit of the dwelling in signlessness (*animitta-vihāra*).

[In the preceding stages], up to the end of the fifth ground, there is much observation of signs (*sanimitta-darśana*) and little observation of signlessness; in the sixth ground, there is little observation of signs and much observation of signlessness;
in this [seventh] ground, there is exclusively observation of signlessness, such that one possesses the application (*prayoga*) for distancing oneself from the practice of signs toward signlessness.
Therefore, regarding the two [points]: prior to this stage, the cultivation of wondrous practices in all preceding stages involved effort (*sābhoga*); upon reaching this stage, such effort ceases.
Third, because it transcends the worldly paths of the two vehicles: in the first, second, and third stages, one's conduct is similar to that of worldly ordinary beings;
in the fourth, fifth, and sixth stages, one's cultivation is similar to that of the two vehicles.

Because one observes [the path] and, in the seventh stage, remains far removed from those [hindrances], one is able to perform superior practices within [the stages]; thus it is named the "Far-Reaching Stage" (Dūraṃgamā-bhūmi).
[Commentary]: As for the "Immovable Stage" (Acalā-bhūmi), because non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) proceeds spontaneously and uninterruptedly, by virtue of this—
If, in this stage, there are any activities, any effortful practices, or any afflictions, they all do not [arise], and it is called the Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*).
[Commentary]:
Regarding the "habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of form and mind," these refer to the two categories of the innate obstacles (*sahaja-āvaraṇa*), which are collectively termed as such. One is... named.

The fetters of afflictions regarding form (*rūpa-kleśa-bandhana*) and those regarding mind (*citta-kleśa-bandhana*) arise by taking two or many objects as their conditions. Each of these two has two types:
namely, those that arise by taking form as an object and are of a superior degree of coarseness, which are severed one portion each in the first, second, and third stages;

and those that arise by taking mind as an object and are of a superior degree [of coarseness], which are severed one portion each in the fourth, fifth, and sixth stages. There are two categories of those that arise by taking both form and mind as objects.

The inferior [hindrance] is subtle and difficult to eliminate; it refers to the simultaneous abandonment of both form and mind, along with their latencies (*vāsanā*), across the seventh, eighth, and ninth stages.
This term "latency" applies to both seeds and manifest states, as well as other heavy residues (*dauṣṭhulya*). Here, manifest activity acts as the perfumer and the seed acts as the perfumed.
Because both the perfumer and the perfumed are subtle, this constitutes the residual portion of the coarse hindrances of those [stages].

Therefore, the term "habitual tendencies" (*vāsanā*) refers specifically to the insensitivity (*akarmaṇyatā*) and heaviness (*dausthulya*) of the two obstacles; this is what is properly called "habitual tendency. [Commentary:

Regarding the "Dharmameghā-bhūmi" (Cloud of Dharma Stage): the noble wisdom is like a cloud, and because one realizes the Dharmakāya through this cloud of wisdom and gives rise to the Great Dharma, it is the stage of the cloud of that Dharma;
thus it is named the Dharmameghā-bhūmi. As the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* says: "The great dharma-cloud of wisdom..."

Containing all virtues, its waters are as vast as space; because the coarse and heavy [afflictions] still fill the *dharmakāya*, the term "Equal Enlightenment" (*samyaksambuddha*) signifies a state of similarity.
Because his awakening is equal to that of a Buddha, he is called "Equal Enlightenment"; however, because he has not yet attained even the minor path of liberation, he is not yet named a Buddha.

[Commentary] Some say that what is explained extensively below refers to the passage in the *Awakening of Faith* which states: "It is only the mental characteristics (*citta-lakṣaṇa*) that are extinguished, not the substance of the mind (*citta-svabhāva*).
'Extinction' means severance... and so on, up to: "Now, when ignorance is exhausted through awakening, the characteristic of movement is extinguished accordingly;
however, it is only the mental characteristics that are extinguished, not the substance of the mind. Regarding those who feel compassion, there are various sutras...
The treatise states that there are four supreme virtues possessed exclusively by the Tathāgata and not shared by other noble ones:

first, great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*), which has non-delusion and non-harming as its essence; second, great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), which has non-delusion and non-harming as its essence; third, great sympathetic joy (*mahāmuditā*), which has non-delusion and [joy] as its essence;
and fourth, great equanimity (*mahopekṣā*), which has non-delusion and virtuous relinquishment as its essence. Each of these four consists of three aspects. One...

[The three types of great compassion are: first, that which has sentient beings as its object; second, that which has phenomena as its object; and third, that which has no object. It is said that "great compassion" arises by taking *tathatā* (suchness) as its object.

The other two are to be understood accordingly. [Commentary: "You all" refers to you sentient beings who, due to prior afflictions and karma, have summoned and experienced the five aggregates as the dwelling of birth and death.
Therefore, it is said that they "enter this house. Regarding the two meanings of "entering," one interpretation is based on the sense of "not emerging":
because they do not cultivate sublime practices and remain submerged without emerging, this is called "entering the house. The second interpretation is based on the sense of "dwelling place":
because they dwell within birth and death and seek no way out, it is not a case of first emerging from suffering and subsequently entering the dwelling. The father beholds the fire breaking out.
Fearing that his sons might be burned and their spirits terrified, the Buddha saw the rise of delusion and, concerned lest living beings be harmed, felt compassion;
for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, he entered the three realms, which are like a dilapidated and burning house, just as that elder entered the burning house in alarm to rescue his children.
[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "I originally," etc., he initially established two vows: first, the vow for self-benefit, seeking to realize bodhi;

second, the vow for benefiting others, universally transforming sentient beings. His original vow for self-benefit has now been fulfilled; wishing further to benefit others, he therefore transforms sentient beings so that they all enter the Buddha-way.
