[Commentary: All afflictions—those that are discriminative and deluded regarding principle, and those that are innate and deluded regarding phenomena—arouse karma and moisten rebirth.

The discriminative [afflictions] directly arouse [karma], while the innate [afflictions] assist in its arousal; the innate [afflictions] directly moisten [rebirth], while the discriminative [afflictions] assist in its moistening.
Since both the arousal and the moistening occur together, there is the cycle of birth and death.

[Commentary]: Regarding the "ripened fruit" (*vipākaphala*): the cause encompasses both the wholesome and the unwholesome, while the fruit is exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). Because it ripens as a result of a different category [of nature], it is called "ripened" (*vipāka*).

Furthermore, because the cause was created in a previous life and the ripening occurs in the present life, or the cause is created in the present life and the fruit ripens in a future life—ripening at a different time—it is called "ripened.
This ripening itself is the fruit; thus, it is termed the "ripened fruit."

[Commentary]: Regarding the twenty-two faculties (*dvāviṃśati-indriya*), the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (57) states: "What is the meaning of 'faculty' (*indriya*)? The meaning of 'predominance' (*ādhipatya*) is the meaning of 'faculty.
Why are there exactly twenty-two faculties? Because twenty-two dharmas possess the function of predominance.

[The following verse is cited in the commentary: "Because they possess the function of predominance in apprehending objects, the six faculties beginning with the eye are established; because they possess the function of continuity..."
Because the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) has a predominant function in maintaining existence through the power of karma, it is established separately from the other faculties.

Because they experience the fruits of karma, the five feeling-faculties (*vedanendriya*) are established separately; specifically, the two faculties of sorrow (*daurmanasya*) and suffering (*duḥkha*) experience the fruits of unwholesome karma, while the three feelings of joy (*sukha*), pleasure (*saumanasya*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) experience the fruits of wholesome karma. These [latter] are capable of experiencing both the desirable and the undesirable results of wholesome and unwholesome [actions].
Because the fruits of karma exist within the six destinies, they possess predominant efficacy regarding worldly purity;
because the five faculties such as the eye possess predominant efficacy regarding supramundane purity, the three untainted faculties (*anāsrava-indriya*) are established.

As for the establishment of the twenty-two faculties, other dharmas are not so, for they lack this superior efficacy; therefore, they are not established as faculties. Regarding the three [untainted] faculties: [text fragment].
The nine faculties, beginning with faith (*śraddhā*), belonging to the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) are called the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown" (*ājñātāvya-jñendriya*).

Regarding the final moment of the path of seeing, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states: "From the final moment of the path of seeing onwards, all [faculties] such as faith are of the nature of the faculty of 'knowing' (*ājñendriya*).
All the nine untainted (*anāsrava*) faculties belonging to the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) constitute this [faculty].

This is the faculty of one who has already attained full knowledge (*ājñātāvīndriya*). [Commentary: The five faculties, such as the eye and so forth, and the two sexual faculties—male and female—have matter (*rūpa*) as their substance.
Furthermore, within the one hundred dharmas, there is nothing else that establishes the male and female faculties apart from a portion of the faculty of life (*jīvitendriya*).

The life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) as a distinct entity has the dissociated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) as its essence; the mind-faculty (*manendriya*) generally has the eight consciousnesses as its essence;
the five faculties of faith and so forth each have one dharma from among their respective names within the category of mental factors (*caitta*) as their essence;

the five faculties of sensation (*vedanendriya*) have the factor of sensation (*vedanā*) among the mental factors as their essence; and regarding the three untainted faculties (*anāsravendriya*), it is said that their three natures [are as follows].
Regarding the term "nature" (*prakṛti*) as it applies here, because its essential meaning has already been expressed and one does not wish to repeat it, the word "nature" is used.
The three untainted [faculties] have, according to their respective applications, the nine faculties—faith and the others—as their essence;

that is to say, the mental faculty (*manas*) together with the five beginning with faith (faith, vigor, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom) constitute these nine. Furthermore, another interpretation holds that the intent of this latter phrase is to clarify the three untainted [faculties].
The essence of the faculties (*indriya*) and their categories should be distinguished as follows: among the twenty-two faculties, three are as previously described;
seven are material; these eight are exclusively of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*);
the mind faculty (*manas-indriya*), the five feeling faculties (*vedanā-indriya*), and [the remaining] eight faculties are either exclusively of a wholesome nature (*kuśala*) or may be otherwise.
Regarding sorrow (*daurmanasya*), the verse says: "Only the last eight [mental factors] are exclusively wholesome;
sorrow is both wholesome and unwholesome. The commentary states: [Sorrow is associated with the mental consciousness].

[Sūtra]: Regarding the phrase "the Buddhas manifest guidance," etc., it refers to the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body) that arises through the activity of the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body) to instruct and guide [beings].

Because it is the basis for the various meritorious dharmas of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) and so forth, it is all termed the *dharmakāya* (dharma body). [Commentary]: According to the analysis, following the nature upon which the *nirmāṇakāya* relies, it is called the *dharmakāya*.
It is said that it does not depart from the three realms (*tridhātu*), as it manifests therein in accordance with sentient beings. Thus, it is said: "nor does it depart."
This. [Commentary:
Regarding "non-Buddhists and others," at the end of the eon when human lifespans are immeasurable, there appeared a non-Buddhist named Ulūka, which translates as "owl.
His appearance was hideous; he hid in mountain valleys during the day and traveled about to teach and convert at night. People of the time said:

Because he resembles an owl (*ulūka*), he was given that name. The school is named after its founder; thus it is called the Vaiśeṣika (formerly known as Vaisesi, now known as Vaiseshika), which translates as "Excellence" (*viśeṣa*).
Because an excellent person composed the treatise, and because the treatise itself is excellent and sublime, it is called the *Vaiśeṣika-śāstra* (the Treatise on Excellence).
This is the fourth [section] concerning the six categories (*ṣat-padārtha*) taught by the Vaiśeṣika non-Buddhists.
The *Mahā-sāmānya-pada-śāstra* is so named because it explains that meaning; thus it is called the *Mahā-sāmānya-śāstra*.

As for the six categories (*ṣaṭ-padārtha*), they are substance (*dravya*), quality (*guṇa*), action (*karman*), the Great Universal (*mahāsāmānya*), particularity (*viśeṣa*), and inherence (*samavāya*) (as explained elsewhere).

[Commentary]: If this is so, then since those of the Two Vehicles who have attained the stage of No-More-Learning (aśaikṣa) have already emerged from the fire-hut of the *prātibaddha* (segmented) existence within the triple world (*traidhātuka*), are they not indeed "outside" the triple world?

Furthermore, since Bodhisattvas of the Ten Stages who undergo *pariṇāmika* (transformative) birth emerge from this triple world and dwell in those lands of retribution (*vipākabhūmi*), are they not also "beyond the realms"?

Answer: Those of the Two Vehicles who have attained the stage of No-More-Learning are said to have "emerged" because their subsequent *prātibaddha* existence will never again continue. Thus, they are designated as having emerged.

Those currently dwelling within the three realms still undergo *paricchinna-bheda* (segmented existence); they are not yet those who, outside the realms, undergo *pariṇāma-vikāra* (transformation of change). Even the subtle fruit of maturation (*vipāka-phala*) belongs to the three realms and is not outside them.

[Commentary] Some say that "reaching the wisdom of wisdom" refers to the True Suchness of Original Enlightenment (*mūla-awakening*) according to the *Awakening of Faith*, which is termed "all-encompassing wisdom" (*sarvajñatā*). Conversely...

When delusion returns to the truth and reverts to the source, it is called "initial awakening" (ādikṣānti); thus, the term "wisdom-wisdom" (jñānajñāna) is used. The essence of wisdom is original awakening (mūlapratyavekṣaṇājñāna), which constitutes the Dharma-body;
the function of wisdom is initial awakening, which constitutes the Reward-body. When essence and function are discussed together, it is termed "the wisdom of all-knowledge" (sarvajñajñāna).

[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "from the derivative," etc.: because one knows True Suchness as it truly is and knows the dharma of True Suchness as it truly is, the unawakened mind gives rise to delusive illusions, leading to the cycle of birth and death;

this is termed the "derivative. From the end of this cycle of birth and death, one turns toward Original Awakening, traversing the stages of the five patiences (*pañca-kṣānti*), returning from delusion to truth. Therefore, this Original Awakening is the fundamental basis for the practice of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

[Commentary]: "Seeing events throughout a hundred kalpas of the past and future" refers to a specific class of Bodhisattvas who, upon attaining sudden enlightenment and entering the first bhūmi, are able to know the events of a hundred kalpas through the spontaneous functioning of their innate wisdom (*sahaja*). The *Fahua shu* states:

"The followers of the Two Vehicles can know events of eighty thousand kalpas in the past and future, whereas a Bodhisattva on the first bhūmi can know events of a hundred kalpas; [the former] is inferior [to the latter]."
The remaining merits of the two vehicles surpass those of the [other] two vehicles; they cannot be compared in a single standard.

"The Hundred Dharmas Illuminating Gateway" (*Śatadharma-vyākhyāna-mukha*) refers to the hundred dharmas as explained in the *Śatadharma-śāstra*. "Gateway" (*mukha*) means that which is unobstructed; it is the means by which one enters into understanding.

Its essence consists of the teachings and principles. It is called an "illuminating gateway" (*vidyāmukha*) because it is a gateway of clear wisdom through which one enters by relying upon the gateways of teaching and principle.

Understanding the nature and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and essence and function (*tattva-vṛtti*) of the hundred dharmas: fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) enters into the nature, while subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*) enters into the characteristics.
[Commentary] Regarding the expansion of the "one hundred" of the first stage into a "thousand dharma-gates of illumination": since the number ten is the same as before, it is not mentioned;

however, because the "thousand" and so forth differ from what preceded, they are specifically mentioned. The *Daśabhūmika-śāstra*, fascicle six, states: "Within the first stage, one realizes [the truth] in a single thought-moment."
On the first stage, one attains one hundred samādhis; on the second stage, one thousand samādhis; on the third stage, one hundred thousand samādhis; on the fourth stage, ten billion samādhis;
on the fifth stage, one thousand billion samādhis; on the sixth stage, one hundred thousand billion samādhis; on the seventh stage, one hundred thousand billion nayutas of samādhis;
and on the eighth stage, samādhis equal in number to the atoms within a million three-thousandfold great thousandfold world systems.
In a single moment of thought, a Bodhisattva of the ninth stage attains as many samādhis as there are atoms in hundreds of thousands of Buddha-lands of asaṃkhyeya;

a Bodhisattva of the tenth stage, in a single moment of thought, attains as many samādhis as there are atoms in ten unspeakable hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of nayutas of worlds (as seen in the case of beholding a hundred Tathāgatas and so forth, it may be understood accordingly, as detailed in that treatise).

[Commentary] Regarding the Turning of the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra-pravartana*), based on the meaning of the *Dharmacakra* section of the *Fahua shu* (Commentary on the Lotus Sutra), it is analyzed according to five gates:

first, the essential nature (*svabhāva*); second, the explanation of the name; third, the characteristics of its turning; fourth, its classifications; and fifth, the emergence of the three vehicles. Regarding the first, the essential nature of the wheel, there are five points:

1) the self-nature of the wheel, which refers to the factor of enlightenment consisting of the investigation of dharmas (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*), namely right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) and right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*). The *Yujia jiuwu* (Ninety-five [Treatises on] Yoga) states: "Right view and other such dharmas..."

Because it is that which is accomplished, it is called the Wheel of Dharma (*dharmacakra*). Because it involves three revolutions for oneself and others, and because it pertains to the paths of seeing, cultivation, and no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), the noble eye of wisdom is able to crush the afflictions; thus, it is called a "wheel.

Alternatively, its essence consists solely of the eight branches of the Noble Path, as it possesses the complete meaning of a hub, spokes, and rim. The cause of the two wheels of Dharma refers to the various teachings capable of producing the subsequent Noble Paths.
In various sūtras and śāstras, such as those concerning hearing, reflection, and cultivation, the teachings of the Buddha are called the "Wheel of Dharma" (*dharmacakra*).

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that the three cycles and twelve aspects constitute the means for attaining what is to be attained. Thus, the former serves as the cause for the latter, and their combination constitutes the causal fruit;
this is termed the "means. The retinue of the three wheels refers to the aggregates (*skandha*) that accompany the noble paths, including the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).

This refers precisely to the morality concomitant with the Path (*mārga-sahabhū-śīla*); the remaining four aggregates may be understood as such because they assist wisdom (*prajñā*). The objects of the Four Wheels of Dharma (*dharma-cakra*) refer to the dharmas of the Four Noble Truths, the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, and the Three Natures (*tri-svabhāva*).
Regarding the fruits of the Five Wheels of Dharma, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that they are comprised of the fruits of the four stages of spiritual cultivation (*śrāmaṇya-phala*):
the enlightenment of the Śrāvaka, the enlightenment of the Pratyekabuddha, and the unsurpassed enlightenment of the Buddhas and Tathāgatas. (This term "enlightenment" [bodhi]...)
This penetrates both the general characteristics and specific attributes. Therefore, Bodhi and Nirvāṇa are called the "fruit" that is attained. These five entities do not exceed four types:
first, teaching; second, principle; third, practice; and fourth, fruit. These fully encompass the five entities. To explain their names:

*dharma* (the Dharma) carries the meaning of being a standard for guidance and maintenance, because it is the nature constituted by dharmas such as right view. It is called the "Dharma-wheel" (*dharmacakra*). The wheel has four meanings, the first of which is completeness.
Regarding the "complete meaning" [of the Eightfold Path]: Right View and Right Thought are called the hub (*nābhi*), because they are the foundation.

Right Speech, Right Action, and Right Livelihood are called the spokes (*ara*), because they exist by virtue of the hub. Right Mindfulness, Right Effort, and Right Concentration are called the rim (*nemi*), because they encompass and sustain the others.

Although these eight members of the Noble Path have distinct characteristics when practiced individually, their essence actually extends beyond this [specific stage] and is present throughout all [stages], including the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*).
If one studies the Path in this manner, the World-Honored One would not possess the Eightfold Noble Path;

(2) the sense of "crushing," for these four types of factors—whether they suppress, sever, assist in severing, or directly sever—are all capable of crushing afflictions that have not yet been severed;
(3) the sense of "restraining," for once the afflictions have been suppressed, their power is rendered distant; (4) the sense of "indefiniteness," ranging from one's own views to one's own practice.

From one’s own cultivation to one’s own state of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*); from one’s own state of no-more-learning, one speaks to teach others; through that teaching, others understand the principle of the truths (*satya*);
from the principle of the truths, they give rise to right practice (*samyak-pratipatti*); from right practice, they give rise to the wisdom of the fruit (*phala-jñāna*).
Thus, passing it on in succession, they further speak to others—just as the wheel-treasure (*cakraratna*) of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*) is able to subdue those who have not yet been subdued.
Because it subdues the afflictions and because it has already subdued those [afflictions] that were previously suppressed, and because it proceeds again and again, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"It should be known that the Blessed One transferred the Dharma he had realized into the person of Ājñātakauṇḍinya;
this, in turn, was transferred into another person, and that was transferred into yet another. Thus, it should be understood through the sense of successive transmission."
To say "the wheel of Dharma" (*dharmacakra*) is an *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound. "Turning" (*pravartana*) means to move, to manifest, to transport, and to initiate.

It moves forth the proclamation of the teaching, manifests the sublime principle, transports the Noble Path before the sound [of speech], and gives rise to true wisdom after the words have been spoken.
To perfectly destroy hindrances and afflictions is called "turning the wheel of Dharma. That which is turned is the wheel of Dharma; thus, there are two aspects to the turning of the wheel of Dharma.

Regarding the *śeṣa* (explanatory) compounds: the latter two [definitions] are *tatpuruṣa* (dependent determinative), while the former two are [also] *tatpuruṣa*. As for the "turning of the characteristics," the Buddha himself turned [the wheel] three times as fully described therein.
Regarding the "turning for others": what are the three turnings and twelve aspects? Having personally attained the Way, he further turned the Wheel of Dharma for others three times, saying:
"This is suffering; this is its origin; this is its cessation; this is the path. This is called the first [turning].
"Turning" refers to: "This should be fully known," up to "this should be cultivated"—this is the second turning;
"This has been fully known," up to "this has been cultivated"—this is the third turning. These respectively reveal the path of seeing, the path of cultivation, and the path of no-more-learning.

The first is called the "turning that reveals characteristics," because it reveals the characteristics of the four truths. The next is called the "turning that exhorts practice," because it exhorts the practice of the four [truths].

Because one practices the truths, it is subsequently called "realization" (*sākṣātkriyā*); because one transforms [the practice] into the realization that those [truths] are fulfilled, at each stage of transformation, it causes Ājñātakauṇḍinya and others to give rise to four aspects (*ākāra*) regarding each truth—namely, vision (*cakṣus*), knowledge (*jñāna*), clarity (*vidyā*), and awakening (*buddhi*).

When the noble direct perception (*pratyakṣa-jñāna*) within this very [process] is able to sever the afflictions (*kleśa*) to be abandoned by the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*), at that time it is designated as "Truth" (*satya*).

The noble eye of wisdom (*ārya-prajñā-cakṣus*) is precisely this; because it distinguishes between the past, future, and present worlds, it is designated respectively as knowledge (*jñāna*), clarity (*vidyā*), and awakening (*buddhi*).
This refers to one single wisdom collectively named the "Dharma-eye" (*dharma-cakṣus*), which possesses three modes of activity (*ākāra*) termed knowledge, clarity, and awakening.

It does not arise as four distinct knowledges regarding each individual truth (*satya*), for the Path of True Insight (*darśana-mārga*) consists of only a single moment (*ekakṣaṇa*), unlike the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*).

The lower section specifically observes that while the basis for the designation [of the truths] and the realization of cessation are said to pervade the three time periods, this does not mean that the Truth of Cessation itself exists throughout the three time periods.

(Regarding "designation" (*abhilāpa*): it refers to the manifestation; since it is based upon conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) that the unconditioned nature (*asaṃskṛta-svabhāva*) is manifested, although the nature of the unconditioned is not subsumed under the time periods, the phenomena that serve as its designators—being conditioned—are subsumed within the three time periods. Now, because one speaks of the nature by way of its characteristics, such a statement is made;

for the nature and the characteristics of dharmas are inherently inseparable. As for the second and third turnings, there are likewise four aspects (*ākāra*) per turning; when these three turnings are discussed vertically, they constitute ten.

These two modes of practice, when combined with the Four Truths, total forty-eight aspects; yet because they do not exceed twelve in number, they are collectively termed the "Three Turnings of the Twelve Aspects.
After Cunda had first attained realization and entered the Path of Seeing, the Buddha asked him, "Have you understood?
He replied, "I have understood," and thus he received the name "Understanding" (Ajñāta). This occurred after the second and third turnings were completed.

When Ājñātakauṇḍinya attained the fruit of Arhatship, he gave rise to a mundane thought, thinking, "I have understood the Dharma. When the Tathāgata knew this, he too gave rise to a mundane thought, thinking, "Kauṇḍinya has realized my stage of the Dharma.
When the earth deities knew this, they raised their voices and proclaimed it; in a mere kṣaṇa, muhūrta, and lava, that sound was passed on by successive transmission even unto the Brahma world.
Furthermore, as for what is called a "mundane thought": [it refers to the thought of] "I have understood," "He has realized," and so forth.

The mind that takes phenomena as its object is not distinct from the distracted mind; although it revolves through the characteristics (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) of the Four Noble Truths, it does not differ from those of the three vehicles.
Each person realizes their respective fruit. Those of the *śrāvaka* lineage have already practiced for three lifetimes or sixty eons prior to hearing the Buddha’s teaching.
Relying on the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*), they cultivate and realize the principle of the Four Noble Truths; this is called the *śrāvaka* dharma.

A person of the wheel-turning pratyekabuddha lineage, having previously cultivated [the path] for four lifetimes or a hundred kalpas, hears the Buddha’s teaching on the principle of the Four Noble Truths based upon the twelve links of dependent origination and practices its realization; this is called the Wheel of the Pratyekabuddha.
A person of the bodhisattva lineage, having previously cultivated [the path] for one great asaṃkhyeya kalpa, hears the Buddha’s teaching on the basis of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).

Cultivating and realizing the principle of the Four Noble Truths is called the Bodhisattva Wheel of Dharma; otherwise, since all three vehicles equally contemplate the Four Noble Truths and simultaneously realize the state of holiness, what difference would there be?

Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "World-Honored One, when you first turned the Wheel of the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, at that time immeasurable sentient beings gave rise to the mind of a śrāvaka and realized the fruit of a śrāvaka. Immeasurable...
Sentient beings who have resolved upon the mind of a pratyekabuddha realize the fruit of a pratyekabuddha;
immeasurable sentient beings who have resolved upon the mind of great bodhi realize the first, second, and third bhūmis, and shall attain bodhi in as few as one more birth.

Therefore, we know that at the Deer Park, the Wheel of Dharma of the common practice of the three vehicles was first turned. If this were not so, why would the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra* have been preached during the second seven-day period?

Therefore, it is not called the "Turning of the Wheel of Dharma. Because that [teaching] is not what is practiced in common by the three vehicles, it does not receive the name of the "first turning of the wheel of dharma";

rather, it is the specific wheel of dharma of the Mahāyāna. However, in reality, when the wisdom of others arises at the three times, there are also those who attain the fruit of sainthood after passing through births, which is termed the "three turnings.
Now, to clarify this, [the Buddha] for Ajñātakauṇḍinya and the others— [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.]

At one time in the Deer Park, he caused them to attain these three fruits in succession; this is called "turning the Dharma" (the three fruits refer to the results of the three turnings, as the fruit of Once-returner is not mentioned here).
Regarding the "Three Vehicles," the Buddha, Bodhisattvas, and Śrāvakas are said to turn the wheel of Dharma by teaching others so that they may attain wisdom and sever their afflictions.
The Pratyekabuddhas are not like this; the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states that when a Pratyekabuddha teaches the Dharma, it cannot cause others to [attain such results].

Because [the Buddha] has attained the paths leading to the fruits, such as the stages of Heat (uṣmagata) and Summits (mūrdhan), he turns the wheel of Dharma for the Śrāvakas; however, since the Śrāvakas do not recognize the medicine and the disease, [the Buddha] does not turn the wheel of Dharma for them—though in truth, he is indeed able to do so.

[Commentary]: "Suspended river, limpid and cool" (the first character is pronounced *jǔyǎn*; it is the name of a river; the second character is pronounced *lángdīng*; it means clear, cool water). Here, the meaning of "water-lord" (*shuǐzhǔ*) is taken as being like the pouring of water from a suspended river.
Regarding "like thunder," the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that five kinds of sounds issue from the Buddha’s mouth:
first, they are as profound as thunder; second, they are clear and penetrate far, bringing joy to those who hear them; third, they enter the heart, causing both awe and love.

The Four Truths are easily understood and the five types of listeners never grow weary; such are the seven forms of eloquence (*pratibhāna*), which constitute the fourth of the four types of eloquence.

When spoken of in terms of the arising of wisdom, they are called the four types of eloquence (*catasraḥ pratibhānāni*); when defined by the wisdom that penetrates objects, they are called the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).
[Commentary]: Regarding "the single sound as the perfect sound," the commentary sets forth three meanings. The first is the interpretation of Nāgārjuna and Asvabhāva;

they maintain that the Tathāgata has no body and no speech, possessing only great meditative concentration, wisdom, and compassion to pity sentient beings, thus responding like an echo to the Dharma to benefit the multitudes.

The latter two are the explanations of Dharmapāla and others, who state that the Buddha’s untainted voice (*anāsrava-ghoṣa*) is pure, singular, and unmixed, and is therefore called [the perfect sound].
Regarding "one sound," there are two meanings for its designation as "perfect sound" (*yuan-yin*): first, because this single sound perfectly accords with all faculties, it is called "perfect sound";
second, because this single sound perfectly encompasses both text and meaning, and is unimpeded in its unity and multiplicity, it is called "perfect.
Being perfect and being sound, it is termed "perfect sound."
[Commentary]: Regarding the "Three Mysteries," they are called the Three Mysteries because the three karmas of the Tathāgata are subtle, profound, and hidden.
These Three Mysteries are shown so that all sentient beings may rely upon them to emerge from suffering and enter into bliss; therefore, they are called "gateways."

[Sūtra] Regarding the "merit of the five patiences" (*pañca-kṣānti-guṇa*): "Merit" (*guṇa*) refers to the labor of practice and its functional efficacy; "virtue" (*de*) refers to the fruits of morality, wisdom, and blessings.
Therefore, they are called "meritorious virtues.
[Sūtra] "Only the Buddha alone can exhaust the source": Guangping says that "source" (*yuan*) is like the summit of a mountain, the ultimate limit.

The "place" (sthāna) refers to the mountain source; only the Buddha alone is able to practice to the ultimate limit of the five patiences (pañca-kṣānti), reaching the point where one is named "Able to Exhaust the Source" (or "Origin").
Water’s root is called the "source" (yuan); since the essence of the five patiences is the root of all virtues, it is like a spring source.
Therefore, only the Buddha alone is able to realize and exhaust the original source of the five patiences. Question: Only the Buddha alone?
If the World-Honored Buddha had not appeared, those within the five destinies would be subsumed under the two types of bodies of birth and death;

if he had appeared beyond the five destinies, he would be a non-sentient being. Why, then, is he called a "human"? Answer: All conditioned phenomena of form and mind, whether mundane or supramundane, are generally categorized into three classes:
first, sentient beings; second, non-sentient things; and third, that which is neither sentient nor non-sentient. It is not that the latter does not exist.

The Buddha as a sentient being belongs to the third category: having already transcended the five destinies and departed from the two kinds of birth-and-death, he is not subsumed under the category of sentient beings;
yet, because the category of untainted wisdom realizes the ultimate and penetrates the conventional, he is not subsumed under the category of non-sentient beings either.

Therefore, the World-Honored Buddha is neither a sentient being nor a non-sentient being, but is a distinct category of truly untainted dharmas, standing loftily and independently, transcending the five destinies, and thus is called "Venerable."
Brilliant and peerless, he perfected the four wisdoms to serve as a model for all; how could he be categorized as being of the same class as things sentient or insentient?

[Commentary] Regarding the "middle and lower grades," the *Yingluo jing* (Sutra of the Necklaces) explains them much the same way as this sutra; both state that these pertain to the period prior to entering the kalpas.
Those in the stage of external ordinary beings cultivate the ten paths of wholesome action, which are divided into three grades:

those of the lower grade of the ten wholesome actions become minor regional kings (*kṣullaka-rāja*); those of the middle grade become great regional kings (*mahākṣullaka-rāja*); and those of the upper grade become iron-wheel-turning kings (*cakravartin*).

Regarding "regional kings" (*kṣullaka-rāja*), it is like scattering grains of rice upon the ground; the meaning is intended to convey that the number of such minor kings is extremely vast. Furthermore, this is established [as follows]:

At the end of the kalpa, human beings possessed bodily radiance that illuminated each other. Initially, they consumed the fat of the earth, the essence of the earth, forest creepers, and non-glutinous rice;

this non-glutinous rice grew with husks and was known as fragrant rice (*gandha-śāli*). Because they consumed this rice, excrement and filth appeared upon their bodies, and their bodily radiance consequently vanished.
Out of compassion, the Bodhisattva caused the sun, moon, and stars to arise to illuminate and guide them, and eventually established virtuous people as lords over territories.
Regarding the term *kṣatriya*, which translates as "one whose duty is the field" (田主), it is rendered as "king" (*rāja*), referring to those universally acknowledged as kings.

Because such kings distribute grain and millet to relieve the people, they are called "scattered-grain kings" (*tsubaō*); "scattered" (*san*) refers to the act of distributing and relieving. (The pronunciation of 賑 is *zhěn*; it means to distribute and provide relief.)
[Commentary]: Regarding the four types of equality, the *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā* states: "The Wheel-Turning Kings [appear] above eighty thousand [years];
with gold, silver, copper, and iron wheels, they [rule] one, two, three, or four continents respectively; they subdue [others] by being welcomed, going themselves, using force, or through debate;

they are without contention and possess compassion. Master Ci'en’s commentary explains: "From the time the lifespan increases from sixty thousand to eighty thousand years, there are successively Wheel-Turning Sage Kings."

The appearance of a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin) occurs only during the period of increase (*utsarpiṇī-kalpa*); the appearance of the other three types of wheel-turning monarchs is not restricted to this period.
Thus, the iron-wheel-turning monarch is said to appear one hundred years after the parinirvāṇa of the Buddha.

Furthermore, the gold-wheel-turning monarch named *Roca* appears at the end of the period of increase, whereas Maitreya appears at the beginning of the period of decrease (*avasarpinī-kalpa*), because the lifespan of a wheel-turning monarch is long.

One observes that the domains of the four kings—of gold, silver, copper, and iron—are respectively one continent, two continents, three continents, and four continents as their spheres of transformation;
this is because their spheres of transformation differ according to their sequence. Furthermore, within a single world-system there is only one wheel-turning king, just as a Buddha appears alone.
Since a single king and a single Buddha are able to transform all sentient beings, the majesty and virtue of the four kings are presided over by the seven treasures.

There are differences in the superiority or inferiority of their realms; that is to say, while a wheel-turning king with a golden wheel possesses a thousand spokes, the other three wheels have spokes reduced by half for each successive one.
The remaining jewels likewise become progressively inferior. Furthermore, the way in which the kings establish their authority and govern the lands across the various continents differs:
when a Golden Wheel-turning King appears in the world, the minor kings of the various realms come of their own accord to welcome and invite him.
The land is peaceful, stable, prosperous, and joyful, teeming with many people. We only pray that the Celestial Honored One will personally bestow his instructions upon us;
we are all followers and attendants of the Celestial Honored One. If it is a silver-wheel-turning monarch (rājā cakravartin), he goes there in person, and that region submits as a vassal.

If it is a copper-wheel-turning monarch, having arrived there, he proclaims his majesty and vies in virtue, whereupon that region respectfully submits; this is called "victory through contention. If it is an iron-wheel-turning [monarch]...
The king continues until the battle lines are decisively won, at which point he stops; this is called "Victory in Battle. A Universal Monarch (Cakravartin) never inflicts harm;
having subdued his opponents, he transforms them through the ten wholesome paths of action.

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "if the king is born," the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra* states that when a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*) assumes his office, on the fifteenth day of the waxing moon, he bathes and ascends the throne.

His father takes the waters of the four great oceans in the right horn of a white ox, places all types of seeds within the horn, and pours it over the crown of the prince’s head. At the very moment of this consecration, suddenly from the east there appears gold...
The wheel-treasure appears, complete with a thousand spokes, emitting wondrous light, coming forth to guide and lead the king; this is called the inauguration of a Golden Wheel-turning King.
The inaugurations of the other three types of wheel-turning kings are all likewise.

[Commentary: Regarding the seven treasures, the *Lokadhātunirdeśa-sūtra* (*Qishi jing*) and other texts provide extensive explanations. To summarize their essentials: first is the Wheel Treasure (*cakraratna*), which is golden in color both inside and out;
it measures seven *yojana*s from east to west and twelve *yojana*s from north to south, and is fully equipped with a thousand spokes.

Second is the Elephant Treasure (*hastiratna*), whose body is pure white; it has six tusks and seven limbs that support the ground—namely, the four feet, the tail, the trunk, and the head as the seventh limb. Third...
1. The Horse Treasure (Aśvaratna): with long, pure-colored hair, it can travel through the air, traversing the four continents in a single day.

2. The Jewel Treasure (Maṇiratna): the color of lapis lazuli, it emits light that shines brilliantly. 3. The Woman Treasure (Strīratna): her every movement is exquisite and wonderful; one never tires of gazing upon her. 4. The Steward Treasure (Gṛhapatiratna):
he possesses the divine eye (divyacakṣus) and perceives the treasuries of jewels throughout the four continents. 5. The Military Commander Treasure (Pariṇāyakaratna).
Your servant Bao Shan governs the fourfold army—namely, elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry—and brings them together in assembly according to the King’s will.
Furthermore, there are seven other similar treasures: first, the Sword Treasure; if any territory gives rise to a rebellious or resistant mind, the Sword Treasure flies there and subdues it.
Second, the Leather Treasure; its color is a brilliant white like the radiance of the sun, and merchants offer it up.
The king’s [palace] is five yojanas wide and ten yojanas long; made from the skin of a sea dragon, it cannot be harmed by water, fire, wind, or the like.
It can eliminate cold and heat, and wherever the king travels, it serves as a canopy covering him and his military host.
Each section is partitioned so that men and women dwell separately and do not see one another. Third, the royal bed is soft, supple, fine, and smooth; the king sits upon it.
First, through the cultivation of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), he is free from greed, hatred, and delusion, so that those women who behold him have no defilement in their minds.

Fourth, the Jewel King of Forests: whenever he thinks of wandering in the forest, he immediately enters it; there, flowers and fruits are lush and abundant, and he gathers with his retinue in joyful amusement, while the celestial maidens sing and dance, all according to his wish.
Fifth, the Jewel King of Palaces: while residing within the palace, whenever he desires to see the stars and the moon, the king sees them immediately.
First, having seen this, he sleeps in peace and happiness, free from anxiety; when cold, there is a sensation of warmth, and when hot, there is a sensation of coolness.

Sixth, the precious garments are soft and free from defilement; when the King wears these robes, he experiences neither cold nor heat, nor hunger, thirst, emaciation, or fatigue, and he is not harmed by fire or other elements.
Seventh, the precious sandals: when the King wears these sandals, whether traveling on water or on land, he is always secure.

He travels a hundred yojanas in detail without impairing his majestic deportment. Thus, this Wheel-Turning King is fully endowed with the seven treasures and possesses further similar secondary treasures to enjoy according to his heart's desire.
He rules over the four continents with a full thousand sons, all of whom are brave and capable of defeating the armies of others.
Such are the virtues resulting from the retribution of the ten wholesome paths; although the other three types of Wheel-Turning Kings are gradually [lesser], [they likewise possess these qualities].
The inferior [state] being fully endowed with the seven treasures can be understood by analogy with this.

[Commentary: Although [he possessed] the seven [treasures], etc., it was as when Śāriputra had cultivated the bodhisattva practices for sixty *kalpas* and sought to enter the seventh stage (*vihāra*).
When he encountered a brahmin who came to beg for his eyes, he consequently regressed from the Great Mind. The Tathāgata then used skillful means to transform him.

Those who have slightly inclined toward that [Mahāyāna] basis, having studied and realized the fruits of the Hīnayāna, turn their minds toward the Mahāyāna within the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Such individuals as these will, before long, attain the stage of non-retrogression through faith (*śraddhā-avaivartika*).
[Commentary] Furthermore, regarding the phrase "those who attain faith," this reveals that those with the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) possess clear understanding and do not regress.

The phrase "certainly not regressing" clarifies that this is the stage of non-regression (*avivartika-bhūmi*); prior to this stage, there is still the possibility of regression. The *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra* (Yíngluò jīng) states:
"One who initiates the mind and practices for one kalpa, two kalpas, or even until the completion of the sixth stage and enters the seventh stage will ultimately never regress."
From this point onward, they are categorized as those of the "receding stage" (*hāna-bhāgīya*).

For instance, more than eighty thousand people, including Prince Dharmadatta and others, who were about to enter the seventh stage (*vihāra*), fell back into unwholesome states and even among the non-Buddhist paths (*tīrthika*) due to encountering adverse conditions.

For one kalpa, ten kalpas, or even up to a thousand kalpas, they committed great false views and the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya-karma*). Furthermore, according to the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* (Treatise on the Compendium of the Great Vehicle), there are ten [such cases].
The verse states: "Through the power of purity, the superior force, and the firm mind of progress, one is called a Bodhisattva;

this is the initial cultivation over countless three great eons. The auto-commentary explains: "First, the power of purity refers to roots of goodness such as faith; second, the superior force refers to great vows and virtuous friends;
third, the firm force refers to [the resolve] that even when encountering various adverse conditions and being destroyed by them through all manner of means, [it remains unshaken]."

The non-retrogressive great bodhicitta increases further and further throughout successive lifetimes in both the present and the future; this is called the cultivation [of the path] over three great kalpas.
If that is so, how does the initial mind of the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*), which is firm and non-retrogressive, differ from what is described in the *Necklace Sūtra* (*Ratnavyūha-sūtra*)?
Answer: If there are those of sharp faculties and diligent effort who possess these three powers and encounter virtuous friends, they will indeed not retrogress.
Even if one turns away from the great bodhicitta, wrong views will not arise;

however, for those of dull faculties who lack diligence, and who fail to encounter virtuous friends while meeting with adverse conditions, such a loss of the resolve may occur. This explanation refers specifically to a certain class of individuals who possess sharp faculties and are diligent.
Since the second interpretation in this commentary is superior, it is established that those with sharp faculties and diligence who have already attained faith will certainly succeed.
As for "non-retrogression in stage":
[The Commentary] states that "abiding" (sthiti) carries the meaning of peaceful dwelling and support. That which is able to abide and that which is abided in are both termed "abiding.
Because non-discriminative wisdom realizes the principle of true reality (dharmatā), it dwells immovably and serves as the support for all dharmas of merit.

[Commentary: The first phrase clarifies the object: since the pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*) has no characteristics and the dependent origination (*paratantra*) has no phenomena, there is only the true nature (*pariniṣpanna*);

thus, the other two natures are subsumed, leaving only the perfected nature. The second phrase clarifies the wisdom: because this wisdom realizes that pervasive conceptualization has no essence or characteristics, and understands that dependent phenomena have no self-arising, the single True Suchness (*tathatā*) is named as having a non-dual illumination.

[Commentary: "Fully observing" means fully observing that the nature of all phenomena within all bodily and verbal actions is fundamentally pure, and that the illumination of wisdom is perfectly complete therein. [Commentary:

"Dharma-love that accords with the Path" refers to the merit and wisdom cultivated which accord with and lead toward the fruit of the Path; because they accord with the Dharma, they are called "Dharma."
The "conformity to the Dharma-path" refers to conforming to the dharmas that constitute the path; because this craving desires those [dharmas], it is called "craving for the dharmas of the path.
In the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, the Buddha instructs bodhisattvas to remain free from this craving and to cultivate practice without marks (*animitta*), stating:
"The merit performed by a bodhisattva should not be clung to with craving."
[Commentary]: Regarding "the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of ignorance and the *ālayavijñāna* arise together": "arise" means to relinquish and to attain.

Because the habitual tendencies of ignorance and the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) necessarily exist simultaneously, at the moment of the Diamond-like Samādhi (*vajropamasamādhi*), while the ripening consciousness remains, the habitual tendencies of ignorance likewise persist.

Subsequently, following the Diamond-like Samādhi, one relinquishes the ripening consciousness and attains the Path of Liberation (*vimuktimārga*), [thereby relinquishing] the habitual tendencies of ignorance.
Together with their marks (*lakṣaṇa*), they abandon consciousness (*vijñāna*) and attain the fruit of Buddhahood.

[Commentary: Regarding "quiescent illumination" (*jizhao*): below, there is none equal to it, as it penetrates the three virtues (*triguṇa*). First, regarding the virtue of wisdom (*jñānaguṇa*): quiescent illumination is without equal;

the Buddha’s untainted wisdom (*anāsravajñāna*) illuminates the principle of quiescent extinction (*śānta-nirodha-tattva*), which is termed "quiescent illumination. Furthermore, this wondrous wisdom can quiesce birth.

Death can illuminate both principle and phenomena; because it is named "quiescent illumination" (*jizhao*), it excels all other ordinary beings and sages, and is thus said to be "without equal. Second, regarding the virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*):
unconditioned true liberation has nothing with which to be equal, and the wondrous unconditioned principle of true supreme liberation is beyond comparison.

Because this liberation is manifested by abandoning the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*), it is called the "virtue of abandonment. The true principle is named "abandonment" because it manifests through the abandonment of obstacles.

Therefore, these three possess the virtue of grace (*guṇa*): the Great Compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) that manifests in response [to beings] is peerless; the Great Loving-kindness, Great Joy, and Great Equanimity manifest bodies in accordance with objects without equal;
and they universally rescue both enemies and kin, extending their grace to both the noble and the humble—hence they are called the "Scripture on the Virtue of Grace.

By citing Great Compassion as the standard, the remaining three bodies and three virtues are illustrated in order: the Retribution Body (*nirmāṇakāya*), the Dharma Body (*dharmakāya*), and the Transformation Body (*saṃbhogakāya*).

Regarding the phrase "peaceful and secure" (*sukha*) and so forth: this indicates the appearance of residual hardships such as the "horse-barley" (*aśvaka-yava*) famine, intended to exhort people to sever evil;
in reality, however, the Tathāgata has exhausted all subtle flaws and dwells in serene peace, partaking of the bliss of the Dharma.
The *Dazhidu lun* (Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra) states that in the past, when the World-Honored One was a great Brahmin, he saw the Buddha and the Sangha eating various fine delicacies.
He spoke these words: "The sound of these people eating is like the sound of horses eating barley sprouts.
Because of this, he fell into the Black Rope Hell (*Kālasūtra-naraka*) and suffered for many eons; even after attaining Buddhahood, he still ate horse fodder for three months.
The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states: "The World-Honored One was traveling through the country of Sūrabha, accompanied by a community of five hundred bhikṣus."
While he was dwelling under a tree at Naḷinī on the banks of the river, five hundred horse-dealers from the kingdom of Vārāṇasī arrived at that place.
At that time, there was a famine and it was difficult to obtain alms.
Then, the Brahmin Vairaṇya invited the Buddha and the Saṅgha for a three-month retreat, yet provided them with no offerings whatsoever. During this time, the horse-dealer gave [alms] every day...
The monks were each given five *sheng* of barley, while the Buddha was given one *dou*. After the five hundred bhikṣus had eaten this coarse food, they conceived thoughts of detachment from desire.

When the three months were complete, they all attained the fruits of sainthood (*āryaphala*). As for the five hundred horses, they had previously fallen into the realm of animals due to their violation of the precepts;
the Buddha, employing skillful means to bring about their liberation, bestowed fodder upon them as an act of giving. Thus says the *Vinaya*.
Devadatta hired four strong men for four thousand taels of gold to go up Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa together to move a great rock onto the stone chamber.
He waited for the Tathāgata to emerge from the stone chamber so that they might push the great rock together to crush the World-Honored One.
At that time, a yakṣa deity stood by the side of the road and caught the rock with both hands, hurling it toward another direction. Separately, there was another...
A single stone slab, seventy-odd paces in circumference, pursued the World-Honored One. The World-Honored One, for the sake of the assembly, manifested his past karma;

by the power of samādhi, he soared into the void, and the stone likewise remained in the air. The entire multitude beheld it from all sides—east, west, south, and north—as it followed behind the Buddha.
The Buddha then explained the causal conditions of the stone to the great assembly: "In the past, the Buddha had a half-brother named Suyasa, who [vied with him]..."
The Buddha, by means of his supernatural power, returned to the stone chamber within the mountains. This rock had wounded the Buddha’s toe, and blood flowed profusely.
[The earth] shook violently, and the multitude all gathered. For the sake of the assembly, the Buddha expounded the causes and conditions of his past lives in detail, as recorded in that text.

[Commentary]: "Body" refers to the fruit of direct retribution, which is the internal body composed of the five aggregates; "abode" has the meaning of reliance, referring to the external vessel-world and the land as the fruit of circumstantial retribution.
This [land] relies upon the transformation of the fundamental consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) according to the lands inhabited by sages and worthies.

It is not transformed by the pure, untainted [consciousnesses] of Bodhisattvas on the ten stages—specifically the sixth and seventh consciousnesses—as those are pure and untainted only in the case of the Buddha alone.
If a person can rely upon that which is relied upon—namely, that which is entirely pure and untainted—they will thereby dwell in a land of absolute purity.
[Commentary] "Ascending to the Diamond Foundation (*vajraprākāra*) and remaining forever immovable": Guangping says, "Foundation" (*yuan*) is like the summit of a mountain;

because it is high and level, it is called a foundation. The diamond metaphor refers to the stage of the causal position of settled dwelling; because its summit is high, vast, and level, it is named the "Diamond Foundation."
In the second moment of thought, at the stage of the Path of Liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), one realizes the principle of true permanence, which is serene and immovable.
Regarding what is called "permanence," there are three kinds: first, the permanence of immutability, as the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) is an unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) essence that is immutable;

second, the permanence of non-interruption, as the Reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*), though conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), undergoes the subtle four marks of change yet continues without interruption; and third, the permanence of continuity, as the Transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) benefits sentient beings.

Because this ceases and that arises in constant succession, the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra* states: "The uninterrupted, immovable succession is such that the Dharma-body, Enjoyment-body, and Transformation-body are all eternally abiding.

[Commentary] The meaning of the latter interpretation is that after the Vajra-samādhi, one realizes the principle of the ultimate truth (*tattva*), and thus it is called "ascending to the source of the Vajra."

【Sūtra】 "Attaining the great benefit of the Dharma" is the general heading; specifically, there are two categories: first, those who have not previously understood, who attain awakening and comprehension by virtue of hearing the Dharma;

and second, those who have already attained understanding, who obtain the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*), meaning they enter the correct stage (*samyaktva-niyāma*) and realize the first bhūmi.

[Sūtra] As for the phrase "a single drop of the ocean": when a Bodhisattva of the tenth stage praises the merit of patience according to his own power of wisdom, even a hundredth, a thousandth, or a hundred-millionth part of that merit is like a single drop of water in the great ocean;
the remaining merit is so profound, vast, and inexhaustible as the waters of the great ocean that it cannot be fully described through praise.

[Sūtra] "Not by this gate" means that taking this patience (*kṣānti*) as the gate of entry, those of the three stages of worthiness (*tri-śaikṣa*) and the ten stages of sainthood (*daśārya-bhūmi*)—from the inferior to the superior, from the lower to the higher—all rely upon this patience to enter the ultimate and attain all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*). This refers to that very thing.
As for "place," it means principle (*yukti*); there is absolutely no such path by which one could attain all-knowledge without the gate of patience.

This is the principle. [Commentary] Regarding the eight difficulties (*aṣṭāv akṣaṇāḥ*): the three miserable realms constitute three; being born before or after a Buddha constitutes the fourth; having incomplete faculties constitutes the fifth; being possessed by false views while claiming worldly wisdom and eloquence constitutes the sixth;
being born in a borderland (excluding the northern continent) constitutes the seventh; and long-lived deities, namely those in the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñisattva*), constitute the eighth.
It is "Heaven" (deva).
[Sūtra] Regarding "Anuttara" and so forth, the *Fahua shu* (Commentary on the Lotus Sūtra) states: "An" means "non-"; "uttara" means "above"; "sam" means "correct";
and "yak" means "equal. Furthermore, it says that "bodhi" means "enlightenment," which is thus "Unsurpassed, Perfect, Equal, and Correct Enlightenment" (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi).

There are four types of awakening (bodhi): first, supreme awakening (*anuttara-bodhi*), which is general; that is, the name "supreme awakening" refers to both enlightenment (*bodhi*) and the pure dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

Second, perfect awakening (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), which distinguishes it from the false and deluded awakenings of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). Third, equal awakening (*sama-saṃbodhi*), which distinguishes it from the awakening of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), as their awakening is partial, understanding only the emptiness of sentient beings (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).
Fourth, again, perfect awakening (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), which distinguishes it from the awakening of Bodhisattvas who have not yet fulfilled the fruit.
Because this stage is not yet perfectly complete, these latter three types of awakening separately manifest the four wisdoms of the mind-continuum (*catur-jñāna-citta-varga*) of enlightenment.
The single character "awakening" (*jue*) below is connected to the four above. Because it possesses the latter three, nothing surpasses it;

it transcends all metaphors, and that which is realized through the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is called unsurpassed enlightenment (*anuttara-bodhi*). However, many sūtras and śāstras frequently refer to the ultimate truth itself as unsurpassed enlightenment.

Because they are fundamental, these are explained specifically; now, taking both together, the fruit of Buddhahood—both wisdom and its object—is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).

If a person hears these names of the fourteen patiences (*kṣānti*) and is able to give rise to faith, they will swiftly transcend suffering and hardship and shall attain such a fruit of triple enlightenment (*tri-bodhi*).

[Commentary: Some say that "the first consciousness" and so forth refers to the School of Dharma Characteristics (Faxiangzong), which designates the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) as the "first consciousness" at the moment of rebirth.

This refers to the fundamental consciousness within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) following the existence of death (*cyuty-bhava*), or the fundamental consciousness within the existence of birth (*upapatti-bhava*) following the intermediate state.
Accordingly, at the very first moment of the process of rebirth into any of the five destinies (*gati*), there exists only the eighth consciousness.

Because it arises first, it is called the "first moment of consciousness" (*prathama-kṣaṇa-vijñāna*). Since this consciousness possesses discernment (*vijñapti*) and appropriation (*upādāna*), it differs from wood or stone.

[Commentary: Regarding the *Laṅkāvatāra* and other texts, the sequence proceeds from the false toward the true, and from the derivative toward the fundamental; thus, the "characteristics" (*nimitta*) are transformed first.

Following the characteristic of karma (*karmalakṣaṇa*), there is the characteristic of reality (*tattvalakṣaṇa*); since true suchness (*tathatā*) is the actual nature of consciousness, it is said in general that consciousness has three characteristics.

According to the intent of the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra*, the sequence of arising from the fundamental toward the derivative is first the characteristic of karma, second the characteristic of transformation (*pariṇatilakṣaṇa*), and third the characteristic of manifestation (*pratibhāsalakṣaṇa*).

The Sūtra designates fundamental awakening (*mūlajñāna*) as the characteristic of reality; within the characteristic of transformation, the meaning of the characteristic of manifestation is implicitly contained.
Also, based on the *Awakening of Faith*, the fivefold sequence of the beginning and end of all phenomena arising from the True [Suchness] is clarified (as previously cited).

Within these five, the third, the meaning of "non-awakening" (*abodhi*), has two aspects: first, fundamental non-awakening; in contrast to that True Suchness, which is beginningless original awakening, this is called "non-awakening with a beginning.
The very first moment of delusion and turning away from original awakening is termed "fundamental non-awakening."

Awakening is also termed fundamental ignorance (mūla-avidyā). Second, regarding the secondary and derivative non-awakening: because time elapses after the second thought-moment, the three subtle marks arise.

First is the mark of karma (karma-lakṣaṇa): with original awakening as the cause and ignorance as the condition, the stillness is struck and set in motion, giving rise to the mark of the karmic consciousness.
Second is the mark of transformation (pariṇāma-lakṣaṇa): because it transforms based on the movement of karma, it becomes a subject that perceives; this is called "transformation."
Regarding the three marks: the "mark of manifestation" (nirmita-nimitta) is so called because it manifests various objective realms as illusory appearances based upon the view (*darśana*).
[Commentary]: Regarding the *Laṅkāvatāra* and other texts, for example, just as a bright mirror can manifest and sustain various forms and images, so too does the eighth consciousness [manifest].
Consciousness is able to sustain and manifest all objective realms and locations.
[Commentary] Furthermore, regarding "distant" and so forth: since beginningless time throughout kalpas, there has been no characteristic of a temporal beginning. Why?
Because the past and future lack substantial nature or characteristics; thus, within the present, the perfuming occurs solely within the mind, and this perfuming mind is itself...
Because deluded thoughts arise in opposition to the Truth, the very first thought is called the "consciousness of the initial moment" (*prathama-ksana-vijñāna*).
[Commentary] Furthermore, regarding "perfuming" and so forth: the fundamental ignorance perfumes the inconceivable essence of that original enlightenment (*mūla-avidyā-prabhāvita-tad-amala-vijñāna*).

Due to this perfuming, adventitious defilements (*āgantuka-mala*) cover it; as the inconceivable essence moves in accordance with the adventitious defilements throughout their midst, this is designated as [the movement of consciousness].

Because it explains the nature [of phenomena] by following their characteristics through perfuming, it is called "inconceivable perfuming. As for "inconceivable transformation," the true suchness of original enlightenment is eternally abiding and unchanging;

its substance pervades all dharmas as their nature—namely, the nature of cause, the nature of fruit, and even the nature of the vessel-world and the sentient-being world—which undergo transformation and variation based on events, characteristics, causes, and conditions. Following these...

Because the nature is explained through its manifestations, it is called "inconceivable transformation. This inconceivability is the cause and basis for the manifesting consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), because based on this inconceivability, the three subtle and six coarse levels of consciousness arise.

[Commentary: Furthermore, regarding causes and conditions: fundamental awakening (*mūla-awakening*) acts as the cause and ignorance (*avidyā*) acts as the condition, whereby the active consciousness (*karmic-vijñāna*) manifests;
thus, through such successive development, all phenomena are produced. Therefore, the *Sutra of Immeasurable Meanings* states: "As for 'immeasurable meanings,' they arise from a single dharma.
This single dharma is precisely True Suchness (*tathatā*). From this single dharma, hundreds of thousands of meanings arise; within these hundreds of thousands of meanings, there is the one."
Furthermore, the fact that one gives rise to hundreds, thousands, and tens of millions, and that this process continues in succession to produce immeasurable and boundless meanings,

reveals the principle that ignorance (*avidyā*) and the karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*) are both produced from original enlightenment (*mūla-awakening*). The principle that all phenomena flow forth from the realm of true thusness (*tathatā-dhātu*) is what is meant by "arising."
[Commentary]: Regarding the homogeneous cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) that produces a flow-on fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*), there are three categories:

first, the seed inducing the seed, where the preceding moment serves as the cause and the succeeding moment serves as the fruit; second, the seed producing the manifest state (*pravṛtti*), where the seed-cause produces the manifest fruit;
third, the manifest state perfuming the seed, where the manifest cause produces the seed-fruit. These three categories—wholesome, defiled, and neutral—each relate to one another in this manner.
That which is of the same category is called the *niṣyanda-phala* (outflow fruit).
[Commentary] Some say that the eighth consciousness, being pure, undefiled, and neutral (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*), is constant, pervasive, and unmixed;

it is the true *vipāka-vijñāna* (ripening consciousness), for it is established as the basis for the five destinies and four modes of birth. As the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states: "Undefiled" means...
Because the defiled dharmas obstruct the Noble Path and can also obscure the mind, rendering it impure, this consciousness is not defiled and is therefore termed "unobscured" (*anivṛta*).
It is termed "indeterminate" (*avyākṛta*) because it is neither wholesome nor unwholesome; that is to say, its nature cannot be distinguished as having desirable or undesirable excellent fruits.
The essence of the seventh consciousness is likewise constant and continuous throughout the state of outflows (*sāsrava*), where it possesses afflictions.

The *daurmanasya* (mental distress) associated with these is of an obscured nature (*nivṛta-avyākṛta*). In the state of being untainted (*anāsrava*), it is of a wholesome nature (*kuśala*) and pure. The six preceding [faculties] regarding defilement and purity are to be understood as usual.
[Commentary: Regarding "defiled and pure perfuming (*vāsanā*)": perfuming is a synonym for seeds (*bīja*), and it also carries the meaning of "infusing seeds."
The seed induces the seed; the seed gives rise to the manifest activity (*pravṛtti*); and the manifest activity perfumes the seed. Each acts as its own cause to produce its own kind of fruit.
These three categories all encompass both the newly perfumed (*navābhyasta*) and the originally existent (*prakṛtistha*). Therefore, the Sūtra states:

"The defiled and pure [states] acquired at birth (*upapattilabdha*) each serve as the basis for immeasurable and innumerable defiled and pure consciousnesses. Within these acquired states, the very first moment is exclusively originally existent; from the second moment onward, they encompass both the newly perfumed and the originally existent.
[Commentary]: Some say that the "consciousnesses such as the karma-consciousness" refers to the intent of the *Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna* (Qixin lun).

Taking fundamental awakening (*mūla-bodhi*) as the cause and ignorance (*avidyā*) as the condition, the quiescent is struck and set in motion, giving rise to the distinctions of the three subtleties and six coarsenesses (as previously cited).

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "the former [categories]," the eighth consciousness constitutes the three subtle states; these arise from ignorance (*avidyā*) rather than being simultaneous with it, because the eighth consciousness is pure and indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).
As for the subsequent two categories of consciousness, they are distinguished by their defiled and pure aspects;

that is, the preceding seven consciousnesses are all produced through successive transformation from the *karmic-consciousness* (*ālayavijñāna*), and thus fully encompass the six coarse states. Specifically, the "consciousness of cognition" (*jñānavijñāna*) encompasses the "characteristic of cognition" (*jñānalakṣaṇa*) and the "characteristic of appearance" (*nimittalakṣaṇa*).
The "continuing consciousness" (*anuvartaka-vijñāna*) subsumes the latter five kinds of consciousness because they are associated with the wisdom of the former seven consciousnesses;

furthermore, the sixth and seventh consciousnesses give rise to the grasping of self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-grāha*). Because of this grasping of self and phenomena, one gives rise to afflictions, creates karma, and experiences the fruit of maturation (*vipāka-phala*); thus it is called the "continuing consciousness."
[Commentary]: Regarding the eighth consciousness, the seeds of all phenomena are subsumed under the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness;
therefore, the eighth consciousness as the causal seed acts as the generative cause that brings about the manifestation of the first seven consciousnesses as their resultant fruits.

Conversely, the manifestations of the first seven consciousnesses act as the perfuming causes that perfume and generate the resultant seeds of the eighth consciousness. Thus, the perfumed seeds precede and lead to the subsequent [manifestations]. Such is the process.
The three categories [of afflictions] have served as causes for one another throughout kalpas of vast antiquity;

finally, at the ultimate moment of the vajra-position, they are simultaneously and instantaneously abandoned together with the path of non-interruption (ānantarya-mārga). In the subsequent second moment, within the path of liberation (vimukti-mārga), one is designated as a Tathāgata.
[Commentary]: Furthermore, regarding "causal conditions" (*hetu-pratyaya*): the seeds of the three natures each act as their own cause; this is the meaning of "cause.

The manifesting consciousness refers to the eighth consciousness, which is able to undergo transformation and manifestation; the objects thus manifested each act as conditions for one another; this is the meaning of "condition.

Thus, with their own seeds acting as causes and objective spheres acting as conditions, they are able to give rise to the various defiled and pure consciousnesses; therefore, they are called "causal conditions."
[Commentary] "Flowing on" (*liuzhu*) refers to the eighth consciousness’s phases of arising, abiding, and ceasing continuing in an uninterrupted succession;

this is called the flowing-on of arising, abiding, and ceasing. Now, regarding the phase of arising: with fundamental enlightenment as the cause and ignorance as the condition, the initial activity of the *karmic-consciousness* (*ye-shi*) is termed the "phase of arising.

From the arising of the *karmic-consciousness*, the *evolving-consciousnesses* (*zhuan-shi*) arise; from the evolving-consciousnesses, the *manifest-consciousness* (*xian-shi*) arises; and from the manifest-consciousness, the six coarse characteristics (*liu-cu-xiang*) arise.

The continuation through long kalpas is called the characteristic of abiding (*sthiti-lakṣaṇa*). If one arouses the mind, practices, and passes through the stages to subdue and sever [afflictions] until the final stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-sambodhi*), where in a single thought-moment one eradicates fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*);
at the moment ignorance is severed, the karmic consciousness is suddenly relinquished—this is called the characteristic of the cessation of the flow (*pravāha-nirodha-lakṣaṇa*).
[Commentary: "Arising, abiding, and ceasing" refers to the characteristics of arising, abiding, and ceasing.

Regarding the first seven consciousnesses in relation to the eighth consciousness—whether as mind or as objects—the coarse and manifest phenomenal aspects are termed arising, abiding, and ceasing. Question:

If the seventh consciousness takes the eighth consciousness as its object, and since the seventh is subtle while [the eighth] is its object, why are the first seven mental consciousnesses all collectively described [in this way]?

Question: Is it coarse and manifest? Answer: Although the seventh consciousness is subtle compared to the first six consciousnesses because it takes the eighth consciousness as its object, it is nonetheless coarse and manifest in its transformation of objects because it is accompanied by the four afflictions—delusion (*moha*), view (*dṛṣṭi*), pride (*māna*), and craving (*tṛṣṇā*).

Thus, the objects and minds of the first seven consciousnesses are all coarse. Furthermore, regarding their mutual production: based on their own seeds within the manifest consciousness (*darśana-vijñāna*), various objects arise.
The seven preceding consciousnesses that arise due to the conjunction of conditions are called "the arising of characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa-utpāda*).
When these causal seeds are perfumed by objective conditions over long kalpas, such that cause and effect continue in succession, this is called "the abiding of characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa-sthiti*).

If one resolves the mind to practice, turning from delusion toward truth and proceeding from the derivative toward the fundamental, subduing and severing [afflictions] through the successive stages until the completion of the seventh stage—whereby coarse segmental death is extinguished—this is called "the cessation of characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa-nirodha*).

Upon cessation, one enters the eighth stage (*aṣṭamī-bhūmi*) to receive a body of transformation (*nirmāṇakāya*), practicing until the attainment of Buddhahood; this refers to those who proceed directly with an increase in compassion (*karuṇā*).

For those of increased wisdom (*prajñā*) or those whose wisdom and compassion are equal—namely, the followers of the two vehicles (*dviyāna*) who have turned their minds toward enlightenment—their cessation of characteristics occurs immediately upon the exhaustion of the body of fragmented existence (*pariccheda-kāya*).

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "based on the former," this accords with the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*. When *tathatā* (suchness) serves as the basis for the flowing-forth (*pravṛtti*) and for arising, abiding, and ceasing, it is termed the "basis of delusion and awakening.
When *tathatā* serves as the basis for the manifestations (*nimitta*) and for arising, abiding, and ceasing, it is termed the "basis of defilement and purity.
It should be understood that the former aspect is long while the latter is short.

[Commentary: As for the phrase "Now, however," it means that although all sentient beings have differed from wood and stone since the first moment of kalpas past, it was at the very first moment that the *karmic consciousness* (*karmavijñāna*) began to arise;
at that time, it was called "delusion. Prior to its arising, it was fundamentally awakening.

This reveals that True Suchness (*tathatā*) serves as the basis for both delusion and awakening. Furthermore, it is said that the defiled and pure states acquired through birth are each capable of acting as defilement [and purity].
Since pure consciousness fundamentally relies upon *tathatā* (suchness) and possesses both defiled and pure aspects, it reveals that *tathatā* itself serves as the basis for defilement and purity.
This refers to the period from the first moment—indescribable eons ago—until the final moment of the diamond-like samādhi;
that is, the aforementioned arising, abiding, and ceasing, wherein the long encompasses the short, and arising, abiding, and ceasing are contained therein.

[Sūtra] Regarding the arising of all such [phenomena], following the *Awakening of Faith*, one takes the "phase of karma" (*karmalakṣaṇa*) as the beginning. From the phase of karma arises the "phase of transformation" (*pravṛttilakṣaṇa*);
from the phase of transformation arises the "phase of manifestation" (*nirbhāsalakṣaṇa*); and from the phase of manifestation arise the six coarse [phenomena] (*ṣaḍ-audārikāḥ*).

These extend down to the differentiation of objects, which is called the "dharma of form" (*rūpadharma*), and the differentiation of discernment, which is called the "dharma of mind" (*cittadharma*). Therefore, the Sūtra says: "There are unspeakable [phenomena]."
It can be said that consciousness gives rise to the two dharmas—form and mind—of all sentient beings.
[Commentary] Regarding "the manifesting consciousness manifests objects": the consciousness that is able to manifest objects is called the "manifesting consciousness.

As for the manifested form-objects, they are caused by the six preceding consciousnesses perceiving the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*). These seeds of the five sensory objects are perfumed and reside within the manifesting consciousness; these are the seeds of form.

The manifestation of form as an active state is not the arising of those form-phenomena from the manifest consciousness (*pravṛttivijñāna*). It is, for example, like a bright mirror manifesting the images of various objects;

it does not mean that the bright mirror gives rise to the various objects. The intent of the question is: "Is it because the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) manifests the realm of form that the realm of form must therefore arise from the mind?
Should one then say that objects in a mirror arise from the mirror? [The answer is: The mirror does not give rise to the image; so too with the mind.
The *Shu* (Commentary) answers the intent of the question, "How can the mind produce form-phenomena if form does not arise [from itself]?

as follows: The five consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, take the five objects as their conditions; these are all *xingjing* (objective domains). The mental consciousness that accompanies the five (*wujü yìshí*) also takes the same objects as the five, and this too is an *xingjing*.

When these take the five objects as conditions, they perfume three kinds of seeds: namely, the *xiànfēn* (perceiving aspect), the *xiàngfēn* (perceived aspect), and the *běnzhì* (original object). The *xiànfēn* is the mind; it perfumes the mind.
The substantial characteristic of seeds is that they perfume the seeds of form within the *nimittabhāga* (objective aspect). Those seeds of form are perfumed by the mind;
