because they are subsumed under the *nimittabhāga* of the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), and because form arises from the *nimittabhāga* of the fundamental consciousness, it is said that mental phenomena give rise to material phenomena (the meaning of the three objects is explained elsewhere).

[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "having cognitive objects (*ālambana*) and so forth," the intent of the question is as follows: The first seven [consciousnesses] are capable of perfuming, while the eighth is capable of being perfumed and maintaining what is perfumed.

The seeds of form and mind each give rise to their own respective manifest mental states; the seeds of mind produce manifest mental phenomena which possess the quality of having cognitive objects, and the seeds of form produce manifest form which possesses the quality of being obstructive. Since both form and mind arise from their own respective categories, how is it that...?

If the substance that is perfumed and sustained by mental phenomena (*citta-dharma*) were itself matter (*rūpa*), then it would be illogical for mental phenomena to perfume and sustain material phenomena, because they differ in their nature as being non-obstructive versus obstructive.

Regarding the two meanings explained in the commentary, the first states: "Since both the perfuming of seeds and the sustaining of seeds depend upon the mind, it is said that material phenomena arise from the mind.
If the mind did not produce material phenomena characterized by physical resistance, how could it be called 'consciousness-only' (*vijñapti-mātra*)? It is 'only' [consciousness]..."
The wise understand that all phenomena arise from consciousness, and thus the mind gives rise to form; this accords with the meaning of the Middle Way of Consciousness-Only (*vijñaptimātra*).
[Commentary: Regarding the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, chapter three, and so forth, the intent of the *Laṅkā* is to say that conditioned phenomena flow forth from that true nature (*dharmatā*). All...

This delusion exists within delusion; therein are the four great elements, which are the perfuming of the conceptualizing mind and the sustenance of the conceptualizing mind, termed the "capable" great elements of conceptualization.
This is because fire possesses the capacity to ripen things and destroy vessels.

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "if obstructive," etc.: if one holds that obstructive matter and the mental factors of discernment possess distinct, independent entities, how can one practice so as to sever attachment to phenomena and attain uncontaminated wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*)?

Since the matter transformed by such wisdom is identical to the transforming mind and thus also becomes uncontaminated, and because the matter transformed [by the mind] is identical to the transforming mind and likewise becomes uncontaminated, it follows that these mental factors give rise to matter.
The Dharma accords with the principles of the teachings. [Commentary:

Furthermore, regarding "the Buddhas and so forth," ordinary beings and other such classes do not sever their attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*). They perceive material form as obstructive and space as non-obstructive.
Because of this attachment to phenomena, they are constrained and hindered by form; since form and space are mutually contradictory, they cannot function with mastery. The Buddhas...

Because the Bodhisattva has severed the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) consisting of attachment to phenomena and has realized the inconceivable, unimpeded principle, he is not constrained by form;
rather, form and emptiness interpenetrate with sovereign mastery. Thus, he is able to manifest inconceivable feats:
the great ocean is contained within the pores of a single hair-tip, and Mount Sumeru is received within a mustard seed, such that the large and the small enter one another.
Such matters as these, characterized by unimpeded mastery, are called inconceivable phenomena (*acintya-vastu*). If someone were to ask:
"In order to receive the great ocean within a single pore, do you expand the pore to make it wide, or do you contract the great ocean to make it minute so that it enters the pore?
If you expand the pore, since the hair-tip is already sharp and small, its original state remains as it was; how, then, could it be expanded? If you contract the ocean...
The great ocean remains as it was in its original state of depth and breadth; how could it be contracted? The question of how a mustard seed can contain Mount Sumeru is likewise.

Please show the mode of operation. Answer: If there were a mode of operation for expansion and contraction such as you have described, and if a principle for such a manifestation were evident, then it would be conceivable.
However, because the mode of operation for inconceivable expansion and contraction cannot be discussed through the process of unfolding and rolling up, [it remains beyond the reach of thought].
For this reason, it is called "inconceivable" (as further explained in the Commentary).
[Commentary] Regarding the "five sense objects" (*pañca-viṣaya*) and so forth, the *Abhidharma-kośa* states that there are twenty-five kinds of form (*rūpa*). Now, a verse is composed as follows:
Blue, yellow, red, white, Long, short, square, round, Coarse, fine, high, low, Regular and irregular, and light.
Shadow and light, darkness, smoke, clouds, dust, and mist differ from one another; manifest color (vyañjanavarṇa) differs from distinct color (viśiṣṭavarṇa);
including the single manifest color of space, up to the tangible objects, there are twenty-six [types]. It is said in verse: "Namely, earth, water, fire, and wind;

along with roughness, smoothness, lightness, heaviness, softness, laxity, tension, cold, hunger, satiety, thirst, strength, weakness, fainting, itching, stickiness, old age, sickness, death, fatigue, respiration, vigor, and smallness."
Because the *Abhidharmakośa* is extensive, I shall stop here for now.
[Commentary: Earth upholds, water gathers, fire matures, and wind causes growth; these are called the functional activities of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
In this text, the meaning of "solidity" defines the essence of the earth element, while the meaning of "upholding" defines its function.

The names are listed by enumerating both their manifest functions and their essential natures. Regarding the three elements of water, fire, and wind, the text omits the enumeration of their functions;
this omission or inclusion is for the sake of stylistic smoothness and consistency.

[Commentary] "In relation to the preceding" refers to the fact that the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, in its third fascicle, states that earth, water, fire, and wind are called the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), and describes their nature.

They are called "great elements" (*mahābhūta*) because they serve as the seeds for production. There are four meanings of "great": first, the greatness of being the basis, because everything depends upon these formative causes;
second, the greatness of essential characteristic, because they pervade all that is derived; third, the greatness of physical form, because earth, water, fire, and air pervade all locations;
and fourth, the greatness of initiating activity, because, like the earth, they cause all things to grow. This refers to the seeds.
"Element" (*dhātu*) refers to the sense of being a cause; these four serve as causes for the arising of various forms. Although space is vast, it cannot function as the causal substance for others;
therefore, it is not called an "element. Earth, water, fire, and wind are both "great" and "elements," and are thus termed "great elements" (*mahābhūta*). The sixth fascicle of the *Fayuan* states:

"In distinguishing the six causes based on the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), when the great elements are considered in relation to derived form (*upādāya-rūpa*), there are only three [causes]."
1. Because the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) provides the power of non-obstruction; 2. because the similar-type cause (*sabhāga-hetu*) causes increase; 3.

because the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*)—the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*)—must arise simultaneously; [it is] not a mental or mental-concomitant [cause], and thus not an associated cause (*samprayuktaka-hetu*);
[it is] neither wholesome nor unwholesome, and thus not a ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*); [it is] not of the nature of affliction, and thus not a pervasive cause (*sarvatraga-hetu*).

Because they function as causes, there are no [other] three types of causes. When derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) is considered in relation to the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), it also has three causes:
first, the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*), because this cause is broad in scope; second, the co-existent cause (*sahabhū-hetu*), because they are inseparable;

and third, the retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*), because the morality of restraint (*saṃvara*), non-restraint (*asaṃvara*), and the morality concomitant with meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samvara*) can all bring about the primary elements. Thus, one should understand that there are no other three [causes]. Having finished explaining the production of causes, what is the production of conditions (*pratyaya*) like?

The primary elements (mahābhūta) are related to derived matter (upādāyarūpa) solely as a dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*), because when they manifest in relation to one another, they are not of the nature of mind and so forth;

thus, the other three conditions do not apply. If all the derived matter contained within a single collection of primary elements exists in mutual dependence upon them, it may be called "derived" (*kṛta*) and can mutually bear the sense of being "derived.
The third *Yogācārabhūmi* states that within a collection of material form, there may be only a single primary element, such as a mani-jewel.
Regarding the "Wind of Dustless River-Lamps of the Pearl River," some possess two [of these qualities], while others possess three or four, varying according to the circumstances.
[Commentary]:
As for the "fivefold" [classification], both the *Pañcaskandhaka* and the *Yogācārabhūmi* explain that the five faculties, such as the eye, consist of derived translucent matter (*rūpaprasāda*).

By nature, the mind apprehends the derived matter of visible form, odor, taste, and tangible objects as the substance of the five faculties; because the substance of sound is porous and largely discontinuous, it is not so apprehended.

Some say that the eight factors—both the primary elements (*bhūta*) and the derived matter (*bhautika*)—constitute their substance. However, according to the *Yogācārabhūmi*, based on their manifest characteristics, only the derived matter is mentioned.
Nevertheless, there are five reasons why they are designated as "faculties" (*indriya*): first, the sense of adornment, referring to the eyes and so forth.
1. The sense of "adornment," because it adorns the body of sentient beings; 2. The sense of "continuity," because the two [mental] continuities persist throughout the course of a single lifetime;

3. The sense of "basis," because it is the support for consciousness (*vijñāna*); 4. The sense of "arousing," because it is capable of arousing consciousness; 5. The sense of "pervasiveness," because it pervasively serves as the basis for the primary mind (*rājasaṃtati*) and its associates.
The Sūtra relies on these manifest and predominant meanings to designate them as "faculties" (*indriya*). There are two kinds of faculties: the first is...

The first is the ultimate sense organ (*paramārtha-indriya*), which is called "supreme" because its essence is subtle and is known only by the wisdom of the noble ones (*ārya-jñāna*). The second is the conventional sense organ (*saṃvṛti-indriya*);

because it serves as the physical basis for the former, it is also called the "supporting material organ" (*rūpa-paṭala-indriya*). These ultimate sense organs reside within the supporting material organs;

like a polished gem, they illuminate objects and give rise to consciousness, and are thus termed "organs. Regarding the manner of apprehending objects—whether through contact or non-contact—the eyes and ears apprehend form and sound through non-contact.

Regarding the objects of perception, "seeing" refers to the eye; "hearing," the ear; and for the triad of nose, tongue, and body, the combined perception of odors, tastes, and tangibles is termed "cognition.

As for the general classification of the four great elements and the five sense-fields, the third chapter of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that within all material aggregates there are briefly fourteen types of entities:

namely, the four great elements, the five sense organs, and the five sense fields. Such material aggregates arise from their own seeds as the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*) undergoes a simultaneous transformation.

Furthermore, within this, there are various distinctions among the sense faculties—such as the eye—and their objects, which are composed of multiple causes and conditions consisting of primary and derivative matter;
these are categorized by type as explained at length therein. Regarding the presence or absence of these elements across the realms (*dhātu*) and stages (*bhūmi*):

the five faculties, as well as visible form, sound, and tangibility, exist throughout the five stages of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), as they pervade the four dhyānas. The two types, odor and taste, exist in two realms and two stages, namely the first dhyāna.

Because it exists, it can produce the four great elements; because it is pervasive among all derivative forms, its existence or non-existence is determined according to the derivative matter (*upādāya-rūpa*).
[Commentary: That which is conventionally designated as the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) is collectively called the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*).

This is because feeling, through its reception of what is favorable, unfavorable, or neutral, gives rise to afflictions and karma, thereby inducing the fruit of the aggregates. Since these five aggregates exist by virtue of that feeling, it is named the aggregate of feeling.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "although perception (*saṃjñā*) and so forth," this addresses the question: since the essence of grasping at false signs and the essence of false mindfulness and retention are not themselves feeling (*vedanā*), how can they be called "contemplating the designation of feeling"? The intent of the commentary’s explanation is as follows:

although the essences of perception and mindfulness are not feeling, because perception and mindfulness arise from the mind having apprehended an object through feeling, perception and mindfulness—being associated within the same aggregate—assist feeling in apprehending the object.
This is collectively termed "feeling" (*vedanā*).

[Commentary: Although it is said that karma and so forth... [The question is: Since the performance of action is volition (*cetanā*) and the experience of the fruit is consciousness (*vijñāna*), specifically the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*), why is it called "contemplating feeling"?

The intent of the commentary's explanation is as follows: although karma and its fruit are in essence volition and consciousness, they are nonetheless designated by the term "feeling" because of the act of experiencing and receiving (*anubhava*).
It is called "receiving" (*vedanā*) because it receives the fruits of karma through its objective spheres and activities.

[Commentary]: *Kṣatriya* means "one whose duty is the fields"; in Chinese it is translated as "royal lineage. This refers to the time at the beginning of the eon when people contended for fragrant rice;
consequently, they divided the lands and fixed their boundaries, establishing virtuous men whom all agreed upon as kings and enfeoffing them over the fields.
First, there are those who feel aversion toward the household life and delight in dwelling in quietude, diligently cultivating pure karma;

for this reason they are called *brāhmaṇa*, which is translated as "Pure Conduct" or "Pure Resolve. Next are the *vaiśya*, which is translated as "Sitting to Collect"; sitting to collect profit refers specifically to merchants and traders.
Next are the *śūdra*, which is translated as "Plowing the Fields. Originally, fragrant rice grew spontaneously within the fields, but later...

Because they are unarisen, one plows the field and sows them; these four constitute the beginning. Thereafter, based on causal conditions, various lineages (*gotra*) are established, as explained in the *Yogācārabhūmi*.

[Commentary: Regarding "Vijñaptimātratā" and so forth: just as one clings to the existence of various objects within a dream, yet upon awakening, they are suddenly dispelled, one comes to know that dream-objects are [unreal].

When the Bodhisattva of Emptiness perceives the arising of true awakening upon the Path of Seeing, he suddenly dispels deluded conceptions and realizes that the dream of birth and death is entirely empty.
He reflects back upon their origin within this birth and death, wherein one erroneously clings to self and dharmas, falling into the inversion of thinking they exist.

[Commentary: Regarding the statement that "names express the common characteristics (sāmānya-lakṣaṇa) of the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of all phenomena": "intrinsic nature" is also termed "specific characteristic" (svalakṣaṇa).
This specific characteristic serves as the substantial basis (āśraya-bhūta), while the common characteristic constitutes the conceptual meaning (artha) supported by it.

Since the meaning depends upon the substance but is not the substance itself, and since the substance of the phenomenon—the specific characteristic—is beyond words, the expression of a phenomenon through words is termed its "common characteristic. As the saying goes: [omitted].

Water and fire merely possess the conventional designations (*vyavahāra*) for the meanings of "moisture" and "heat," but they cannot be separated from the words "moisture" and "heat. This is because words do not [directly] grasp the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of those phenomena;

rather, the natures of moisture and heat are what are apprehended by the body (the sense-faculties). Thus, they possess the conventional designations for their common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), which are the objects of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

As for the "remaining additional factors" (*dharma-śeṣa*), these refer to the further, additional meanings upon the substance of the phenomenon itself. This is because they cannot be separated from those [meanings].

Because it refers to the essence of phenomena (*dharmatā*), all names are merely provisional designations (their specific and general characteristics, their mutual relations, and their various categories are as explained elsewhere).
[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "because the supramundane verbal teachings are understood through the transcendence of characteristics":

because sentient beings do not understand the supramundane nature, characteristics, causes, and effects, Buddhas and Bodhisattvas provisionally establish verbal teachings within that ineffable Dharma to manifest it for them.
Furthermore, by teaching the transcendence of words and the departure from signs, one understands the cultivation of causes and the realization of fruits;
thus, all verbal teachings are unreal, like an echo in a valley.
[Commentary] As for the "second moon," it is because of an eye disease that one perceives an illusory moon beside the actual moon; regarding this illusory moon...
Furthermore, upon these [illusory things], there arise further conceptualizations of blue, yellow, red, white, and so forth; yet in reality, these do not exist.

Sentient beings, afflicted by their attachments, perceive illusory phenomena within true nature, and upon those illusory phenomena, they further give rise to conceptualizations of existence and non-existence, identity and difference, and so forth; yet in reality, these do not exist.
Therefore, all illusory phenomena—whether existent or non-existent, identical or different—lack any substantial reality.

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "the former refers to the equal," the previous statement that all phenomena (*dharma*) are produced through conditions—namely the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*)—is as follows:

within dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), the factor of "volitional formations" (*saṃskāra*) acts as a predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) to evoke the factors of birth, old age, and death; thus, the aggregates, bases, and elements are established.

As for the statement that "all phenomena are produced through causes," this means that the five factors beginning with consciousness (*vijñāna*) act as the direct causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) to generate and bring about the actual manifestation of birth and old age.
The limb of death is termed "sentient being" (*sattva*); yet in reality, a sentient being is not separate from the three aggregates (*skandha*).

However, the scriptural text establishes these as two distinct meanings based on the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) and the direct causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), respectively. There are three types of causal conditions:

namely, the seed inducing the seed, the seed inducing the manifestation of the actualized state (*samudācāra*), and the actualized state perfuming the seed. Of these, the first category refers to cause and effect occurring at different times; the latter [two] refer to simultaneous cause and effect.
The second category: simultaneous cause and effect (as may be understood from the Commentary).

Wù (five-huqie). Ōu (wū-houqie). Jiǎn-chì (upper: jū-liǎnqie; lower: jū-yǐqie). Pài-sǎ (upper: xū-màiqie; lower: sā-xiàqie). Shū (chāng-zhūqie; means beautiful).
Bīn (bì-línqie). Yā (wū-gǎiqie). Bèng (běi-jìngqie). Chèn (rèn-rènqie). Shuōu (suǒ-lùqie). Sān-miǎo (in the ancient *Yùpiān*, wáng-lüèqie).

Compiled by the Great Master Yu-rong, who extensively expounded upon the translation of scriptures, the realization of their meaning, and the lectures on the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Śāstras.

[Commentary]: Regarding "external grasses and so forth," these are the seeds of material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) within the eighth consciousness; they lack physical form and are transformations of the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*).

Regarding the seeds that cause the production of currently manifesting, substantially obstructive material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*), these seeds, in relation to the manifestation, are direct causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).

Just as seeds of grain produce sprouts within the manifest material forms, this is an explanation of the meaning of "cause-condition" (*hetu-pratyaya*) within the context of "dominant condition" (*adhipati-pratyaya*),
and not a direct cause-condition.
[Commentary]: Regarding the good and evil of the three periods of time, the fruits induced by good and evil karma are experienced throughout these periods. What is the mode of their manifestation?
There are four general types of good and evil karma: first, karma performed in this life that is experienced in this life, called *sadyavedanīya-karma* (karma to be experienced in the present);
second, karma that is experienced in the very next life, called *upapadyavedanīya-karma* (karma to be experienced upon rebirth).
There is karma that is to be experienced in the third birth, or even in the hundredth or thousandth birth;

such karma, which is certain to be experienced within a definite number of births, is called "karma to be experienced in subsequent lives" (*aparaparyāya-vedanīya-karman*). Furthermore, there is karma that, due to its being slight, may or may not yield its retribution;
because both the timing and the retribution are uncertain, it is called "karma of indefinite experience" (*aniyata-vedanīya-karman*). This is from the *Yogācārabhūmi*.
The sixty-fourth category of analysis consists of two parts: first, karma that is determinate in its retribution but indeterminate in its timing;
this refers to karma whose fruit of retribution is certain to be experienced—either in this life, in a future life, or in subsequent lives—but whose timing is not fixed.

Second, karma that is determinate in its timing but indeterminate in its retribution; this refers to the aforementioned three types of karma where the specific time for experiencing the fruit of retribution is fixed, as follows: [text continues].
Unwholesome karma need not necessarily result in retribution due to the power of repentance when encountering superior conditions;

this refers to the third category where both time and retribution are determinate. Fourth is that where both time and retribution are indeterminate; this refers to the fourth category of indeterminate karma mentioned previously.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "seeds within consciousness" and so forth: that the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) maintains various formless aspects is precisely what is subsumed under the objective portion (*nimittabhāga*) of the fundamental consciousness.

The fundamental consciousness is like the sky, and the mind is like clouds. The empty sky is bright, pure, and stainless, yet dragon-drums [thunder] and clouds fly about, pervading the sky extensively;
furthermore, with thunder and rain increasing, there are all manner of distinctions. The various phenomena are likewise thus.

Consciousness is a bright and pure seed without form; when it encounters conditions, it manifests as the various distinctions of material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) and mental phenomena (*citta-dharma*).
Accordingly, it pervades the three realms and nine stages, wherein beings experience the retributions of suffering and pleasure according to their respective causes and karma.

The intent is to dispel these false and illusory matter and mind and to purify the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*); thus this Dharma-gate is revealed, extending even to the good and evil causes of the three periods of time.
The fruits are all like clouds in the sky. The second interpretation is as follows: "Space" is a metaphor for the true nature (*dharmatā*); "clouds" are metaphors for form and mind.

Just as the void is brilliant and pure but becomes obscured by clouds, if those floating clouds are dispelled, the sky is immediately brilliant and pure; so too, the true nature is fundamentally pure but becomes obscured by the aggregates (*skandhas*).

If delusive aggregates are dispelled, the fundamental nature is immediately pure. This is taught to instruct Bodhisattvas to contemplate the purity of the fundamental nature and thereby dispel [delusion].
"False appearances are like a torrential rain (pùgài, where pù is pronounced as in pǔgài, meaning a great downpour).
[Commentary] Regarding the phrase 'the above' and so forth, the first sentence of the commentary's ten phrases indicates the heading; the next four phrases concern the practices that act as remedies;

the following four phrases concern the obstacles to be remedied; and the final sentence provides the conclusion. First, regarding the nature of the contemplative method: whether it be form or mind, all..."
1. Because all phenomena are like illusions, they are clarified as being conventionally designated; this serves as the antidote to the inversion of clinging to phenomena as truly existent. 2.

One contemplates that the performance of karma and the experiencing of its results are like what is seen in a dream; this clarifies that experience is unreal, serving as the antidote to the inversion of clinging to the subject of reception.

3. One contemplates that essence, function, and names are merely provisional designations, like echoes following a call; this reveals that names are conventional, serving as the antidote to the inversion of clinging to names. 4. Fourth contemplation.
The arising and ceasing of phenomena are like a mirage; through the fifth contemplation on the continuity of luminosity, one remedies the inversion of grasping at annihilation and permanence.

The eighteen *dhātus* exist momentarily by depending on conditions, like a flash of lightning; through the sixth contemplation on existence and non-existence, unity and difference—like a second moon—one remedies the inversion of grasping at spontaneity (*svabhāva*).
Phenomena appear through the coming together of conditions, such that the aggregates, bases, and elements are revealed to be like bubbles upon water.

The seven contemplative methods for curing the perversion of clinging to emptiness through the conditions of dharmas arise from causes; cause and effect are both identical and different across the three periods of time.
Just as clouds appear in the sky, one clearly understands that they arise from conditions and are provisional.
This teaches Bodhisattvas how to cure the seven perversions, abide in non-perversion, and dwell in the signless for the benefit of oneself and others, observing reality as it is.
[Commentary]: "Defiled consciousness" (*kliṣṭa-vijñāna*) refers to the first seven consciousnesses, which are called "defiled consciousness" because they are associated with afflictions (*kleśa*).

Alternatively, it is a general term for all eight consciousnesses when they are contaminated (*sāsrava*), as they are equally bound by the bonds of characteristics (*nimitta-bandhana*) throughout all eight consciousnesses.

[Commentary]: Regarding "bondage by characteristics" (*lakṣaṇabandhana*): when the eight consciousnesses with outflows (*sāsrava*) perceive objects, the characteristics of the objects bind the seeing-faculty, rendering it not independent;
these characteristics themselves are the binder and are thus called "bondage by characteristics. The two types of bondage are as explained below.
[Commentary]: Regarding "the conventional is itself the truth" (*saṃvṛtir eva satyam*), the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* explains the Four Noble Truths as follows:

within the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*), there are three aspects—the fact (*vastu*), the principle (*naya*), and the suchness (*tathatā*)—all of which are termed "truth. The other truths are likewise each threefold. Herein, the aspect of the factual phenomenon (*vastu-lakṣaṇa*) is called "truth";

this is termed "conventional truth" (*saṃvṛti-satya*) because it is a conventional [reality] that is itself a truth. The principle and suchness are termed "truth," and because they are the truth of the conventional, they are termed "conventional truth. Within this context...
The two truths subsume those four truths; therefore, this explanation is given.

[Commentary] That which is ultimate is itself the truth; this refers generally to both the dependent and perfected natures. That which is examined and found to be real is called "truth" (*satya*); the truth that is ultimate is termed "ultimate truth" (*paramārtha-satya*).

[Commentary] Regarding "middle wisdom" (*madhyama-prajñā*) and so forth: the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states that the wisdom of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) can take [the truths] as objects but cannot realize them;
this is termed "inferior wisdom" (*hīna-prajñā*), in contrast to middle and superior wisdom.

[Commentary] Regarding "distinguishing the truths (*satya*) based on the Dharma" and so forth: the various schools establish four general types of the establishment of the truths (*satyavyavasthāna*). The first is that of the Hīnayāna...
Regarding the establishment of those [two truths], at the initial stage, it is generally taught that they are established by means of informative intimation (*vijñapti*).
The *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā* states: "Just as a jar or a garment are conventional, that which differs from these is called the ultimate.

Thus, provisional phenomena such as jars and garments constitute conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), while the remaining five sense objects and other conditioned or unconditioned phenomena possessing substantial reality constitute ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Second, both are ultimate...
The Śūnyatāvāda school, based on the teachings of the second turning of the wheel which predominantly expound emptiness, establishes the meaning of the two truths (*satyadvaya*):

within the gate of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), the progressive stages of cultivation and realization may be said to exist; within the gate of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), there is neither cultivation nor realization, and all is empty.

Thirdly, the Yogācāra school (the School of Reasonable Perfection) also relies on the teachings of the second turning which predominantly expound emptiness to establish the meaning of the two truths according to the *Prajñāpāramitā*.

The treatise explains that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) constitute conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), while unconditioned reality (*asaṃskṛta-tattva*) constitutes ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

Fourth, the *Yogācāra* school (*yukti-pariniṣpanna-naya*), based on the teachings of the third turning of the wheel regarding the Middle Way—which is neither empty nor existent—establishes the meaning of the two truths:
first, conventional truth; second, ultimate truth. Each of these two truths has four aspects, together forming eight truths, as detailed in the commentary.

[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "dharmas have superiority and inferiority," etc.: dharmas possess superiority and inferiority by mutually depending upon one another to constitute the ultimate and the conventional.

Based on the five dharmas, these are paired in four groups to collectively form the eight truths: first, the two truths of reality and falsity; second, the conventional [truths] such as a jar or a forest.

Regarding the two truths of principle and phenomena: the aggregates, bases, and elements as they appear conventionally are the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), while their actual reality as the ultimate is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

Regarding the two truths of the coarse and the subtle: the phenomena of the aggregates and so forth, in their coarse aspect, are the conventional truth; the principle of the Four Noble Truths, in its subtle aspect, is the ultimate truth. Regarding the two truths of the shallow and the deep:

the fourfold establishment of the Four Noble Truths, in its shallow aspect, is the conventional truth; the suchness of the two emptinesses, in its deep aspect, is the ultimate truth. These are the four modes of designation.

The essence of the two truths and two emptinesses is that *tathatā* (suchness) accompanied by verbal expression constitutes the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), while the one true *dharmadhātu* (dharma-realm) devoid of verbal expression constitutes the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

Regarding the four kinds of conventional and four kinds of ultimate truths, each has its own distinct names. The *Fayuan* (Garden of the Dharma) commentary states: "The four types of conventional truth are:
first, the worldly conventional truth, also called the 'truth of having a name but lacking reality,' which conceals the true principle according to worldly sentiment."

Those who fall into falsehood are called worldly commoners (*loka-prākṛta*). This refers to those who establish names based on subjective sentiment; these are "nominal conventionalities" (*prajñapti-saṃvṛti*).

The "worldly" (*loka*) refers to the mundane world, which is the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*); thus it is called "worldly conventional truth. All other [conventional truths] are *dharmadhāraya* (possessive) compounds.

Furthermore, conventional truth is also called "truth according to the differentiation of phenomena" (*vastu-viśeṣa-satya*), referring to the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) according to their respective meanings.
The establishment of the aggregates, bases, and elements is called the "truth of the manifestation of the characteristics of the path and phenomena" because it is easy to know;

this is termed the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). Furthermore, the conventional truth of realization (*adhigama-saṃvṛti*) is also called the "truth established through skillful means" (*upāya-prajñapti-satya*);

that is, the designation of the distinctions between defilement and purity, and cause and effect—namely, suffering, origin, cessation, and the path—which leads one toward the fruit, is called "realization. That which possesses marks and can be known is termed [the conventional].
The four conventionalities of the mundane world and the ultimate conventional truth are also called "provisional designations" (*prajñapti*) and are not "unestablished truths.

This refers to the suchness of the two kinds of emptiness, which is wondrously transcendent from among all phenomena and is known by the noble ones; this is termed the "ultimate. Because it is established through provisional characteristics and its essence is not separate from its verbal expression, it is termed "conventional.
This refers to the suchness of the emptiness of persons and the suchness of the emptiness of phenomena, which are provisionally designated and accompanied by [conceptual] designations.

Regarding the four types of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) as explained by the [text]: first is the worldly ultimate truth (*loka-paramārtha-satya*), also called the truth of the manifestation of essence and function.

This refers to the coarse and manifest phenomena of the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*), which, because they fall within the realm of the false and deceptive, are termed "worldly.

Furthermore, because they are known by the noble ones (*ārya*) and transcend the first type of conventional truth, they are termed "ultimate. Thus, the worldly itself being the ultimate truth is called the "worldly ultimate truth."
The remaining truths are all *dharmatā-samāsāsa* (nominal compounds). The ultimate truth of principle (*tattva-paramārtha-satya*) is also called the truth of the differentiation of cause and effect;
that is to say, the differentiation of cause and effect regarding the knowledge, abandonment, realization, and cultivation of suffering, origin, cessation, and the path is termed "principle.

It is the object of untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*), and because it transcends the two preceding conventional truths, it is called "ultimate" (*paramārtha*). The ultimate truth of realization (*adhigama-paramārtha-satya*) is also called the truth of revealing reality by means of the gate (*dvāra*).

This refers to the true suchness of the two-fold emptiness, which is realized through the noble wisdom that relies on the gate of emptiness as expressed by linguistic conventions; thus it is called "attainment.

It is unfathomable to ordinary fools and transcends the three conventional truths, hence it is named "Ultimate" (paramārtha). This Ultimate Truth of the Ultimate is also called the "Truth that Sets Aside Conventions to Discourse on the Essential Meaning" (zhenti).
This refers to the essence of the one true dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), which is wondrously detached from linguistic expression and utterly transcends all phenomena; thus it is named.

Because it is the ultimate noble wisdom realized within oneself, which transcends the four preceding conventional [truths], it is further called "ultimate" (*paramārtha*), as explained extensively in that text.

[The Commentary] states: "Regarding 'one view,' etc., within the gate of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), there are characteristics of speaker and listener; because the ultimate truth (*tattva-satya*) is established in contrast to conventional truth, the two truths are formed, and thus they are not identical.
However, according to the primary ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), there are no characteristics of speaker or listener, and thus [the two truths] are not established."

Because conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) lacks the nature of conventional truth, there is likewise no ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Since the conventional and the ultimate are mutually defined, when the conventional vanishes, the ultimate perishes;

this is called "non-duality" (*advaya*). Beyond the conventional and the ultimate, there is neither the true nor the conventional; this ineffable dharma is called the "ultimate truth" (*paramārtha-satya*).
As stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi*, beyond the four truths there is the "non-established truth" (*avyavasthāna-satya*); thus, beyond these two truths lies the ultimate truth.

[The text says: "The Truths. [Commentary: Regarding the phrase "the two, etc.," some say that having speech and hearing is called "not one," which reveals the meaning of the distinction between the two truths;
that there is no speech and no hearing is called "not two," which reveals that the essence of the dharmas, in which the two truths are extinguished as verbal designations, is without differentiation.
The meaning is that "neither one nor two" is precisely the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). For example, waves arise depending upon water;
if there were no waves, the original substance of the water would remain, and there would be no separate dharma of water. It is likewise:
conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) exists depending upon the true truth; if conventional truth did not exist, the original true truth would remain, and that true truth is itself the ultimate truth.
The ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) does not exist separately outside of the conventional; this is intended to refute the first interpretation, which is why the commentary states "it is not.
[Commentary] That which exists like an illusion through causes and conditions—whether form (*rūpa*) or mind (*citta*)—constitutes the body of a sentient being.

With wholesome and unwholesome karma as the cause that summons and evokes it, and with the various afflictions (*kleśa*) as the conditions that moisten and impel it, one undergoes diverse results of maturation (*vipāka-phala*) by means of these causes and conditions; this is called [the conventional].

Because these are dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for sentient beings rather than direct causal conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*), they are said to be "resembling causes and resembling conditions.
Since these causal conditions are not ultimately real, they are like magical illusions (*māyā*). Alternatively, it may be that cause and condition are identical;

that is, the direct causal condition—the seed—is the cause that directly produces its own fruit, giving rise to all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), whether mental or physical, which exist like a magical illusion. Or, as for "causes and conditions," there are ten types.

The meaning of the two conditions—cause (*hetu*) and dependence (*pratyaya*)—is as follows: by means of the power of the preceding members acting as causes, there is a dependence that serves as the condition for drawing forth the subsequent members.
That is to say, ignorance conditions volitional formations, and so on, up to birth conditioning aging and death. Since all these are illusory, they exist like a magical illusion.
Sentient beings each draw forth the subsequent from the preceding through the principle of cause and condition; it is not created by oneself, nor by another.
"I created [this] which is not suffering; I created [this] which is not without cause. [Commentary]:

Regarding the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) do not arise from their own seeds or causes, because they lack inherent power and must rely on the assistance of others.
Thus, they necessarily arise only through the convergence of various conditions. As that verse says: "All phenomena do not [arise] from themselves..."
Arising does not come from another, nor is it non-common, nor is it without cause; therefore, one knows there is no arising.
[Sūtra] "The nature of phenomena is fundamentally without nature" means that the true nature of all phenomena is fundamentally without false nature. Why?
Because, according to the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*), it is solely the emptiness of suchness (*tathatā*).

[Sūtra] Regarding "Neither non-existence nor supreme": the first verse previously revealed the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*) because it is devoid of marks (*animitta*), thereby transcending the dependent nature (*paratantrasvabhāva*).
In the second verse, one transcends the imagined nature (*parikalpitasvabhāva*). This third verse transcends both natures simultaneously;

because there is nothing to be grasped upon the ultimate, it is called "neither non-existence nor supreme. Here, "supreme" (*anuttara*) refers to that which can negate (*nirākaraṇa*), while "non-existence" (*abhāva*) refers to that which is negated (*nirākṛta*); thus, [the extremes] are extinguished.

The ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) is the true nature of phenomena, which is truly nameless; its reality is that there is no substantial entity of ultimate meaning. Being free from the clamor of birth and death, it is called "nirvāṇa.
Being empty, harmonious, and unimpeded, it is called "ultimate emptiness" (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*).
[Sūtra] Regarding those who understand [this], the preceding sūtra asks: "Is there conventional truth within ultimate truth?
If one says there is not, then wisdom would not be twofold; if one says there is, then wisdom would not be unitary. What is the meaning of this unity and duality?
In the Blessed One’s response, the first three verses clarify both truths simultaneously to reveal the Dharma and bring about understanding; the following two [verses...]

This verse distinguishes between the object and the cognition through the aspects of "one" and "two. This single verse presents both the object and the cognition together to establish the meaning of "one" and "two":
regarding the cognizing wisdom, it is always "one," because it illuminates the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) with a non-conceptual aspect;
regarding the truth being cognized, it is always "two," because conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) remains unimpaired while realizing the ultimate truth. If one can penetrate this...
The establishment of these two meanings and one meaning is based on the conventional nature of the speaker and the listener; thus they are not one—this is called "two meanings.

Because they vanish in the speaker and the listener within the ultimate truth, they are not two—this is called "one meaning. When a bodhisattva mahāsattva illuminates and understands this in such a way, this is the true entry into the understanding of the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).
If one does not penetrate this meaning of one and two, it is a semblance of entering into the ultimate.
The "ultimate truth" (paramārtha-satya) refers to those who have erroneously understood the ultimate truth.

[Sūtra] Regarding "conventional truth" (saṃvṛti-satya) and so forth: because sentient beings have been deeply attached to the "disease" of existence since beginningless time, this conventional truth is extensively elaborated as being unreal.
It arises like an illusion and is designated as an "illusion" (māyā) because it resembles an illusion; it is like flowers in the sky appearing due to an eye disease.

There is an analogy for the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature): it is like the appearance of emptiness when the mind's grasping has ceased, serving as a metaphor for the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature).

Because the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature) exists based upon the *pariniṣpanna*, it is like a shadow following a form; from that form, the shadow arises. This serves as a metaphor for the *paratantra*.

Just as a mass of hair appears to those with impaired vision due to karmic conditions, this illustrates the two natures combined: the *paratantra* is unreal, yet it exists through causes and conditions, while the *parikalpita* is entirely [unreal].
There is no following after delusory attachments, which are like the appearance of falling hairs due to an eye disease.
[Commentary] Regarding "Vimalakīrti" and so forth: the layman Vimalakīrti received a necklace offered by the son of an elder, Sudatta;
he divided it into two portions—one portion he gave to the lowest beggar, and one portion he offered to the Tathāgata Duṣprasaha.

Because one bestows gifts equally upon the Buddhas and sentient beings as they are conceptually distinguished, their merit is equal; this is called the gift of Dharma (*dharmadāna*), because it is the practice of observing the Dharma and because it is the Dharma of merit.

[Sūtra]: It is empty because it is "emptiness-of-emptiness" (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*). This means that the former [emptiness] is able to negate emptiness, and subsequently, that which is negated is also empty. Thus, emptiness is the conclusion.
The meaning of emptiness is taught in order to dispel the illness of [clinging to] emptiness.
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "some say," the Dharma-character (Faxiang) school asserts that ignorance is the root and the formations (*saṃskāra*) and so forth are the branches.

They maintain that by contemplating the twelve links of dependent origination and practicing toward the state of a sage, one eventually attains Buddhahood and all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñatā*). According to this view, all such phenomena lack both self-nature and other-nature.

Because of these characteristics, it is called "emptiness. The second point of the doctrinal intent explains that in the distant past, *ālayavijñāna* (fundamental awakening) served as the cause and ignorance (*avidyā*) as the condition;

striking the stillness caused it to move. First, the three subtle states arose; next, the six coarse states arose. Thus, one revolves through birth and death, proceeding from the root to the branches.
Fundamental awakening is the root, while all else is the branches. Fundamental ignorance conforms to its own delusive darkness and opposes [awakening].

Because it is one's own original awakening (*mūla-bodhi*), one sleeps within birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*). When awakening from delusion and returning to the source, one departs from the periphery of birth-and-death and returns to the nature of original awakening.

By opposing one’s own delusive darkness and conforming to that other—original awakening—one passes through the stages of abiding, cultivation, realization, and proof until reaching the stage of Buddhahood, where one attains all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñatā*).

Within the realm of birth-and-death, the characteristics of delusion and awakening are distinguished; thus, ignorance is taken as "self" and original awakening as "other. This constitutes the relationship between self and other.

By relying upon this mutual dependence and opposition, non-conceptual wisdom arises to illuminate and understand the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), wherein all characteristics are extinguished and all dependencies are severed;

thus, there is no distinction between self and other, and everything is empty. This passage explains the reason why, as previously stated, the Buddha and sentient beings are one and not two in their mode of being (*ākāra*).

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "Some say," etc., this is the doctrine of the *lakṣaṇavāda* (Characteristics School). When a Bodhisattva has not yet attained Buddhahood, they take the characteristics of bodhi as their afflictions (*kleśa*).

Because the characteristics of affliction depend upon the nature of awakening (*bodhisaṃbhāva*), and because characteristics are explained in accordance with that nature, it is said that they take bodhi as affliction.
When a Bodhisattva attains Buddhahood, they take the nature of affliction as bodhi; [this concerns] the characteristics of affliction.
Because the nature of cessation remains, and because the nature is explained in accordance with its characteristics, it is said that afflictions are *bodhi*.
Just as when salt is in water before it has been boiled, the salt is the water; and once boiled, the water is the salt—this is also like that.
The meaning of the second school, the Nature School (*Xingzong*), is as follows: just as waves depend upon water, the moving characteristic of water is transformed and termed "waves."
It is like the case of waves and water: although one speaks of waves as distinct from water, in reality they are a single dharma. It is the same with this:
afflictions (*kleśa*) are dependent upon the nature of awakening (*bodhicitta*); when the defiled aspect of that nature manifests, it is termed "affliction.

While one speaks of the nature of awakening as being divided into two categories in relation to the aspect of affliction, in reality, affliction is itself awakening (as explained further in the commentary).
[Sūtra] Regarding *geya* (應頌): in the Sanskrit language it is *geya*, which is translated as "to be chanted" (*ying song*) or "repeated verse" (*chong song*).
*Gāthā* (伽陀) is translated as "chanting verse" (*feng song*), or simply "verse" (*song*). The character "recitation" (*song*) used by some is not in accordance with the Sanskrit.

[Sūtra] "The true nature (*tathatā*) is precisely equality," and so forth. Because the twelvefold teaching (*dvādaśāṅga-pravacana*) elucidates the true nature, the *prajñā* of words (*vyañjana-prajñā*) serves as the mother of the Buddha’s wisdom;

"mother" here signifies the cause and the sense of growth and development. Through hearing this teaching, the seeds of wisdom are perfumed (*vāsita*), and by gradually growing, the wisdom of all Buddhas is produced.
Therefore, the teaching that elucidates the true nature further serves as the wisdom for sentient beings at the noble stages (*ārya-bhūmi*).
Ordinary sentient beings who are mothers [of the Dharma] give birth to the roots of goodness because they produce those virtues through the sūtras and other teachings.
If one takes refuge in the twelvefold teaching in its ultimate sense, that is itself the true mark (*dharmatā*); thus, the true mark serves as the mother of the Buddha’s wisdom.
For both ordinary and noble sentient beings, it is the root of goodness and the mother of wisdom, which accords with the meaning of the *Anantārtha-sūtra*: "The immeasurable arises from the one."
The Dharma arises.

[Sūtra] Regarding the phrase "the Buddhas, etc.": for what reason was it previously stated that "the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is the mother of wisdom," and subsequently stated that "this is called the essence of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*)"?
This commentary explains: before one has attained Buddhahood, it is called the mother of wisdom; if...

Having already attained Buddhahood, it is named the "essence of wisdom" (*jñāna-dhātu*); these names differ according to their respective stages of cause and fruit. Furthermore, when the true nature (*dharmatā*) has not yet been realized, it is called the "causal nature";
once the true nature has been realized, it is called "fruition-wisdom. By means of these two sections, the preceding text is explained and established:

the "mother of wisdom," the "essence of wisdom," and their respective names, meanings, characteristics, and functions. There are four [points], all of which are pronounced with the level tone (as in *ye*, *shi*, *ye*, *shi*).

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "by the power of hearing and perfuming" (*śrutavāsanā-bala*), it means that by hearing the teachings that express the true nature of reality (*tathatā*), one perfumes the *prajñā* of words;

furthermore, from the wisdom of hearing (*śruta-mayī-prajñā*) arises the wisdom of reflection (*cintā-mayī-prajñā*), and from the wisdom of reflection arises the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mayī-prajñā*).
Furthermore, from the impure wisdom of cultivation arises the pure wisdom of cultivation (*anāsrava-bhāvanā-mayī-prajñā*), which perfumes the fundamental consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*) internally.
The originally existing untainted seeds gradually increase through the permeation of untainted seeds by the wisdom of cultivation;

these seeds then give rise to actual manifestations, beginning from the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*) where the wondrous, equanimous wisdom arises to realize the principle of true reality (*tathatā*), continuing until the stage of Buddhahood where one perfectly realizes true reality.
Because all of this is induced by hearing the teachings that explain true reality and by taking the principle of true reality as an object, it is said to be "real."
The marks are the mother of Buddha-wisdom; because all Buddhas have already attained Buddhahood, they are the true nature of the wisdom of omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*).
As the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "Awakening (*bodhi*) and the abandonment [of afflictions] are both called awakening. This omniscience is precisely awakening and abandonment.
[Commentary]: "That which has not yet been attained is its nature" means that "nature" (prakṛti) signifies the sense of cause.

When one has not yet realized the principle, the hearing of the Dharma perfumes the mind, causing the untainted seeds to increase gradually until the Buddha-wisdom arises; thus, this very reality-mark (dharmatā) is the causal nature of that Buddha-wisdom.
If one has already realized the principle of the reality-mark, it then constitutes the actual nature of the resultant Buddha-wisdom.

[Commentary: "That awakening and understanding reach their ultimate perfection is itself wisdom" refers to the intent of the Nature School (Xingzong): this very *dharmatā* (real mark) is precisely awakening and understanding.

Within the causal stage, original awakening possesses a superior capacity that causes ignorance and the like to gradually diminish, so that the original awakening of the *dharmatā* manifests bit by bit.
It is like polishing a mirror: as one portion of dust is removed, one portion of clarity appears. All [phenomena] are thus.

Now, when the obscuration is suppressed as in the initial polishing of a mirror, the aspect of clarity has not yet appeared; for a Bodhisattva of the tenth stage, the obscurations are extinguished part by part and the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma) become clearly manifest.

At the final stage of Equal Enlightenment, within the Path of Liberation, it is then that Original Awakening (mūla-āśraya-parāvṛtti) appears in its perfect culmination, which is named "All-Knowledge" (sarvajñatā).

[Commentary]: That which has not yet been attained is its nature; "nature" here carries the meaning of "cause. Within the causal stage, it obstructs and covers the fundamental awakening (mūlabodhi) and the principle of nature.
Because fundamental awakening is called the Buddha-fruit once it is free from obstructions, it is said that the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa) constitutes the causal nature of the Buddha.

[Commentary]: Because sounds serve as the medium for manifesting names and phrases (*nāma-pada*), they are called "perfumers" (*vāsana*). These sounds, through their various articulations, establish names and phrases that manifest the true nature (*dharmatā*).

By hearing these names and phrases that manifest the true nature, one repeatedly perfumes and activates the originally non-outflowing seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*) within consciousness, causing them to gradually grow until the wisdom of a Buddha is attained and the principle of the true nature is realized. All of this is due to...

Because the correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*) arises by taking the name of that true reality (*tathatā*) as its cause and having the principle of true reality as its condition, true reality is said to be the mother of the Buddha's wisdom.

[Sūtra] "Protecting the fruit of Buddhahood" refers to the *Tathāgata-parivarta* (Chapter on Contemplating the Tathāgata), which protects the fruit of Buddhahood and the transformation of sentient beings; it protects the ten... [text truncated].

The "Chapter on the Bodhisattva Practice" within the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* protects all ordinary beings and noble ones through fourteen types of patient acceptance (*kṣānti*) and the practice of transforming sentient beings.
Based on this sūtra, the first two chapters specifically explain the ten stages (*bhūmi*). These two chapters display the causal practices and the resultant virtues of the dependent;

this "Chapter on the Two Truths" displays the conventional and ultimate truths upon which they depend. The former [two chapters] are specific and the latter is general, both clarifying the internal [nature].

[Commentary on the] "Protection. [The Sub-commentary] states: "Regarding the clarification of the preceding principles and phenomena": in the first three chapters, the principles and phenomena were clarified to lead [the practitioner] toward cultivation and study;
from here on, the general meaning of the preceding text is summarized and explained, and the meanings not yet fully understood in the preceding text are revealed.

[Sūtra] It is said: "Because all sentient beings—regarding the characteristics of the five aggregates of clinging, both material and mental, up to the characteristicless and the non-characteristicless—are not infinite, this distant explanation [demonstrates that] while the capacities, faculties, and conducts of the disciples to be converted in the preceding two chapters are infinite, the Dharma-gates by which they are transformed are likewise infinite.
Although these Dharma-gates are many, they ultimately all accord with the true reality of the ultimate mark."

The *Li* (Principle) further states: "If a bodhisattva, in accordance with the perceptions of sentient beings, perceives one or perceives two—and so on up to this point—therefore this dharma-gate is neither one nor two.
This is a proximate conclusion that explains the meaning of "one" and "two" within the "Chapter on the Two Truths.

To perceive that there is one or two is the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*); to realize that one and two are neither one nor two is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). It further states: "One..."
"All Buddhas preach Prajñāpāramitā until they attain *samyak-saṃbodhi*": this passage comprehensively reveals the meanings not yet clarified in the preceding three chapters.
It demonstrates that the merit and excellence of this Prajñā are such that they cannot be fully described;
those who give rise to pure faith will transcend all hardships and sufferings, and those who uphold it shall attain *bodhi*. Of these two points, the first two [refer to the former].

The summary of the preceding and succeeding meanings clarifies two senses of "manifesting virtue" (*guṇa-vyañjana*): the first sense is a remote and general summary, while the latter sense is a proximate and specific summary.
[Commentary]: "Yet it is not 'immeasurable'" means that although the cognizing wisdoms (*jñāna*) capable of realization may be numerous, the principle realized (*tattva*) is one and only.
The characteristics of the outflows (*āsrava*) are one; the flavor of liberation is not manifold.

[Sūtra]: "How much more so," etc., means that if even a single moment of pure faith surpasses suffering and hardship, how much more so the merit obtained by those who copy, uphold, explain, and practice the *sūtras*—which is equal to the fruit within the causal stage of all Buddhas.
The reason why the merit of one’s station is no different [from that of others] is that one shall attain the fruit of *sambodhi*.

[Commentary: As for the title of this chapter, "Protecting the State" (*Rāṣṭrapāla-parivarta*), one might ask: since the general title of this sutra is the *Rāṣṭrapāla-prajñāpāramitā*, why is this specific chapter alone given that name?
The answer is: because King Prasenajit and others requested the World-Honored One to expound the Dharma for protecting the state; therefore, as in this...
First, for the sake of the Bodhisattvas, this explains their internal protection (*adhyātma-rakṣā*), demonstrating that Prajñā possesses supreme efficacy;

by receiving and practicing it, one subdues Māra and his enemies until the attainment of Buddhahood. Next, in response to the request, the methods for protecting the state are taught for the sake of the kings;
the intent is to reveal that the supreme function of Prajñā is noble and capable of subduing Māra, severing the suffering of birth and death, and securing the peace of the nation.
Because the people of that time engaged only in minor matters and the various kings fulfilled their original requests and aspirations, this chapter alone received the name "Protection of the State.

Question: Before the Buddha appeared, when Yao and Shun governed through transformation, the realm was abundant and joyful; since there was no Buddha-dharma at that time, what was it that could provide protection?

Answer: At that time, the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the people were slight; they were benevolent, compassionate, filial, and obedient, and the virtue of the kings and ministers was such that [the state was protected].
When a supreme ruler causes those below to follow [the Way], the people are at peace and the state is prosperous; there is no need to protect it.
Since the Buddha did not appear in this world to preach the methods for protecting the state, it is not so in the present age; therefore, one must protect it. Question:

Take for example Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty, who venerated and established the Triple Gem, studied the Buddhist scriptures with great precision, practiced frugality in his imperial attire, and governed the people by honoring the Buddha. Why was his reign not auspicious, and how did he meet his end? Answer: [The answer follows].
This was likely because Emperor Wu of Liang had long harbored enmity toward Hou Jing, which led to such consequences. Had he not honored the Buddha, his holy reign would not have endured for long.
Because he established the Three Jewels and caused Buddhism to flourish, he remained on the throne for nearly fifty years, during which the realm was prosperous and peaceful.
When his life reached its natural end and he grew old, he further commanded his loyal ministers—due to their past karmic causes—to ascend with him to the celestial palace.

[The Emperor of Liang reigned for forty-eight years and lived to the age of eighty-six; when his minister Hou Jing rebelled, the Emperor perished in anxiety. Examples such as these need not cause doubt; therefore, the Sūtra-verse says:
"Even if one passes through a hundred kalpas, the karma one has created does not perish; when the causes and conditions meet, the fruit and retribution must be experienced by oneself.
Since it is said that past causes are the basis for both calamity and fortune, and all arise from past causes, why [is there a need for...]?

Regarding the methods for protecting the state, there are two kinds of causes: first, the cause of retribution for past karma, such as Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty or King Ajātaśatru who killed his father;

second, the cause of initiating present action, wherein the creation of an evil cause inevitably results in an evil effect, and the creation of a virtuous cause inevitably results in a virtuous effect. Furthermore, there are two types of causes: first, past causes; second, [present causes].

These manifest causes are assisted by past karmic causes; when these manifest causes support them, their fruits will necessarily arise. If even one of these causal factors is missing, the fruit will certainly not arise.
As it is said here, by relying on the Dharma and accumulating goodness, internal virtues increase while external calamities are extinguished.

Furthermore, there are two types of causes: first, karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya-karma*); second, karma to be experienced in the next life and subsequent lives (*upapadyavedanīya-karma*, etc.). As the *Shiji* (Records of the Grand Historian) states regarding Zou...
In the prison of Jūci, frost fell in the summer; in the state of Qin, red lacquer turned white. The *I Ching* says:

"A family that accumulates goodness will surely have an abundance of blessings; a family that accumulates evil will surely have an abundance of calamity. These are all examples of causes and effects manifesting in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavipāka*). Question:
If disasters can be averted by the recitation of sutras performed by ordinary monks, then it should also follow that when ordinary monks commit evil, [calamities would likewise arise].

When calamities arise, one must distinguish between the teachings established by the Buddhas and those practiced by the devas. The kings and ministers who govern and transform the people follow the Dharma of the Buddha and dare not disobey him;
they follow the ways of the devas and dare not disobey them. If one disobeys the devas, one does not accord with the Buddha and will be abandoned by the devas.
Because one is abandoned by the devas, demons and spirits will incite chaos and disasters will arise in the land. If one relies upon the Buddha-dharma, [calamities will cease].
Because establishing the state and bringing peace to the people accords with the will of the heavens, the protective deities of heaven guard it; thus the land is abundant and joyful.
When monastics revere the Buddha and preach or recite according to the Dharma, they share in the same accord with the Buddha-mind as kings and ministers.

Kings and ministers hold rank and possess sovereign power, enabling them to bring about the suffering or happiness of the state and its people; yet ordinary monastics hold no such rank—if they should commit evil—[the consequences would differ].

If one brings calamity only upon oneself and not upon the people, and if there is recitation and study that brings blessings to assist the king and his ministers so that the state is secure and the people are at peace—this is precisely due to the king, the ministers, and the Sangha acting in concert; it is not otherwise.
[Commentary]: "Furthermore, one obtains a pure livelihood and an excellent, wondrous mat" refers to the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, which states that the four dhyānas constitute the bed. Pure.
"Life as a bedding" refers to pure livelihood (*pariśuddhājīva*), which is the bodily, vocal, and mental karma arising from non-attachment (*alobha*).
"Bedding" refers to such things as patterned rugs and fine woolen carpets.
[Sūtra] "Twice daily" refers to the times at dawn and at dusk; this indicates that the teaching of Prajñā is like the sun first rising.

Because it destroys the darkness of ignorance, when the sun is about to set and the signs of darkness gradually increase, it symbolizes that for sentient beings of the final age, the darkness of delusion grows ever more intense;

thus, the *Prajñāpāramitā* is taught to destroy this darkness of delusion. Furthermore, the explanation of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* occurs at midday, when brightness is at its peak, symbolizing that the *Prajñāpāramitā* illuminates all things.
The explanation of the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* occurs during the first watch of the night, symbolizing [the manifestation of] the Pure Land.
Because this profound sūtra gives rise to clear wisdom and destroys the darkness of delusion, it accords with the intent of those two sūtras; that is, the meaning of this very sūtra.

[Commentary: Regarding "last year" and so forth: the translation of the sūtra was completed within the fourth month of the first year of the Yongtai era (the *wuyin* year), and on the eleventh day of the second month of the second year of Yongtai, by imperial decree, Dharma Master Liangben entered the palace at the Southern Peach [Garden].
Since Enshū composed his *Gisho* (Commentary on the Meaning), he refers here to last year.

The *Shinkō Shō* states that when this sutra was being translated, an imperial edict ordered the Tripitaka Master Amoghavajra to establish a ritual arena at the Shōmyō-den, and another edict summoned ten great virtuous monks, including Kaikan, to the Southern Peach Garden to perform a face-to-face translation with the Tripitaka Master; they began on the first day of the fourth month and continued until the fifteenth.

On the day the Japanese translation was completed and presented for inspection, at the hour of You (the sixth hour), an imperial decree was issued for the two Dharma Masters Liangben and Zili to come on the following day to the ritual arena in the Chengming Hall.

At that time, the Tripitaka Master held the Sanskrit manuscript, the Emperor spread out the old Chinese translation upon the imperial desk, and holding the new translation in his own hand, they read them side by side without rising from their seats; thus, one entire fascicle was concluded.

Emperor Bìdì, in great joy and celebration, issued an edict praising the *Lǐjīng* (Ritual Sūtra) and summoning the various Great Virtuous Ones to recite it within the inner palace chapel until the end of the fifth month.
On the eighth day of the eighth month, he decreed that fifty monks from each of the Zìshèng and Xīmíng Monasteries—making one hundred seats in total—should lecture and recite it together.
From the middle of the seventh month, autumn rains fell continuously until the eighth month.

An imperial decree was issued to establish a *amogha-pūjā* (unrestricted assembly) on the first day of the ninth month, ordering that all monastics (*śrāmaṇera*) within the capital should assemble at Guānghuá Gate to welcome the scriptures.
At the hour of the Rabbit (*māu*) on that day, as the scriptures emerged from within the palace, the sky suddenly cleared, becoming as transparent and still as a mirror.

The various officials offered their congratulations, and an edict was issued for all close ministers, from the Chancellor downward, along with the court officials of the ninth rank and below, to escort the scriptures to [the assembly].
On the long north-south street by Wàngxián Gate, the carriage and horsemen crowded together, while the sounds of song and music boiled up to the heavens.
Five-colored clouds appeared near the sun, spanning more than ten *qǐng* in breadth; their myriad transformations were beyond the reach of even the finest painting.

A multitude of several hundred thousand monastics and laypeople watched the clouds and paid homage to the scriptures, their tears falling like rain. Led by incense and flowers, the scripture-carts moved slowly southward for seven [li].
Eight *li* away lay Ziseng Temple, where multicolored clouds spread and curled gracefully through the air.

As the scripture-carrying palanquin entered the temple, the clouds followed the scrolls, swirling for a short while before parting to send half of the scriptures to Ximing Temple. As the banners and flowers emerged from the temple, men and horses followed in procession to Tianmen Street;
there, by the side of the sun, the multicolored clouds appeared as before. Among the officials, scholars, and commoners along the road, there was none who did not [marvel].
Upon seeing this, as soon as he had entered the temple, the five-colored clouds vanished (the Imperial Edict commending and praising him was as recorded in the memorial).

From the beginning of the ninth month until the middle of that month, the weather was clear and the moon bright; smoke and dust did not stir. On the fifteenth day, Ximing Temple held a *sansiang* (lecture-distribution) vegetarian feast.
The Military Commissioner obtained a report stating that Pugu Huaien, having turned against his duty, had gathered troops from the Western Rong and Northern Di tribes numbering in the tens.
Ten thousand people were terrified from the northwest at Fengtian County to the southwest at Zhouwu County, and from the northeast at Tongzhou;

the entire court was struck with alarm and the officials turned pale. Before the troops of Gao Lingsong (Ziyi) from Hedong had arrived, and before the officers and soldiers of the Shenche Army in Guanzhong were fully prepared, Yu Cha’en, the Military Commissioner, set fire to the Buddha Hall of Ximing Temple.
The Incense Master made this vow: "The incense has risen from the hundred seats and the heavens are utterly clear and serene; this bright clarity manifests the power of the sutra.

Now that the barbarian tribes have arrived from three sides of the realm and our national troops have not yet engaged them, the *Ratnarakṣita-rāja-prajñāpāramitā* truly is able to protect the state. May it continue from tomorrow until the twenty-fourth or twenty-fifth."
The rains fell again on the day before yesterday, preventing those barbarian hordes from advancing their troops toward Hedong.

That the Lord Commandant was able to return here and that there was a plan to avoid the loss of our defenses must surely be due to the protective power of Prajñā for the state. Weeping, he concluded his solemn admonition;
having finished speaking, he returned to the palace garden. From the afternoon of the sixteenth until the end of the month, the rain poured down continuously, day and night.
The troops from Hedong had all arrived at the capital, and the generals and soldiers were stationed north of the palace gardens.

At that time, an envoy from Fengtian County reported that after the rain had slightly subsided late on the twenty-sixth, a large army of the Tubo had surrounded Fengtian County with some one hundred encampments;
although they had filled the moats, they did not dare approach the city walls. When the Tubo army asked for the reason, [the envoy] explained it to them.
It is recorded that from within [the camp], they saw a man on the city wall wearing armor and over ten feet tall;
the Tibetans were terrified and retreated, killing one another as they fled westward beyond Liangzhou, where they lay prostrate in ditches and ravines until Pugu himself died.

An imperial edict was issued for all military camps to install images of the Heavenly King (Tianwang), and every day at the hour of Shen, they were to offer a solemn sacrifice of a hundred flavors to repay his merit.
[Commentary: "How could the title 'Hall of Good Dharma' (Śubhadharmasabhā) be in vain? This refers to the name of the lecture hall at Zisheng Monastery.
On the fifteenth day of the ninth month, after the hundred-seated assembly at Ximing Monastery had concluded, the various virtuous monks (mahāsthaviras) moved into Zisheng Monastery.

At that time, as bandits were pressing in from all sides, a celestial fragrance emanated from within the monastery; consequently, the Emperor issued an edict for Dharma Master Liangfen to resume his lectures in the lecture hall according to former custom.

When Dharma Master Daoli preached the sutra at the Prajñā Hall of Ximing Monastery, the various virtuous ones (mahāsattvas) were urged to apply themselves with even greater sincerity in recitation and chanting.
Each night, the assembly gathered in the lecture hall to recite the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra;
their collective resolve was so devout that they prayed for the Tibetan army to retreat and disperse. This continued until the intercalary tenth month.

On the twenty-third day, an imperial decree was issued to establish an Unrestricted Great Assembly at Zisheng Temple. The decree stated: "The hundred-seated Dharma site fortunately relies upon this temple;
