The Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) is twofold. First is the True Path of Seeing (*tattvadarśanamārga*). As stated in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (Treatise on Consciousness-Only) in the verse on the Path of Seeing:

"When, with respect to the object of cognition, the wisdom [of the practitioner] perceives nothing at all, at that time one abides in consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*), because one is free from the characteristics of the two graspings (*grāhyagrāhaka*). The commentary states:
"When the Bodhisattva, with respect to the objective realm, perceives nothing at all through non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpajñāna*), because he does not apprehend its characteristics."

At that time, it is called "truly abiding in the ultimate nature of consciousness-only" (*vijñaptimātratā-paramārtha-svabhāva*), because this wisdom is equal and co-equal with *tathatā* (suchness), being free from both the characteristics of the grasper (*grāhaka*) and the grasped (*grāhya*).

(The Commentary states: "Mind and object correspond; as wisdom and [suchness] merge in profound union, they are both free from the two graspings and cut off all conceptual proliferation; therefore, it is said 'equal and co-equal'."). It continues:

"When this wisdom arises at the stage of immediate succession (*ānantarya*) following the stage of application (*prayoga*), its realization of *tathatā* is termed the 'Stage of Thorough Comprehension' (*prativedha-avasthā*). (The Commentary states: "Its essence is pervasive...")

It is also called the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*) because it first illuminates the principle. Regarding the phrase "realizing *tathatā*": this refers to the realization of the all-pervading *tathatā*.

All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are termed "formations" (*saṃskāra*), and since this *tathatā* pervades all formations and serves as their true nature (*dharmatā*), and likewise serves as the true nature of the realizing wisdom, it is therefore called the all-pervading *tathatā*.

However, the first moment of the true path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) is called the "uninterrupted path" (*ānantaryamārga*), because at the time when the wisdom that correctly severs the seeds of the two obstacles of conceptualization arises and delusions perish, there is no interval between them;

thus it is named the uninterrupted path. The subsequent second moment is called the "path of liberation" (*vimuktimārga*), because having already severed the seeds of the obstacles, one correctly realizes *tathatā* (suchness) and achieves the state of turning away from and abandoning [the obstacles]; thus it is named the path of liberation. Liberation itself is the path.
The path of liberation is called the *vimuktimārga*. The subsequent three moments of thought are called the *viśeṣamārga*, because they proceed with superior advancement.
Thus, these are collectively termed the stage of the True Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*) within the state of single-mindedness. The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:

"That is to say, it is the aforementioned non-conceptual wisdom which truly realizes the ultimate truth revealed by the two kinds of emptiness and truly severs the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the two obstacles arising from discrimination."

Although the process is completed over many moments, because they are equivalent, it is collectively termed "one mind. Regarding the realization of the principle through the abandonment of hindrances, there are two masters' explanations:
first, that the two emptinesses and the two hindrances are realized and abandoned gradually, because there are differences of depth and coarseness;
second, that the two emptinesses and the two hindrances are realized and abandoned instantaneously, because the power of the aspirational intention possesses such capability.
Subsequently, this is the Path of Vision (*darśana-mārga*) in its aspect as the "correct two. Prior to this, the True Path of Vision directly realizes suchness (*tathatā*);
this is the Fundamental Wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*). All that follows is subsumed under Subsequent Wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*). It transforms images to take suchness as its object;

all other conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are transformed into the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) of an image, which is called the Path of Vision in its aspect. This, in turn, has two types: first, that which takes the non-established truths (*apratiṣṭhita-satya*) as its object, known as the [Threefold]... [text truncated].
Regarding the sixteen moments of mind of the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) established by means of the two conditions of the non-established truths (*avyavasthāpita-satya*):

as for the first three moments of mind, the treatise states that there are three grades of mind observing the non-established truths: (1) the wisdom that internally eliminates the provisional designation of sentient beings (*sattva-prajñapti*), which can eliminate the weak-grade latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) of conceptualization;
(2) the wisdom that internally eliminates the provisional designation of phenomena (*dharma-prajñapti*), which can eliminate the medium-grade conceptual latent dispositions.
The separate elimination of the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) universally dispels the conceptual designations of all phenomena pertaining to sentient beings;

this wisdom capable of removing all discriminative latent tendencies is explained in the Commentary as follows: "Internal elimination" refers to eliminating conceptual designations by taking only the internal body as the object.

Thus, the designation of "sentient being" is first conceived through the false attachments of sentient beings; there is only the internal mind appearing as a sentient being, and when its lack of intrinsic substance is discussed, [the designation is eliminated].

That which is called "the wisdom that takes conventional conditions as its object" refers to this very wisdom of the subject that takes the internal body alone as its object, thereby dispelling the conventional designation of a sentient being.
Next, one dispels attachment to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*), and subsequently, one universally dispels both attachments to persons and phenomena; this is explained by analogy.
Although the terms "person" and "phenomena" are used, the intent is to sever both types of conceptualized obstacles (*vikalpa-āvaraṇa*) simultaneously, for both arise from these two attachments.
However, these two obstacles are each divided into upper and lower levels: the coarse are the upper and the subtle are the lower. Thus, there are four categories in total.

The two coarse types are eliminated separately, while the two subtle types are eliminated together. Because the power of the first two grades of wisdom is still weak, they cannot sever both simultaneously;
rather, they sever the coarse upper levels individually. Upon reaching the upper grade [of the subsequent stages], [they are able to sever them together].

Because the cultivation of wisdom is superior, both types of hindrances (āvaraṇa) are simultaneously severed, including their lower-grade, subtle aspects. In the first two moments of mind, because they are not yet particularly distinguished, they take only the internal body as their object and eliminate the false designations of self and phenomena.
The third moment of mind is able to extensively and universally take all internal and external objects as its sphere, eliminating the false designations of self and phenomena;
therefore, these three moments of mind sever the four grades of hindrances. According to the power of that wisdom, it is described as "mild" (mṛdu).
The initial arising of the middle-superior [wisdom] is called "soft" (*mṛdu*); the subsequent wisdom is called "middle" (*madhya*); and the final arising is called "superior" (*adhimātra*).

These all pertain to the single mind of the True Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), wherein one abandons what is to be abandoned by oneself and realizes what is to be realized by oneself. The distinctions between the uninterrupted path (*ānantaryamārga*) and the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) are established collectively and individually for the three moments of mind. The translation reflects the technical terminology and the logical structure of the passage as it stands.)*
Because they share a single flavor and because they encompass all phenomena, the three knowledges and sixteen mental states constitute the Path of Vision (*darśana-mārga*).
This, in turn, has two aspects. First, regarding the sixteen mental states of the apprehended and the apprehender, the *Śāstra* states:

"First, based on the observation of the distinctions between the apprehended and the apprehender, one establishes sixteen types of minds, namely the Dharma-minds and the Subsequent minds. Regarding the Truth of Suffering, there are four types of minds: first, the Suffering-Dharma mind..."

The patience of knowledge (*jñāna-kṣānti*) refers to the contemplation of the suchness (*tathatā*) of the truth of suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) within the three realms, whereby one correctly abandons the twenty-eight types of conceptual proclivities (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned through the vision of suffering.

The two knowledges of the dharma regarding suffering (*duḥkha-dharmajñāna*) refer to the patience (*kṣānti*) and the subsequent non-outflow wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñā*) that arises immediately after [the patience], which contemplates the aforementioned suchness and realizes the liberation from the afflictions previously abandoned.
The patience of subsequent knowledge regarding suffering (*duḥkha-anvayajñāna-kṣānti*) refers to the non-outflow wisdom that arises immediately after that knowledge.

The patience regarding the dharma (*dharmakṣānti*) and its corresponding knowledge (*jñāna*) are each individually realized within; that is to say, all subsequent noble dharmas are of this same category. Regarding the subsequent knowledge of suffering (*duḥkhānvayajñāna*):

immediately following this [patience], an untainted knowledge (*anāsravajñāna*) arises which definitively confirms and validates the subsequent knowledge of the patience regarding suffering. One should know that it is likewise for the truths of origin, cessation, and the path.
These sixteen moments of mind consist of eight observations of suchness (*tathatā*) and eight observations of correct knowledge (*samyagjñāna*); this is the true path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).

The section on the establishment of the names and characteristics of the Path of Insight (*darśanamārga*) through the distinctions of the liberated intervals and the self-realized portion (end of the treatise).

According to the commentary on that [text], the "apprehended" (*grāhya*) refers to the principle of the Truths (*satya*), while the "apprehender" (*grāhaka*) refers to the wisdom that takes that principle as its object. The "Dharma-patience" (*dharmakṣānti*) and "Dharma-knowledge" (*dharmanirjñāna*) take the principle of the Truths as their objective domain and contemplate the apprehended;
the "Subsequent Patience" (*anvayakṣānti*) and "Subsequent Knowledge" (*anvayanirjñāna*) take the preceding category of wisdom as their objective domain and contemplate the apprehender. Within this:

The uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*) and the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) are each established separately as sixteen moments of mind. Regarding "the receptivity to the knowledge of the dharma of suffering" (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*):

"suffering" (*duḥkha*) refers to the teaching that elucidates the truth of suffering; "knowledge" (*jñāna*) is the wisdom that takes that teaching on the dharma of suffering as its object during the stage of the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*).

"Receptivity" (*kṣānti*) is untainted receptivity; it is the receptivity that precedes the knowledge of the dharma of suffering. As for "knowledge," because it functions through decisive resolution, although there is no distinction between receptivity and knowledge, they follow one another accordingly.

This is used to designate the names. Regarding "Dharma-knowledge of suffering" (*duḥkha-dharma-jñāna*): "dharma" refers to the suchness of suffering; the knowledge that can take the suchness of suffering as its object is called Dharma-knowledge of suffering.
Regarding "Receptivity to subsequent knowledge of suffering" (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna-kṣānti*): this refers to the subsequent noble dharmas which are of the same category as this knowledge of suffering;

it is called subsequent knowledge of suffering. The wisdom that takes this as its object is called Receptivity to subsequent knowledge of suffering. Regarding "Subsequent knowledge of suffering" (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*): it is the confirmation of the taking of the subsequent [category] of suffering as its object.

The knowledge termed "subsequent knowledge of suffering" (*duḥkha-anvaya-jñāna*) is established as distinct [from the preceding] because it consists of the following: within the sixteen moments of mind, it takes the category of phenomena (*dharma-pakṣa*) as its object; it is a knowledge that takes the category of subsequent [moments] as its object;

it is the dharma-knowledge-acceptance (*dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*); it is the true uninterrupted path (*anantarya-mārga*) of dharma-knowledge; it is the seeing aspect (*darśana-bhāga*) of the true liberation path (*vimukti-mārga*) of dharma-knowledge;

it is the subsequent acceptance (*anvaya-kṣānti*) of the seeing category; it is the self-witnessing aspect (*svasaṃvedana-bhāga*) of the uninterrupted path of subsequent knowledge; and it is the self-witnessing aspect of the liberation path of subsequent knowledge, which serves to confirm the preceding knowledge. Thus, it is established through these distinctions.

Regarding the second [point], the *Treatise on the Sixteen Minds of the Lower and Upper Truths* states: "Second, based on the distinction between contemplating the objects of the lower and upper truths, sixteen types of minds—namely, the 'Dharma' and 'Subsequent' [minds]—are established.
This means that for each of the four truths, such as suffering (*duḥkha*), within both the manifest and non-manifest realms, there are two types of mind:

first, the patience of clear observation (*abhisamaya-kṣānti*), and second, the wisdom of clear observation (*abhisamaya-jñāna*). These constitute, as appropriate, the true path of vision (*darśana-mārga*)."

In the path of vision (*darśanamārga*), which consists of the uninterrupted liberation (*ānantaryavimukti*) and the aspect of seeing (*darśanabhāga*), one contemplates the truths and abandons the one hundred and twelve types of conceptual proclivities (*anuśaya*) to be abandoned by vision.

According to the commentary on that [text], the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), subsequent knowledge (*anvayajñāna*), and the knowledge of the four noble truths do not differ in terms of their mode of activity (*ākāra*);

however, their distinctions are described according to their respective functions. Within the true path of vision (*tattvadarśanamārga*), it may also be explained figuratively that there are sixteen moments.
The *Cittayoga* (Heart Yoga) in fifty-five [verses] states that from the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), sixteen moments of mind arise, consisting of lower and upper [stages].

This means that from the non-conceptual (*apratiṣṭhita*) Path of Seeing, one gives rise to this contemplation of the established truths (*prajñaptisatya*). It is not entirely outside the Path of Seeing;

rather, it arises within the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*). "The manifest realm" refers to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), because one enters the Path of Seeing while manifesting in the desire realm.

That is to say, in the two higher realms, these [factors] do not manifest. Regarding the *darśana-mārga*, the *anantarya-mārga* aspect of the *kṣānti-dharma* (receptivity) is the "seeing" (*darśana*) portion, while the subsequent *jñāna-dharma* (knowledge) aspect of the *darśana-mārga*—the *vimukti-mārga* portion—is not [such seeing].

This is because the self-witnessing portion (*svasaṃvedana-bhāga*) performs this contemplative practice after the sixteen moments of mind; since the contemplation is relatively coarse, it differs from the preceding sixteen moments.

By means of contemplation, the number of dharmas that sever the hindrances can be known. These three aforementioned types all constitute the *sākṣātkāra-mārga* (path of realization through direct perception);

they are practiced in order to bring the mind of contemplation to maturity. One performs this contemplation prior to the path of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) in order to enter into the path of seeing. Question:

Why does the root verse explain the true path of seeing (*tattva-darśana-mārga*) but not the path of realization through direct perception? Answer: The Treatise states: "The aforementioned true path of seeing..."

After realizing the nature of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātratā*), there are two types of realization within the path of characteristics and the path of seeing; since the former is superior, the verse specifically addresses it.
Regarding the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-kārikā* states: "Non-apprehension and the inconceivable are supramundane wisdom;

by abandoning the two types of heavy obscurations (*dausthulya*), one realizes the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*). The commentary says: "Once the Bodhisattva has arisen from the preceding path of seeing, in order to abandon..."
To realize the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) and eliminate remaining obstacles, one repeatedly cultivates non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).

Because this wisdom is free from the grasped (*grāhya*) and the grasper (*grāhaka*), it is said to be "non-attainment" (*anupalambha*) and "inconceivable" (*acintya*). Alternatively, being free from conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), it is called "non-attainment";
its wondrous function being difficult to fathom, it is named "inconceivable. It is supramundane non-conceptual wisdom because it severs the mundane world; thus, it is called "supramundane."

The latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the two-fold grasping in the world are the root of the world; only this [wisdom] can sever them and thus alone receives the name "supramundane" (*lokottara*), or is established by that name based on two meanings:
its essence is untainted (*anāsrava*) and it realizes suchness (*tathatā*). Because this wisdom possesses these two types of meaning, it alone is named supramundane;
other wisdoms are not so. This refers precisely to the non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) of the ten stages (*bhūmi*), which is cultivated repeatedly.
Therefore, by abandoning the two types of *dausthulya* (coarseness/heaviness)—the seeds of the two obstacles—the term *dausthulya* is established.

Because its nature is unserviceable and contrary to the subtle and light, it causes those [seeds] to be eternally extinguished; thus, it is said to be "abandoned. Since this [path] is able to abandon those two types of *dausthulya*, one is then able to realize the vast transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*).
(The above is from the treatise) This serves as a general exposition of the broad meaning of cultivation, abandonment, and realization throughout the ten stages (*bhūmi*). Cultivation.
Each practice eliminates one hindrance and realizes one truth, such as attaining the fruit of Buddhahood upon entering the first bhūmi; this may be understood according to the sūtras.

[Commentary: Regarding "the first bhūmi and so forth," it signifies entering the first bhūmi and practicing the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*); because one bestows gifts according to one's will, various treasuries of jewels manifest.

[Commentary] Regarding "the Stage of Joy" (*pramuditā-bhūmi*) and so forth, the Master of the Commentary cites a sūtra to explain the names of the ten stages, which is identical to that in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*.

As for the "Stage of Joy": because one first attains the nature of an ārya, fully realizes the two kinds of emptiness (*dvaya-śūnyatā*), and is able to benefit both oneself and others, giving rise to great joy;
as the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra* states: "Seeing the Truth and seeing the Benefit—both are collectively termed 'Joy'—therefore it is called the Stage of Joy."
[Commentary: Regarding "severing all ignorance," the Bodhisattva of the First Stage severs the obstacle of the nature of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjanatva*).
This refers to the seeds of the two obstacles of conceptualization which possess the functional capacity to cause one to proceed toward various states of existence;

this is termed the "nature of an ordinary being. Because this nature is designated by the class of beings toward whom it leads, it is called *pṛthagjanatva*. Thus, the nature of an ordinary being is itself the name for the obstacle.
When the obstacle to the nature of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*) is severed, the seeds upon which it depends—the temporal supports—likewise follow in being severed.

Alternatively, the obstacle to the nature of being an ordinary person is called the "obstacle to the nature of an ordinary person" because it obstructs the nature of an *ārya*. This nature of an ordinary person is precisely the state of being a worldling (*pṛthagjana*).

Upon entering the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), one abandons this state of being a worldling and attains that state of being an *ārya*, whereby one is termed an "Ārya. This occurs based on the fact that the untainted seeds (*anāsravabīja*) have already arisen.
The nature of the noble ones (*āryatva*) is established based on the capacity residing upon the seeds that manifest.
[Commentary]: Those who cling to the ignorance of the marks of self and phenomena do so because of their deluded attachment to those marks;
thus, the clinging to marks is called "clinging to marks. To cling to marks is precisely what is termed "clinging to self and phenomena. This is called "clinging to marks."

Regarding the phrase "ignorance that is proximate to the grasping at self and phenomena": it is explained as "proximate" because it is close to that grasping at self and phenomena. Regarding "ignorance regarding the fear of saṃsāra and the evil destinies":
the term "saṃsāra" here refers in intent to the long-lived gods of the northern continent (*Uttarakuru*) and so forth, as these are summoned by wholesome karma.

As for the three evil destinies and the eight difficult conditions (*aṣṭākṣaṇa*), they are so designated because they are censured as the results of suffering—the fruits of afflictions and karma—which constitute the general and specific defilements.

All that is termed "frightened by the evil destinies" and "frightened by birth-and-death," as well as the categories of ignorance pertaining to the evil destinies, are subsumed within this [category of delusion].

Thus, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "It should be known that the category of delusion (*moha*) is generally designated as 'delusion' (*mūḍha*). Hereafter, one should interpret according to this explanation (the Commentary states:
"Because it is the karma produced by delusion, the fruit experienced by delusion, and the category of delusion, all are called 'delusion'").

[Commentary] Regarding "the distinctions of abandonment" and so forth: there are three kinds of abandonment, namely, that which is abandoned by seeing (*darśana-heya*), that which is abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), and that which is not to be abandoned (*aheya*).

That which is abandoned by seeing consists of what arises from conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*) along with its associated mental states (*citta-pakṣa*), as well as the karma produced thereby and the retribution for the eight difficult conditions;

all these are abandoned by seeing. Specifically, ignorance (*avidyā*) and the like are termed "abandonment by intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva-prahāṇa*), while the associated mental states are termed "abandonment by association" (*saṃprayoga-prahāṇa*).

The bodily, verbal, and mental actions produced by discrimination, along with their resulting fruits, are abandoned according to the nature of that which produces them; these are also seen as abandoned through vision (*darśana-heya*).

Wholesome and neutral phenomena are termed "abandoned by detachment" (*visamyoga-heya*). Unwholesome karma and the retributive fruits of the eight difficult conditions are termed "abandoned by non-arising" (*anutpāda-heya*).

That which is abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) refers to those innate [defilements] which can only be severed by repeatedly cultivating the Noble Path after one has emerged from the Path of Vision.

The three types of karma and all contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena produced by mental states associated with the afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*)—whether abandoned through their intrinsic nature, abandoned through dissociation from their associates, or abandoned through separation from their bonds—are termed "abandoned by cultivation" (*bhāvanā-heya*).
Those that are not to be abandoned (*aheya*) refer to all unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena and all uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) conditioned phenomena; these are termed "not to be abandoned."

[Commentary]: Regarding the five sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*): first, the inner science (*adhyātma-vidyā*), which clearly understands the internal causes and effects of the Buddha-dharma; second, the science of grammar (*śabda-vidyā*), which clearly understands the diverse verbal expressions of all phenomena;
third, the science of logic (*hetu-vidyā*), which establishes one’s own school through formal syllogisms (*pramāṇa*) to refute the heterodox and manifest the correct;

fourth, the science of medicine (*cikitsā-vidyā*), which clearly understands medical texts to prescribe medicines according to the ailment; and fifth, the science of arts and crafts (*śilpa-karma-sthāna-vidyā*), which pertains to worldly arts and crafts of the body.
Because all that is expressed can be understood.

[Commentary] Regarding the five types of fear and so forth: first, the fear of not being able to subsist (*ajīvikā-bhaya*) arises from the conceptualization of self and attachment to the necessities of life;

its essence consists of the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) and greed (*lobha*). Second, the fear of ill repute (*aśloka-bhaya*) arises from performing non-beneficial acts while harboring expectations; it has greed as its essence.

The essence of the three fears of death consists in the arising of the notion of loss due to the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*). That which is distinct from the first [fear] takes the innate view of self (*sahaja-ātma-dṛṣṭi*) as its essence.
The distinction from the first is as follows: the first fear is the fear of not surviving; this [second] fear is the fear of perishing;

the fourth is the fear of the four evil destinies (*apāya*), which arises from unwholesome karma and has delusion (*moha*) as its essence; the fifth is the fear of the majesty of the great assembly, which arises when one knows that one's own realization is inferior and is surpassed by others.
Arising also has delusion as its essence.

[Commentary] Regarding "because of false wisdom, erroneous grasping, perception, views, and attachment": through false wisdom and erroneous grasping, one gives rise to the fear of not being able to subsist;
through false wisdom and deluded conceptualization, one gives rise to the fear of ill repute; and through false wisdom and deluded views, one gives rise to the fear of death.

Due to the arising of deluded craving through wisdom, there is fear of the evil realms; due to the arising of false attachment through erroneous wisdom, there is fear of the majesty and power of the great assembly.
Because one's roots of merit are slight—that is, because one has cultivated few roots of merit and goodness—one lacks material resources and thus has fear regarding livelihood.

Because one’s roots of merit in both merit and wisdom are slight, one frequently commits transgressions and offenses, resulting in fear of ill repute, death, and the evil realms. This is because one’s roots of wisdom and goodness are deficient.
Therefore, there is the fear of being surpassed by others and being inferior to them, as well as the awe inspired by the majestic virtue of the Great Assembly.
[Commentary] Furthermore, regarding the "arousing" and so forth, the sentient beings to be converted are distinguished into five categories: (1) the three realms; (2) the six destinies;

(3) the birthplaces, namely the nine stages; (4) those subsumed within the aggregates; and (5) those who obtain benefit until the end of the future, whose conversion and benefitting continue without ceasing. (Correspondence with the text)
[It can be understood].
[Commentary]: Regarding "Great Mindfulness" and so forth, the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states that one enters the Buddha’s Pure Land briefly by way of four meanings:
first, taking great mindfulness and wisdom as the vehicle; second, taking the dharma-nature of great emptiness as the path for travel; third, the vast flavor of the Dharma...

Taking the joy and bliss thus produced as one's food and drink, and taking the four great elements, emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*) as the gateways of entry, one enters the Pure Land through such principles.
First, one contemplates pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*); because the intrinsic nature of both self and phenomena is empty, it is called the liberation door of emptiness.
Next, one contemplates the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*); because all contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) are not objects of aspiration, it is called signlessness.

The gate of liberation subsequent to the vow is called the "Gate of Signlessness" (animitta-vimokṣa-mukha), as it contemplates the signless ultimate truth of the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva).

Because these three contemplations abandon all obstructive defilements, they are designated as "liberations. Because the contemplative practice that performs the observation is unimpeded with respect to the object of observation, they are called "gates.
Because one enters the Pure Land by means of this contemplation, it is called the "Gate of the Pure Land. There are two kinds of Pure Lands.

First is the land of the principle of dharma-nature (*dharmatā*), which refers to the single True Suchness (*tathatā*); second is the land of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), which refers to the ten levels of the *paranirmita-vaśavartin* lands.

If one speaks in terms of the land of principle, when one attains accomplishment through the cultivation of the three gates of liberation and enters into the realization of True Suchness, this is called "entering the Pure Land.
This is because, in this case, wisdom confronts the object, and wisdom serves as the gate to the object. If one speaks in terms of the land of phenomena...
The three gates of liberation serve as the entrance for eliminating false attachments and for not indulging in outflows;

by contemplating the principle of signlessness (*animitta*), one takes this contemplative practice as the causal gate and attains birth in the Pure Land as the resultant fruit. Both the primary retribution and the environmental retribution are termed "fruit.
Thus, the cause is contrasted with the fruit, and the cause serves as the gate to the fruit. To summarize this meaning: one travels by means of the vehicle of mindfulness and wisdom.

The path of the *dharmatā* takes joy and bliss as its sustenance; by relying on the gates of liberation, one enters the land of intrinsic nature and characteristics to behold the *saṃbhogakāya* Buddha.
[Commentary: "Habituation" refers to habit-energies (*vāsanā*) that encompass both seeds and manifest activities. There are three types of habit-energies:

first, habit-energy is a synonym for seeds, so it is called "habit-energy" because it is the perfumed portion of the habit-energy of manifest phenomena; second, it is the manifest activity that acts as the perfumer...
It is called "habitual tendency" (*vāsanā*) because it consists of the seeds of the perfuming portions that are repeatedly cultivated.
Thirdly, the residual power of the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*) apart from their seeds and manifestations is called habitual tendency.

Here, when we speak of "karmic habitual tendencies," it refers to those arising from discrimination based on these [first two] habitual tendencies; therefore, it is said that in the first stage (*bhūmi*), there is no karma of the three realms.
"One practices so as not to create new karma.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "If this were so, those on the stages of realization (*bhūmi*)..."—the intent of the question is: if innate afflictions (*sahaja-kleśa*) do not trigger karmic action, then for those on the stages of realization who possess superior retributions such as the bodies of the Ten Kings, there would be no cause for them.
The intent of the answer is that it is due to the discriminative afflictions (*vikalpa-kleśa*) prior to the stages of realization.
By giving rise to the ten wholesome karmas, with those karmas as the cause, one receives a body among humans or devas and acts as one of the ten kings;
it is not meant that the superior retribution of the ten kings exists without a cause.

[Commentary] As for the statement that some say they are "gradual enlighteners" and so forth, the meaning is that among both gradual and sudden enlighteners, these are bodhisattvas in whom wisdom has increased at the beginning.
Having already transcended the stage of the earth, they no longer experience the bodily sensations of the fragmented [realm] as they receive the retribution of the ten kings.

Nevertheless, those bodhisattvas, by virtue of their power of wisdom, untainted concentration, and vows, assume a body of transformation (*nirmāṇakāya*); it is by relying upon this body of transformation that they act as the ten kings.

If this were not the case, would the fruit of retribution of the ten kings not belong to those types of bodhisattvas? If one admits that they do exist, then one must know that it is precisely through transformation [that they attain it].
"The transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) acts as the Ten Kings.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "if within the realms," etc., the question is raised: since the transformation body is born outside the three realms (*tridhātu*) and does not produce the *prādeśika* (segmented) birth, ordinary beings do not see it;
how then can it perform the transformative governance of ordinary beings? This passage explains that if one considers the transformation body to be within the three realms...
Regarding those born externally who are not within the realm of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), would even the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas not see them as being outside their realm?
If it is granted that they do see them, then these beings of transformation (*pariṇāmikakāya*) receive the rank of the Ten Kings;

by the power of their compassion and vows, they can cause ordinary beings of lower stations to see them. Furthermore, the dimensions of their bodies also appear in accordance with what is appropriate for those of lower stations.
The "small [retribution]" corresponds to the intention of this Master.

[Commentary] Therefore, regarding the phrase "the seven [stages] and so forth": for Bodhisattvas prior to the seventh stage who have increased their compassion, the reception of the retribution of the ten kings is indeed *pariccheda* (segmented birth).

The term "and so forth" (*deng*) refers to taking birth according to the species [of beings] to benefit others—all of which are actual bodies. This applies to Bodhisattvas of gradual enlightenment as well.
Those whose wisdom predominates all undergo the transformation body (*pariṇāmikakāya*) and do not possess the bodies of the Ten Kings;

however, it is said that by the power of a bodhisattva’s merit, one should act as the Ten Kings, though it need not be fixed. Alternatively, there may be those who do so, acting through a manifested body (*nirmāṇakāya*). The second interpretation in the *Sūtra Commentary* is the same as the explanation of Cien.

[Commentary: Regarding the latter two types of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) and so forth, this means that beneficial conduct (*arthacaryā*) and cooperation (*samānārthatā*) involve only the power of faith, understanding, and practice, but do not yet constitute thorough penetration;

because they are not extensively increased or superior, they are omitted [from the primary list]. Nevertheless, they are mentioned here according to their capacity and portion, as they still constitute beneficial conduct and cooperation.
[Commentary]: "The ground is as level as the palm of a hand" symbolizes that within the second bhūmi one cultivates the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) with equality toward enemies and kin.

"Various colors and so forth" manifest the excellence of the purity of its ethical discipline (*śīla*). Having cultivated the preparatory practices (*prayoga*) of the second bhūmi at the beginning and middle, once these practices have been perfected and the stage attained, one gives rise to the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) to sever and exhaust the obstacle of the second type of wrong conduct (*mithyā-pratipatti-āvaraṇa*), which subsumes the two delusions (*moha*).

In the second moment of thought, one gives rise to the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), abandons the latencies (*vāsanā*) of the two obstacles, realizes the most supreme *tathatā*, and ascends to the second stage, the Stainless (*vimalā-bhūmi*). [Commentary:
Regarding "the latencies," the former refers to seeds and the latter to habit-energies; both are afflictive obstacles (*kleśāvaraṇa*), and these are what are now being severed.
"Practice.
[Commentary: Regarding "the two meanings, etc.," the first refers to the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the latter to the obstacle to the knowable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
[Commentary: Regarding "ignorance concerning subtle points of training and transgressions": coarse and manifest heavy precepts and subtle and light precepts arise from the former.
A portion of the innate ignorance (*sahaja-avidyā*) within the stages (*bhūmi*) can cause a Bodhisattva to err and commit transgressions regarding even subtle precepts.
Regarding the ignorance that gives rise to various karmic activities: this ignorance initiates those three types of karmic actions resulting from such transgressions.

The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states that all ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) are Bodhisattva stages; in each stage, one hindrance (*āvaraṇa*) and two delusions (*moha*) are abandoned, which is identical to the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*.
The commentary does not further cite this. [Commentary:

Regarding the phrase "Vijñaptimātra" (Consciousness-Only) and so forth, it clarifies that within the ten stages (*bhūmi*), one subdues the manifest afflictions (*kleśa*) but does not sever their seeds; rather, it refers to the elimination of the "coarse heaviness" (*dauṣṭhulya*).

This is explained in terms of functional capacity. It indicates that from the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*) upward, one completely subdues the afflictions so that they never again arise; however, there may still be manifest [afflictions].
The intentional decision to retain [the afflictions] does not mean that one lacks the power of wisdom to subdue them.

[Commentary] Regarding the answer concerning "clarity" (*vidyā*) and so forth: although these two categories differ, the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) is not separately initiated outside of the abandonment of the cognitive obstructions (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*) to abandon the heavy residues (*dauṣṭhulya*) of anger and other afflictions within the afflictive obstructions.
This is because the single wisdom of the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) simultaneously dispels the heavy residues of both obstructions.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "at the ten stages (*bhūmi*) and so forth," it means that one eliminates the seeds of the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) by means of the path of uninterrupted realization (*ānantarya-mārga*), and subsequently eliminates the latencies (*vāsanā*) of the two obstructions by means of the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*). [Commentary]:

Regarding the statement "according to the [Sarvāstivāda] school, there are seven material [factors] and three mental concomitants (*caitta*)," this refers to the three [unmanifest] actions of the body, the four [unmanifest] actions of speech, the manifest form (*rūpa*) of bodily and vocal action, and mental action (*manas-karman*).
The three types of non-attachment, non-hatred, and non-delusion—these three mental factors arise because delusion lacks correct wisdom and thus gives rise to false views;

conversely, non-delusion arises together with right view and is therefore called "upright. The Sautrāntika masters state that this classification is identical to that of the Mahāyāna (as in the commentary). The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
"The volition capable of moving the body is called bodily action (*kāyakarman*); the volition capable of producing speech is called vocal action (*vākkarman*); [the volition] that deliberates..."
It is determined that mental action (manas-karman) is so called because it consists of volition (cetanā) associated with the mind and because it moves the mind;

however, since it causes the manifestation of bodily and vocal intimation (vijñapti-rūpa), volition is metaphorically designated as form (rūpa), taking volition as its essence while also including the metaphorical intimation-form.

[Commentary] Regarding the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* and other texts: because the ten paths of wholesome karma (*daśa-kuśala-karmapatha*)—as the causes and conditions of the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*)—induce the results of the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*) in the realms of humans and devas, the intermediate [stages] of these ten wholesome karmas induce the fruit of the human realm, while pure ten wholesome karmas induce the fruit of the celestial realm.
Within the ten wholesome karmas, different types of merit and immovability (*aniñjya*) induce rebirth among the heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and the form realm (*rūpadhātu*).

[Commentary: Regarding "the highest-of-the-high" and so forth, the ten paths of wholesome action (*daśa-kuśala-karmapatha*) are collectively categorized into two grades as causes for the mundane world:
they serve as the lower grade for the supramundane, and the higher grade for the mundane. Within the three grades [of the mundane], the lower grade is the cause for rebirth in the human realm;

the middle grade is the cause for the desire-realm heavens (*kāmadhātu-deva*); and the higher grade is the cause for the form and formless realms (*rūpa-ārūpyadhātu-deva*). As for the supramundane, there are likewise three grades: those of the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and the Mahāyāna.
Next, regarding the "superior-superior" (shang-shang-pin) category, which consists of the superior-inferior, superior-middle, and superior-superior, there are further two types:

first, the ten wholesome actions of Bodhisattvas at the causal stage, termed "superior-superior"; second, the ten wholesome actions of Tathāgatas at the resultant stage, termed "extremely superior-superior."

[Commentary]: These are established by being the opposites of the ten wholesome and ten unwholesome [paths of action]. Regarding the paths of action (*karmapatha*), they are based on the gravity of the ten wholesome [actions], while those that extend to the lighter [degrees] have the sense of being causes.

Because karma necessarily brings about its fruit, it is called a "path of action. The opposite of these are the ten unwholesome paths of action, which likewise possess degrees of lightness and gravity.
Generally speaking, the paths of action can yield five fruits: first, the ripened fruit (*vipākaphala*); second, the concordant fruit (*niṣyandaphala*); third...
The four fruits of disconnection (*visamyoga-phala*) and the five fruits of sovereign power (*adhipati-phala*) are obtained through wholesome contaminated (*sāsrava*) karma;

these exclude the fruit of disconnection [as a distinct category for this specific type]. Uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) wholesome karma also obtains four fruits, excluding the ripening fruit (*vipāka-phala*).

Because uncontaminated superior dharmas destroy contaminated ones and are not their cause, the ten wholesome paths of action—whether contaminated or uncontaminated—are said collectively to obtain five fruits. The same applies to the ten unwholesome paths of action.

One can attain the four fruits, excluding the fruit of disjunction (*visamyoga-phala*). The Commentary clarifies that there are three fruits; the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*) is not mentioned because it is easily understood.
[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "the sutra says next," etc.: the previously cited *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* is an exposition of the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*. [The ten non-virtues...]

Regarding the paths of karma, after one has experienced the ripening fruit (*vipāka-phala*) in the three miserable realms, upon obtaining a human body, each individual karma produces two kinds of distinct fruits:
the specific retribution (*viśeṣa-phala*) and the concordant fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*).
[Commentary] As for the dominant fruit (*adhipati-phala*): through the karma of killing, one’s own internal body lacks luster; through stealing...
Karmic actions that bring about frost and hail which damage crops are caused by the karma of sexual misconduct; those that result in bodily impurities are caused by the karma of frivolous speech;
those that result in foul breath are caused by the karma of divisive speech—also called speech of sowing discord—which alters circumstances and incites strife among the virtuous;
and those that result in seasonal changes that damage crops are caused by the karma of harsh speech, such as [the growth of] thorns and stony debris upon the fields and sprouts.
Due to false speech, the environment becomes treacherous and crooked; due to increased avarice, the stalks and other parts yield few fruits;
due to increased malice, the fruits and other parts become pungent; and due to increased wrong view, the stalks and fruits are either deficient or non-existent.

With these ten unwholesome actions serving as causes possessing dominant power, these ten types of results are induced; these are called dominant results (*adhipati-phala*). Among these ten, three are internal dominant results.

The seven kinds of external dominant results (*adhipati-phala*) are merely presented here in brief regarding their modes of manifestation; in reality, all ten non-virtuous actions (*daśākuśala*) induce both internal and external dominant results.
[Commentary: Regarding "the three stages," etc., it first manifests the display of courage and the adornment of armor and weapons, signifying the intent to subdue the obstacles of this stage.

Therefore, the enemies and thieves of this stage are all subdued within the second stage. Having cultivated the preparatory practices (*prayoga*) for the third stage and completed those practices, one gives rise to the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*), whereby the third obscuration of dullness and the two types of delusion are completely severed.

Subsequently, in the second moment, one gives rise to the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), abandons the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the two obscurations, realizes the *tathatā* of the superior flow, and ascends to the third stage, the Luminous (*Prabhākari*).
[Commentary]: Regarding "the light of the samādhi of immeasurable wisdom": because one attains superior samādhi and gives rise to wisdom, it is the samādhi of immeasurable wisdom.
This possesses three virtues: first, attaining superior samādhi and giving rise to the light of wisdom;
second, the excellence of the practice of patience, such that one cannot be shaken or overcome by adverse conditions, as anger has been subdued; third, the attainment of supreme mastery.
Taking the *dhāraṇī* as its basis, it gives rise to supreme wisdom that illuminates the Mahāyāna Dharma; this is called the Ground of Radiance (*prabhākārī-bhūmi*).

[Commentary: Regarding the "obscuration of dullness and darkness" (*tama-mandya-āvaraṇa*): ignorance (*avidyā*) and so forth are, by their very nature, deluded and dark, lacking clarity and sharpness; thus, being both dark and dull, they constitute an obscuration, hence the name "obscuration of dullness and darkness."

[Commentary: Regarding "the ignorance of attachment to what was not yet attained but is now attained": because ignorance is proximate to that craving, it is termed "ignorance of attachment" through the method of proximity (*upacāra*).

"What was not yet attained but is now attained" refers to the superior meditative concentration and the wisdom of cultivation, which were previously unattained and are now for the first time acquired;
since this ignorance obstructs those virtues, it is called the ignorance of attachment to what was not yet attained but is now attained.
The ignorance that consists of attachment to what was previously unattained and what is now attained is able to obstruct superior dhāraṇī;
this ignorance is itself the obstruction, and thus it is called "the ignorance that acts as an obstruction.
Since this ignorance obstructs superior hearing, reflection, and dhāraṇī, the ignorance that acts as an obstruction to superior dhāraṇī is termed "the ignorance that obstructs superior dhāraṇī."
[Commentary]: This statement that *dhāraṇī* has mindfulness and wisdom as its essence is because its excellent function of discernment and clear recollection is preeminent.

There are two types of *dhāraṇī*: first, the *saṃgraha-dhāraṇī* (retaining *dhāraṇī*). "Retaining" (*saṃgraha*) means holding; it refers to the ability to hold all dharmas heard, whether their words or their meaning.

(This refers to the *śrutadhara-dhāraṇī* cited in the Commentary. Second, the *vibhāga-dhāraṇī* (dispersing *dhāraṇī*). "Dispersing" (*vibhāga*) means bestowing; it refers to the bestowal of the Dharma upon others.
Therefore, there are likewise four kinds: first, the dhāraṇī of phenomena (*dharma-dhāraṇī*), because within a single name, phrase, or syllable, all names, phrases, and syllables are manifested;

second, the dhāraṇī of meaning (*artha-dhāraṇī*), because within a single meaning, all meanings are manifested (the commentary explains that it is called "retaining" [dhāraṇī] in the sense of self-benefit);

third, the dhāraṇī of patience (*kṣānti-dhāraṇī*), because by attaining the Bodhisattva’s patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), one teaches and demonstrates it to others; fourth, the dhāraṇī of mantras (*vidyā-mantra-dhāraṇī*).

The meaning of the commentary is as follows: Because one has internally realized the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*), one is able to expound the various distinctions of the Dharma according to all directions;
thus, the unimpeded analytical knowledge of language (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*) is the very retention (*dhāraṇī*) of that patience.

Because one has internally achieved the unimpeded analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*), one possesses mastery in preaching the Dharma and is able to recite and bring forth all divine mantras (*vidyā-mantra*) to bestow them upon sentient beings.

For the sake of all sentient beings, the unimpeded analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*) is precisely the dhāraṇī of incantations (further verify this in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*).
[Commentary] Regarding "the fourth stage and so forth," the manifestation of signs first shows the winds arising from the four directions;

this symbolizes that within the fourth stage, the virtue of benevolence is like the wind, gathering and transforming the four modes of birth and crushing those who lack faith, which is why the wind-circle (*vāyu-maṇḍala*) appears. The various wonderful flowers symbolize the inclination toward the four [noble truths].

Because it is the fruit of the patient acceptance (kṣānti) that accords with the ground, the flowers are spread upon the ground so that all sentient beings may cultivate the flowers of causal practices within the ground of birth and death to attain the wondrous fruit.
Within the third ground, one cultivates the preparatory application (prayoga) for the fourth ground;

once this application is perfected, one gives rise to the path of uninterrupted transition (ānantarya-mārga) to sever and exhaust the subtle afflictions of the fourth ground—the obstacle of active manifestation and the two types of ignorance. This is the second stage.

By giving rise to mindfulness as the path of liberation, one abandons the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the two obstacles and realizes the *tathatā* (suchness) that is free from grasping, thereby ascending to the fourth stage, the *Arciṣmatī-bhūmi*.
[Commentary:

Regarding "free from grasping," this is a passage from the treatise itself. The sub-commentary explains it as follows: "Truly being without attachment means it is not [the object of] the grasping of a self."
Because it is the basis for the grasping of pride, self-love, ignorance, extreme views, and so forth, it is called "unappropriated suchness.
Prior to this stage, suchness was subject to attachment and had a locus of dependence due to being grasped; this stage is not like that.
[Commentary]: Regarding the subtle view of self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), it is a defilement to be abandoned through cultivation within the sixth consciousness.

Because it previously frequently arose together with the view of grasping at a self (*ātmagrāhadṛṣṭi*) and other such views, it is called a "dark and dull obstacle" (*andhabhūta-āvaraṇa*). It obstructs what has been heard, contemplated, and cultivated, causing one to forget them;

it also obstructs superior meditative concentration (*samādhi*), dhāraṇī, and superior wisdom (*prajñā*). This [obstacle] pertains to the superior concentration and the Dharma that have been attained...

It gives rise to attachment that obstructs the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*). Regarding its subtlety, the treatise explains it through three meanings: First, because it is of the lowest grade.

This refers to those dharmas such as the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) that arise from discrimination within the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*); because they are coarse and violent, they are called "superior grade.
Solitary greed (*rāga*) and the like, being generally unwholesome (*akuśala*), are called "middle grade. This [subtle attachment] is innate (*sahaja*) and neutral (*avyākṛta*).

First, it is called "inferior" by nature; second, it arises spontaneously without the condition of deliberate attention (*amanasikāra*), for it does not arise through the forceful reflection of conceptual discrimination;

third, it follows along with present activity from distant eons, persisting throughout the course of one's life without being abandoned, for unlike conceptual discrimination, it is not discarded when encountering specific conditions.

[Commentary]: Regarding "attachment to the joy of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) through ignorance": because one craves and becomes attached to that meditative attainment, this attachment to the flavor of attainment is called "attachment to the flavor of meditative attainment.
This craving for the flavor of attainment, together with the feeling of joy (*sukha-vedanā*), is termed "attachment to the joy of meditative attainment.
Because ignorance is proximate to that craving for the flavor of attainment, it is designated by this name. It is a subtle and wondrous pure dharma.
Regarding "attachment to ignorance": within the afflictive hindrances, there is an attachment that craves those subtle and pure dharmas;
because this ignorance is proximate to that attachment, it is so named.

[Commentary: Regarding "the fifth stage and so forth," the manifestation of a precious woman first indicates that one is approaching the fifth stage (*pañcamī bhūmi*) and giving rise to superior virtues.
That the woman adorns her body with necklaces signifies that within the fourth stage (*caturthī bhūmi*), the adornment of all virtues has already been perfected.

That the woman wears a flower crown on her head symbolizes the arising of the fruit of the noble path (*āryamārga-phala*) in the subsequent stages; thus, within the fourth stage, one cultivates the five [perfections].

Once the preparatory application for the stage has been perfected, the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) arises, severing the fifth obstacle to parinirvāṇa of the lower vehicles and the two types of delusion.

Subsequently, in the second moment, the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) arises; one abandons the latencies (*vāsanā*) of the two obstacles, realizes the non-distinctive suchness (*tathatā*), and ascends to the fifth stage, the Difficult to Conquer (*Sudurjayā-bhūmi*).

[Commentary: Regarding the Ground Difficult to Conquer (*Sudurjayā*): the two wisdoms—the fundamental and the subsequent—have distinct modes of activity (*ākāra*) when realizing the ultimate and penetrating the conventional.

At this stage, through the power of preparatory application (*prayoga*), the Bodhisattva causes them to arise simultaneously. Because he has attained this "difficult-to-conquer" wisdom, it serves as the name for this ground.
[Commentary: The four fearlessnesses of the Buddha-fruit refer to the ability to know for oneself with total confidence and fearlessness regarding four matters.

Because one is without timidity, inferiority, doubt, or dread, they are called "fearlessnesses. There are four such fearlessnesses: first, the fearlessness of perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi-vaiśāradya*).
This refers to perfectly awakening to all phenomena and being fully awakened to all phenomena; thus it is called "perfect enlightenment," as it is not a partial awakening or a false awakening.
Second is the fearlessness regarding the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-vaiśāradya*), because all seeds and habitual tendencies of the outflows of affliction have been exhausted.

Third is the fearlessness regarding the teaching of obstructive dharmas (*antarāyika-dharma-vaiśāradya*), because the Buddha declares that defiled dharmas which constitute obstructions will necessarily act as hindrances.

Fourth is the fearlessness regarding the teaching of the path leading to liberation (*niḥsaraṇamārga-vaiśāradya*), because he declares that the noble ones, through cultivation, certainly emerge from suffering by means of the path of transcendence. If anyone should question him, the Buddha correctly perceives these four [fearlessnesses].
The understanding that the fearlessnesses of the Tathāgata—such as the fearlessness of being perfectly awakened (*samyaksaṃbuddha-vaiśāradya*)—are all *tatpuruṣa* compounds [is as follows].
[Commentary: The wisdom that realizes [this] is the fearlessness of being perfectly awakened. While Bodhisattvas possess a portion of the meaning of "perfect awakening," they lack "equal awakening";
the remaining three [fearlessnesses] are as stated in the text.
[Commentary]: Regarding the characteristic of pure equality and non-differentiation, the *Śāstra* states:

"The universal non-differentiation of True Suchness" means that this True Suchness is universally undifferentiated (its essence being a single dharma), unlike the eye and other faculties, whose universals possess distinctions.

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "severing the [afflictions] that follow," the *Śāstra* states: The obstacle to the parinirvāṇa of the lower vehicles refers to a portion of the innate (*sahaja*) cognitive obstacles (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
This causes one to loathe birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and delight in nirvāṇa, similar to the two lower vehicles who loathe suffering and aspire toward cessation.

This obstacle is severed at the fifth stage by the path of non-differentiation. (The "path of non-differentiation" is so called because, in contrast to the differentiated objects of aspiration and aversion, it realizes the non-differentiated *tathatā*; thus it is named the path of non-differentiation.)

[Commentary]: Regarding these two types [of practitioners], the former loathes birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) while the latter delights in *nirvāṇa*. However, since birth-and-death and *nirvāṇa* are fundamentally without distinction, how could there be such loathing and likewise such delight in pursuit?
It is solely due to the power of the influence of ignorance (*avidyā*) that these arise.
Rejoicing in [virtue] and wearying of [suffering], and the tracing back of faults to their source, constitute the two types of ignorance within the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

[Commentary: Regarding the four pairs: (1) the pair of vows and aspirations versus compassion; (2) the pair of the roots of goodness versus non-abandonment; (3) the pair of correct practice versus tirelessness;

and (4) the pair of protecting others versus one’s own excellence. Of these, the first two correspond respectively to benefiting oneself and benefiting others, while the latter two pertain to benefiting oneself.
(One may understand this by examining the text).

[Commentary]: Regarding these "sufferings" and so forth, the essential nature (*dharmatā*) of the objects of knowledge consists of both the coarse and the subtle; the wisdom that knows them likewise has higher and lower levels.

Based on this, the *Śrīmālādevī-sūtra* speaks of eight truths: namely, the four noble truths of conditioned activity (*saṃskṛta*) and the four noble truths of unconditioned non-activity (*asaṃskṛta*).
These eight noble truths are not what is known by the two vehicles, because they discern the four truths as having immeasurable aspects of practice.

There are those who posit four noble truths that are further subject to transformation and change, which can be cultivated through practice: namely, *paricchinna-jarāmaraṇa* (segmented birth and death) is called suffering;

afflictions and karma are called the origin; unconditioned cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) is called cessation; and the category of wisdom regarding the emptiness of living beings (*pudgala-śūnyatā-jñāna*) is called the path.

Regarding the "path of the four noble truths without effort" (*anabhisaṃskāra-catur-āryasatya*): because there is no superior dharma to be cultivated or performed beyond this, it is said that the cycle of birth and death through transformation (*pariṇāmi-jarāmaraṇa*) is suffering;
the category of cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) is the origin; non-abiding nirvāṇa (*apratisthita-nirvāṇa*) is cessation;

and the category of the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmaśūnyatā-jñāna*) is the path. This reveals the bodhisattva’s correct contemplation of the four truths without effort. As for the "immeasurable truths," whether they be real or... [text fragment].
The mundane categories of immeasurable meanings all converge upon the truth of immeasurable objects; thus, the truth of immeasurable truths is called "immeasurable truth.
If the wisdom that realizes it and its practice and understanding are immeasurable, the truth of immeasurable truths is likewise called "immeasurable truth. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"The four truths, when analyzed, possess immeasurable aspects; since the immeasurable is itself truth, it is called 'immeasurable truth.'"
[Commentary: Regarding the sixteen heterodox doctrines: 1) the thesis that the effect exists within the cause; 2) the thesis that [the effect] is manifested from conditions;
and so on, up to the sixteenth, the thesis of false conceptualization regarding auspiciousness, as set forth in the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*.

[Commentary]: Regarding the "obstacles to the path" and the "path leading out," within the ten stages (*bhūmi*), each has three mental states—namely, the entering, the abiding, and the exiting mental positions—which are termed "obstacles to the path.

This is because the state of entering severs the obstacles. The state of abiding is the correct cultivation, and the state of exiting is the fulfillment of cultivation; both are termed the "path leading out," as they constitute the path of transcendence.
Furthermore, within the stage of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana-bhūmi*), these are termed "obstacles to the path" because there are various afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*).

Because it is the Noble Path, the names of the stages of the noble ones of the Three Vehicles are called the "Path of Departure" and the "Path of Transcendence. Furthermore, Bodhisattvas fully know the path that emerges from birth and death, the path that severs hindrances, and the path that purifies defilements.

[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "the sixth stage and so forth": this indicates that the wisdom of dependent origination abides in the three gates of liberation, is accompanied by the seven noble riches, and removes all impurities.

The defilements and fetters ripen into the fruit of Bodhi, like flowers or a pond manifesting four stairways that represent the transformation of the four modes of birth and entry into the path of the Four Noble Truths.
Golden sand is spread upon the ground to signify its preciousness and its capacity to relieve all who are impoverished. Regarding the water of eight virtues, the *Nāgarāja Sūtra* explains them as:
first, clarity; second, lightness; third, coolness; fourth, softness; fifth, fragrance; sixth, sweetness; seventh, not harming the throat when drunk; and eighth, [not distressing the stomach].
Eighth, having drunk [the water], it does not harm the abdomen; because the eight concentrations nourish merit and wisdom, there are blue, red, yellow, and white lotuses.

These four colors correspond, in sequence, to the Sanskrit term *utpala* and others, representing the forty-four types of wisdom—the flowers of causal practice—cultivated through the contemplation of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) within the six stages.
Because one relies on the wisdom of dependent origination, one sports with supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) in the lotus pond of liberation, remaining far removed from worldly attachments.
Experiencing the cool bliss of the sublime Dharma that extinguishes the heat of affliction, one cultivates the preparatory practices (*prayoga*) for the sixth stage within the fifth stage.

Once these preparatory practices are perfected, one gives rise to the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) to sever and exhaust the sixth obstacle—the active manifestation of coarse characteristics. This subsumes two delusions.

Subsequently, in the second moment, one gives rise to the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), abandons the latencies (*vāsanā*) of the two obstacles, realizes undefiled and pure *tathatā*, and ascends to the sixth stage.

The Sixth Ground: The Ground of Presence (*Abhimukhī-bhūmi*). [Commentary: As for the Ground of Presence, one contemplates the twelve links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) within conditioned formations as they continue in succession.

These appear with perfect clarity before the contemplative mind, like reflections in a mirror. By virtue of this contemplation, non-conceptual wisdom (*animitta-jñāna*) is induced and brought into manifestation.
The preceding is named the Ground of Presence (*abhimukhī-bhūmi*).

[Commentary: "In accordance with those" means that this dwelling has the sense of being a basis; it refers to entering into and realizing the equality of true suchness (*tathatā*) by relying on the three gates of liberation through the wisdom of superior patience (*adhimātra-kṣānti*).
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states: "There is neither defilement nor purity in true suchness," meaning that the intrinsic nature of this true suchness is [free from these].
Because it is untainted and cannot be said to become pure only later.

[Commentary] Regarding the cause of accumulation (*saṃudaya-hetu*): innate greed and so forth act as the cause for moistening rebirth, while the five members beginning with consciousness act as the productive cause;

because they produce the *paritta-kalpa* (limited) existence, they are called the "cause of accumulation. The three types of karma—merit and so forth—that induce the fruit of *paritta-kalpa* existence are called "accumulative karma" (*saṃudaya-karma*).

Since the non-meritorious karma that brings about the fruits of the three miserable realms does not arise for abandonment upon the Path of Seeing, the causal karma that brings them about is abandoned at this stage;
thus, the fruit is coarse while the cause is subtle, and they are abandoned sequentially.
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "the manifestation of coarse characteristics," this wording is inverted. The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states:

"The obstacle of the manifestation of coarse characteristics refers to a portion of the innate cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) that clings to the coarse characteristics of defilement and purity as being manifest. This obstacle pertains to the sixth stage, where the path of non-defilement and non-purity is realized.

As for the term "coarse characteristics," it refers to clinging to the relative aspects of the Four Noble Truths; because these are coarse compared to the subsequent subtle [truth], they are called "coarse characteristics."
The manifestation of coarse characteristics is itself an obstruction; thus it is called the "obstruction of the manifestation of coarse characteristics.

Contrary to the preceding [stage], the true suchness (*tathatā*) of this stage is termed "non-defiled and non-pure," and the wisdom that takes suchness as its object is termed the "path of non-defiled and non-purity."

[Commentary]: Regarding the ignorance of the flowing and turning of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-caryā*), it refers to the manifestation of coarse characteristics of the defiled causes and effects of the flowing and turning of contaminated formative actions (*saṃskāra*) within the truths of suffering and origin.

Regarding the ignorance of grasping at the pure causes and effects of cessation and the path, because one apprehends the characteristics of untainted purity, there is much contemplation with signs (*sanimitta-bhāvanā*);
for the most part, one is unable to abide for long in signless contemplation (*animitta-bhāvanā*).

[Sūtra] Regarding the phrase "enveloped by the darkness of ignorance" and so forth, the meaning of dependent origination is analyzed through five gates: first, the determination of its essential nature; second, the explanation of its name; third, the characteristics of its conditions;

fourth, its reliance upon the [three] periods of time; and fifth, the sequence of defilement and purification, as well as the forward and reverse orders. First, regarding the determination of its essential nature: the essential nature of the member of ignorance (avidyā) has delusion (moha) as its intrinsic character.

According to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, there are two types of ignorance: namely, ignorance that is deluded regarding the internal body and ignorance that is deluded regarding external [phenomena].
Regarding the object, ignorance (*avidyā*) takes only the first [of the three types] as the branch of ignorance. This, in turn, has two aspects:

first, delusion regarding the true meaning, which is confusion concerning the principle of reality and encompasses the lower and middle grades; second, delusion regarding the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*), which is exclusively of the superior grade and arises from confusion regarding the internal body as the fruit of maturation.
These three grades of delusion are all capable of inciting karma; specifically, it is through the inferior-grade delusion that one incites immovable (*āniñjya*) karma.
Karma arises from middling-grade delusion as meritorious karma, and from superior-grade delusion as non-meritorious karma. Furthermore, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
"That which directly initiates karma is exclusively abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*); its auxiliaries are not fixed.

Thus, taking only such initiating agents as the branch of ignorance (*avidyā*), this refers to all four types of ignorance—both associated and dissociated, as well as active outbursts (*paryavasthāna*) and latent tendencies (*anuśaya*). Question: Regarding the seeds...

Question: Do those who currently generate karma for existence have equal strength in their primary (direct) and auxiliary (indirect) conditions? Answer: For ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) generating karma, the manifest [karma] constitutes the primary condition while the seeds constitute the auxiliary;
this applies to those non-Buddhists (*bāhyaka*) who are not heedless. For those who are heedless, both the manifest and the seeds constitute the primary condition.

Regarding the members of the path of action, their substance (*svabhāva*) encompasses the three types of action (*trividha-karman*); however, all three types of action have volition (*cetanā*) as their essential nature.

The two types of action—bodily and vocal—are also conventionally designated as having form and sound as their essence. Consequently, this branch of conduct (*caryāṅga*) applies to both seeds and manifest states.

Its essence consists of formative volition (*rūpa-cetanā*). It is taken exclusively as being tainted (*sāsrava*), wholesome, or unwholesome bodily, vocal, and mental karma capable of producing future ripened results (*vipākaphala*).
Therefore, it functions solely as the nature of the branch of conduct that produces either the collective retribution (*nikāya-sabhāga*) alone, or both the collective and individual retributions.

Since karma that results in individual retribution (*pratiniyatavipāka*) is not the constituent of formations (*saṃskāra-aṅga*), the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "That which is produced by it [ignorance] is what is called formations.
This implies that all karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya-karman*) and all auxiliary karma for future lives are not the constituent of formations.

The meaning is that there are two types of maturation fruits (*vipākaphala*): first, the collective retribution (*sāmānyavipāka*), which is the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) as it is the master of collective retribution; second, the individual retribution.
Retribution consists of the fulfillment of that collective retribution through the individual completion of the six consciousnesses, the material sense faculties (*rūpīndriya*), and so forth;

therefore, the karma capable of inducing this has three categories: first, that which induces only collective retribution; second, that which induces only individual retribution; and third, that which induces both types of retribution.
Thus, it is collectively designated as "formations" (*saṃskāra*) because they are produced by that very ignorance. Among these three categories, one takes only...

Those [karmas] that evoke a collective retribution (*saṃvartanīya-vipāka*) or evoke both types of retribution constitute the constituent members of *bhava* (becoming). Those that evoke only specific retribution (*pratiniyata-vipāka*), however, do not constitute the member of *bhava*;
because the power of this karma for the cycle of birth and death is inferior, it is merely termed a "specific auxiliary" to the primary karma.
Furthermore, karma to be experienced in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya-karma*) is excluded because its power is inferior and it is not a karma that causes the flow of birth and death. Next...
The five members refer to consciousness (*vijñāna*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), and feeling (*vedanā*);

these take seeds as their essential substance. At the stage of the seeds, there are no distinct active characteristics; they are subtle, hidden, and difficult to know. Therefore, we describe their appearance based on the manifest activities (*samudācāra*) that arise from them.

Thus, we designate those seeds as the five members through differentiation. Furthermore, regarding the member of consciousness, it refers exclusively to the eighth fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*).
Because it is the aggregate that serves as the primary subject of retribution, it is called the "limb of name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*).
The four aggregates are called "name"; these four aggregates—feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness—are collectively termed "name.

Just as in the world, "name" refers to that which follows sound and converges upon phenomena, so too these four aggregates—the mind and mental factors—converge toward and proceed toward their objects of perception.
Regarding the statement that the four formless aggregates are collectively called "name" (*nāman*):

it is because they conform to and proceed toward various objects of perception (*ālambana*). Alternatively, it is because, based on verbal expression, they conceptually differentiate various objects of perception;
therefore, they are called "name. Why is the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) called "form"? Because, in each respective [case]...
It is called "form" (*rūpa*) because it has the sense of being planted in a location, of increasing, and of being subject to transformation and resistance.
As for the limb of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), its substance consists of the five faculties—the eye and so forth—and the faculty of mind (*manas*).

This means that when the first six consciousnesses, which are of the nature of maturation-born (*vipākaja*) and neutral (*avyākṛta*), serve as the support for subsequent moments of consciousness, they are termed the "faculty of mind. The seventh [consciousness] is not included.

Because they are results of maturation (*vipāka*), these six factors are established as the "six sense bases" (*ṣaḍāyatana*) because they serve as the gateways and locations for the growth of mind and mental factors.
As for the two members of contact (*sparśa*) and feeling (*vedanā*), they take the single factor of contact or feeling respectively as their essence according to their specific functions.

Now, taking the seeds of consciousness and so forth as the essence of the five members, this is because they constitute the actual substance that produces the fruits of birth and death (*saṃsāra*). Thus, the seeds of consciousness and so forth are of an indeterminate nature (*avyākṛta*) and cannot [function] by themselves.
At the stage of birth (*upapatti*), before the [five] constituents (*skandha*) have been determined, one dwells in a state of dispersion within the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*).

This refers only to the seeds of designations (*nāma-vyañjana-bīja*) of the eighth consciousness and so forth; they do not yet belong to the five constituents such as consciousness (*vijñāna*).
