It is only through being gathered by the preceding constituent of formations (*saṃskāra*) that they are then subsumed under the five constituents beginning with consciousness.

Furthermore, the constituent of consciousness (*vijñāna-aṅga*) is precisely the seeds of designation of the fundamental consciousness; being summoned by formations, it constitutes this specific constituent.

Regarding the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of the member "name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*): while the term "name-and-form" generally refers to everything except the six unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena, here the member "name-and-form" takes as its essence the seeds accumulated by formative forces (*saṃskāra*). This is not the general sense [of the term]. This essence is twofold:

first, the essence derived from a comprehensive inclusion, wherein the seeds of all five members are the essence of the member "name-and-form," because these five members do not transcend form (*rūpa*) and sensation (*vedanā*).
The members of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) are likewise of the nature of the five aggregates (*skandha*). Among these, the aggregate of "name" consists of four aggregates.

Within the hundred dharmas that constitute name-and-form, one takes the entire eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), a portion of the first six consciousnesses—totaling seven types of consciousness seeds—and a portion of each of the eleven mental factors (*caitta*), namely:

the five universal (*sarvatraga*), the five object-specific (*viṣayapratiniyata*), and the one from the indeterminate (*aniyata*) category, which is sleep (*middha*). Together, these constitute the seeds of the eleven mental factors.

The five faculties (*pañcendriya*) and the five objects (*pañcaviṣaya*) constitute ten material phenomena (*rūpadharma*). When these are totaled with their seeds, they comprise twenty-eight dharmas as the seeds for this limb [of dependent origination].

Other factors—whether provisional (*prajñapti*) or lacking distinct seeds—are excluded; even if they possess seeds, they do not belong to this limb because they are not accumulated by formative forces (*saṃskāra*) and are not results of maturation (*vipāka*).
Such meanings may be understood as usual. Second, to avoid confusion, the essential nature (*svabhāva*) is established and distinguished.
The remaining four branches consist of other dharmas which constitute the body of the *nāmarūpa* branch;

these twenty dharmas form its body because, from among the previous twenty-eight, eight dharmas—the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), the five sense organs, contact (*sparśa*), and feeling (*vedanā*)—are excluded and established separately as distinct branches. (The above refers to the desire realm.

As for the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), in the first dhyāna, odor, taste, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, and the mental factor of torpor (*middha*) are excluded because they do not exist there.

If the seeds of the aggregate consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) are considered in their mixed state, there are five types of mental factor seeds and eight types of material phenomenon (*rūpa-dharma*) seeds; thus, twenty-three dharmas are reckoned as constituting the essence of these seeds.

If they are not considered in a mixed state, one must further exclude the seeds of the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*), contact (*sparśa*), feeling (*vedanā*), and the five sense organs—these eight dharmas—and instead take the four types of aggregate consciousness seeds (namely, those of eye, ear, body, and the sixth consciousness). Furthermore, there are eight types of mental factor seeds.
This refers to the seeds of fifteen dharmas: the three universal [mental factors], the five object-specific ones, and the five kinds of form—namely, visible form, sound, and tangibility.
If one is in the second dhyāna or above, the first five consciousnesses are absent because there is no *vitarka* (applied thought) or *vicāra* (sustained thought);
thus, the body of this branch consists of the seeds of twenty dharmas, namely two types of consciousness-seeds and the mental factors.
There are ten types of seeds of form and eight types of seeds of form; if they are not conflated, their substance consists of twelve factors. These are the seeds of this branch:
the seed of consciousness is one, being exclusively the sixth consciousness; the seeds of mental factors are eight; and the seeds of form are three.

If one excludes the formless realm, five further [factors] are removed—the five sense organs and the three types of form—because there is no form there. If they are conflated, the substance consists of ten.

The two dharmas refer to the seeds of the two consciousnesses and ten mental factors (*caitta*) as their substance; if they are not conflated, the substance consists of only nine dharmas—namely, one consciousness and eight mental factors.

Although there are *dharmāyatana-rūpa* (matter included in the sphere of phenomena) produced by the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), which resemble the physical sense organs (*upādāya-rūpa*) and are generated by the power of concentration, they are not *vipāka* (maturation).
Therefore, in the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), these exist only nominally. For this reason, various treatises [state] either...

One might argue that the seeds of form from other realms are taken up to constitute "name-and-form" (nāmarūpa) there; however, since this treatise discusses the factors of the specific stage [of existence], those are not included here.

If one were to contemplate dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), it should be stated as: "volitional formations condition consciousness; consciousness conditions name; name conditions the sense-base of mind (*manāyatana*); the sense-base of mind conditions contact," and so forth.
As for the member of the six sense-bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), its substance consists of the five faculties and the seeds of the first six consciousnesses, provided they exist as maturation (*vipāka*).
That which was called "mind" (*manas*) in past lives is here distinguished by way of two time periods within a single mind; thus, it is explained as distinct.
That which belongs to the past is termed "mind," while that which is present is subsumed under the branch of "name-and-form. If this were not the case, there would be no consciousness within "name.
This is discussed in terms of the five [aggregates] existing simultaneously at one time. If, however, one speaks of those seeds in terms of the stages of future rebirth, then first...

The locus of birth, which in the past life was called "mind" (*manas*) and is also subsumed under the "middle" [link], is designated as "mind" because it serves as the support for the subsequent consciousness.

At that time, it is not yet termed the "limb of the six sense bases" (*ṣaḍāyatana*). Therefore, with respect to the remaining stages, even in the present life, it is subsumed under the six sense bases.
Thus, the essential natures (*svabhāva*) of these two types of seeds are each distinct. As for the essential nature of the limb of contact (*sparśa*), excluding...

The seventh consciousness grasps the entirety of the contact (*sparśa*) associated with the eighth consciousness, as well as the maturation-contact (*vipāka-sparśa*) associated with the six consciousnesses;
all seeds are its substance. Regarding the limb of sensation (*vedanā*), its substance is as explained for contact, because its functional states and meanings are identical.
Regarding the limb of craving (*tṛṣṇā*), craving is itself greed (*lobha*); among the three grades of greed, it refers to the inferior and middling grades.
The limb of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is included within the limb of grasping (*upādāna*) because it consists of superior-grade greed;

thus, the nine limbs of grasping have as their essence all afflictions (*kleśa*), since the afflictions of all realms (*dhātu*) cause rebirth and are all capable of seizing the phenomena of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*). Therefore, they are collectively termed the limb of grasping.

Both the limbs of craving and grasping are able to moisten [the seeds] both in their latent state (*bīja*) and in their manifest state (*vartamāna*); hence, there are ten limbs of existence (*bhava*).

As for the "entity" (*tattva*), it refers to the seeds of the six branches beginning with "prior existence" (*pūrvakālabhava*); once moistened by craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*), they are designated as the "present existence" (*vartamānabhava*) and the "future existence" (*āyaty-ambhava*).
Therefore, this consists solely of the eleven branches of the seed-stage. Regarding the entity of the twelve branches of aging and death (*jarāmaraṇa*), the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states:

"From the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) until one reaches the fundamental state (*mūlabhava*) and before undergoing decay and transformation, all are subsumed under the branch of birth (*jāti*). This constitutes the entity of the twelve branches of aging and death.
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "All states of transformation are collectively termed 'aging' (*jarā*); the disintegration of the body and the end of life are termed 'death' (*marana*).

Aging is not necessarily present [in all beings], yet it is established as a link [of dependent origination] in conjunction with death. The essence of these latter two links is comprised of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) and consists exclusively of manifest active states (*samudācāra*) categorized as the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*).
Question: Why is illness (*vyādhi*) not established as a link? Answer: The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "Because illness is not universal, it is not established [as a link]."
"Branch" (*aṅga*) refers to [the factors] that do not pervade the three realms, because they are absent in the higher realms and because they do not necessarily exist within the desire realm.

Regarding the second explanation of the name, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, chapter ten, states: "Because one proceeds through the various destinies (*gati*) bound by afflictions (*kleśa*) and arises again and again, it is called 'dependent origination' (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
Furthermore, the fifty-sixth [chapter] explains: "The cause is named dependent origination, and the fruit is named dependently arisen; [it is so called] because it acts as a condition."

It is called "dependent origination" (*pratītyasamutpāda*) because it gives rise to results, and it is called "dependently arisen" (*pratītyasamutpanna*) because it is produced from conditions. Regarding the third characteristic of conditions: ignorance (*avidyā*) has three grades;

delusion regarding the true nature of reality (*tattvārtha-moha*) ranges from the lower to the middle grade, while delusion regarding the result of maturation (*vipāka-phala-moha*) is exclusively of the upper grade.

All of these arise in dependence upon the internal body as the result of maturation. Volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) are of two kinds: first, wholesome (*kuśala*), and second, unwholesome (*akuśala*). Or...
They are divided into three: first, the immovable; second, merit; and third, non-merit. The karma of the two upper realms is called immovable karma.

Wholesome karma of the desire realm is called meritorious karma, meaning it brings about the maturation of the happy destinies and includes all wholesome karma that accords with the maturations of the five destinies;

thus, all such karma is termed "merit. However, the designation "merit" applies generally to the wholesomeness of all three realms, yet the wholesome karma of the upper realms possesses its own distinct excellence.
The term "immovable karma" (*āniñjya-karma*) is a collective designation for the wholesome karmas of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

Unwholesome karmas that result in rebirth in the miserable destinies (*durgati*), produce intense heat (*tāpa*), and lead to maturation (*vipāka*) within the five destinies are called "non-meritorious karma" (*apuṇya-karma*). The seeds of the five links beginning with consciousness—the power of the perfuming of names and phrases (*nāma-pada-vāsanā*)—are weak and inferior;
they cannot arise spontaneously in their respective locations and must await the impelling force of the link of formative action (*saṃskāra*) to bring them forth.
Accumulation arises from the following: through weak-grade delusion, one generates immovable karma; through medium-grade delusion, one generates meritorious karma;

and through strong-grade delusion, one generates non-meritorious karma. Once these karmas have been generated, by their force, the seeds of the five factors beginning with consciousness are accumulated.
These are subsumed under *saṃskāra* (formative forces) and *bhava* (existence), which pertain to the place of rebirth—that is, the various forms of future birth, aging, and death.
Regarding the determination of stages, there is no sequence of before and after; rather, the cause is explained in terms of the stage that is about to arise. As the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
"That is to say, taking as a condition the delusion regarding internal matured fruit (*vipākaphala*), one produces the various karmas capable of truly summoning future existence.

Taking these as conditions, they trigger and directly produce the seeds of the five fruits in the stage of future birth, aging, and death. Subsequently, based on the delusion regarding external dominant fruit (*adhipatiphala*), one takes [the seeds] as a condition.
When objects of perception give rise to feeling, craving arises; conditioned by craving, the four types of grasping—desire and the rest—are produced.

When craving and grasping combine to moisten the seeds of projecting karma and their associated causes, these are termed "existence" (*bhava*). Regarding the four types of grasping: first, grasping at sense-desires (*kāma-upādāna*), which has as its nature greed for the five sensory objects.
Second, grasping at self-theory (*ātma-vāda-upādāna*): because of attachment to a self, one conceives of the discourse concerning a self; this is called grasping at self-theory.

Third, the clinging to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) consists of clinging to the other three views. Fourth, the clinging to precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) consists of clinging to the precepts and prohibitions maintained by those three views.

From the time of this retribution at the end of life until entering the subsequent existence—specifically from the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) until reaching the fundamental existence (*mūlabhava*)—before the aggregates have undergone decay, the factors of birth and the factors of aging and death manifest; thus, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction arise in various ways as they follow upon birth.
Ignorance arises once more, and it is able to accumulate the karma that serves as the cause for future existence;

when the previous retribution has been exhausted, the subsequent retribution is born again—this is called the characteristic of the revolving wheel of the members of existence (*bhavāṅga*). Fourth, regarding the dependence on time, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states:

"The ten causes and two fruits definitely do not belong to the same time period, because cause and fruit are distinct. That is to say, the ten members of the past are the causes, and the two members of the present are the fruits."

Regarding the ten factors of the present as the causes for the two factors of the future, which constitute the fruit: from ignorance (*avidyā*) up to sensation (*vedanā*), when compared with craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and existence (*bhava*), they may be either identical or different.

That is to say, if ignorance produces the seeds of consciousness (*vijñāna*) and so forth from karma that is to be experienced in the next life (*upapadyavedanīya-karman*), then the factors of craving and grasping arise in the present body;
moistening those six seeds, they transform into what is called "existence" (*bhava*). This is identical to the [present] world. If, however, ignorance...

Regarding those karmas that are to be experienced in subsequent lives (*aparaparyāya-vedanīya*) and a portion of indeterminate karma (*aniyata-karman*) whose retribution is received across successive lifetimes:

the seeds of ignorance, formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are projected in the present life; however, the branches of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) do not arise in the present life because their retribution has not yet been received.
Consequently, in the life immediately preceding the actual experience of that retribution in a later future life, craving finally arises.
Taking up [craving] and moistening it constitutes "existence" (*bhava*), because one experiences its fruit in a subsequent life;

or, having previously arisen in former lives, the first seven members arise in the present life, and only then does craving and grasping moisten them to constitute existence, such that one experiences the fruit in a subsequent life.
This is precisely what distinguishes the first seven members from the next three members in terms of not belonging to the same lifetime. If the first seven and the next three...
Regarding the latter two, they are mutually determined by being of the same temporal period (*adhvan*), arising from similar potentiality (*śakti*), and having similar power (*bala*).

As for the fifth point, defilement and purification in their forward and reverse orders, the *Abhidharma* (the *Abhidharmakośa*, Chapter 4) states: "Because of the forward and reverse order of defilement, and because of the forward and reverse order of purification.

First, regarding the forward and reverse order of defilement: this refers to the practice performed during the seven stages of preparation (*prayoga*) prior to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) of the Pratyekabuddhayāna.

These contemplative practices of direct and reverse order are called "defiled" (*saṃkleśa*) because they are with outflows (*sāsrava*). In reality, however, they are also practiced by those in the noble stages (*āryabhūmi*);

here, they are said to be performed by ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) because the discussion concerns the stage of the ordinary person. When performing this contemplation, one first proceeds from cause to effect in direct order, which is called "direct" (*anuloma*) because it follows the sequential order;
then, one examines the cause by means of the effect, which is called "reverse" (*pratiloma*) because it proceeds in the opposite direction.

Because it follows the sequence of the forward progression (*anuloma*), that is, when one contemplates that ignorance conditions formations, formations condition consciousness, and so on up to birth conditioning aging and death—this is the forward contemplation by which one knows the succession of the faults and afflictions of birth and death.

When one performs the contemplations of the seventy-seven knowledges (*jñāna*) and the forty-four knowledges, it is called the reverse (*pratiloma*). Because it follows the reverse sequence, first [we shall discuss] the contemplation of the seventy-seven knowledges.
This means that one contemplates how, in the present, the factors of dependent origination such as old age and death exist through conditions and do not exist without conditions;

the former is the knowledge that investigates the cause, and the latter is the knowledge that examines the cause. Because this birth and old age and death arise within one's own present self, these two types of knowledge are established.
Furthermore, one contemplates that all past instances of old age and death from beginningless time likewise depend upon conditions for their arising.

There is that which is not non-conditioned arising; furthermore, existence (*bhava*) also constitutes two types of knowledge. Although future phenomena have not yet arisen, they can possess the sense of being subject to defilement (*saṃkleśa*) and subsequent cessation.
Therefore, one now contemplates the conditioned arising of old age and death as defilement, giving rise to two types of knowledge: first, inferring the cause and examining the cause;
second, within the three periods of time, the former knowledge contemplates that the effect has a cause to reveal its origin, while the latter knowledge contemplates that the effect exists.
Because the cause is not indeterminate, one refutes the externalists' false conceptualization that things arise without a cause; this collectively constitutes six types of knowledge.

One then gives rise to a further type of knowledge that universally contemplates and articulates the teachings on dependent origination throughout the three periods of time, which is called the "knowledge of the stability of phenomena" (*dharma-sthiti-jñāna*), because it abides by means of the teachings on phenomena;
added to the preceding, these constitute seven. In this manner, up to the link of *saṃskāra* conditioned by ignorance and *bhava* conditioned by *upādāna*, each is established as such.

Due to the seven knowledges (*jñāna*), they collectively constitute seventy-seven knowledges. Since ignorance (*avidyā*) is without cause and the cycle of rebirth (*saṃsāra*) ceases of its own accord upon the mere severing of ignorance, eighty-four knowledges are not established.
Following this, one enters the forty-four knowledges by contemplating the Four Truths (*catur-āryasatya*), as this is proximate to the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*).
Thus, the forty-four knowledges that arise subsequently refer to the contemplation of old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*). Old age...

Regarding the contemplation of the arising of death, the cessation of death, the path leading to the cessation of death, and so on down to the arising of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), the cessation of volitional formations, and the path leading to the cessation of volitional formations—each of these eleven factors possesses the four truths. Consequently, four types of knowledge arise for each, totaling forty-four.
Within the twelve factors, there is no separate contemplation of the arising of ignorance (*avidyā*); therefore, the total does not reach forty-eight types of knowledge. However...
Because the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) ceases of its own accord upon the severance of ignorance (*avidyā*), it is pure. Regarding "purity in the forward and reverse order":

this refers to observing according to the forward and reverse sequences once the stage of severance has been reached and the ultimate fruit attained; thus, it is called "pure. Specifically, observing that because ignorance ceases, volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) cease;

because volitional formations cease, consciousness (*vijñāna*) ceases; and so on, up to: because birth ceases, old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*) cease—this is the forward observation based on severance.

The sequential contemplation proceeds as follows: by the absence of what is there no aging-and-death? By the cessation of what does aging-and-death cease? The former is the knowledge that investigates the cause;
the latter is the knowledge that examines the cause. In this manner, it continues until: by the absence of what is there no volitional formations (*saṃskāra*)?

By the cessation of what do volitional formations cease? This is the reverse contemplation, which relies on the contemplation of the reverse order at the stage of the ultimate attainment of the fruit.
Therefore, by means of such contemplations as these, one is liberated from birth and death, and the cycle of transmigration is forever stilled.

[Commentary] Regarding ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and grasping (*upādāna*): the Sūtra states that these three are collectively subsumed under the two links of ignorance and craving-grasping, because they belong to the category of ignorance and assist ignorance.
The link of formations (*saṃskāra*) is karma; the five links beginning with consciousness (*vijñāna*) and the link of birth-and-death (*jāti-maraṇa*)—these seven [links]...

This "existence as fruit" (*phala-bhava*) consists of the six factors beginning with volitional formations (*saṃskāra*); therefore, it pertains to both cause and fruit. The Commentary (*Śū*) uses the term "pertaining to" (*tong*) because it speaks of it in reference to one portion, namely "karmic existence. [The Commentary states:
"The two periods and the three periods do not contradict the Sūtra," because the Sūtra presents the general characteristics; thus, the ten causes of the past and the present...
The two fruits are present, while the ten causes are future; thus, the two classes of fruits span both time periods, and together they encompass all three periods.

[Commentary: Regarding the clarification of cause and effect from beginning to end: among the twelve links, ignorance (*avidyā*) possesses the strongest power, as it is precisely what initiates karma and evokes the fruit of suffering.
Therefore, the Sūtra specifically mentions ignorance, karma, and the fruit; by citing the superior, it subsumes the inferior. Ignorance directly gives rise to craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
Grasping (*upādāna*) assists in arousing craving (*tṛṣṇā*), while clinging (*upādāna*) itself directly moistens the rest; alternatively, it assists in moistening.

Because these three members—ignorance (*avidyā*), craving, and grasping—are afflictions (*kleśa*) that function as the basis for arousing and moistening [karma] to summon suffering, they constitute the causes of karma and suffering.

The members of birth, aging, and death (*jāti-jarā-maraṇa*) are the matured fruits (*vipāka-phala*) summoned by the karma that was aroused and moistened by those two [sets of] members. As for the members of formations (*saṃskāra*) and existence (*bhava*)...

The *saṃskāra* link and the five links beginning with consciousness (*vijñāna*) pertain both to causes and to results. Specifically, the *saṃskāra* link brings about the results of birth, aging, and death;

the five links beginning with consciousness produce those results of birth, aging, and death. Thus, the *bhava* link possesses a dual significance: the sense of bringing about the result of future existence and the sense of manifesting the present result.

Furthermore, because ignorance (*avidyā*) acts as the cause that sets the *saṃskāra* link in motion, the *saṃskāra* link serves as the cause that gathers the five results beginning with consciousness.
Because [the seeds] exist, the two links of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) moisten the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) and so forth, causing them to evolve;
thus they are called "existence" (*bhava*). [Commentary: Regarding "the causal origination of the sequence," "sequence" means the sense of leading forward.

Because each preceding link serves as a condition and possesses the power to lead forward each subsequent link, there is a succession of prior causes and subsequent effects—namely, from ignorance conditioned by which there are formative forces, up to birth conditioned by which there is aging and death.
Aging and death.
[Commentary: Regarding the statement that "the object of wishlessness (*apraṇihita*) and compassion (*karuṇā*) are non-dual," this means that wishlessness is wisdom;

because wisdom and compassion both take dependent origination as their common object, the objects are non-dual. Thus, through the arising of compassion—which itself does not form a wish—one brings about deliverance.

[Commentary] Furthermore, regarding the phrase "not [identical]," because one contemplates that dependently originated phenomena (*pratītyasamutpanna*) do not exist substantially, it constitutes the gate of liberation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣamukha*).

Because the characteristic of the flowing and turning of illusory phenomena is not non-existent, yet cannot be craved, it constitutes the gate of liberation of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-vimokṣamukha*).

Because one contemplates that the nature of dependent origination is a single, quiescent mark without distinct characteristics, it constitutes the gate of liberation of signlessness (*animitta-vimokṣamukha*). It is said that these three contemplations take a single object.

Non-dual. [Commentary] "The seventh stage and so forth" means that by relieving the suffering of hell and causing those beings to be free from fear, it indicates that the body of the seventh stage shall emerge from the suffering of the *paricchinna-bhava* (segmented existence).

Having cultivated the preparatory practices (*prayoga*) for the seventh stage within the sixth stage, once these practices are perfected, one gives rise to the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*) to sever [the afflictions].
The exhaustion of the seventh obstacle—the manifestation of subtle characteristics—comprises two delusions;

subsequently, upon the arising of the path of liberation, one abandons the latencies of the two obstacles, realizes the non-distinct true suchness of phenomena, and ascends to the seventh stage, the Far-Reaching (Dūramgamā).
[Commentary: Regarding the Stage of Far-Going (*dūraṅgamā-bhūmi*): "Far-going" has the sense of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*).

Because it is untainted (*anāsrava*), uninterrupted, and consists of a continuous flow of exclusively signless contemplation (*animitta-vipaśyanā*), this signless concentration realizes the principle of liberation and is thus called the "liberation samādhi.
Because it is far removed from practices involving signs and dwells in the signless, it is named the Stage of Far-Going (as explained in detail previously).

[Commentary]: "The non-distinctiveness of phenomena" refers to the non-distinctiveness of True Suchness (tathatā). The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (Wei-shi shu) states: "Although many teachings establish various designations, True Suchness has no distinction;

that is to say, although names such as 'Ultimate Reality' (paramārtha), 'Dharma-realm' (dharmadhātu), and so forth differ, since True Suchness itself has no distinction, it is called the 'non-distinctive True Suchness of phenomena.'"
[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "the manifestation of subtle characteristics," this wording is inverted. The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states:

"The obstacle of the manifestation of subtle characteristics refers to a portion of the innate cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) that clings to the existence of subtle characteristics of arising and ceasing in their manifestation; this obstructs the seventh stage, the path of wondrous signlessness.

To say that there is the manifestation of subtle characteristics of arising and ceasing while clinging to them means that within the sixth stage, one is engaged in the practice of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
Contemplating that dependent origination which possesses the relative states of arising and ceasing is the objective domain of the preceding stage; this is called the subtle characteristic.
The manifestation of this subtle characteristic is itself an obstruction, and thus it is termed the "obstruction of the manifestation of subtle characteristics."
[Commentary]: Regarding "the ignorance of the manifestation of subtle characteristics": "subtle characteristics" refers to the characteristics of saṃsāra.

All categories of ignorance consisting of the active clinging to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) are subsumed under ignorance. This active [clinging] is itself ignorance, hence it is called "active ignorance.
The ignorance of the manifestation of these subtle characteristics is termed "the ignorance of the manifestation of subtle characteristics."

For those who grasp at existence through ignorance, the flow of the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) has birth as its primary feature; yet in reality, all that exists within the realm of outflows (*sāsrava*) is subject to cessation.
When one mentions the characteristic of birth among these outflows, it does not mean that one fails to grasp cessation; rather, it means one grasps the characteristic of the flow [of existence].

To apply mental attention with delight toward the signless (*animitta*) is to apply mental attention with delight toward the categories of ignorance, all of which are subsumed under ignorance. To apply mental attention with delight...
Delight is itself ignorance; it is called the mental attention that delights in ignorance, for by the power of ignorance one produces a delight in the perception of signlessness.
This mental attention that delights in the signless ignorance is called the mental attention that delights in signless ignorance.
Those who cling to cessation, regarding it as existing within the untainted state, do not fail to cling to arising when they cite even a single characteristic of cessation.
This refers to grasping the characteristic of cessation and extinction.

[Commentary] To explain this term: the total extinction of the first six consciousnesses and the cessation of one portion of the defiled mind and mental factors of the seventh consciousness so that they do not temporarily function is called "cessation-extinction" (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
For those of the Two Vehicles, this excludes only the grasping at a self (*pudgala-grāha*); for Bodhisattvas, both are excluded.

Excluding the two types of grasping at persons and phenomena, it is taught that each, in relation to its own vehicle, is considered defiled; yet, because it brings peace and harmony to the body, it is also called "concentration" (*samādhi*).

The concentration that is to be abandoned and exhausted by this [attainment]—that which can extinguish and exhaust—is itself termed the "attainment of cessation" (*nirodhasamāpatti*), or the "attainment of the cessation of feeling and perception" (*vedanā-saṃjñā-nirodha-samāpatti*), because during the stage of preparatory application (*prayoga*), one specifically feels revulsion toward the coarse characteristics of feeling, perception, and mental formations.
[Commentary: Regarding the emergence of this essence, when practicing the preparatory application (*prayoga*), one first uses the subtle mind to cultivate weariness toward the coarse mind;
next, one uses the minute mind to cultivate weariness toward the subtle mind; and finally, one uses the extremely minute mind (*sūkṣma-sūkṣma-citta*) to cultivate weariness toward the minute mind.
At the moment this extremely minute mind suddenly ceases, twenty-two dharmas permeate and form seeds within that extremely minute mind; upon these seeds reside the obstructive mind and other factors.
The non-arising of active functioning constitutes the essence of the cessation attainment (*nirodha-samāpatti*). The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:

"When practicing meditative concentration, because one feels aversion toward the coarse movement of the mind and mental factors during the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) of that concentration, one generates a superior aspiration to obstruct the mind and mental factors, causing them to become increasingly subtle, until at the moment of the extremely subtle mind, an impression is infused into the ripening consciousness (*vipāka-vijñāna*), becoming ultimate."
Because the seeds of the mind and its associates are suppressed by these seeds of intensified revulsion (*udvega*), coarse and agitated states of mind do not temporarily manifest;

based on this state, the two meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) are provisionally established (the term "two attainments" refers to the attainment of non-conception and the attainment of cessation, which are spoken of together because their modes of operation are similar when the preparatory practices are cultivated).

As for the twenty-two mental factors: there are five each of the universal (*sarvatraga*) and object-specific (*viniyata*) factors, and eleven wholesome (*kuśala*) factors; these, along with the primary mind (*citta-rāja*), are reckoned [to arise simultaneously].
Regarding these twenty-two dharmas, according to the principles of this collective treatise, among the eleven wholesome [dharmas], the latter three are merely nominal and lack distinct seeds.

Since they are already perfected at the stage of Buddhahood, they do not perfume seeds; rather, the attainment of the cessation-concentration (nirodha-samāpatti) is established based solely upon innate seeds.

[Commentary] Regarding the clarification of the basis (*āśraya*) and so forth: the intention of those of the Hīnayāna for entering [this state] is to produce the notion of cessation and to weary of the toil and anxiety of contaminated (*sāsrava*) consciousness, or to weary of the coarse movement of uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) consciousness; therefore, they enter the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).

The intention of Bodhisattvas for entering it is likewise to give rise to the supreme merit of mindless tranquility; therefore, they enter the meditative absorption of cessation. As the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (Treatise on Consciousness-Only), fascicle 7, states: "This..."

When first entering meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one must necessarily rely on the contemplation of the untainted (*anāsrava*) state at the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) as the preparatory practice (*prayoga*), because it occupies the final position among the sequential concentrations (*anupūrvavihārasamāpatti*).
Once this concentration has been cultivated and mastery attained, the mind of other stages may subsequently manifest;
by performing the contemplation of suchness (*tathatā*), one is thus able to enter.
[Commentary: Although it relies on the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*), the Sarvāstivādins claim that the meditative absorption of that stage is exclusively contaminated (*sāsrava*).

If this were so, one would have to admit that a contaminated mind of preparatory effort (*prayoga-citta*) enters the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*). Therefore, he explains this: although it relies on the Peak of Existence, it is nonetheless uncontaminated (*anāsrava*).

Why? Because this concentration is subtle and wondrous; to realize the two kinds of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), one must rely on the subsequent realization (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) as appropriate, which is uncontaminated.
Because it is produced by a concentrated mind (*samāhita-citta*), the Sarvāstivādins claim that [the Sautrāntika position] is incorrect.
[Commentary: Regarding those who attain it, Vasubandhu’s *Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya* states: "Five types of persons attain the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*):

those in the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) of the three vehicles, non-retrogressive Bodhisattvas, and body-witnessed Anāgāmins. The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states: "If Bodhisattvas, having previously been in the stages of the two vehicles..."

Those who turn their minds [toward enlightenment] after attaining the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) can give rise to this absorption in all stages (referring to those of gradual awakening).
Were it otherwise, some might only be able to permanently suppress all afflictions upon reaching the final mind of the seventh stage;

yet even though they have not yet permanently severed the afflictions of the desire realm to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), they are as if they had already severed them and are able to give rise to this absorption. The treatises state that such individuals have already entered the Stage of Far-Reaching (*dūraṅgama-bhūmi*).

Because it is only Bodhisattvas—as explained in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*—who are able to manifest the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), they are those for whom compassion predominates.
There are, however, those who from the very first stage (*prathamabhūmi*) are able to permanently suppress all afflictions (*kleśa*) and manifest this attainment throughout all ten stages;

as the sūtras—the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* and the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*—state, Bodhisattvas are also able to manifest the meditative attainment of cessation during the first six stages. Therefore, they are those for whom wisdom predominates. His commentary explains:

Among Bodhisattvas of the ten stages, there are those who give rise to afflictions—namely those for whom compassion (*karuṇā*) predominates—and those who do not give rise to afflictions—namely those for whom wisdom (*prajñā*) predominates.
Alternatively, it is explained that while the compassion and wisdom of all Bodhisattvas are equal, there are two types of intentional orientation (*āśaya*) regarding their preferred practice:

first, those who, out of fear of afflictions, suppress them so that they do not arise; and second, those who, being unafraid of afflictions, allow them to manifest as active occurrences (*samudācāra*).

Regarding the distinction between being subdued and not being subdued, concerning the term "body-witness" (*kāyasākṣin*), the *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā* states: "The Non-returner who attains the meditative absorption of cessation is called a body-witness.

Since the absorption of cessation is mindless, it is established as a "body-witness" because it is realized through the body. Regarding this, two masters of the Vijñaptimātra school offer the following views:

one says that among the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation in the eight lower stages, one must completely abandon those of the desire realm, while the others are either suppressed or abandoned.

Only then can one first enter this meditative absorption (*samādhi*). Because the seeds of the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are of two natures—mixed and complex—and because they strongly obstruct meditative absorption;

and secondly, because it is necessary to sever the afflictions abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) of the four lower stages, whether by suppressing or severing them, before one can first enter this absorption, as the seeds of affliction associated with transformed sensations (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*) strongly obstruct meditative absorption. Both masters state this.

Having subdued and severed [the afflictions] from the sphere of nothingness downward and having attained the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), it is revealed that among those in training (*śaikṣa*), only those who have attained the third fruit [of the non-returner] can achieve this. [Commentary:

Regarding the phrase "only in... and so forth: the initial arising of the absorption of cessation occurs only within the human or celestial realms of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), specifically within the three continents.

Because it arises through the power of the teachings of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, and the assembly of noble ones, those who have practiced for a long time can manifest it even within the two upper realms.

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that once the eighth consciousness has been established, one enters the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) in the formless realm by relying on the existence of the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) as its support.
[Commentary]: Regarding the *siṃhavijṛmbhita-samādhi*, the Sūtra states: "The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva enters the Bodhisattva *siṃhavijṛmbhita-samādhi*;

he leaves behind the joy and bliss born of seclusion and enters the first *dhyāna*; he leaves behind the joy and bliss born of concentration and enters the second *dhyāna*, and so on, up to entering the cessation of perception and feeling (*saṃjñāvedayitanirodha*).
Then, arising from the cessation of perception and feeling, he returns to enter [the first *dhyāna*]."
Arising from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one enters the sphere of nothingness;
continuing in this manner down to arising from the second dhyāna and entering the first dhyāna—this is called the Lion’s Stretching Samādhi (*siṃhavijṛmbhita-samādhi*).

Arising from a lower stage while possessing the mind of a higher stage is called "stretching" (*vijṛmbhita*); entering a lower stage while possessing the mind of a higher stage is called "stretching" (*vijṛmbhita*). Thus, it is named the Lion’s Stretching.
Therefore, this concentration is so named.
[Commentary] Regarding the "Samādhi of Gathering and Scattering," the Sūtra states: "Leaving behind the joy and bliss born of seclusion, one enters the first dhyāna;
arising from this, one enters the second dhyāna; arising from this, one enters the third dhyāna; and so on, up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception."
Having emerged from the concentration of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he enters the attainment of cessation; having emerged from this, he enters the first dhyāna;
having emerged from this, he enters the attainment of cessation; having emerged from this, he enters the second dhyāna; having emerged from this, he enters the attainment of cessation;
and so on, until having emerged from the concentration of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he enters the attainment of cessation.

From the attainment of the perception of cessation, one arises and dwells in an unconcentrated mind; from that unconcentrated mind, one enters the attainment of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Having arisen from this, one dwells in an unconcentrated mind; from that unconcentrated mind, one enters the attainment of the sphere of nothingness.
Having arisen from this, one dwells in an unconcentrated mind; from that unconcentrated mind, one enters the sphere of infinite consciousness.

From meditative concentration up to entering the first dhyāna from a non-concentrated mind, and arising from the first dhyāna to abide in a non-concentrated mind—this is called the samādhi of gathering and dispersing.
When a bodhisattva dwells in this samādhi, they attain the equal true nature of all phenomena;
entering the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling from all stages is called "gathering into one."
Because everything emerges from the ground and is called "scattered" (*vīpaśyanā*), this meditative absorption is so named.

[Commentary: Although the sixth consciousness in its entirety and the defiled portion of the seventh consciousness are both extinguished and do not arise, the pure portion of the seventh consciousness—the mental state associated with the Wisdom of Equality—relies upon the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body) to extensively benefit sentient beings. (From the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra-ṭīkā*)
It is said that the ox-cart of the causal stage takes the two wisdoms—the wondrous and the level—as its essence; thus, the *Fayuan* states:

"Although the great Bodhisattvas enter the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), they constantly manifest dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*) while roaming through various pure lands.

This is because, prior to entering the concentration, their intentional resolve strikes and activates the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) of the fundamental consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), causing the various modes of deportment to appear. Even after the mind has ceased [in cessation], the deportment does not perish, due to the second..."

Regarding the statement that "the eight consciousnesses maintain [the seeds] by taking them as objects," it means that because the eighth consciousness maintains those seeds and takes their manifest activity as its object, the bodies resulting from meditative attainment (*samāpatti-phala-kāya*) and the modes of deportment (*īryāpatha*) do not perish.
The intent of the sūtra here is that although one attains the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) during the first six stages (*bhūmi*), one has not yet attained mastery over it;
only upon reaching the seventh stage does one attain mastery and abide in the meditative absorption of cessation while manifesting a body to benefit sentient beings.
[Commentary]:

Regarding "the eighth stage and so forth," this signifies that within the eighth stage, through effortless practice (*anābhoga-caryā*), the non-conceptual wisdom (*animitta-jñāna*) that benefits both self and others spontaneously subdues Māra;
because of this fearlessness and mastery, the lion king appears on both sides of the body [of the Buddha] at the seventh stage.

Having completed the preparatory application (*prayoga*) for the eighth stage through its middle cultivation, one gives rise to the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantaryamārga*) to sever the eighth [category of affliction].

Within the signless (*animitta*), one eliminates the obstacles to preparatory application and severs two delusions (*moha*). Subsequently, in the second moment, one gives rise to the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*), abandons the latencies (*vāsanā*) of the two obstacles, realizes the *tathatā* that is neither increasing nor decreasing, and ascends to the eighth stage, the Immovable (*acalā-bhūmi*).

[Commentary]: Regarding the Immovable Ground (*acalā-bhūmi*): because one has already attained mastery over the practice of signless contemplation (*animitta-bhāvanā*), neither sign-associated practices (*sanimitta-caryā*), nor effortful practices (*sābhoga-caryā*), nor any afflictions (*kleśa*) can cause it to waver. It is for these three reasons that it is called the Immovable Ground.

[Commentary]: "The essence is without increase or decrease" means that the essence is the realization (*saṃvitti*). It refers to the realization of True Suchness (*tathatā*) as being without increase or decrease.

The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (Treatise on Consciousness-Only) states: "Non-increasing and non-decreasing True Suchness. The commentary by *Asvabhāva* explains: "Being free from the increase of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) and free from the decrease of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), it is called 'non-increasing and non-decreasing.

Vasubandhu’s commentary states: "Because defilement is severed without decreasing and purity is attained without increasing, it is called 'non-increasing and non-decreasing. (The following is the passage cited in the Commentary).
[The term] *vijñaptimātra* (consciousness-only) is as stated in the text). [Commentary: Regarding the "severing of all functional efforts," the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states:

"The obstacle to applying effort within the signless (*animitta*) refers to a portion of the innate aspect of the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) which prevents the signless contemplation from arising spontaneously. It continues until it says: "It obstructs the eighth stage (*bhūmi*)."

Regarding the path of non-effort (*anābhoga-mārga*) within this stage, it is taught that the essence of the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) associated with the first seven consciousnesses—whether in their state as seeds or as manifest activity—possesses the power to prevent the noble qualities from becoming particularly sublime. While the obstructions of the first six consciousnesses never manifest again, they remain only as seeds;
however, the obstructions of the seventh consciousness exist both as seeds and as manifest activity, exerting effort through the power of those obstructions.
By further shifting the blame, one returns to the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), which acts as an obstacle to the application of effort within the signless (*animitta*).

This is called the "obstacle to the application of effort within the signless. It obstructs the path of effortless spontaneity (*anābhoga-mārga*) of the subsequent stage; upon entering the eighth bhūmi, it can be permanently severed.

[Commentary]: Regarding "ignorance regarding effort in the contemplation of signlessness" (*animitta-bhāvanā-prayoga-avidyā*): by the power of ignorance, it causes the contemplation of signlessness to proceed as an application of effort;
therefore, it is called "ignorance regarding the effort of the contemplation of signlessness. Regarding "ignorance regarding the autonomous grasping of signs" (*nimitta-svatantra-grahaṇa-avidyā*):
by the power of ignorance, one is deludedly attached to those signs, and because of this grasping of signs, it is called "grasping of signs" (*nimitta-grahaṇa*).

That which is called ignorance is the ignorance that grasps at signs; this ignorance obstructs those dharmas of sovereign and supreme merit, and thus this ignorance that grasps at signs regarding sovereignty is called the ignorance of grasping at signs regarding sovereignty.

[Commentary]: Regarding the question "What are the characteristics?"—this indicates the characteristics of manifested physical forms as well as the characteristics of objective realms such as gold and silver.
As for "lands" (*kṣetra*), there are the characteristics of the distinctions in size and dimension of great and small lands, and the characteristics of broad and narrow lands.
These are the real, general bases of support, while the lands are the provisional, specific supports. Within these characteristics, lands are distinguished individually.
[Commentary: "Attaining the two masteries" means that because one attains mastery within the signless (*animitta*), one attains mastery in manifesting signs and manifesting lands.

[Commentary: "The seventh [ground] and so forth" refers to the coarse afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*); from the eighth ground onward, they are permanently suppressed and do not arise, following the sixth [consciousness].

It is said that although the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) is subtle, it can still manifest because the fruit of the wisdom realizing the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmyajñāna*) is subject to interruption;

"fruit" refers to either the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) or subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*), as the arising of these does not contradict the fundamental and subsequent [realizations] of emptiness.

Regarding the phrase "the mind and mind-objects are quiescent": this means that the mental states and their concomitants accord with the principle of quiescence, such that their characteristics are obliterated;
whether body or mind, they lack any sign of movement or arousal, such that their functions are obliterated; all are like empty space, entirely still and silent.
[Commentary]: "To be free from all discrimination of mind, thought, and consciousness" means that the eighth [consciousness] is named *citta* because it has the sense of accumulating and arising;
the seventh is named *manas* because it constantly and critically deliberates; and the first six are named *vijñāna* because they discern coarse objects.

To be free from mind, thought, and consciousness is to extinguish dependence on others (*paratantra*), which is the absence of anything grasped or attached to; it is to extinguish pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*), and like empty space, it is the realization of perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna*).
[The text] generally dissolves the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), entering into the realization that all phenomena are like empty space.
[Sūtra]: Regarding these bodhisattvas, the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "It is like a person who dreams that his body has fallen into a great river;
he exerts great courage and employs great skillful means (*upāya*) desiring to emerge from the river. While exerting such courage, he suddenly awakens. Having awakened—"

In the same way, the Bodhisattva Sarvashura, from the very beginning, having seen all sentient beings fallen into the river of birth and death, gave rise to great diligence and zealously cultivated superior progress until reaching the Immovable Stage (*acalā-bhūmi*).

Having abandoned all conceptualizations and effortful practices (*sābhoga-prayoga*), at that time the Bodhisattva no longer engages in any activity; it is for this reason that all Buddhas extend [their hands to him].
Seven Exhortations.

[Commentary]: Regarding "various types of vitarka and vicāra," *vicāra* refers to deluded conceptualization; it denotes various kinds of false awakening and inverted delusions that afflict and harm sentient beings.

[Commentary: Regarding "merely having attained," etc., "merely" (適) means "just now. You have just now attained this one dharma; as for "one dharma," it refers to the truth that the nature of all dharmas is non-arising.

"Clarity" (明) refers to non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*). You have attained only a small portion of this. Furthermore, the Tathāgata possesses immeasurable clarities of dharma which you have not yet realized.
Briefly pointing out three types, they are: entering, acting, and transforming the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), as well as the teaching on entering.

Understanding the cultivation of practices that transform one into successively higher stages (this may be understood by cross-referencing the *Śāstra*). "Nayuta" is here translated as *hai* (a large number).
[Commentary: Regarding the *Avataṃsaka* and other texts, having reached this stage, the merit obtained within a single thought-moment is twice that obtained during the previous two kalpas;
each subsequent moment is twice as superior as the preceding one, increasing progressively until it surpasses all others.
"Because he practices all practices within the practice.

[Commentary: Regarding "the ninth stage and so forth," this indicates that within this stage, having attained the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), he skillfully turns the wheel of Dharma to benefit sentient beings;
thus, he manifests as a Universal Monarch (*cakravartin*) surrounded by a multitude. The white parasol atop his head, adorned with various jewels, symbolizes the absence of... [text truncated]

Because he is the foremost among those who possess unimpeded wisdom, and because he covers and protects all sentient beings with loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, serving as a refuge for the multitude and adorned with manifold virtues, he manifests a white parasol adorned with various jewels.

Having cultivated the preparatory practices (*prayoga*) for the ninth stage within the eighth stage, and having perfected those practices, he gives rise to the path of uninterrupted realization (*ānantarya-mārga*).
Thereby, he exhausts the ninth category of obstacles to benefiting others—specifically, the obstacle of being unwilling to act—and [the obstacle of] the two-fold [obscuration].

Following the sequence of the various delusions, in the second moment of thought, one attains the Path of Liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), abandons the latencies (*vāsanā*) of the two obstacles, realizes the sovereignty of wisdom, and ascends to the ninth stage, the *Sādhumatī-bhūmi*, which is the suchness (*tathatā*) that serves as the basis for this realization.
[Commentary] Regarding the *Sādhumatī-bhūmi*: it is the stage where one attains mastery over all phenomena (*dharma*) and their manifold meanings (*artha*); these two are suchness.

Next, I shall explain the two analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) of teaching and principle. To speak according to various dialects so that the multitude may be free from affliction and without fault or reproach is the analytical knowledge of language (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*).
To possess mastery in preaching the Dharma is the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*).
[Commentary]: Regarding the "obstruction to the unimpeded" (*anāvaraṇa-āvaraṇa*), this refers to the obstruction to the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*). The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:
"The obstruction to the lack of desire to act for the sake of others within the context of benefiting others" refers to a portion of the innate (*sahaja*) cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

This causes one to lack the desire to diligently engage in activities that bring benefit and happiness to sentient beings, and instead delights in cultivating one's own benefit; it obstructs the four analytical knowledges of the ninth stage.

[Commentary] Regarding the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* and other texts: the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) have wisdom as their essence. As for that which is induced by them, both the primary [wisdom] and its associated mental states have meditative concentration and wisdom as their essence, with the four aggregates as their nature.
As for the accompanying factors, they have the five aggregates as their nature; since the morality coexistent with the path (*mārga-sahaja-śīla*) constitutes the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*).

[Commentary] First, regarding the essence of phenomena (*dharmatā*): it refers to all phenomena subsumed under the characteristics of dependent origination and the nature of dependent origination, which are free from the extremes of the two views of existence and non-existence as clung to.
For example, the characteristic of form-dharmas is resistance; the characteristic of mind-dharmas is cognitive discernment;
and the characteristic of the nature of phenomena is eternal constancy. All such things are the objects of knowledge for the unimpeded analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*).
Therefore, this is the unimpeded analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*).

[Commentary: Regarding the essence of the objective sphere of phenomena: within the phenomena subsumed under the nature and characteristics of the non-arising that is free from the two extremes mentioned previously, it refers to the objective sphere of knowledge as it truly is (*yathābhūta-jñāna-viṣaya*).

"As it truly is" means to accord with reality; it refers to the essential nature of the objective sphere known by correct knowledge in accordance with reality. This refers to the categories of meaning.
This is the essence [of the object]. "Object" (*viṣaya*) is a name for the essence itself; thus, it is called the "essence of the object. Regarding the meaning of "object":

because the essence depends upon those phenomena (*dharma*), the essence of the object of phenomena is called the "essence of the object of phenomena. When a Bodhisattva dwells within the sphere of wisdom (*jñāna-viṣaya*) subsumed by dependent origination, they correctly know the meanings of form (*rūpa*) and so forth.
What is the meaning of form? It refers to the collection of the eye and visible forms, the ear and sounds, and so forth.

Because they give rise to delusion, they engage in false conceptualization regarding permanence, bliss, self, and purity; the Noble Ones, however, thoroughly understand the meaning of impermanence and so forth—this is the unimpeded analytical knowledge of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*).

[Commentary] "Correctly attaining and bestowing upon sentient beings" means that once the Bodhisattva has attained the Dharma through correct wisdom and understanding, he explains it and bestows it upon sentient beings.
To be able to correctly understand all the various dialects that others prefer and to speak to them according to their own speech while knowing their underlying intentions—
all such [abilities] constitute the analytical knowledge of language (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*) regarding the diversity of the verbal expressions of sentient beings.

[Commentary]: Regarding "properly bestowing through immeasurable gateways": this means that in accordance with the correct views of sentient beings who seek the Dharma, one should preach immeasurable Dharma-gateways according to their capacities.

Having attained correct knowledge regarding all such verbal expressions, one preaches according to their faculties—whether by means of the essence or the characteristics, whether briefly or extensively, and through immeasurable distinctions of nature or depth—to provide various benefits and meanings.
To explain things according to what [the listener] knows constitutes the various distinctions of eloquence; this is the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*).

[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "that treatise, etc.," that [treatise] states: "By means of the unimpeded knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*), one correctly knows that all phenomena are subsumed within non-differentiation."
In the One Vehicle, through the unimpeded analytical discernment of meanings (*artha-pratisaṃvid*), one distinguishes the various differences among the vehicles;

through the unimpeded analytical discernment of words (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*), one is able to expound all vehicles without destroying their distinct natures; and through the unimpeded analytical discernment of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*), one teaches each individual vehicle by means of immeasurable gateways of Dharma-illumination (*dharma-prabhāsa-mukha*), as is explained at length in that treatise.

[Commentary: Regarding the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* and other texts, this Bodhisattva attains two types of dhāraṇī: first, the dhāraṇī of collection (*saṃgraha-dhāraṇī*), by which one suddenly comprehends the meaning of all syllables upon hearing the meaning of a single syllable;
second, the dhāraṇī of dispersion (*vikiraṇa-dhāraṇī*), by which one suddenly expounds the meanings of all syllables within the meaning of a single syllable.
Thus, one is able to receive and expound [the teachings] instantaneously (as can be understood from the corresponding commentary).
[Commentary: Regarding the "Tenth Stage" and so forth: because the causal stage is about to be fulfilled and one is adjacent to the state of Buddhahood, he manifests the body of a Tathāgata.
Because he intends to save sentient beings, he appears in a golden color; because he demonstrates the culmination of the causal stage, there are perfect rays of light and the offering of Brahmā.
The transformation Buddhas whom he honors turn the wheel of Dharma, signifying that this Bodhisattva is about to attain the fruit of Buddhahood.
Because the Brahmā King waits specifically for the request to preach the Dharma, one cultivates the preparatory practices (*prayoga*) of the tenth stage within the nine stages.

Once these preparatory practices are perfected, the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*) arises, whereby one completely abandons the tenth [stage’s] obstacle—the obstacle to attaining mastery over all phenomena—which comprises two delusions.
Immediately thereafter, in the second moment, the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) arises; one abandons the latencies (*vāsanā*) of the two obstacles and realizes mastery over karma and so forth.
Regarding the *tathatā* (suchness) that serves as the basis for attaining the tenth stage, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states:

"These ten stages collectively subsume all conditioned and unconditioned merits as their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Because they serve as the supreme support (*adhiṣṭhāna*) for the practices one cultivates, enabling them to grow and develop, they are collectively termed 'stages' (*bhūmi*).
Furthermore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 47, states: "Because they are able to sustain the meaning of a bodhisattva."
It is called "ground" (*bhūmi*) because it serves as a basis for experience and habitation; it is called a "stage" (*avasthā*) for that same reason.

[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "great dharmas," Asvabhāva explains: "Because one attains the wisdom that takes all phenomena as its object—wisdom that takes all dharmas such as the sūtras as its object collectively and is inseparable from true thusness (*tathatā*)—it is like the *mahāmegha-dhāraṇī-mukha-samādhi*."
The gateway is like pure water, for wisdom is its treasury; it is like clouds holding water, for it can produce those supreme qualities.
Furthermore, just as a great cloud covers and conceals the sky, so too does this Dharma-wisdom cover and conceal the two vast obstructions that are like the sky.
Moreover, just as a great cloud pours down pure water to fill the void, so too does this Dharma-wisdom give rise to the immeasurable.

Because the supreme qualities such as supernormal powers and the preaching of the Dharma completely fill the realization of the boundless *dharmakāya*, and because the noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*) is like a cloud for these three reasons—acting as a cloud for this Dharma—it is called the "Dharma-Cloud Ground" (*dharmameghā bhūmi*). This ground of the Dharma-cloud is named the Dharma-Cloud Ground.
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "such as these," this refers to observing in this manner from the initial generation of the bodhicitta through the practice of the successive stages.

This cognitive wisdom of observation is called the Path of Application (*prayogamārga*); it induces the wisdom that realizes [the truth], which realizes the principle of quiescence—namely, the inferior grade of the patience of quiescence (*śāntikṣānti*).

[Commentary] Regarding the realization of mastery over karma, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states that it is the True Suchness (tathatā) which serves as the basis for mastery over karma and so forth (meaning that once this True Suchness is realized,
one possesses the three masteries, as explained in the commentary).
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "Although there are ten," etc., the question is: how can True Suchness (tathatā), which is of a single characteristic, be divided into ten? The answer is:

although the nature of True Suchness is in reality without differentiation, because there are distinctions according to the excellence of its virtuous qualities (guṇa), ten names are provisionally established.
[Commentary: Regarding the severance of the obstacles to the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states:

"The obstacle consisting in not yet having attained mastery over all phenomena refers to a portion of the innate aspect (*sahaja*) of the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). It prevents one from attaining mastery over all phenomena.

This obstacle [obstructs] the Great Dharma-Wisdom Cloud (*mahādharmanirdeśajñānamegha*) of the tenth stage, as well as the activities (*karmasamudācāra*) arising from what it contains. The intent of this treatise is to say that it is by means of the cognitive obscuration [that these are obstructed].
Because it obstructs all virtues, one has not yet attained mastery; this lack of mastery is itself termed the "obstruction to the non-attainment of mastery.
Alternatively, if one considers that which causes all virtues to lack mastery, the obstruction to that lack of mastery is termed the "obstruction to the non-attainment of mastery."

[Commentary: Regarding "the ignorance of activity toward the subtle secrets that have not yet been realized": the "subtle secrets" refer to the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmamegha*) stage and the virtues therein.
Due to the power of ignorance, one has not attained mastery or perfect realization regarding those supreme virtues;
thus, when various activities arise, this ignorance regarding such activities is termed "ignorance of activity. Because it has not yet been realized... [it is called ignorance].
Regarding the interpretation, this [term] applies to both the subject and the object; two explanations may be understood in relation to ignorance (*avidyā*).
However, since this ignorance obstructs those subtle and secret qualities, it should be understood as a *tatpuruṣa* (possessive compound).

[Commentary: "Transformation" (*parāvṛtti*) refers to that which is based upon the eighth consciousness and the principle of True Suchness (*tathatā*), as they serve as the support for all phenomena of defilement and purity, or delusion and awakening.

"Transformation" means the relinquishing of what is abandoned and the attainment of what is gained; through the repeated cultivation of the untainted noble path (*anāsrava-ārya-mārga*), one eliminates the heavy residues (*dauṣṭhulya*) of the two obstacles within the fundamental consciousness, thereby relinquishing the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) arising from the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
Furthermore, regarding the dharmas of birth and death, one is able to transform and attain the *pariniṣpanna* (perfected nature) within the *paratantra* (dependent nature) and so forth;

this refers to the basis of transformation and abandonment, and the basis of transformation and attainment. Both are *tatpuruṣa* (possessive) compounds. As the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra-vyākhyā* states: "The combination of the supported (*āśrita*) and the support (*āśraya*) is termed 'transformation of the basis' (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*); therefore, it is not a *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound."

[Commentary]: Regarding "diminishing power" and so forth (these six points on the transformation of the basis [āśraya-parāvṛtti] are all from the tenth fascicle of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*):

the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* by Vasubandhu states that "resolute belief" (*adhimukti*) refers to the stage of practice through resolute belief (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*), while "shame" (*hrī*) and "embarrassment" (*apatrāpya*) are the superior characteristics of the practice of resolute belief. Furthermore, Cien (Kuiji) explains that because these are included among the mental factors of resolute belief, they attain decisiveness;

and because of shame and embarrassment, one honors the worthy and rejects evil, thereby possessing this superior virtue which permeates both the preparatory (*sambhāra-mārga*) and the application (*prayoga-mārga*) stages.

In the stage of cultivation, one diminishes the power of the defiled seeds within the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) so that the seeds of the two obstacles do not arise as active manifestations;
this is termed "diminishing power. Simultaneously, one causes the capacity of the pure seeds within the fundamental consciousness to flourish and increases the capacity of the untainted seeds;

this is termed "augmenting power. These two capacities—diminishing and augmenting—are distinct and mutually exclusive, as explained by the term *vyatireka* (contradiction). Although the terms "diminishing" (*hāni*) and "augmenting" (*anuśaṃsa*) are used...

"Transformation" (*parāvṛtti*) refers generally to both the agent and the object; specifically, it refers here to the functional capacity of the seeds of defilement and purity that are respectively diminished and augmented within one's own continuum.
"Transformation" as the agent refers to the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*), which acts as the transformer, while the two dharmas of defilement and purity act as the objects transformed.

It transforms the power of defilement by diminishing it and transforms the merit of purity by augmenting it. This transforming path derives its name from those [objects], and is thus called the "transformation that diminishes power and augments capacity."
[Commentary: Regarding "transformation through penetration" (*prativedha-parāvṛtti*): beginningless obstructive defilements hinder the true nature, blocking it so that it does not flow.

Within the stage of the Path of Seeing (*darśana-mārga*), noble wisdom manifests, severing these obstructions and penetrating the principle; thus, it is called "penetration. There are two ways to understand this: first, the act of penetrating is itself the transformation; second, the transformation is that which is penetrated by the penetrating [wisdom]. Both explanations are valid.

[Commentary: Regarding the "transformation through cultivation" (*bhāvanā-parāvṛtti*), it refers to the transformation of obstacles through the excellence of cultivation; thus, "cultivation" itself is termed the "transformation through cultivation.

The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (Wei-shi shu) states: "This means that within the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), excluding the stage of seeing (*darśana-mārga*) of the first stage, the remaining first stage and the other nine stages constitute the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*).
All that is cultivated throughout the ten stages is the 'transformation through cultivation.'"

[Commentary: Regarding "Vajra and so forth," when the Vajropama-samādhi (Diamond-like Samādhi) manifests, one eternally severs all subtle seeds of the two hindrances that have existed from the beginning;

this is called the "severance of the heavy burdens" (*dauṣṭhulya*). Immediately thereafter, in the next moment, the Path of Liberation arises, wherein one abandons the four matters and suddenly realizes the Buddha-stage—the perfection of Bodhi and Nirvāṇa—and this is called the "perfection of the transformation of the basis" (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*), which is the "transformation of the abandonment."
The transformation that attains the perfection of the fruit is called the "transformation of the perfection of the fruit. [Commentary:

Regarding "inferior transformation" and so forth, this refers to the stage of the two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas), including both those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*). It possesses six characteristics and is thus termed "inferior transformation":

first, self-benefit; second, the attitude of aspiration and aversion; third, the realization of the principle of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*); fourth, the abandonment of the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*); fifth, the realization... [text continues].
Regarding the six types of true analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) that lack superior capability (the first two being like the [stream-enterer]), the treatise states:

"The latter four are able only to penetrate the suchness of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā-tathatā*), severing the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and realizing true analytical cessation; because they lack superior capability, they are termed 'inferior transformation.'"

[Commentary]: Regarding "vast transformation" (*vipula-parāvṛtti*) and so forth: this is termed "vast" in contrast to that which is inferior; it reverses the six preceding meanings (the first two are as explained in the commentary). Regarding the latter four, the *Treatise* states: "Possessing the capacity to thoroughly penetrate the true suchness (*tathatā*) of the two emptinesses, to simultaneously sever the seeds of the cognitive obstacles (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) and the afflictive obstacles (*kleśāvaraṇa*), and to suddenly realize unsurpassed bodhi and nirvāṇa—having such superior capability is called 'vast transformation. The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra-vyākhyā* states: ... [The text continues with the detailed explanation of the transformation of the basis. ... Thus, the transformation of the basis is established through the power of the cultivation of the path. It is called "transformation" because the former state is abandoned and a new state is attained. It is called "basis" because it is the support for all conditioned phenomena. It is called "vast" because it transcends the inferior stages and possesses the aforementioned superior capabilities. It is called "transformation" because the nature of consciousness is fundamentally pure, yet through the influence of adventitious defilements, it undergoes delusion; when these are severed by the power of the path, it returns to its original purity. This is what is meant by "transformation. Furthermore, the term "transformation" implies that while the substance remains constant, its mode of activity changes. It is like water becoming ice, or gold being fashioned into various ornaments. Although the substance is not lost, its functions differ. Therefore, it is called "transformation.
