As for "basis," it refers to the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*). Because it is the root of all phenomena, it is called the "basis. When this consciousness undergoes transformation, it is called the "transformation of the basis. It is also called the "Great Mirror Wisdom" (*ādarśajñāna*). Why? Because it reflects all objects without distortion, it is called a "mirror. Because it is free from the two obstacles and is supremely pure, it is called "wisdom. Because it is vast and great, it is called "great. Because it is the basis for the other three wisdoms, it is called the "basis. Thus, the Great Mirror Wisdom is established. The remaining three wisdoms are: the Wisdom of Equality (*samatājñāna*), the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*), and the Wisdom of Accomplishing Tasks (*kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna*). These four together constitute the transformation of the basis. The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* says: "The transformation of the basis is the abandonment of the seeds of the two obstacles and the attainment of the four wisdoms. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the term "transformation" is used because the former impure state is discarded and the latter pure state is attained. It is like the transformation of milk into curds, or the transformation of a base metal into gold. Although the substance is not destroyed, its qualities change. Therefore, it is called "transformation. As for "basis," it refers to the mind and mental factors. Because they are the support for all worldly and supramundane dharmas, they are called the "basis. When these undergo transformation, it is called the "transformation of the basis. It is also called the "Wisdom of the Dharma-realm" (*dharmadhātujñāna*). Why? Because it realizes the equality of all dharmas, it is called "equality. Because it is free from the two obstacles and is supremely pure, it is called "wisdom. Because it is the source of all virtues, it is called the "Dharma-realm. Thus, the Wisdom of the Dharma-realm is established. These four wisdoms are the fruit of the transformation of the basis. They are also called the "four bodies of the Buddha": the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), the Enjoyment-body (*saṃbhogakāya*), the Transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*), and the Nature-body (*svabhāvakāya*). The Dharma-body is the Wisdom of the Dharma-realm. The Enjoyment-body is the Wisdom of Equality and the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation. The Transformation-body is the Wisdom of Accomplishing Tasks. These four bodies are the ultimate fruit of the transformation of the basis. Therefore, it is said: "The transformation of the basis is the attainment of the four wisdoms and the four bodies. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the term "transformation" is used because the former state of bondage is discarded and the latter state of liberation is attained. It is like a prisoner being released from jail, or a sick person recovering from illness. Although the person is the same, their status changes. Therefore, it is called "transformation. As for "basis," it refers to the seeds and the manifested dharmas. Because they are the support for the continuity of birth and death, they are called the "basis. When these are transformed, it is called the "transformation of the basis. It is also called the "Unobstructed Wisdom" (*anāvaraṇajñāna*). Why? Because it is free from the two obstacles, it is called "unobstructed. Because it clearly perceives all objects, it is called "wisdom. Because it is supreme and peerless, it is called "unobstructed. Thus, the Unobstructed Wisdom is established. These are the various aspects of the transformation of the basis. One should understand them according to the scriptures. This concludes the explanation of the transformation of the basis. It is called "transformation" because the former is discarded and the latter is attained. It is called "basis" because it is the support for all phenomena. It is called "vast" because it transcends the inferior and possesses superior capabilities. It is called "transformation" because the nature of consciousness is fundamentally pure, yet through the influence of adventitious defilements, it undergoes delusion; when these are severed by the power of the path, it returns to its original purity. This is what is meant by "transformation. Furthermore, the term "transformation" implies that while the substance remains constant, its mode of activity changes. When this consciousness undergoes transformation, it is called the "transformation of the basis. It is also called the "Great Mirror Wisdom. Why? Because it reflects all objects without distortion, it is called a "mirror. Because it is free from the two obstacles and is supremely pure, it is called "wisdom. Because it is vast and great, it is called "great. Because it is the basis for the other three wisdoms, it is called the "basis. Thus, the Great Mirror Wisdom is established. The remaining three wisdoms are: the Wisdom of Equality, the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation, and the Wisdom of Accomplishing Tasks. These four together constitute the transformation of the basis. The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* says: "The transformation of the basis is the abandonment of the seeds of the two obstacles and the attainment of the four wisdoms. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the term "transformation" is used because the former impure state is discarded and the latter pure state is attained. It is like the transformation of milk into curds, or the transformation of a base metal into gold. Although the substance is not destroyed, its qualities change. Therefore, it is called "transformation. As for "basis," it refers to the mind and mental factors. Because they are the support for all worldly and supramundane dharmas, they are called the "basis. When these undergo transformation, it is called the "transformation of the basis. It is also called the "Wisdom of the Dharma-realm. Why? Because it realizes the equality of all dharmas, it is called "equality. Because it is free from the two obstacles and is supremely pure, it is called "wisdom. Because it is the source of all virtues, it is called the "Dharma-realm. Thus, the Wisdom of the Dharma-realm is established. These four wisdoms are the fruit of the transformation of the basis. They are also called the "four bodies of the Buddha": the Dharma-body, the Enjoyment-body, the Transformation-body, and the Nature-body. The Dharma-body is the Wisdom of the Dharma-realm. The Enjoyment-body is the Wisdom of Equality and the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation. The Transformation-body is the Wisdom of Accomplishing Tasks. These four bodies are the ultimate fruit of the transformation of the basis. Therefore, it is said: "The transformation of the basis is the attainment of the four wisdoms and the four bodies. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the term "transformation" is used because the former state of
The "perfection of fruition" (*phala-parāvṛtti*) is taught for Bodhisattvas; the "vast transformation" (*vipula-parāvṛtti*) is taught for those of the Two Vehicles.

Perfection belongs exclusively to the Buddha, while vastness pertains to the causal stage. Furthermore, it is said that since the "vast, luminous, and perfect transformation" is mentioned, it also exists within [the stages of the Two Vehicles].

Among these six, the first is designated as a "provisional transformation" because the true transformation has not yet been attained; the remaining five are "true transformations" because they constitute actual realization.

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "now, first," etc., this now reveals the meaning of the third transformation through cultivation (*bhāvanā-parāvṛtti*), which accords with the progression toward the fourth transformation as the fulfillment of the fruit (*phala-paripūri-parāvṛtti*).
It manifests in accordance with the cultivation of the sixth transformation, and not the other three, because those have already been transcended.

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "the meanings of the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) differ," the preceding six [categories] were explained in terms of stages to demonstrate the process of realization;

these four now clearly elucidate the essential meaning of the body [of the path]. Although there are four names, they comprise eight categories, all of which were established by the Master [Asaṅga]. The treatise states: "The first is the path capable of transforming. This, in turn, has two types:

(1) the path capable of subduing, which means it subdues the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the two obstacles so that their power does not give rise to the manifest activity (*samudācāra*) of the two obstacles. This applies to both [obstacles].

Regarding the two paths—the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*)—the three types of knowledge (preparatory, fundamental, and subsequent) subdue those [afflictions] either gradually or instantaneously as appropriate.

(In the preparatory path, subduing occurs only gradually; in the fundamental and subsequent knowledges, subduing occurs both instantaneously and gradually. The two paths capable of abandonment (*prahāṇa-mārga*) refer to those that can permanently sever the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the two obstacles.
These paths are certainly not contaminated preparatory paths, because contaminated states are induced by the habitual grasping at signs and have not yet eliminated such characteristics.

Therefore, because the preparatory application (*prayoga*) seeks what is to be realized and induces what has not yet been accomplished (the Commentary states that there are four meanings regarding the contaminated preparatory wisdom and the contaminated subsequently attained wisdom:

first, being contaminated and previously practiced; second, being induced by the grasping of signs; third, being unable to eliminate, suppress, or extinguish these signs; and fourth, the preparatory application seeking the *tathatā* to be realized and seeking the non-conceptual wisdom to be induced, which have not yet been accomplished—due to these four meanings, it cannot sever the afflictions;

however, the uncontaminated path of preparation can also sever the afflictions). Second, the basis of transformation (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), which is further twofold: first, that which maintains the seeds (*bīja-dhāraka*).
"Support" (*āśraya*) refers to the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*), which is able to maintain the seeds of both defiled and pure phenomena and serves as the common basis for them.

Because the Noble Path transforms it so that one abandons the defiled and attains the pure, it is called "transformation of the basis" (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*). (The essence of this transformation of the basis is the manifest fundamental consciousness itself, as it encompasses both the outflowing and the non-outflowing, and spans both cause and fruit.
Second, the "basis of delusion and awakening" refers to True Suchness (*tathatā*), which can serve as the fundamental root of both delusion and awakening. All defiled [phenomena]...

Pure phenomena depend upon this [basis] for their arising; because the Noble Path transforms it so that one abandons defilement and attains purity, it is called "transformation of the basis" (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*).
Regarding that which is transformed and abandoned, there are two types: first, abandonment through what is to be severed. This refers to the seeds of the two obstacles;

when the true path of immediate succession (*anantarya-mārga*) manifests, the obstacles and their antidotes are mutually contradictory, whereby the obstacles are immediately severed and extinguished, never again to be actualized. This is termed "abandonment," referring to the abandonment of those seeds.

Because they have been severed, the false attachments to the self and phenomena no longer manifest; furthermore, since the self and phenomena as grasped objects do not confront deluded cognition, they are also said to be "abandoned.

By this, it is called the abandonment of the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*). That which is discarded refers to the remaining seeds of the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the inferior uncontaminated (*anāsrava*);
when the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) manifests, it induces the extremely perfect, luminous, and pure fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*), and not those [seeds].

"Because they are the basis, all are forever abandoned" (the above is from the treatise). According to the correct principle, these two types of seeds are abandoned simultaneously with the Path of Non-interruption (*ānantarya-mārga*).
While the Path of Non-interruption arises, those [seeds] have not yet been abandoned, because they are not incompatible with the Path of Non-interruption.

It is through the Diamond-like Samādhi (*vajropama-samādhi*) that one is able to induce the Great Fundamental Consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*), which is the extremely perfect, extremely luminous, and utterly pure Path of Liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).

It is associated with the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom. Because the sixth consciousness, together with the Vajra Holy Path, can induce the fundamental consciousness (ālayavijñāna) to become untainted (anāsrava), it is called "inducing.
"Utmost perfection" distinguishes this from the support of the Bodhisattvas prior [to Buddhahood], which was not yet perfect;

"extreme clarity" distinguishes this from the fact that their wisdom was not yet pure and bright; and "purely untainted" means being unmixed with outflows, as was the case during the previous stage of the causal path.

The middle [stages] are untainted (anāsrava), while the sixth and seventh [consciousnesses] are pure (śuddha) but not "pure" (viśuddha); the eighth consciousness-aggregate is both pure and pure (viśuddha), yet it is not "pure" alone.
Here, it is shown that the untainted eighth consciousness of the Buddha-fruit is perpetually continuous; therefore, it is termed "pure and pure" (viśuddha-viśuddha).

Because this pure fundamental consciousness is not the locus for those tainted or inferior untainted seeds, they are all eternally abandoned. To distinguish this from a mere "cutting off and abandoning," the term "abandoned and discarded" (parityakta) is established.

Because it is not a defiled dharma (*kliṣṭadharma*), it is not termed "abandonment" (*prahāṇa*); rather, it is the abandonment of its seeds. Once these have been abandoned, the manifest outflows (*sāsrava*)—which are inferior even among the untainted (*anāsrava*)—never arise again.

For this reason, it is called the "abandonment of inferior dharmas of saṃsāra. This accords with the explanations in various scriptures regarding the relinquishing of four matters within the path of liberation (*vimuktimārga*).

These four matters consist of: (1) tainted wholesome states (*sāsravakuśala*), (2) the two obstacles (*dvivibandha*), and [the remaining two]. The outflows of saṃsāra are subsumed under three of these matters. First, the tainted wholesome; second, the two obstacles.

The three types of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), along with all indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) phenomena and inferior outflow-free (*anāsrava*) states, together constitute four things that are also abandoned by the diamond-like path (*vajropama-mārga*).

As the treatise says: "There are four things that are transformed and attained; these further comprise two types: first, those attained through manifestation, namely Great Nirvana (*mahāparinirvāṇa*).
Although this is inherently pure by nature from the beginning, it was not manifest because it was covered by adventitious obstructions; now, through the true Noble Path..."

Because birth severs those obstacles, it causes their characteristics to become manifest; this is called "attaining nirvāṇa. This is established based on *tathatā* (suchness) as being free from obstacles, and its essence is the pure *dharmadhātu*.
(There are four types of nirvāṇa, as explained in detail therein. Second, that which is produced and attained is called "great bodhi" (enlightenment).

Although the seeds capable of producing it exist primordially, it does not arise because of the obstruction of the objects of knowledge (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*). Through the power of the Noble Path, these are severed.

Because those obstacles have been removed, it causes [the seeds] to arise from their seeds; this is called "attainment" (*prāpti*). Once awakened, this continues in succession until the end of the future.
This is precisely the mental complex associated with the four wisdoms, which is termed "that which is produced by attainment" (the four wisdoms are as follows).

[Commentary]: Regarding "the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) and so forth," this refers to the afflictions that arise in association with the cognitive obscurations; when these are severed, the afflictions are simultaneously suppressed.

This is because, on the first bhūmi, the practice of *dāna* (generosity) opposes craving and attachment; on the second bhūmi, the cultivation of the four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) opposes ill-will (*vyāpāda*);

and on the third bhūmi, the cultivation of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), the great dhāraṇīs, and the emission of wondrous radiance oppose the darkness of ignorance (*moha*). Such is the case for all the bhūmis.

Those [afflictions] that are particularly predominant are suppressed prior to the ten stages (*bhūmi*); within the six consciousnesses, the seeds of afflictions are suppressed, their manifestations are severed, and their latencies are eliminated;

by means of the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*), the three realms are instantaneously severed in a single moment. Within the seventh consciousness, those [afflictions] are intermittently suppressed prior to the eighth stage;
after entering the eighth stage, they are permanently suppressed and do not arise; at the time of the diamond-like concentration, [the seeds of affliction are likewise eliminated].
The three realms are severed instantaneously.

[Commentary: Regarding the seeds of the cognitive obstacles (*jñeyāvaraṇa*)—those to be abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*) are all severed instantaneously upon entering the mind of the first stage (*bhūmi*);
those to be abandoned by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) are severed gradually throughout the ten stages, culminating in the present moment of the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*).

In a single preceding moment, all [afflictions] are completely severed; because they arise by taking as objects both internal and external, coarse and subtle realms, and because there are many categories [of afflictions], they are severed gradually.

[Commentary]: Regarding "gradual and sudden" in principle, it means that while the meanings and principles are understood gradually, the True Principle (tattva) is illuminated suddenly. Within the state of fruition, the "accomplishment of the object" (*sādhyālambana*) is briefly omitted.
The realization of wisdom is also attained instantaneously and perfectly.
[Commentary: "Constantly abiding in the single nature like one sitting upon a bed" means that it is like a person in a dream who, amidst the delusions of movement and stillness, suddenly awakens;

the delusions then vanish entirely. One knows the body is resting on the bed, while the dreaming mind was mistaken. Here, the bed is a metaphor for the awakened nature, and birth-and-death is a metaphor for the dreaming mind.
When one suddenly awakens from the dream of the inversion of movement and stillness, realizing that the dreams of birth and death are entirely non-existent,
one knows that the original nature has always resided in the essence of fundamental enlightenment.
[Commentary]: Regarding the *Suvarṇabhadra-sūtra*, this is a new title for an old translation; it refers to the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*. Its second chapter states:

"Suppose a person, as if in a dream, sees a great river flooding their body. They move their hands and feet to cut across the current, crossing over without slackening or retreating, and thus reaches the other shore.
Suddenly they awaken from the dream, and both the river and the other shore can no longer be found. It is not so.

It means that even for mindless dharmas, it is likewise so: through diligence within the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), one does not retreat, cuts off the stream of birth and death, and reaches the other shore.
Once awakened, both the dream-like appearances of birth and death and the "other shore" are found to be unobtainable.
This extinction of birth and death is pure awakening; it is not a state of being without awareness.

[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "dwelling in the fourth [stage]" and so forth: the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, and other texts all state that there is a wondrous Pure Land beyond the Akaniṣṭha heaven, wherein Bodhisattvas of the tenth stage are born.
The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* also says that there is a wondrous Pure Land transcending the triple world, where Bodhisattvas of the tenth stage are born.

The *Cien* commentary states: "Birth" means manifestation, departure, and abiding. When one is about to reach the stage of the Vajra Path, one then departs for the wondrous and pure land atop the Akaniṣṭha Heaven.

Regarding the statement that there is a Pure and Wondrous Palace of Mahāvaśavartin outside the Five Śuddhāvāsa Heavens, as taught in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and other texts, this also belongs to the Realm of Form (*rūpadhātu*).
As for the claim that it transcends the Three Realms, this refers to the state following the bodhisattva’s untainted (*anāsrava*) realization.
Because the transformed body obtained through wisdom is untainted (*anāsrava*), this Pure Land transcends the three realms (*tridhātu*).
Furthermore, it is understood that although this wondrous Pure Land is subsumed under the Heaven of Ultimate Form (*Akaniṣṭha*), its essential nature is a transformation produced by the Buddha;
since its substance is untainted and does not fall within the bonds of the realms, it is said to transcend the three realms.
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "its flowers are vast and great," the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, fascicle 12, states:
"There is a great precious lotus throne whose dimensions equal ten hundred-thousand *asaṃkhyeya* trichiliocosms; a Bodhisattva of the tenth stage sits upon it to realize perfect enlightenment.
This King of Flower Thrones manifests ten characteristics: first, the characteristic of sovereignty, which [stands] in relation to all the minor thrones."
1. The characteristic of the sovereign (*adhipati-lakṣaṇa*), because it consists of ten *asaṃkhyeya* hundreds of thousands of three-thousandfold great thousand-world systems;

2. The characteristic of the intermingling of supreme jewels (*ratna-vyavakīrṇa-lakṣaṇa*), because the various jewels are interspersed throughout; 3. The characteristic of pervading all realms (*sarva-dhātu-vyāpana-lakṣaṇa*), because the ground extends through all worlds; 4. The characteristic of the cause (*hetu-lakṣaṇa*), because supramundane roots of goodness arise from it;

5. The characteristic of accomplishment (*pariniṣpatti-lakṣaṇa*), because it is endowed with all marks; 6. The characteristic of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-lakṣaṇa*), because it is most excellent and wondrous.
Ninth, regarding the characteristic of its multitude of merits: it transcends all realms of humans and devas; tenth, regarding the characteristic of its adornment:
it has a body made of *maṇi* jewels with nine facets, and its surface is covered by an immeasurable net of jewels interspersed with a thousand flowers.
[Commentary]: Regarding "receiving the rank of a king," at that time the crown prince enters the category of Kṣatriya kings; the Bodhisattva is likewise so.

By being consecrated upon the head with the water of the Buddhas' wisdom, he receives his rank and enters the category of Buddhas, possessing the ten powers and immeasurable merits as extensively described therein.

[Commentary] "Relying on these" means relying on this supreme Vajropama-samādhi (diamond-like concentration) to give rise to the uninterrupted path (*ānantarya-mārga*), which exhausts the tenth [level], the obstacles to the stage of Tathāgatahood.

This subsumes the two delusions; subsequently, in the second moment, one gives rise to the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), abandons the four matters, realizes the two types of transformation-basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), and is named the Wondrously Enlightened Tathāgata, possessing the three bodies (*trikāya*) and four wisdoms (*caturjñāna*), as well as conditioned and unconditioned dharmas.
The wondrous merits are all perfectly fulfilled.

[Commentary: Regarding the "obstructions to the stage of the Tathāgata," the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states: "Although one has attained mastery over phenomena on this stage, there remain residual obstructions that prevent it from being called 'ultimate.
These consist of innate subtle cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) and spontaneous afflictions (*kleśa*)."
When the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*), which obstructs the seeds of affliction, manifests, they are all severed instantaneously, and one enters the stage of a Tathāgata.

The intention [of this] is that because of these obstructions to the Buddha-stage, Bodhisattvas of the ten stages perceive the realm of the Buddha as if looking at the moon through a thin silk veil—vague yet distinct.
These obstructions to the Buddha-stage are established based on the two types of obstructions; specifically, they belong to the category of the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
The seeds of the afflictive hindrances are gradually severed stage by stage; it is taught that they are severed by a single momentary path of diamond-like concentration.
Because the two hindrances are discussed in combination, it is said that they are severed instantaneously upon entering the stage of the Tathāgata.

[Commentary]: Regarding "the ignorance that constitutes a subtle obstruction to all objects of knowledge," this refers to a portion of the innate category of ignorance within the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
All such types are subsumed under ignorance. Thus, what is called a "cognitive obstruction" is in fact ignorance;
it is designated as a "cognitive obstruction-ignorance. Although Bodhisattvas of the tenth stage have attained mastery over all phenomena, they nevertheless...
There exists this one portion of subtle cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) which prevents these Bodhisattvas from attaining the most ultimate and preeminent excellence;
because it is an extremely subtle ignorance that acts as an obstacle, it is called "subtle cognitive obscuration-ignorance.
As for the aforementioned "all objects," it is so named because this ignorance obstructs all those objects.
[Commentary]: Regarding the phrase "the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) and so forth," two masters of the Vijñaptimātra school offer the following views:

The first master says that the seeds of contaminated phenomena (*sāsravadharma*) and the inferior uncontaminated seeds (*anāsravadharma*) are both abandoned at the moment the diamond-like concentration (*vajropamasamādhi*) manifests, because they are discarded simultaneously with the seeds of the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*).

The second master says that at the time the diamond-like concentration manifests, those [inferior uncontaminated seeds] have not yet been abandoned, as they do not contradict the path of immediate succession (*ānantaryamārga*).

Therefore, it is only when the subsequent paths of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*) regarding the remaining outflows arise that the eighth pure consciousness can be relinquished, for [the latter] is not the support for those [outflows].
(This subsequent section correctly explains the meaning.

[Commentary: Regarding "the stage of Equal Enlightenment," this refers to the moment when the path of liberation arises at the final stage of Equal Enlightenment and ignorance is exhausted; it is the characteristic of movement.

The fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) ceases along with the extinction of ignorance; however, it is only the active, outflowing characteristics of the karmic consciousness (karmavijñāna) that cease, while the essence of the mind (cittasvabhāva) does not.
The essence of the mind is like water, and its active characteristics are like waves; when the waves subside, the water becomes still, yet the water itself is not extinguished.

[Commentary]: Regarding these two types [of practice], the former relies on *Vijñaptimātra* (Consciousness-Only) to sever the subtle seeds of obstruction within the first seven evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*);

the latter relies on the *Awakening of Faith* to sever the "mark of karma arising from ignorance" (*avidyā-prabhava-karma-lakṣaṇa*), which is precisely the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*). Each is based on a partial aspect of the principle;

in reality, it is only when all obstructions—including those of the eight contaminated consciousnesses (*sāsrava-aṣṭa-vijñāna*) and ignorance—are extinguished that one attains the fruit of Buddhahood. Thus, they are combined.
"Taking the two texts and following the principles of the teachings.

[Commentary: This stage is still inferior and has not yet attained equality with the Buddha; because this stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) has exhausted all obstacles and its realization of the ultimate and conventional truths resembles that of a Buddha, it is called "Equal Enlightenment.
Since "equal" (*sama*) signifies similarity, there is but a slight difference from the Path of Liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
He is not yet called a Buddha.

[Commentary: The Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*) is, in reality, the eighth consciousness which is both principle and wisdom, untainted (*anāsrava*), and manifests the body, the land, and the images of the other three wisdoms.
However, because at the stage of fruition wisdom is predominant and consciousness is subordinate, it is said that "wisdom manifests all things."
The dharmas are reflections, like a perfect mirror; thus the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "This mental state is free from all conceptualization;

its objects and modes of activity are subtle and difficult to know. It serves as the support for both manifest [dharmas] and seeds, and is able to manifest and produce the reflections of bodies, lands, and wisdoms.
Because it manifests various forms and images like a great perfect mirror, it is called the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*mahādarśanajñāna*)."
[Commentary]: The Wisdom of Equality (*samatājñāna*) is the wisdom that realizes equality; it is thus named the Wisdom of Equality.

Furthermore, during the impure stage (*sāsrava-avasthā*), the seventh consciousness (*manas*) clings to the eighth consciousness as a self, causing the sixth consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*), which depends upon it, to be unequal toward itself and others.
Upon reaching the pure stage (*anāsrava-avasthā*), this [seventh consciousness] becomes associated with wisdom, thoroughly comprehending non-self and becoming free from [such clinging].
Because it is established as "equality" by overturning inequality, its nature is equality; this nature of equality is wisdom, and is thus called the Wisdom of Equality (*samatā-jñāna*).
As the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "This mental state contemplates all phenomena and all sentient beings—self and others—as entirely equal.
It is constantly associated with great compassion and other such qualities, manifesting enjoyment bodies (*saṃbhogakāya*) according to the inclinations of sentient beings."
Because it differentiates the various images of the earth and so forth, continuing as a single flavor until the end of the future, it is called the Wisdom of Equality (*samatājñāna*).

[Commentary: The Wisdom of Wondrous Observation refers to the wisdom associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*); it is so named because its divine function in observing all phenomena is without fixed direction.
Thus, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "This mental state skillfully observes the specific and general characteristics of all phenomena without obstruction."
Furthermore, because it revolves to encompass and observe immeasurable gateways of dhāraṇī and samādhi, as well as the precious jewels of merit produced thereby;
because it can manifest infinite varieties of functional activity within great assemblies and attains mastery over them all;

because it rains down the great rain of Dharma, severing all obstacles and causing all sentient beings to obtain benefit and happiness—it is therefore called the Wisdom of Sublime Observation (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*).
[Commentary: The wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*) subsumes the mental states associated with the five sensory consciousnesses;

because their functional activity is similar, they are combined into a single wisdom. This wisdom is able to accomplish the benefit of others, and thus it is called "the accomplishment of what is to be done.

Since this very wisdom is the accomplishment of what is to be done, it is termed the "wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done. As the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "This refers to the mental state..."

For the sake of benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings, it universally manifests various transformations of the three karmas throughout the ten directions to accomplish the tasks required by its original vow-power;
this is called the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is to Be Done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*). The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states:

"The Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is to Be Done discriminates the differences in the mental activities of sentient beings and initiates transformations of the three karmas to benefit and bring happiness to the various classes of sentient beings according to their needs."

Therefore, it is further said that the *nirmāṇakāya* Buddha is called both "with mind" and "without mind. It possesses a dependent mind (*paratantra-citta*) but lacks a self-dependent mind (*svatantra-citta*).
It is merely comprised within the aspect of the real mind (*bhūta-citta-vijñapti-bhāga*), like fire in a mirror that has no separate self-substance.

It manifests greed, anger, and so forth to cause other inferior classes of beings to understand the Buddha’s mind; yet, if it were the Buddha’s actual mind, even the great Bodhisattvas would be unable to perceive it.
How much less could ordinary beings or other sages understand it? This is explained in detail in that treatise. [Commentary:
As for the meaning according to reality, the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is To Be Done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*) arises only at the stage of Buddhahood;

what reason is there for it to exist during the causal stages? This is because the eighth consciousness is the sovereign of total retribution and is of a contaminated (*sāsrava*) nature. Thus, the contaminated...

Because the eight consciousnesses transform into the five impure sense-faculties (*indriya*), and based upon these five impure sense-faculties, the five impure sense-consciousnesses arise, the mental states associated with the *kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna* (wisdom of accomplishing activities) are only attained at the stage of Buddhahood, not during the causal stages. This is because in the causal stages, the seventh and eighth consciousnesses are continuous, while the first six are intermittent.
Thus, although each of these four wisdom-associated mental states definitely possesses twenty-two [mental factors], [the specific composition differs].

Because the function of wisdom (*jñāna*) is superior within the Dharma, it is manifested by the name "wisdom"; thus, these four wisdoms collectively encompass all conditioned merits (*saṃskṛta-guṇa*) of the Buddha-stage without exception.

[Commentary] Although, in the stage of the Buddha’s fruition, the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) realizes suchness (*tathatā*) such that there is no distinction between subject and object, here we rely on the five...

The nature of the Dharma-body (dharmakāya) has distinctions: with True Suchness as its self-nature body (*svābhāvikakāya*) and the collection of the four wisdom-minds as its enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*), it belongs to these two bodies.

[Commentary] "The treasury of perfected merit" refers to the treasury of merit containing all virtues, wherein the divine and wondrous wisdom and understanding, as well as the essence itself, are complete. This is the treasury of merit.
Not yet having reached the full status of a Bodhisattva, one dwells in the stage of a Tathāgata through the fulfillment of the treasury of virtues;
profoundly tranquil and unmoving, it is like the great ocean, limpid and free of waves.

[Commentary] Regarding the "three bodies" (*trikāya*) and so forth: according to the *Awakening of Faith*, the three bodies are explained in terms of the single meaning of True Suchness (as may be seen in the commentary).
[Commentary: Regarding the prior refutation of "definitive identity," this was taught for the sake of those who cling to the view that the Buddha is a single entity without distinction;

thus, by stating that the three bodies (trikāya) differ in essence, characteristics, and function, it dispels the affliction of their attachment to oneness. Regarding the subsequent refutation of "definitive difference," this was taught for the sake of those who cling to the view that the Buddha is definitively distinct;
thus, by stating that the three bodies are in fact only one True Suchness (tathatā) without separate entities, it dispels that [attachment].

The illness of clinging to difference: the preceding section accords with the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, while the subsequent section accords with the *Mahāyānaśraddhotpāda-śāstra*. By combining the intent of these two texts, both the illnesses of [clinging to] identity and difference are simultaneously dispelled.
[Commentary]: "Jambudvīpa" is an archaic name for the continent formerly known as Yánfútí; it is a corruption. This [name] translates as "Purple Cinnamon Continent. Within this continent...
Because there is this purple cassia tree, it is named Purple Cassia Island. The *Qishi jing* (Sūtra on the Arising of the World) states:

On the northern shore of the northern continent of Mount Sumeru, there is a Jambū tree. Its roots penetrate twenty yojanas into the earth; its trunk is seven yojanas wide and one hundred yojanas high;
its branches and leaves spread downward for fifty yojanas; its fruit is very large, and its flavor is sweet and delicious. The tree...
Below is Jambūnada gold, which eclipses the light of the sun and moon. To the east is Pūrvavideha, translated here as "Victorious Body" (Shengshen Zhou);

because the bodies of the people on this continent are exceedingly excellent and wondrous, the *Qishi jing* states that there is a tree on the Eastern Continent named Kātanba, seven yojanas in girth, and for this reason the name of the continent was established. To the west is Aparagoyānī.
The continent of *Nir-māṇarati* (translated here as "Cow-Trade" or "Ox-Goods") is so named because its inhabitants use precious oxen as their medium of exchange.

The *Qishi jing* (Sūtra on the Arising of the World) states that on the Western Continent there is a tree called *Tiāntóujiā* (*Tinduka*), seven *yojanas* in trunk-width, described in the same manner as above.

Beneath this tree stands a stone ox one *yojana* in height; it is for this reason that the name of the continent was established. The Northern Continent, *Uttarakuru*, is translated here as "Without."
Because the physical forms and conduct of the people on that continent are superior, it is called the "Superior Birth" (*uttara-kuru*) and also the "Exalted" (*uttara*).

The *Lokadhātu-vibhāga-sūtra* states that the wealth and happiness of the Northern Continent are like those of the second heaven; lotuses bloom there, one constantly hears exquisite fragrances and various kinds of music, and it is exceedingly delightful compared to the other three continents.
For this reason, it is named the Exalted Continent. As for the shape of the continent: [The text continues with a description of the shape of the continent.]
Regarding their dimensions, the *Abhidharmakośakārikā* states: "Among these, the characteristics of the great continents are as follows: Jambudvīpa in the south is like a chariot;

its three sides are each two thousand [yojanas], and the southern side is three and a half [yojanas] (the 'three and a half' refers to one-half of those three sides, or alternatively, three and a half yojanas); the shape of the continent is like a sacrificial altar in India.
Pūrvavideha in the east is shaped like a half-moon; its three sides are like those of Jambudvīpa, and the eastern side is three hundred and fifty [yojanas]."

A *yojana* (is the unit of measurement). This continent calls that [continent] its eastern boundary, while that continent refers to it as its southern boundary, because it has its back turned toward Mount Sumeru. The western continent, Aparagoyānī, is circular and without deficiency;
its diameter is two thousand five hundred [yojanas], and its circumference is three times that. Regarding the dimensions of Uttarakuru, each side is equal at two thousand [yojanas].
As for the lifespan, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states that the lifespan of humans in Jambudvīpa is not fixed.

The lifespan is sometimes immeasurable years, referring to the period of formation (*vivartakalpa*); sometimes it is eighty-four thousand years, referring to the beginning of the period of abiding (*vivṛttasthāyikalpa*) before its decline;
and at other times, the lifespan gradually decreases until it reaches ten years, referring to the period when the three calamities arise.
Regarding the people of Pūrvavideha, their lifespan increases to a fixed two hundred and fifty years; regarding the people of Aparagoyānī, their lifespan increases to a fixed five [thousand years].
The lifespan of those in the northern continent, Uttarakuru, is fixed at one thousand years.
[Sūtra] Regarding the phrase "the color of the sun changes," the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra* states that at that time, the asuras take various colored jewels and gems for their armor;
its radiance is brilliant, and their bodies are like Mount Sumeru, with the light of their jewels appearing in blue, yellow, red, white, and black.

Adorned with the five colors and harboring arrogance, they claimed to be equal to the gods. At that time, the Heavenly King caused various swords and blades to rain down from the sky into the dwelling place of the asuras.
When the asuras ascended into the air, the rising sun emitted a thousand rays of light, which obscured and eclipsed the moon so that the celestial palaces could no longer be seen.
The Asura King raised his right hand to block the solar disk for Jambudvīpa.
Seeing the sun change its appearance, those teachers of false views fail to recognize the law of karmic retribution and recklessly speak of abundance or scarcity;
the moon changing its appearance is likewise so. As for "eclipses," this refers to the waning of the sun and moon, like insects eating grass, gradually diminishing until they are exhausted.

[Sūtra] A comet is a malevolent star. According to the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna*, there is a great yakṣa who gives rise to intense wrath and emits smoke from his mouth as he travels through the air; the people of Jambudvīpa call this a comet.
As for the "earth-stars" and other such stars, they are equivalent to Rāhu, Ketu, and various other portentous stars.
【Sūtra】 Regarding "a hundred grains," Yang Qian’s *Wuli Lun* states: "Liang" is the general name for *shu* and *ji*; "diao" is the general name for *ging* and *nuo*;
"shu" is the general name for various beans. Each of these three grains has twenty varieties, totaling sixty.

When the fruits of vegetables and trees that assist the grains—each numbering twenty—are added, they collectively form the "five grains," which, when categorized individually, constitute the "hundred grains."
[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "composed and expounded" (*xiūshù*), the *Xiǎochāo* states: I personally questioned the Master of the Commentary (*shǔzhǔ*), who replied:
"In that year, having received an imperial decree, I was in the Southern Peach Garden composing this commentary. When we reached this section of the sutra, there had been a long drought.

The Emperor dispatched envoys to various places to pray to the mountains and rivers, yet after more than a month, it did not rain. At dawn and dusk, the Governor Yu [Yìkāng] approached with the utmost sincerity."
It is said that when they were traveling together to Xingtang Monastery, the monk Zhijing remarked: "The state is greatly propagating the ultimate teaching;

the translation of sutras and the compilation of commentaries are intended to save the age. Yet the sutra says, 'When heaven and earth suffer from extreme drought and the ponds and pools run dry,' and so forth—that such disasters would be extinguished upon the lecturing and reading of this sutra.
Now, even as we reach this point in the commentary, the disaster has not yet been extinguished. If it cannot be eliminated now, how could it possibly remove the calamity hereafter?"
Liang Ben reproached himself for his ordinary sentiments not conforming to the ultimate principle.

In the past, when Dharma Master Tanyan finished his commentary on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, he made a vow to seek a sign, pledging in writing: "If this commentary accords with the principle, may fire not burn it;

if it does not accord with the principle, may it be consumed by the flames. He cast the commentary into the fire; when the fire was spent, the text remained intact, its brilliance shining through clearly. It continues to circulate to this day.
Fahu has now completed this commentary; since it has not rained for a long time in this region, what is the use of this?

On the morning of the fourteenth day of the sixth month, he placed a written petition before the Buddha, burned incense, and made a sorrowful plea: "If it does not rain within the next seven days, I pray that this written commentary be consumed by fire.
From now on, I shall no longer unroll these scrolls, but will remain upright and silently recite [the scriptures]. Thus he proceeded.

On the fifteenth day, an imperial edict was issued for forty-nine virtuous monks (*bhadanta*), including the presiding elder (*sthavira*) Chengru of An Guo Monastery in the capital, to recite the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra* at the Penglai Hall. By the time of the *xu* hour on the sixteenth day, a heavy rain fell;
by the morning of the seventeenth day, this was reported in full to the throne, and in the memorial it was stated: "This is truly [the result of] Your Majesty’s propagation of the Sūtra."

Reflecting on the merit of this entrustment and reception, how could it lie within the capacity of a humble monk? That such a noble vow has been fulfilled is what monks like Liangben and others privately consider a mere coincidence;
its verification is insufficient as proof. Your Majesty, with celestial wisdom, has deigned to look down upon us and condescended to inquire into these matters.

This humble monk is filled with shame and trepidation and dares not presume to issue a command. We respectfully present this memorial to convey our sincere sentiments for Your Imperial Knowledge. (The imperial edict was as stated in the petition.)

[Commentary: As for the "specifically twenty-nine," there are twenty types of calamities common to the first four difficult conditions, and three types each in the latter three difficult conditions, totaling nine;
thus, there are twenty-nine distinct varieties of calamities in all.

[Sūtra]: Regarding the various calamities of the earth—its cracking and its violent quaking—it is taught in the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna* that when great and evil nāgas give rise to intense wrath, they shake the great waters for one hundred, two hundred, or three hundred yojanas; since the earth rests upon these waters, the great earth trembles.

Furthermore, proponents of false views falsely claim that auspiciousness or misfortune causes the earth to move. Moreover, there are other conditions that cause the great earth to quake, namely: [the movements of] all...
Due to the causal conditions of sentient beings performing wholesome and unwholesome karmas, the great earth trembles.

Beneath the earth there is wind; because the wind moves, the water moves; because the water moves, the earth trembles. If it is moved by wholesome karma, there will be abundance, joy, and no calamities; if it is moved by unwholesome karma, disasters and difficulties arise.
The masters of false views speak falsely of abundance and scarcity. The *Book of Jin* states that during the Yuankang era of Emperor Hui of Jin...

In the fourth year [of the Yongjia era], a mountain in Shu Commandery shifted. In the seventh month of the eighth year of Dàkāng, there was a great rain, and the ground in front of the palace collapsed over an area five feet square and several zhang deep;
within it were found three fissures in the earth, each three zhang wide and three hundred paces long, occurring during the third year of Yuǎnxǐ of Emperor Huài.
These were all omens that ministers and subordinates would be divided and scattered in defeat.
[Commentary]: "What are the causes and conditions... and so forth, asks both regarding the presence and absence of obstacles.

What are the causes and conditions by which evil nāgas and asuras diminish and destroy the various worlds? What are the causes and conditions by which evil nāgas and asuras do not prevail and do not inflict decay or destruction upon the various worlds?
[Commentary]: Vāsuki, also known as Andhaka-vāsuki, means "nine-headed single-body" in Chinese; he is the most eminent among the nine-headed dragons.

Furthermore, there are the seven-headed Dragon King, the Elephant-Faced Dragon King, and so forth, up to the Bāṣpaha Dragon King, the ten kinds of Dharmic-practicing Dragon Kings, and the non-Dharmic-practicing, afflictive Dragon Kings, who all determined their relative superiority and inferiority.
[Commentary]: "Vajra" signifies the meanings of firmness and sharpness. Because its substance is firm, nothing can destroy it; because its function is sharp, it can crush all things.
The noble wisdom (*ārya-jñāna*) is shown to be like this: its substance is firm, so evil cannot break it; its function is sharp, so it can destroy all evils.
Because the Bodhisattva holds a vajra in his hand, he is named Vajrapāṇi Bodhisattva.

[Commentary: The three-headed, eight-armed Trailokyavijaya Vajra is an alternative manifestation of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva. The three heads symbolize the external subduing of the demonic adversaries of the three worlds;
the eight arms symbolize the internal accomplishment of the Eightfold Noble Path. Maheśvara is here called Mahādeva (the Great Sovereign).
According to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and the *Lokadhātu-sūtra*, he is listed among the deities of the six heavens of the desire realm.
Externally, it is separately stated that the palace of the Māra-devas is high and magnificent; this refers to Maheśvara.

[Commentary: As for the emission of blue light, among all various colors, blue is supreme. This signifies that having already subdued Māra, one causes him to cultivate correct practice and attain superior, exalted virtues.
Regarding the Piśācas, the original term is Piśāca, which is translated as "ugly ghosts."

[Commentary: Regarding the emission of white light: white is the source of all colors; it signifies that [the Buddha] has already caused the asuras and others to abandon flattery and crookedness, and to cultivate upright conduct.
Because being upright and free from flattery is the root of all virtues, he honors the pāñcika.
Their old name is *kumbhāṇḍa*, which means "ghosts with hidden forms" (*yīnxíng guǐ*) or "ghosts of shadows and forms. They are called "hidden form" because their shape resembles a winter melon.
He is also called the Winter-Clawed Ghost (*Piḷitā*), which is translated as the "Possessing-Ghost" (*yànmèiguǐ*).
[Commentary: His manifestation as the wrathful Six-Footed Vajra represents this Bodhisattva’s wandering and transforming activity within the six realms of existence to bestow happiness upon them.
His having six arms signifies that he rescues those in the six realms, causing them to emerge from suffering. His sitting upon a water buffalo symbolizes...
The *Fahua shu* (Commentary on the Lotus Sūtra) states that the ox-king possesses three virtues: first, the virtue of subduing enmity, because he has severed the two obstacles;
second, the virtue of majestic beauty, because he is endowed with all the [auspicious] marks; and third, the virtue of transport, because he delivers both himself and others.

Possessing these three virtues, he is able to subdue venomous dragons and restrain evil winds and rains; thus, he sits upon a water buffalo. If the Victorious and Sublime Body sits upon a lion, it symbolizes wisdom and valor.
The "Fierce One" (Māra) is able to sever all obstacles; he manifests various forms according to the capacities of sentient beings, for their mental dispositions differ.
[Commentary] The emission of golden light signifies that he has already subdued the venomous dragon and cultivated meritorious virtues of compassion as precious as gold.
The *Pūtana* is a spirit of feverish disease.
[Commentary]: *Yakṣa* means "one who can subdue yakṣas"; its meaning is translated as "majestic power" (*vīrya*).
If it refers to those subdued, it is translated as "valiant and strong," or alternatively as "violent and evil" because they lack majestic power. Those that fly are called *yakṣa*;
their old name is *yecha*. Those that move upon the earth are called *rākṣasa*, which is translated here as "the terrifying."
[Commentary: Showing a body with four arms signifies the subduing of the yakṣas of the four directions and the uprooting of the four modes of birth.

[Commentary: Emitting light of the color of lapis lazuli symbolizes the subduing of various yakṣas, bhūtas, and other spirits, causing them to practice various sublime deeds, just as a lapis lazuli gem possesses all manner of colors.
[Commentary: "Emitting five-colored light" means emitting light of the five colors—blue, yellow, red, white, and black—to signify that this Bodhisattva is adjacent to the rank of Buddhahood;
the five wisdoms (*pañca-jñāna*) are about to be perfected, and he is forever emerging from the signs of the five paths of rebirth (*pañca-gati*).
[Sūtra] Regarding *dhāraṇī*, the full term is *dhāraṇī-mantra-dharma-artha-mantra-kṣānti*; this constitutes one category.

Because of this total retention (*dhāraṇī*), one recites and brings forth all secret divine mantras. If one maintains this mantra, one will certainly be able to eliminate calamities, pacify difficulties, establish the state, destroy evil, subdue heterodoxy, transcend the mundane, and enter the sacred.
[Commentary: "The Holy One, the Universal Illuminator" refers to the wisdom of the *saṃbhogakāya* (reward body), which destroys the darkness of afflictions and illuminates the true *dharmakāya*.

Because it illuminates both itself and others, it is called "Universal Illuminator. "Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha" refers, respectively, to the three bodies: the *dharmakāya*, the *nirmāṇakāya* (transformation body), and the *saṃbhogakāya*.
"Samyak" (perfect) and "Saṃbodhi" (awakening) combined are termed "Samyaksaṃbuddha" (Perfectly Awakened One).

[Commentary: Regarding the eight case endings (*vibhakti*), according to the *Record of the Western Regions*, the syllable *va* is pronounced with a departing tone from the mouth; the eight cases—namely, the agent (*kartṛ*), the object (*karman*), the instrument (*karaṇa*), the purpose (*sampradāna*), the point of departure (*apādāna*), the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), the vocative (*sambodhana*), and the nominative (*prathamā*)—are so designated.
[Commentary]: The term *yogācāra* in the Sanskrit language means "correspondence" (*yoga*). There are five types of correspondence: first, the correspondence between the teaching and the principle;

second, the correspondence between the mind and its object; third, the correspondence between meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*); fourth, the correspondence between practice and the fruit;

and fifth, the correspondence between the medicine and the illness—for example, treating the illness of excessive greed with the medicine of the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*). This is the practice of yoga.

One who attains the contemplation corresponding to the gateway of the letter A acquires the inexhaustible treasury and awakens to the fact that the fundamental nature of phenomena is non-discriminative wisdom;
this is precisely the correspondence between mind and object, while other meanings are also encompassed therein.

[Commentary]: "The consecration by the rain of Dharma" means that Bodhisattvas of the tenth stage receive the water of the Buddha-dharma poured upon their hearts and heads, just as one is consecrated with water.
[Commentary]: "Those who have achieved perfection," etc., refers to the Bodhisattvas of the tenth stage, who are persons who have perfected holy wisdom; they pay homage.
This is the ritual for paying homage to the Buddha.
[Commentary] Regarding "masculine sounds" and "feminine sounds": in the phonological systems of this land (China), there are clear (*qing*), dark (*zhuo*), and neither-clear-nor-dark sounds.

In the *śabda-vidyā* (science of grammar) of India, there are masculine sounds, feminine sounds, and neuter sounds. According to the intent of this commentary, "masculine sounds" refers to the clear sounds.
Although the female voices calling out differ, their intent is no different; they all take the World-Honored One as their object.
[Commentary]: Regarding *svāhā*, there are five meanings as explained in the commentary, just as the term *bhagavat* contains many meanings.

[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "subsuming the preceding," the three types of retention (*dhāraṇī*)—namely, the retention of dharmas, the retention of meaning, and the retention of patience—are all subsumed within the mantra-retention (*vidyā-dhāraṇī*).
These are collectively termed the "prose subsumption of dharmas, meanings, and patience" and consist of sixteen phrases, which manifest sixteen modes of practice (*ākāra*).

These range from the "practice of the lamp of wisdom" and the "fundamental practice" up to the "practice of giving birth to all Buddhas. The intention behind subsuming those ten characters into the single character "earth" (*pṛthivī*) is that they are themselves *tathatā* (suchness).
The letter *Dhī* serves as the seed-syllable (*bīja*) because it signifies that all phenomena do not depart from True Suchness (*tathatā*).

[Commentary: Therefore, regarding the phrase "informing the various kings" and so forth: in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, the Śrāvakas were entrusted with the task of studying the profound and secret meaning of Prajñā;
whereas in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, the Bodhisattvas were entrusted with the task of transforming the Śrāvakas. Thus...
[The text] entrusts this to the kings so that they may establish and protect the Triple Gem, fulfill the wishes of the patrons, and guard the land.
[Commentary]: Regarding the "impurity of lifespan" (*āyuṣkaṣāya*), the very essence of lifespan is impure; thus it is called the "impurity of lifespan. The others are all *karmadhāraya* compounds.
[Commentary]: Regarding this sequence: sentient beings dwelling in the world take their lifespan as primary; because life is shortened, it is called the *āyuṣka-kaṣāya* (corruption of lifespan).
Life depends upon material requisites; because these requisites are impaired, there follows the *kalpa-kaṣāya* (corruption of the eon).

Greed and other dull afflictions (*moha*) disturb and vex body and mind, while evil views and sharp, acute afflictions gradually increase. There follow the next two corruptions: because of these dull and sharp afflictions, various evils are committed.

Due to karma, there is the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kāluṣya*). Regarding the causes and conditions for the fruit that depends upon suffering and its origin (*duḥkha-samudaya*): both the primary retribution (*pratyaya-vipāka*) and the secondary environment (*upādāna*) are termed "fruit.
That is to say, the life-span and the turbidity of the eon (*kalpa-kāluṣya*), along with the sharp or dull afflictions (*kleśa*), serve as the conditions for arousal and moistening.

Following these, there are the two subsequent turbidities; because of the afflictions, one cultivates the causal karma of evil deeds. This agent of such action is called the turbidity of sentient beings. The first two and the last one depend upon suffering.
The afflictions and the turbidity of views are established based on the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*).

[Commentary: As for life-span being based on the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), which has consciousness as its nature—this refers to the length or brevity of the life-span as explained in reliance upon the life-faculty.

The life-faculty is established based on the functional capacity of the seeds of the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*). "Life" refers to the non-interruption of form and mind; the "faculty" refers to the seeds of consciousness.
The capacity induced by karma, distinguished by its specific functional power, is termed a "faculty" (*indriya*). That which is the faculty of life is called the "life-faculty" (*jīvitendriya*).
Because the power of wholesome karma is weak while the power of the karma of killing is strong, resulting in a short lifespan, it is called the "impurity of life" (*āyuṣka-kaṣāya*).

Famine, disease, and weapons constitute the "impurity of the eon" (*kalpa-kaṣāya*), having the four sense objects as their substance. Furthermore, another interpretation holds that an "eon" (*kalpa*) refers to a period of time.

In terms of its meaning, time has no separate essence; it is established by relying upon phenomena (*dharma*). The discordance among the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and the four great elements (*catvāri mahābhūtāni*) is termed "sickness.

Depending on which phenomena it relies upon, its essence consists of the five aggregates; thus, it is still subsumed under "time" within the category of non-associated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*). The *Fahua shu* (Commentary on the Lotus Sūtra) states:

"As for the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*), it should be understood as having the eighth consciousness and the five aggregates as its nature. Although the eighth consciousness exists, [it is so designated].

Regarding the essential nature [of these defilements], it is now explained: due to the power of external conditions consisting of proximate evil causes, the provisional entity of the five aggregates commits evil and lacks goodness;

this constitutes the *sattva-kaṣāya* (defilement of sentient beings). Greed and other primary afflictions (*kleśa*) along with their secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) constitute the essence of the *kleśa-kaṣāya* (defilement of afflictions). The five views constitute the essence of the *dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya* (defilement of views).
Among these five, the *āyuḥ-kaṣāya* (defilement of lifespan) is established based on seeds, while the remaining four defilements are all established based on the manifestation of form (*rūpa*).
The mind is established [in this state].

[Commentary: Regarding the phrase "due to the subsequent," etc.: due to the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*), the wholesome factors (*kuśala-pakṣa*) decline; due to the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*), one engages in speculative investigation.
Consequently, some take pleasure in self-mortification, while householders give rise to dull afflictions, and those who have left the home life among non-Buddhists give rise to sharp afflictions.

All afflictions (*kleśa*) damage the collection of wholesome qualities (*kuśalapakṣa*). Following that, there are two further corruptions (*kaṣāya*) that cause the decline of sentient beings (*sattvakaṣāya*), namely, the decline of physical stature up to freedom from disease; thus, they cause deterioration and decay.
[Commentary: As for "antidotes," by means of the three roots of goodness, one remedies the turbidity of afflictions; by giving rise to various correct views, one remedies the turbidity of views;
by practicing the ten virtuous actions, one remedies the turbidity of sentient beings; by the excellence of internal fruits, such as the prolongation of life, one remedies the turbidity of lifespan;

and by the excellence of external fruits, such as the absence of the three calamities, one remedies the turbidity of the eon. Therefore, the preceding commentary states that those of sharp and dull faculties perform their respective deeds.

This meaning is explained through the distinction between internal and external fruits, and through abandonment by means of their respective antidotes (*pratipakṣa*). Among the five corruptions (*pañca kaṣāyāḥ*), the corruption of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*) and the corruption of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*) are abandoned by way of their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-prahāṇa*), because they are of the nature of afflictions.
As for the remaining three corruptions, they are termed "abandoned by non-arising" (*anutpāda-prahāṇa*);
once one has entered the stage of the noble ones (*ārya-bhūmi*), one no longer commits evil, and even if one were to live for an entire eon, these would not be called corruptions.

[Commentary: Regarding the "three types of persons" and so forth: during the period of the increasing eon (*vivarta-kalpa*), the lifespan of sentient beings is long, the three calamities are slight, afflictions (*kleśa*) are thin, and wrong views (*mithyā-dṛṣṭi*) are weak;
sentient beings incline toward the wholesome, and at that time it is a state to be rejoiced in, not called a "defilement" (*kaṣāya*).

As the decreasing eon (*saṃvarta-kalpa*) gradually proceeds, the lifespan of these sentient beings becomes short, the three calamities gradually arise, afflictions become increasingly thick, and wrong views gradually flourish; sentient beings incline toward... [the unwholesome].

The ten evils are loathsome and are called the five turbidities; out of compassion, the Buddha therefore admonishes kings and ministers to establish the Buddha-dharma, forbidding them from relying on their own nobility to establish unlawful regulations that destroy the Buddha-dharma.

[Commentary: Regarding the seating arrangement where laypeople and monastics sit at different heights: when laypeople occupy high seats to expound various heterodox doctrines, the King orders the bhikṣus to stand upon the ground to listen.
[Sūtra] Regarding "evil bhikṣus" and so forth, the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* states: "One should accept invitations in their proper sequence and must not accept individual invitations.

Once one has received offerings, if one then accepts a separate invitation, one is taking the property of the Sangha of the ten directions for oneself. The seven Buddhas had no such practice of accepting separate invitations, as it does not accord with the way of filiality."
[Commentary]: Regarding the statement that "evil ghosts and evil dragons create various hardships and difficulties," this refers generally to the disruption of the true cause;
the meaning will become manifest as it is stated twice below.

[Sūtra]: "That which is not Dharma and not Vinaya" means "not" (fei) is equivalent to "no" (bu). It refers to not relying on penal law and not relying on formal regulations, being without any [valid] basis.
The bhikṣu who is bound, fettered, and constrained is thus called "transverse" (*tiryak*).

[Sūtra]: Regarding the decline of the True Dharma, this refers to the Dharma of Right Practice. As for the "six relations," the commentary on the *Zhou Li* states they are father, mother, brothers, wife, and children.
The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā-śāstra* explains that there are two types of six relations: first, the six paternal relations—paternal uncles, brothers, and so forth.

Regarding the second [category], children and grandchildren: the six relations—maternal uncles, maternal aunts, brothers, and children and grandchildren—are all kin of the same breath (*sagotra*) and bound by natural affection, not mixed with those of different surnames;
therefore, they are called the "six relations. [Commentary]:

The two manifestations of the character for "fire" serve as a metaphor for a single manifestation. That is, the fire and the character are both manifest phenomena (*pravṛtti-dharma*), which serve as metaphors for volition (*cetanā*).
Regarding the single dharma-seed, there is currently a distinction between the metaphor of fire for the manifest [action] and the metaphor of letters for the seeds.
When volition (*cetanā*) manifests as action, it is like the extinction of fire because the volition has ceased; yet the seeds of volition do not perish, just as the letters remain.

Since both the manifest action and the seeds of volition take volition as their essence, they are termed "not yet seen at the limit. The Sūtra cites the letters of fire as an example of a dharma already seen at the limit, thereby revealing that the volition of that action is not yet seen.
The peripheral dharmas cause people to understand. [Commentary]:

Furthermore, regarding "present" and so forth, there are four types of karma: namely, karma that ripens in the present life (*dr̥ṣṭadharmavedanīya*), karma that ripens in the next life (*upapadyavedanīya*), karma that ripens in subsequent lives (*aparaparyāyavedanīya*), and karma that is indeterminate (*aniyatavedanīya*), as previously explained.
[Sūtra] Regarding the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra-śāstra* (The Commentary on the Lotus Sūtra) by Bodhisattva Vasubandhu, there are three meanings to "joyfully receiving and practicing":
first, the purity of the speaker; second, the purity of the Dharma taught; and third, the purity of attaining the ultimate fruit based upon that taught Dharma.
It is by virtue of these three meanings that one joyfully receives and practices it.

[Commentary]: "Vastly refining the profound vehicle" (*xū táo xuán yùn*) means refining with joy and riding upon the vehicle. "Remaining radiance" (*yú huī*) refers to when the Buddha was in the world, like the moon at its zenith with its flowing light brilliant and dazzling;
now that the Dharma he left behind remains in the world, it is like the sun having already set yet leaving behind its remaining radiance.

The purport of the Commentary’s main intent is this: to rejoice in encountering the Buddha-Dharma, the profound and wondrous True Vehicle, and to sorrowfully revere the Bequeathed Teaching—the lingering rays of the Buddha-sun.

[Commentary]: Regarding "the four seas have come to pay their respects," the *Erya* states that the Eastern Yi, Western Rong, Southern Man, and Northern Di—those in the four directions who are obscured by darkness and lack knowledge—are called the "four seas.
Furthermore, because the four directions are as vast as the great ocean, the majestic light of the Son of Heaven shines upon and oversees those four seas.
[Commentary] Regarding the phrase "inquired of all," I consulted ancient meanings and followed established precedents to compile these chapters and explain the meaning of the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
Fearing that my interpretation might not accord with the intent of the Sūtra, I have been filled with anxiety day and night, as if standing on the brink of a deep abyss.
My phrasing and terminology are crude and clumsy, resembling overgrown weeds; I am deeply ashamed and fear the ridicule of others.

[Commentary: Regarding "collecting," etc., this work compiles essential points to assist and extol the *Prajñāpāramitā*, benefiting all sentient beings and together bringing about the realization of Great Enlightenment.

Thus, it says in verse: The meaning of *Prajñā* is profound and vast; this collected commentary extols its subtle depths. It benefits all living beings, so that together they may achieve All-Knowledge (*sarvajñatā*).
*Commentary on the Benevolent Kings’ Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra for the Protection of the State: The Faheng Draft*, Scroll Six.

Lì (lì). Pí lì (upper character pronounced pí-jì; lower character pronounced lì-jì). Shǎn (shī-ràn). Mán [kuáng-yán] (upper character pronounced mò-huán; lower character pronounced dí). Jìng tì (upper character pronounced jū-líng;
lower character pronounced tā-lì). Wú (pronounced wú; refers to overgrown weeds). Xún (xiāng-lún). Nǎn (nǚ-bǎn). [Xuē/hóng] (wū-hóng; refers to deep water).
